title: ‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaos | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Service charges used to be a matter of choice, but now consumers feel obliged to pay them for even a cup of coffee. How do we navigate this minefield and who is really profiting?
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Service charges used to be a matter of choice, but now consumers feel obliged to pay them for even a cup of coffee. How do we navigate this minefield and who is really profiting?
Content: Composite: Rouzes/sellyhutapea/Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Rouzes/sellyhutapea/Getty Images/Guardian DesignSocial etiquette‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaosService charges used to be a matter of choice, but now consumers feel obliged to pay them for even a cup of coffee. How do we navigate this minefield and who is really profiting?Emine SanerMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a London pub, Greg Double was brutally confronted with the reality of Britain’s evolving tipping culture. “I was annoyed about the pint being eight quid, but then when you put service on top, it’s absolutely criminal,” he says. In the past, you might have told the bar staff to keep the change or have a “drink” on you, but since when did we routinely tip in pubs? Or coffee shops? Or, worst of all, at self-service machines? Tip creep is happening.Tipping was awkward enough in the UK when the general rule was 10% at a restaurant, plus anxiety about whether you should tip the hairdresser, babysitter or food-delivery driver. Now, with tipping suggested ever more frequently, US-style, it has become a minefield to Britons. The amounts edge higher – in fancier London restaurants, a 15% service charge is relatively commonplace. And it’s often asked for – in coffee shops for example, when you pay –beforeany service is delivered.Tipping may be a social behaviour, but politics and economics also inform it. Since October 2024, all service charges and tips in Great Britainmust go to staff, which boosts low salaries. Hospitality businesses, struggling with the rises in minimum wage and national insurance, are surely happy that it’s tipping customers who are supplementing wages, rather than themselves. As the news site London Centric pointed out recently in an article headlined “How American tipping culture came to London”, adding an “optional” service charge avoids tax, puts more money in the pockets of staff and means businesses don’t have to raise prices, which puts off customers.But how “optional” is a service charge when the person serving us is looking expectantly as they hand over the card machine? Now, the variables around tipping seem endless and changeable, with each of us having to create our own rules.View image in fullscreenIf a server smiles, it can have a substantial impact on tipping.Photograph: LordHenriVoton/Getty Images; posed by a modelDouble, a creative director for a PR company, says that in a coffee shop without table service, he wouldn’t tip – but he might if he were sitting there, working, “to take into account that I’m going to make this coffee last”. He wouldn’t tip if he’d walked up to a bar and bought a drink for himself, but he might acquiesce if he bought a round.Since drinking Guinness became fashionable, it almost calls out for a tip. “Because you’re like: well, you’ve had to wait around for five minutes for every pint being poured,” says Double. “If you order four pints of Guinness, you immediately see the bar staff think: ‘Oh, for god’s sake.’”Double also highlights a new tipping anxiety. Sometimes a bar worker will press zero on the tip screen before handing you the payment machine, “if they don’t think they’re worthy. There’s even that Britishness of the bar staff.” But what if they don’t? “It almost makes me think that if they’ve not pressed ‘no’ to the tip, that means they think they deserve one.”Many of those I speak to think tech has pushed this change forward – and rapidly. The shift away from cash towards card and digital payments is usually framed as removing “friction”, says Prof John Vines, the chair of design informatics at the University of Edinburgh’s School of Informatics.“It’s about being more convenient. This is all a trend towards making it easier for us to spend our money.” The software in point-of-sale terminals prompts the customer for a tip. “These systems are presented as a way of making giving a tip easier. We don’t have to think about it too much, we don’t have to fiddle with coins and notes. But, really, it’s about encouraging us to spend more.”Faced with three options on a screen, with the third perhaps an outrageous 35% tip, I often panic and go for the middle box. I wouldn’t want to seem cheap by going for the first option, but I end up feeling bullied into giving a generous 20% or more.double quotation markThese systems are presented as a way of making giving a tip easier. But, really, it’s about encouraging us to spend more“Again, that’s presenting those options to you partly to reduce that friction – it’s taking away the need for you to mathematically calculate things. But, of course, it’s a way of controlling the options as well,” says Vines. “While we have the ability to press zero, the act of getting asked at the point of sale likely increases the chances of someone giving something, especially in situations where, at least in the UK, we culturally don’t expect a tip to be given in the first place.”Is it too cynical to suggest that tech companies who run the software, and who take a cut of every transaction, are making more money from pushing tips? “That probablyisa bit cynical, but also probably true,” says Vines, with a laugh.It goes deeper than tech companies skimming a percentage. “A lot of our technological infrastructure is dependent on platforms and systems that come from the US and, in particular, California,” says Vines. “We tend to import a lot of the values and customs that are embedded with them. Even if it’s not intended, they get inscribed into these systems and flatten out the diversity of other cultures, the things that would be acceptable or normal elsewhere.” The example of tipping, while small, he says, “actually is an example of how [US tech companies] that get imported actually have quite significant long-term consequences, because it rewrites social expectations.”View image in fullscreenConsumers are often confronted with three tipping options.Photograph: Rouzes/Getty ImagesIt’s embarrassing, says Peter, who works in a pub in Lincolnshire, to ask customers for tips. A few months ago, they got new card machines that automatically suggest adding one. Peter always presses no before he hands it over to customers. “It can rub people up the wrong way,” he says. The pub’s manager occasionally asks people if they want to add a gratuity, “but even he doesn’t do it very often. It just feels pointless to us. You only tip someone if they’ve looked after you, you’ve been sat down and it’s been good service. You don’t tip someone for just pouring you a pint.”Tipping culture was also changed by the pandemic, even in the tip-heavy US. “During Covid, we started tipping people that we didn’t traditionally tip,” says Michael Lynn, an emeritus professor of consumer behaviour and marketing at Cornell University and the author of The Psychology of Tipping. It was akin to “hazard pay”, he says, plus there was a perception that some people were more likely to be struggling financially. “People started being willing to tip and businesses took that as a message that consumers will bear it.”The accepted level has always increased over time, says Lynn. This could be due to any number of factors. “The population of the US is more urban than it used to be and urban peopletend to tip more than rural people,” he says. Then there’s the move away from cash. “People who pay with a card or digitally tend to tip more than people who pay with cash.” And big tippers – who do it for reasons of status, or to ensure good future service – ruin it for the rest of us. “It creates this upward pressure,” says Lynn. “It’s got to stop somewhere, right? We’re at close to 20% today [in US restaurants].”Several times a year, I have a gnawing anxiety about whether or not to tip my hairdresser. It’s not that I don’t think he deserves it, but would it be condescending? “One of the impediments to tipping is concern about status and power implications,” says Lynn. “Money commodifies the relationship. If you view it as a social relationship, you don’t want to contaminate it with tips. It’s very hard to tip people that you have a long-term relationship with.”View image in fullscreenDo you tip your hairdresser? The jury’s out …Photograph: Spiderstock/Getty Images; posed by modelsWhy do I tip my hairdresser (I’m too embarrassed to press “no”), but not the plumber or the dentist? It’s usually because with the latter two – or an accountant, a lawyer or a doctor – “I’m worse off than they are”, says Lynn. “Not only financially, probably, but also they’re helping solve a problem for me. When I go to something in a hospitality context, or even for a haircut, it’s generally something positive. I’m enjoying myself and that worker is doing not such pleasant work.”The late anthropologist George M Foster, says Lynn, “argued that tipping began as an attempt by patrons to say: ‘Don’t envy me because I’m having fun and you’re working.’ The primary evidence he had for this was that the word for tip in many languages is ‘drink money’.”Social expectation is the main reason people leave a tip. The second, he says, is “social connection and rapport. If a server is attractive, if a server is the opposite sex, if the server smiles, calls you by name, squats down, there are so many variables that impact the social connection, but they all have a pretty substantial impact on tipping.”This, of course, is affected by blatant bias, sometimes unconscious, in the person leaving a tip. Some research shows that Black waiters and cab driversreceive lower tips, says Lynn. “Having said that, there are also a number of studiesnot finding this. There’s enough data on both sides that my conclusion is clearly there is racial discrimination, but it’s not universal and we don’t fully understand when it occurs and when it doesn’t.”You getmore tips from the opposite sex, says Lynn, so “waitresses tend to get slightly better tips. And attractive waitresses get better tips than less-attractive waitresses.”When British football fans went to the US earlier in the summer for the World Cup, many were baffled and frustrated by the tipping culture. One fantold the BBCit was “weird” to be asked for a tip when buying a bottle of water. Ollie Thomas, a football content creator, says he went “with the expectation of [tipping] being very much in your face and quite intrusive. But I live in London and I didn’t think [restaurant tipping] was any different, really.“The main difference I found in the US was that the service was a lot better. I guess the backdrop of the US tipping culture is that there is a massive weight of expectation on the customer’s shoulders to tip because the waiters don’t earn much money. Whereas it feels like there’s not that level of pressure on the customer in London because the general living wage is a bit higher here.”But even in the US, says Lynn, tip fatigue is real. “In surveys, I was asking people: ‘Would you rather tipping be eliminated?’ In 2016, about 32% of people said yes. By 2018 it was 42% and by 2022 it was 52%. I haven’t repeated that since, but other surveys have asked similar questions. It seems to have gone back down to about 40%. But, absolutely, people say they’re being asked to tip for more services than ever before and, even for traditionally tipped services, they’re being asked to tip larger amounts. It negatively impacts consumer sentiment.”So, how do we deal with this emerging tipping nightmare? We could do with some guidelines that everyone can agree on, perhaps beginning with a national discussion on how much we really want US tech companies to influence our proud British cheapskate culture. As for current good practice, Jo Bryant, an etiquette coach and training director at The English Manner, says we should continue to tip in restaurants, but watch out for the service charge. “People shouldn’t feel pressure to double tip. For restaurants, generally, it’s around 12%.”View image in fullscreenThe US has always had a tip-heavy culture.Photograph: Catherine McQueen/Getty ImagesHowever, there’s no reason to tip at the bar in pubs or coffee shops “apart from for food or table service”, says Bryant. But if it’s somewhere you go regularly, you may want to consider tipping: you don’t want to become known as the non-tipper. It’s completely acceptable to press the “no” button to a tip request in a place we wouldn’t usually tip, even with the person serving you in front of you, but do it briskly and confidently. “As soon as you start apologising and making a thing that you’re not tipping, then it becomes awkward.”What about in more grey areas? If in situations that feel more condescending or uncomfortable – tipping someone who cleans your house or looks after your children, say – Bryant suggests just giving a generous tip at Christmas. “If you wrap it up into the Christmas cheer, it can feel less awkward.”It’s very British, says Bryant, to view tipping through a lens of anxious social appropriateness and class. “Americans don’t have that feeling at all. I’ve provided etiquette classes to Americans and get tipped. It’s a great novelty. They’ll say goodbye to you and put a note in your hand. I think it stems from the Brits not talking about money. We’ve always been awkward about wealth and class and status.”It’s why, she says, we never developed a tipping culture – and why it feels unsettling. “We all just find it so brazen to be getting out your wallet and handing money to people … we’ve been left in this slightly muddy zone.” We could fight it – and I’m open to fighting the influence of US tech – but faced with an expectant barista offering me the choice of three buttons, I’m more likely to panic-hit the middle one and hope it wasn’t 25%.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Michael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than good, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Michael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than good, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: GCSE students taking an exam at a school in Kent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGCSE students taking an exam at a school in Kent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionGCSEsHow can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a startPolly ToynbeeMichael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than goodMon 24 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareGCSE results day was marked with the usual front pages filled with pictures of beaming students. What you didn’t see was the invisiblethird of 16-year-oldsin England who failed their maths and English GCSEs, the obstacle to their future.That’s 360,000failedin a system designed by Michael Gove as education minister to mark out winners from losers. It’s a cast of mind shared by many in his party who still yearn for the11-plus, which consigned a random number of children to failure before they’d hardly begun. A few councils still do it.Once failed, this one-third must resit English and maths to do any other course: colleges cannot provide them with a blessed start from failed schooling, as they are refused funds for any student not taking repeated resits. Onlyabout 17%of the wretched resitters ever pass. Quite apart from the despair, David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, points to the waste: of the far-too-few 16 teaching hours a week for students on post-16 study courses, resitters must be taught seven hours of hated English and maths that most of them will fail. That leaves just nine hours for the vocational courses they choose. No wonder UCL research shows the damage done: self-confidence is lost, many drop out altogether. That doesn’t happen in Wales and Northern Ireland,where resits are not mandatory for continuing study.Labour gets it. Both the previous education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, and the current,Lucy Powell, well understand the damage done by this Gove-devised torment: finally compulsory resits will end in 2028. Instead, those who fail can take a new “stepping stone” qualification in functional maths and English, proving adequate literacy and numeracy skills.But an ideological dispute remains among Powell’s advisers. They will still make every 16-year-old take English and maths GCSE in the first place, even if they will probably fail. Many only need the stepping-stone qualification anyway. This doesn’t sit well with Andy Burnham spreading his successfulGreater Manchester baccalaureate(MBacc) nationally, ascheme that offersvocational courses suited to local employersalongside academic subjects from age 14, to keep them engaged and avoiding Neet status: not in education, employment or training.But ideological purists think dividing them early between GCSE groups and stepping-stone groups sets up a two-tier discrimination, downgrading some who might have passed a full GCSE. But with a million Neets, the key priority must be making school encouraging, not rejecting.Gove sticks to his Gradgrind resits. He calls Burnham’s approach “bring back stupid”, anti-intellectual and hostile to ambition. But had he invested in nursery education, where destinies are most surely set, there might be fewer 16-year-olds with failing grades to bully now. New researchreported by the Institute for Fiscal Studiesshows how entering childcare one year earlier gives an average 10% improved maths score by age 14 to 15, and a 28% higher score for those with a mother without qualifications.The good news is that Labour’s emphasis on skills has been infectious, with asurge in applications to technical courses, well beyond the current demographic bulge, while university applications still rise by 3%. Alan Milburn’s commission to solve the crisis of1 million Neetshas real policy steam behind it to urge more skills training.But further education (FE) has a lot of catching up to do. There are many ways England has not just neglected but discriminated against non-academic education. Despite recent extra funding for colleges, this stilldoesn’t cover the entire costof any extra student accepted, an additional 25,000 are expected to enrol this autumn,and colleges lack space and staff after colossal cuts in the Tory years: over-19s adult education fellfrom £5bn in 2002 to £1.5bn in 2025.Recent extra money for pay “only stopped the gap getting wider”, Hughes says, when FE staff are paid£10,500 lessthan school teachers, and are in short supply when construction and engineering jobs pay so much more. Why, he asks, do colleges pay VAT costing £200m, while schools are reimbursed?The spur of Labour’s new growth and skills levy is incentivising employers to take on beginners with short courses. But as applications quadrupled for degree apprenticeships, more sought-after than Oxbridge places for earning while learning,places have halved.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy do university students get maintenance loans, but FE students can’t? “Because too many will never earn enough to pay them back,” says Hughes bluntly. Worse still, Neets on benefits are barred from full-time courses, which is perverse.Needless barriers need fixing. Neets who need driving licences for jobs and apprenticeships, essential from care to plumbing, find the waiting time for a driving test is21 weeksor more.Burnham’s eloquence on valuing “the hard hat as much as the academic cap” earns Gove’s contempt, but it has raised FE spirits. Talking to college heads, they see that Labour knows what to do. As ever, the problem is overcoming Britain’s forever low esteem for technical education. It will take heavy lifting to shift mentalities towardsencouraging that third of 16-year-olds instead of tormenting them.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGCSEsOpinionFurther educationExamsHigher educationSchoolsMichael GoveLucy PowellcommentShareReuse this content

title: Problems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership falls | Pubs | The Guardian
description: Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinational breweries are threatening to squeeze out independents
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinational breweries are threatening to squeeze out independents
Content: ‘We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular,’ Camra’s chief executive said.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular,’ Camra’s chief executive said.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesPubsProblems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership fallsCost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent  breweriesHelena HortonMon 24 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer. But now problems are brewing for the proper pint, as the Campaign for Real Ale has seen its membership sink to an eight-year low and its accounts show it is firmly in the red, making an £800,000 loss last year.Real ale is a traditional draught cask beer, a “living” product that is produced and stored in its cask. It differs from a cold, fizzy lager, in which the yeast is killed and carbon dioxide is added. Real ale contains live yeast so it continues fermenting until it is served.Outside the Devonshire pub in Soho, central London, there is an ever-present horde of drinkers downing pints of Guinness, a stout made by the multinational company Diageo. But the landlord and co-owner Oisín Rogers says: “Real ale is all I drink.”He says: “It is a properly handmade British product produced in exactly the same way it has been for centuries. It has never been industrialised like some of the other drinks that are for sale in bars in London.” His favourite tipple, is, appropriately, a pint of Landlord, made by the family-owned Timothy Taylor brewery in Keighley, West Yorkshire.View image in fullscreenThe Devonshire pub in London’s West End.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesTom Stainer, Camra’s chief executive, says independent breweries are facing unfair competition from multinationals. If you walk into a pub on the high street, you are often confronted with the same few beers, most of which are made by the same large companies, Stainer says.“Our recent beer report highlighted that the beers people want aren’t available in bars because of the ways the huge international brewers operate – they have a stranglehold on the industry,” he says. “We call it an illusion of choice – a lot of people walk into bars and don’t realise everything in front of them is owned by the same big company.”Big brewers ‘misleading drinkers’ over craft beer credentials, says CamraRead moreHe says these “big global brewers who have deep pockets and huge influence” make it “hard for small brewers to get to market”. The incentives offered to large pub companies include cheap packages for beers, wine and soft drinks, with a multi-year tie-in, and minimum purchase orders where “pubs are forced to sell a certain amount of this product”.Stainer adds: “We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular and stop people buying that product they have a minimum purchase order for.”Camra is calling for the Competition and Markets Authority to investigate the big beer companies’ stranglehold on the market.There are no such problems at the King Charles I pub in King’s Cross. As an independent, community-owned venue, the team can choose what’s on tap. They have a healthy range of cask beers, swapped out every five weeks.Matt Roberts, the manager, says: “I like to choose local beers – today we have one from Southwark, some from Kent and one from the West Midlands. Cask ale is still very popular, it makes up around 30% of our sales. We are lucky we don’t have a big pub company telling us what to sell.”Despite the delicious range of cask ale on offer, including the very drinkable Bankside Blonde by Southwark Brewing Company, Guinness still appears to be the order of the day among the customers.View image in fullscreenVisitors at the Camra Great British Beer festival in 2017. This year’s event was cancelled.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesCamra is facing a nadir: last September it announced it had been forced tocancel its pivotal Great British Beer festival, formerly the largest of its kind in the UK, for the foreseeable future due to financial pressures. Writing in the accounts, the chair, Ash Corbett-Collins, said it had been “one of the most challenging years Camra has faced”, pointing to a restructuring in which “a number of roles were sadly made redundant”.The cost of living crisis is making it more difficult to run a membership organisation, Stainer says. “When you look at your bank balance each month, membership might be something you might economise to offset your huge energy bill or the rise in food prices.” A Camra membership is £35 a year.Explore more on these topicsPubsBeernewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US
Content: Andy Burnham (left) and Volodymyr Zelensky during a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (left) and Volodymyr Zelensky during a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/PAAndy BurnhamAnalysisBurnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for UkraineLuke HardingandDan Sabbaghin Pavlohrad, UkraineAs well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the USMon 24 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTShareSince moving into Downing Street in July,Andy Burnham– a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.The occasionwas the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots.In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France have been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.Burnham hands secret missile technology to Ukraine – The LatestRead moreIt was now handing over British blueprints for key components, Burnham said, so Ukraine could eventually make its own version with France.More Storm Shadows could go some way to dealing with Ukraine’s biggest problem: thewave of ballistic missiles fired by Russia that rain down on Kyivand other cities most nights. As of now, Ukraine has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting them down. The Trump administration is disinclined to provide more.Graph of the number of civilians killed by Russia in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasionThe British cruise missiles carry a larger payload than the long-range drones favoured by Kyiv. They could be used to destroy enemy ballistic missile launch systems, which can be quickly moved, and are dotted around sites in western Russia. Depending on their range, they could also disable military runways and aerodromes.But nobody expects production to start soon. In the meantime, the Kremlin has responded with characteristic belligerence. Vladimir Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow would destroy any Ukrainian Storm Shadow factories, and accused London of taking part in the war and adding “fuel to the fire” though it is France that is helping with building them.Last week Russia threatened “consequences” over the supply of British drones to Kyiv andwithdrew its ambassador from London. It is unclear how Putin might escalate further. He has already sent assassins to poison Russian dissidents on UK territory including the murder in 2006 of Alexander Litvinenko, killed with radioactive tea.Burnham appears unmoved by what he dubbed “outrageous” Russian threats, an encouraging sign for Kyiv. On Monday he pointed out that it was Putin who “started the fire” with his illegal and unprovoked invasion, and assured Zelenskyy of his “personal commitment” to Kyiv’s existential cause.Ukraine has warmly welcomed the Storm Shadow initiative. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian he hoped manufacturing could begin in “months, not years”. “We have proved many times we can do impossible things in producing weaponry,” he said, adding that the missile strengthened Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Moscow.Of Burnham’s visit, he added: “For us, it’s hugely symbolic and important. It illustrates that for the UK Ukraine remains a top priority. You are an important bridge and have rectified the situation whenever we have a crisis in our relations with the US. Your king is a valuable diplomatic tool and puts in a good word for us with Trump.”The trip also signalled to allies that the UK will continue to play a leading role in the coalition of the willing after the departure of Keir Starmer. Co-hosting a coalition meeting for the first time, Burnham said Europe would do everything it could to source more Patriotic interceptors for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has asked for 300 to help the country survive the coming winter.Burnham’s speech made clear that he regards Ukraine’s struggle as Britain’s too – at a time when the US has in effect given up on its attempts to broker a peace deal, and has halted direct military aid. “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security but the frontline in keeping Europe safe,” he said. “The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”Ukrainian leaders and soldiers are grateful for British diplomatic and moral support, though they know that London’s military power is limited. Storm Shadow is deemed to have been one of the UK’s most useful contributions but stockpiles were modest.Ukraine’s focus has been on developing its own long-range drones and cruise missiles, such as Fire Point’s Flamingo, which have been used to strike refineries and warehouses deep inside Russia. The goal is to attack Russia with 1,000 drones and some missiles a day this year, not when Storm Shadow production lines are ready.But the deal that Burnham has agreed with Zelenskyy is an important renewal of goodwill. At some point Zelenskyy will probably need the help of European allies whenever the White House re-engages with the peace process. Burnham may become an important interlocutor with Trump, and today’s trip is from Ukraine’s perspective an encouraging start.Betrayal by Luke Harding (Guardian Faber, £20) is published on Thursday.
