title: ‘Better than The Godfather’: how we made brutal Yorkshire crime classic Red Riding | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: ‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’
Content: ‘I had to eat a raw Findus Crispy Pancake’ … Mark Addy as lawyer John Piggott in Red Riding.Photograph: CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYView image in fullscreen‘I had to eat a raw Findus Crispy Pancake’ … Mark Addy as lawyer John Piggott in Red Riding.Photograph: CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYHow we madeCulture‘Better than The Godfather’: how we made brutal Yorkshire crime classic Red Riding‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’Interviews byMichael HoganMon 24 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Grisoni, screenwriterI’d been writing screenplays with Michael Winterbottom and in 2006, his producer Andrew Eaton said: “There’s this quartet of novels by David Peace. Are you interested in adapting them?” I read the first, 1974, and was drawn to it and repelled at the same time. It was strong meat, full of anger and injustice. It’s anchored in reality, especially thePeter SutcliffeandStefan Kiszkocases, but heightened and stylised. “Fiction torn from the facts,” David called it.I was scared stiff because the novels were so experimental but I desperately wanted to do it – even if adapting all four would mean waving goodbye to several years of my life. The books span a decade with a huge cast of characters, so I condensed a lot.Eaton was keen on a different director and format for each film. It meant each had its own reference points. I thought about Chinatown a lot with 1974. The design and costumes were all smoky and brown, like the 70s. The cast went for the material big time. David Morrissey really did his research and Sean Harris is nothing if not method. It’s a very masculine story but we wanted strong female characters too – we had Maxine Peake and Rebecca Hall. I kept the most horrendous violence off-screen. Violence you imagine is much worse than anything you’ll see. Your mind does the work.double quotation markI kept the most horrendous violence off-screen. Violence you imagine is much worseThe police interrogation scenes, where they torture suspects, are terrifying and deliberately so. Stefan Kiszko, on whom Daniel Mays’s character is based, was released in 1992 and died 18 months later, having been wrongly imprisoned for 16 years. A man with a mind of a 12-year-old who just wanted his mum. The corruption and brutality in Red Riding are bleak, but so is the real world. While I was writing, the headlines were full of cases like Stephen Lawrence, Madeleine McCann, Natascha Kampusch, Shannon Matthews, Josef Fritzl …I was warned that Sutcliffe was litigious, so I should use what he actually said in his police interview. That was fine. I couldn’t have made it up anyway. Red Riding was compared to James Ellroy and described as Yorkshire noir, which is spot-on, although David said it was a pity they used a French word. He preferred Yorkshire dark. I added some redemption at the end because I needed to save somebody and finish on a note of love.Allow dailymotion content?This article includes content provided bydailymotion. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWe made 1974, 1980 and 1983 but, for budgetary reasons, not 1977, which broke my heart. It was always intended as a quartet, so it felt like vandalism. I hold out hope that somehow we’ll get to do the missing fourth. The films got a theatrical release in the US, screened back-to-back, which is full-on, but a cult audience went for it. Critic David Thomson called it “better than The Godfather”. Nic Pizzolatto said it influenced True Detective. People are still discovering it. They tend to say: “But you seem like quite a nice guy!”Mark Addy, actorMy agent sent me the scripts but said: “Just to warn you, there’s no money in this.” I got halfway through the first episode, phoned her back and asked: “Who else is attached?” She said: “Sean Bean, David Morrissey, Paddy Considine, Peter Mullan and Maxine Peake.” I said: “Put my name on the list please.” The scripts were so well-written, it was a no-brainer.Everyone was on Equity minimum, there were no trailers, not even a green room area. It was a tremendous experience to have a cast of that calibre, throwing their all into something that wasn’t going to buy them more than a pair of shoes.David Peace’s books put you inside the mind of each character and are dense with detail. They were a major resource for building my character, washed-up solicitor John Piggott. In one scene, he flashes back to finding his father’s body. They literally strapped a camera rig on to me, so viewers see it through Piggott’s eyes. He becomes the unlikely hero, despite being a dope-smoking, heavy-drinking loser. He takes on the might of the crooked West Yorkshire police and partly succeeds. Amid the darkness, he’s a bit of light at the end of the tunnel.Piggott’s a shoddy, unkempt idiot – he sleeps in his suit and at one point, he eats a raw Findus Crispy Pancake – but he saves the girl at the end. He carries her out of a mineshaft in his arms, like a Bruce Willis action hero. Shooting scenes in the underground paedophile’s lair was grim. There was a room with the dentist’s chair in it, mattresses on the floor, a child’s shoe. It brought home the horrors of what these monsters were doing. You needed a shower at the end of the day.View image in fullscreen‘People are still discovering it’ … Sean Bean in Red Riding.Photograph: Contract Number (Programme)/CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYI grew up in York during the 1970s and vividly remember the Ripper era. I used to cycle back from my then-girlfriend’s house in the pitch black. Tension on the streets was palpable – you’d pedal home as quickly as you could. Everyone felt Sutcliffe’s elusiveness and how the police were overwhelmed. The show’s hardly a tourist advert for Yorkshire. On location, set dressing would be a burnt-out car on the grass verge, maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals were like: “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”Red Riding is an extraordinary achievement. Three different directors and formats. It’s hard for me to fault it. It had ripple effects on my career. Ridley Scott had just started work on Robin Hood with Russell Crowe. The casting director gave him a Red Riding DVD because it had so many British actors. He watched it one weekend and, on Monday morning, phoned up to acquire the US rights, then cast me as Friar Tuck. He must’ve seen me eat the frozen Crispy Pancake and thought: “That’s my man!”The Red Riding Trilogy is available to stream on Amazon’s Studiocanal Presents channelExplore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeTelevisionDavid PeacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’? | Dana Frank | The Guardian
description: The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left
Content: ‘The Times is shoring up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party.’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreen‘The Times is shoring up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party.’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APOpinionNew York TimesWhy does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’?Dana FrankThe newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the leftMon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTShare“El-Sayed and Stevens Project Party Unity After Divisive Race,”announcedthe New York Times on 5 August, the day the progressive Abdul El-Sayed beat out his centrist Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in the Michigan senatorial primary. “Divisive” is now the Times’s favorite attack word, deployed repeatedly to disparage and try to undermine the astonishing recent advances by progressive candidates.Four days after that first story, the Times againlanded“divisive” under “Obama and El-Sayed Discuss Unity After Ugly Michigan Primary.” El-Sayed, it asserted, had “narrowly prevailed in a divisive primary after campaigning on a progressive and anti-establishment platform”.On 12 August, the Timesreported thatDavid Crowley, who narrowly beat out Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, “promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany”, his Republican opponent. Other stories slip it in more subtly. That same day, in a piece about representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez allegedly distancing herself from “Woke 1.0”, the TimescitedMiddlebury College professor Erik Bleich, who “pointed to the calls to defund the police as a divisive goal”.By disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s leadRead more“Polarizing”, a close cousin to “divisive”, appears regularly, too. The Times especially likes to apply it to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. Areporter insistedin October 2025, for example: “As Mamdani’s campaign upends New York politics, no single stance has polarized New Yorkers as passionately as his pro-Palestinian activism and caustic criticism of Israel.”Perhaps most outrageous was the Times’s choice ofheadlinefor a recent review of David Zirin’s new book about Howard Zinn: “America’s Most Divisive Historian Gets a New Biography.” How, exactly, was Zinn “divisive”? And who are those other historians who are also divisive, just not as bad? Neither Adam Hochschild, in his review, nor Zirin, in his biography, nor any discussion of I’ve ever seen in 40 years as a practicing US historian (and co-author, along with Robin DG Kelley, of a book with Zinn), talk about Zinn that way.The Times’s choice to cast Zinn as divisive out of the blue, on top of its repeated usage of the word since the midwest primaries, suggests there’s a conscious campaign underway to utilize the concept however it can.Overall, the Times’ repeated charge of “divisive”, along with “polarizing”, implies a previous and virtuous whole that is currently being destroyed by the left. It assumes voters agree that in the face of deep fear of Trump and his allies, we have to stick together, and that progressive candidatescan’t beat Republicansin the midterms.But the Times’s mythical unified country never existed. The United States has always been riven by race, class, gender, religion, immigration status and much more. And vigorous debate has always been at the core of truly democratic politics.For the Times, “unity” is a stand-in for the powers-that-be in the Democratic party and “their preferred strategy of running moderate campaigns that won’t offend aging incumbents, never-Trump Republicans, and the multimillionaire-and-up donor class,” as the editors of Hammer & Hope Magazinerecently put it.The mealy-mouthed, centrist candidates the party’s leadership has chosen in the name of unity have repeatedly alienated or failed to energize voters, especially African Americans.Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not? | Nesrine MalikRead moreThe Times does on occasion employ “divisive” todescribe far-right Republicans, such as with Florida governor Ron DeSantis. But that, in turn, colors its usage against the left, which, implicitly, is behaving fanatically and dangerously, too. As the paperclaimedon 16 August, after the midwest primaries, “Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment.”Note, moreover, the recent actions by “moderate” Democrats the New York Times has apparentlynotdeemed divisive: James Carville, the political consultant, whocalled Democratic socialists“a pack of fools” on Fox News, or Abigail Spanberger, the governor of Virginia, who in Mayvetoed a billgranting collective bargaining rights to public workers, betraying the union base that had elected her.In Michigan, it’sIslamophobiathat’s in fact “divisive”, not the Muslim candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who, along with many of the other candidates the Times calls divisive, is not coincidentally a person of color.By charging progressives – and especially democratic socialists – with divisiveness, theNew York Timesis doing everything it can to shore up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party, and the rest of us fall into line to vote however they like.But it’s the Times that’s trying to divide us, as we form ever broader, ever more dynamic and ever more effective coalitions to challenge the masters it serves.Dana Frank is professor of history emerita at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Her newest book, Balancing Acts: How a Japanese Immigrant Built a Life in the Face of Racial Danger – Until Federal Agents Arrived, will be out from Beacon Press in April 2027This article was amended on 24 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly referred to Abdul El-Sayed as a democratic socialist.Explore more on these topicsNew York TimesOpinionUS politicsNewspapersUS press and publishingNewspapers & magazinesDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Immense drop-off’ in support contributing to care leaver deaths in England, review says  | Social care | The Guardian
description: Death rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on  isolation of those leaving care
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Death rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on isolation of those leaving care
Content: Suicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher than in the general population.Photograph: Lucy Lambriex/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSuicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher than in the general population.Photograph: Lucy Lambriex/Getty ImagesSocial care‘Immense drop-off’ in support contributing to care leaver deaths in England, review saysDeath rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on isolation of those leaving care‘He was left on his own’: the care-leaver lives lost to a system that abandons them at 18Jessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfound isolation contributed to the deaths of more than 100 care leavers inEnglandin a year, with a dramatic drop-off in support from social services at 18 leading to catastrophic consequences, a review has found.A government-commissioned report into the early deaths of young people who left care described the problem as a national tragedy and said many were left on their own “at the height of vulnerability” before they died.Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, said: “Care leavers have been left so isolated, so lonely, and that is the core of the problem. Both adult and children’s social care need to be humanised and need to focus on building those enduring, loving connections. This is a stain on society because all of us have failed.”The review, led by the social work leader Clare Chamberlain and the broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, looked at the deaths of 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 in 2025.It found that the death rate among this group was three to four times higher than among the general population, and suicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher.In total, 36% of the care leavers probably died by taking their own lives, including 24 women. One-fifth of the deaths were at age 18, which the review said highlighted the “immense drop-off in support services” when care leavers reach adulthood.John-Baptiste, whogrew up in the care system, said the review was the “most emotional and triggering piece of work I’ve ever had to do”.He said: “I remember being in a meeting at 17 where my foster parents said: ‘If we’re not getting paid, we don’t want to look after him.’ Why do services change when children reach 18 and should they have to change?“I think there is certainly a case for a 0-25 service. If 112 deaths doesn’t compel us to try and reform things quickly, there’s a big problem in our society.”Among the deaths examined were care leavers in custody, mothers whose children had been removed, people undergoing gender transition, young asylum seekers, murder victims and people who died from medical conditions.One case was that of David (not his real name), who died in the summer of 2025 from a lack of insulin after he lost access to the children’s diabetes nurse who had been helping him keep track of his condition since he entered the care system at 14.The care leavers’ hub he socialised in was closed for refurbishment and his personal adviser was on leave. After his death, his body wasn’t found for two weeks. The review found that when he turned 19, many of the connections he had made “fell away and he was left on his own”.Young people leaving care are assigned a personal adviser to help them transition into independent adulthood up to the age of 21. The review found many of these advisers “hardly knew” the young people they were working with and were only required to see them once every two months. It said many were untrained, ill-equipped and “avoided the emotional side of the transition”.It called for a “major national review of the knowledge and skills” of the workforce tasked with monitoring care leavers, including better mental health expertise.The review found that young people were often attracted to the “lure of living alone and being free of constraints” but were unprepared for the significant drop in support, which “no amount of transition planning will compensate”.In response to the review, the government said it was investing £25m in connected housing options for care leavers, which would include supported housing and shared housing for groups of care-experienced people.MacAlister said this was part of the government’s strategy to make “loving, trusted relationships around care-experienced people the central focus of the care system”.Since December 2023, local authorities must report the deaths of care leavers through a serious incident notification system. MacAlister said “the same thing happening over and over again” compelled him to commission the review.He said it should be a call to action not just for the government and the social care sector. “We need more foster carers, we need mentors for care leavers, we need neighbours to show an interest in a young care-experienced person who might have got their first tenancy and to extend the hand of friendship,” he said.“This is about connections and relationships, and you can’t pay people to do that – it has to be grown organically and nurtured over time.”Explore more on these topicsSocial careYoung peopleEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes | Housing | The Guardian
description: About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership
Content: Andy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesHousingBurnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homesAbout 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownershipKiran StaceyPolicy editorMon 24 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.He saidwhen launching his campaignto become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year | EditorialRead moreThe Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnhamhas promisedwill be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”Ministers drop plan to relax affordable housing rules after negative responseRead moreOfficials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”The plans contrast withthose announced by Reform UKon Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.Explore more on these topicsHousingSocial housingAndy BurnhamLabourAngela RaynernewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French language | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Prime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from dispute
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Prime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from dispute
Content: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc at a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via APView image in fullscreenPrime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc at a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via APTrump tariffsMark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French languagePrime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from disputeAre you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from youLeyland Ceccoin TorontoMon 24 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Carney said on Monday that while American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant … in Quebec, these are rights,” days after receiving widespread praise from political leaders for rejecting a US trade proposal that many perceived as weakening the country’s Francophone culture.The prime minister’s remarks came hours after the US president,Donald Trump, showed little interest in retreating from the spat, posting on social media that Canada had been “ripping off the United States of America for years” and threatening a swath of new, economically devastating tariffs on cars and trucks.Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week.Tariffson an array of Canadian products took effect over the weekend, affecting around 5% of Canada’s exports to the US, and Canada said it will retaliate in early September.On Monday, Carney toured a shipyard with Quebec’s premier, telling attendeesCanada“could not accept” a proposed trade deal that would have weakened French language protections after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, adding that his government “will not give what they have asked”.The prime minister’s decision to abandon trade talks with the US spurred declarations from political leaders and pundits in Canada that the country is now fully locked into an economic war with its longtime ally.Quebec, Canada’s predominantly French-speaking province, has long sought to protect its distinct identity, at times with laws thatclashed with the federal governmentand the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms.In recent years those rules have also frustrated US negotiators, who have framed them as trade irritants. Bill 96, for example, requires products sold in Quebec to have a French description and for trademarks using generic terms to be translated into French, while Bill 109 compels media services such as Netflix, Spotify and Apple to promote and prioritize French content for Quebec users.Quebec’s premier, Christine Fréchette, said Carney had made the right decision in walking away from talks that looked to cross a “red line” for Francophones.“Our culture, our language is central to our identity and it is important to exclude that from the negotiation table,” she told reporters over the weekend. “It’s something that is crucial for us and it won’t change, even though we are threatened with different tariffs, it won’t change. We will stay the way we are.”Polling from earlier in the month shows that dislike for Trump is highest in Quebec. Separatists in the provincehave seen a sharp decline in supportamid the economic wounds inflicted by the US.Last week, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the sovereigntist politician most likely to emerge victorious in upcoming provincial elections, said his party would delay a possible referendum into seceding from Canada until Trump is out of office. He wrote that deciding Quebec’s political fate “must not be hijacked by the upheaval of American politics, the outbursts of an unpredictable president or by a campaign of fear”.The Quebec Federation of Chambers of Commerce (FCCQ) called the tariffs a “worst-case scenario” for the province’s businesses.“Quebec, in fact, has been the most affected by these tariffs since the very beginning of this trade war,” Fréchette said. “In all our regions, businesses risk losing contracts. In fact, it has already begun.”On Monday, Trump’s top trade representative, Jamieson Greer, called reports that French language protections were up for debate a “a funny fake story”.“That is not true,” Greer told CNBC. “I like the Quebecois and I like that they speak French.” He said both he and his sons speak the language.He claimed the issue at stake was that Americans did not like Canada “forcing” streaming giants in the US to pay some of their profits to support Canadian content. Canada had already dropped that position, however, previously abandoning elements of digital services tax.“I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content. We think that’s a really valuable thing and we encourage countries to really put their own country first and put their national identity first.”Carney rejected that framing, telling reporters it was not “funny” and there was an “enormous spread” in perspectives.Also on Monday, Trump redoubled his efforts to wage economic war against his country’s longtime political, security and economic ally.“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trumpwrote on social media. Criticizing Canada’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers, Trump wrote: “Not sustainable, and not anymore!”The president, whofaces mounting domestic unease over his trade spatwith Canada, pledged to increase tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel beginning on 1 January . “We don’t need Canada, they need us!” he wrote, using capital letters.The move has provoked an increasingly predictable backlash from political leaders.The Conservative premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, told local media Trump can “kiss my ass”.“We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at him. He’s arrogant, he’s cocky, and you know, as Ronald Reagan said, if you come to a draw with a bully, what stops that bully from coming after you the next day and the next day. And that’s all Donald Trump is – is a bully,” said Ford. “Well, he’s going to have a rude awakening.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpTrump administrationTariffsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Twelve people arrested after A66 crash that killed seven including two police officers | UK news | The Guardian
description: Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation of events leading to deadly collision
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation of events leading to deadly collision
Content: PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died in a collision between a police vehicle and a car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland police/PAView image in fullscreenPC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died in a collision between a police vehicle and a car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland police/PAUK newsTwelve people arrested after A66 crash that killed seven including two police officersNine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation into events leading to deadly collisionRaphael Boyd,Hannah Al-OthmanandRobert BoothMon 24 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwelve people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including being involved with organised crime as part of the investigation into events leading to a crash on the A66 that killed two police officers and five others.Cleveland police confirmed that nine men and three women were detained by officers investigating the events that led up to PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough dying when a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough collided with their marked armed response vehicle. All five men who were in the second car, aged between 17 and 23, were pronounced dead at the scene.Police said some of those arrested as part of the A66 investigation, whose ages range from 19 to 61, were suspected of various offences.Four people were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and four on suspicion of possessing a firearm, while four of the suspects were also accused of possessing class A and B drugs with intent to supply.Police have said the five men killed in the crash may have had links to “serious and organised criminal activity”, adding that four of those killed in the car that hit the police vehicle had previous convictions.The fatal crash sparked a wave of concern about a social media trend for posting videos of dangerous, high-speed driving, which the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday called “truly reprehensible”.Cleveland police said there was currently “no evidence that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning was for the purposes of TikTok”, but Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, wants assurances from the tech companies and from the online communications regulator Ofcom “that this content is being proactively sought and removed”.At least one of those killed in Saturday’s crash had previously posted reckless driving footage online.The Guardian on Monday found a video on YouTube seen 2.5m times showing a Honda being driven at dangerous speed through a council estate and then down a narrow country road. Google, which owns YouTube, terminated the account after being asked for comment.The arrests have come as part of a “wide-scale investigation into the criminality which took place” in the hours leading up to the crash, which has involved the help of officers and staff from Durham, Northumbria and North Yorkshire police forces.As part of the investigation a Volvo XC60, believed to be associated with the activities of the passengers of the Volkswagen Passat, had been identified and recovered, police said.Assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said his force had engaged in “a fast-moving and complex investigation, with significant links to serious and organised criminal activity” and claimed the “events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect”.He said: “We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice. Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organised crime.“Officers and staff across Cleveland have shown incredible resilience in continuing their work in the face of tragedy. Two of their colleagues lost their lives while serving the people of Cleveland and, while the impact will be felt by our people for a long time to come, they have continued to act with the utmost professionalism.“I am also extremely grateful for the support we have received, and continue to receive, from the public of Cleveland and our wider police family.”Earlier on BBC Radio 5 Live, defence minister, Luke Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies “step up”.“I think we all need to give the police time,” he said. “But there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content.”Earlier this month,five young men were killed in Irelandand four other people injured after the car the men were travelling in was driven the wrong way down the M9 motorway.More than £500,000 has been raised for the families of the two officers who died, while floral tributes have also been left beside the A66 close to the site of Saturday’s crash.One said: “Behind every uniform is a person with a life, family, friends and people whose lives they have touched along the way.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China
Content: Scott Bessent said the objective was to ‘sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone’.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenScott Bessent said the objective was to ‘sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone’.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranUS threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to IranWashington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to ChinaJulian BorgerSenior international correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties withIran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.It is unclear, however, how far theTrump administrationis prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.Iran, meanwhile,vowed retaliationagainst any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign.Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks.The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed.Hardliners appeared to strengthen their grip on government in Tehran and responded by declaring the closure of the strait of Hormuz, attacking ships that ignored its declaration. Trump imposed a counter-blockage on Iranian oil exports through the strait, leading to an impasse that has had profound effects on the global economy.Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, however, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth ⁠told reporters on Monday.In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyTrump administrationIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Rupert Lowe set to be paid as much for divisive posts on Elon Musk’s X as for being MP | Rupert Lowe | The Guardian
description: Restore Britain leader paid up to £1,476 an hour by platform, which critics say is financially incentivising inflammatory content
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Restore Britain leader paid up to £1,476 an hour by platform, which critics say is financially incentivising inflammatory content
Content: Rupert Lowe’s previous posts have included posts demanding mass deportations.Photograph: Jason Bye/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRupert Lowe’s previous posts have included posts demanding mass deportations.Photograph: Jason Bye/The GuardianRupert LoweRupert Lowe set to be paid as much for divisive posts on Elon Musk’s X as for being MPRestore Britain leader paid up to £1,476 an hour by platform, which critics say is financially incentivising inflammatory contentMichael SavageMedia editorMon 24 Aug 2026 12.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRupert Lowe, the leader ofRestore Britain, is on course to earn as much from the social media platform X as he does from his salary as an MP, after surging income from posts that include demands for mass deportations.Lowe has earned £932 an hour for his posts onX, formerly Twitter, since the start of the year, according to his own declarations in the register of MPs’ financial interests, which detail how many hours he has spent on X for each payment he received from the platform.The figure is more than twice the £377 an hour on average he earned last year. His hourly rate rose steeply again this summer, reaching £1,476 since the start of June.X critics claim it is further evidence that X is favouring and incentivising divisive political content, pulling the UK’s political discourse to the right. Elon Musk, the site’s owner, hasrepeatedly amplified Lowe’s posts.Under X’s revenue-sharing scheme, premium subscribers such as Lowe are paid based on the performance of their posts. The scheme resulted inrecord payouts last year. The platform recently announced forthcoming changes, designed to reward original content and commentary.Elon Musk’s X not facing action from UK government over posts inciting violence in BelfastRead moreLowe’s total income from X since the 2024 general election has now surpassed £105,000. He earned more than half of that in the first eight months of 2026.Should his average earnings for 2026 so far continue throughout the year, he would earn just over £93,000 – close to the current MPs’ £98,599 annual salary. He could easily exceed that figure should the higher rate of earnings of recent months persist.Lowe has previously said hedonates his net MP’s salaryto charities and worthy causes in his constituency of Great Yarmouth.The politician’s extraordinary success on X has led to concerns among some campaigners, who fear it is a sign that Musk’s site is effectively funding an MP thatreflects the hard-right views of the billionaire.“We tend to treat a politician’s online reach and their income as two separate stories, but forRupert Lowethey’re part of the same mechanism,” said Ambrose Pym, a researcher covering the far right and technology who analysed Lowe’s rising X earnings. “The more his content is seen, the more X pays him for it.“Scrutiny is rightly falling on other sources of foreign money in British politics. However, a US-based billionaire simultaneously paying and boosting an ideologically aligned British politician through his own platform is going strikingly under-reported. X’s financial and reach incentive structure rewards division and is shaping British politics with almost none of the scrutiny it deserves.”Lowe, who founded Restore Britain after leaving Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, describes his party’s most significant achievement as “dragging mass deportations [of migrants] into mainstream politics”.Asked about his accelerating X earnings, Lowe told the Guardian: “If I wanted to make money, I would not be in politics. I donate my entire net MP salary to local charities in my constituency – being a politician is the most expensive job I’ve ever had.”His recent posts on X show the extraordinary amount of engagement the Restore leader secures on the platform. Over the weekend, one of his posts stated: “An illegal migrant could read ten thousand Home Office pamphlets in some woeful attempt to ‘integrate’, I’d still want him deported.“They broke into our country – they are not welcome here, and they all need to be removed. This is not complicated.” It received 1.3m views, 25,000 likes and 3,000 reposts.Last week, a post about how the UK should replicate Portugal’s ban on the burqa in many public spaces received almost a million views.Lowe’s previous posts have included describing diversity policiesas a“wicked, malicious, viperous cancer” and have criticised illegal migrants as “unvetted foreign males” loitering“where your daughter walks home”.The Guardian has contacted X with a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsRupert LoweRestore BritainXFar rightInternetThe far rightElon MusknewsShareReuse this content

title: Man arrested on suspicion of arson after fire at car park used by Gatwick passengers | England | The Guardian
description: Blaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday night
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Blaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday night
Content: The blaze erupted at the Caldyne business park, a third-party parking site used by people flying from Gatwick airport.Photograph: Eddie MitchellView image in fullscreenThe blaze erupted at the Caldyne business park, a third-party parking site used by people flying from Gatwick airport.Photograph: Eddie MitchellEnglandMan arrested on suspicion of arson after fire at car park used by Gatwick passengersBlaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday nightHarry CockburnMon 24 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire tore through a car park used by people flying from Gatwick airport, destroying about 140 vehicles.The blaze erupted at Caldyne business park near Crawley, about eight miles from the airport just after 9pm on Saturday. Images showed vehicles on fire and enormous plumes of smoke rising close to overhead power lines.As well as causing misery for those returning from summer holidays to find their cars destroyed, the fire led to power cuts at more than 2,000 businesses and homes.Emergency services described extinguishing the blaze as a “significant and complex” operation, with eight fire engines and water carriers deployed to bring it under control.UK Power Networks, which operates the electricity network across south-east England, had to isolate an overhead power cable while crews worked below.A spokesperson for West Sussex fire and rescue service said: “Approximately 140 vehicles were damaged, and a number of the vehicles involved in this fire were parked at a site used for holiday parking. Any affected consumers are advised to contact their operator directly.”There were no casualties, it said.The fire also caused significant damage to two breakdown and recovery businesses and a banger racing team.The Bears banger racing team said ina fundraiserthat they had lost everything.Autocovery and K&L Automotive had also previously donated abandoned vehicles to fire stations across West Sussex for training purposes,according to local reports.Sussex police said a 67-year-old man arrested on suspicion of arson had been bailed pending further inquiries.“Power was shut off to the immediate area, affecting a number of businesses and homes, and nearby roads were closed as a precaution,” a spokesperson said.“Emergency services remain on scene at this time and the public are advised to avoid the area.”A London Gatwick spokesperson said: “We are aware of a fire at an unaffiliated third-party car parking site, which occurred on Saturday evening, and understand how concerning and distressing this will be for any passengers whose vehicles may have been affected.“We are advising any passengers who are concerned that their vehicle might have been affected to contact their parking operator directly.“The parking company is not endorsed or operated by London Gatwick.”Police said anyone with information about the incident was asked to report it online or call 101, quoting serial number 1504.Explore more on these topicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Enough is enough’: players pile pressure on under-fire Gianni Infantino to resign | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: A group of influential current and former footballers have added to the pressure on Gianni Infantino by calling for change at the top of Fifa
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: A group of influential current and former footballers have added to the pressure on Gianni Infantino by calling for change at the top of Fifa
Content: Gianni Infantino was at a youth tournament in the Dominican Republic on Saturday in an attempt to smooth relations with smaller Caribbean member associations on whose support his Fifa fate may hinge.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino was at a youth tournament in the Dominican Republic on Saturday in an attempt to smooth relations with smaller Caribbean member associations on whose support his Fifa fate may hinge.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/ReutersGianni Infantino‘Enough is enough’: players pile pressure on under-fire Gianni Infantino to resignPresident accused by ‘Fifa Legends’ of being power hungrySamuel Eto’o claims chief has not ‘done anything wrong’Nick AmesMon 24 Aug 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of influential current and former footballers have added to the pressure onGianni Infantinoby calling for change at the top of Fifa, saying “enough is enough” in a statement shared widely across social media.The intervention is particularly significant given some of those behind its circulation have undertaken ambassadorial activities forFifaas part of its “Fifa Legends” programme. Among them is the former Manchester United and Arsenal defender Mikaël Silvestre, who also sits on the governing body’s 16-member players’ voice panel designed to assist with anti-racism initiatives.Infantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in CaribbeanRead moreOthers to have shared the statement include the England defender Lucy Bronze, the former England keeper David James and the France 1998 World Cup winner Emmanuel Petit. More signatories are expected to follow in a concerted reaction to Infantino’s ill-fated attempt tosell stakes in the World Cup.“We share the exact same concerns as the millions of fans around the world,” part of the statement read. “Like them, we have watched the game we love drift away from its core values under Fifa’s current leadership. For too long, we’ve seen major decisions taken without players being consulted or considered, and without any regard for the fans who sustain the sport.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Change is necessary. Power has blurred the current leadership’s ability to distinguish between its own interests and what is best for football. Recent events have made silence impossible. Enough is enough.”The group called for efforts to “reshape the future of our sport”, adding: “There are good people within Fifa who want to rebuild trust, but a new era requires a structured change: a real, direct say for players and fans in how football is run. Those who step on to the pitch and those who sit in the stands deserve a genuine voice to help reshape football’s future together.”Infantino has resisted calls to resign and spent Saturday at ayouth tournament in the Dominican Republic, attempting to smooth relations with some of the smaller Caribbean member associations on whose support his fate may hinge.One former player with a different perspective on Infantino is the former Real Madrid, Barcelona and Chelsea striker Samuel Eto’o, who is president of the Cameroonian football federation. In an interview with CNN, Eto’o said Infantino had not committed any missteps and called for the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme to be put back on the table if Infantino is re-elected next March. He said the money from FFE would “reset the balance of power” in football and ensure African countries avoided losing top players to other national teams.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t think that [Infantino] has done anything wrong,” he said. “All of this has happened because there’s an election coming out, that’s all there is.“I want to see all of my colleagues, all of the presidents, re-reading the project. After president Infantino is re-elected, we will have the strength to ask for this project to be put back on the table for discussion. I remain convinced that, if there is a democratic vote, this project will be adopted because it’s good for the majority.”Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Green Man review – Wolf Alice, Shame and secret sets keep the Welsh festival’s flame burning | Green Man | The Guardian
description: The traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Wolf Alice, Tamikrest and Westside Cowboy
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: The traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Wolf Alice, Tamikrest and Westside Cowboy
Content: Commanding … Wolf Alice.Photograph: Patrick GunningView image in fullscreenCommanding … Wolf Alice.Photograph: Patrick GunningGreen ManReviewGreen Man review – Wolf Alice, Shame and secret sets keep the Welsh festival’s flame burningBannau Brycheiniog, WalesThe traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Four Tet, Tamikrest and Westside CowboyOlive PometseyMon 24 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDriving towards the bucolic Welsh valley that’s home to theGreen Manfestival feels a little apocalyptic this year. Charred peat and grassland smoulder on the hillsides, the remnants of one of the 20 wildfires that blazed through south and west Wales the previous week. The dangerously dry conditions pose a problem for the festival organisers: the traditional closing ceremony, during which a towering effigy of the titular Green Man adorned with punters’ handwritten wishes is set alight, has been cancelled. A sensible decision, but one that left longtime festival-goers with a serious question: where would all those wishes go?Then, the heavens open. Manchester quartetWestside Cowboypack out the main stage arena on Friday afternoon, thousands of soggy cagoules bobbing along to the band’s charmingly ramshackle blend of British indie and amiable Americana. “We were over there last year,” grins vocalist and guitarist Jimmy Bradbury, gesturing towards the significantly smaller Rising stage. They’re clearly over the moon – and it’s infectious. To close the set, the band down instruments – save a guitar and a handheld drum – and gather round one mic for a rallying performance of In the Morning. The recorded version sounds like a lullaby, but here they transform it into a euphoric boot-stomping finale.That energy charges through the rest of the day, even as the rain clears up. With his exhilarating blend of highlife, funk and electro, Ghanaian singer Ata Kak bounds across the stage with enough zeal to fuel a small army. London post-punks Shame incite endless moshpits with their rowdy, self-deprecating swagger and calls to “free Palestine”. Dry Cleaning’s Florence Shaw delivers a typically off-kilter performance of her jaded, spoken-word indie, bringing out Jeff Tweedy – of headliners Wilco – for the first ever duo performance of My Soul/Half Pint. Over in the Far Out tent, Karla Chubb of Sprints plucks a teenager out of the crowd to take over her guitar during their final song, Little Fix, freeing her up to crowd surf on one condition: “You have to promise to not touch my bum,” she tells the audience.View image in fullscreenRowdy and self-deprecating … Shame.Photograph: Patrick GunningMalian rock band Tamikrest supply the psychedelic desert blues, and Gambian party-starter Suntou Susso orchestrates a giant conga line through the crowd. Cult producer Daniel Avery maintains the intensity, but in a surprising way:: all headbanging metal guitars and ferocious live drum’n’bass beats, only briefly punctuated by the pulsating techno he’s better known for. Anyone left slightly disappointed gets their fill at Four Tet’s headline slot, which crescendoes from ambient techno into body-rattling bass.Green Man’s lineup is hardly built around old-school star power. Still, both buzzy New York electro duo Fcukers andWolf Alicemake a convincing case for energetic performers, the latter in particular during the weekend’s final headline set. Clad head-to-toe in leather, Wolf Alice’s Ellie Rowsell commands the stage with powerhouse vocals that oscillate between indie crooning, near-operatic belting and snarling, punky screams, and leads the crowd in a collective howl at the moon. After a performance of that wattage, the replacement for the burning ceremony can’t help but feel a bit anticlimactic: Scotland’s Pictish Trail lead an acoustic performance of the Waterboys’ The Whole of the Moon, accompanied by aerial acrobats in glittering costumes, but the restless crowd never really get going.Thankfully, a secret closing set brings together Fcukers, Hot Chip’s Alexis Taylor, Way Dynamic, the Itch, Another Country $$$$ and SNL UK comedian Jack Shep for rounds of back-to-back DJ sets with crowd-pleasing Madonna remixes and a Don’t You Want Me singalong. It makes for a euphoric finale, and wish fulfilment of the highest order.Explore more on these topicsGreen ManFestivalsMusic festivalsWilcoDry CleaningWolf AlicePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things review – a show to make you shudder with laughter | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance art
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: From Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance art
Content: Brooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreenBrooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFrankie Thompson: Horrible Things review – a show to make you shudder with laughterPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghFrom Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance artBrian LoganMon 24 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are plenty of works-in-progress on the fringe.Frankie Thompsoninsists (or has the voice of Peppa Pig do so) that her show is a work-in-regress, an expunging of Horrible Things from the deepest recesses of her, and our, recollection. Thompson, whose brand of clowning-meets-performance art more or less guarantees something interesting will happen on stage, parades these Things as lip-synced audio and audience-terrorising stunts, all marshalled by our brisk and wild-eyed host, brooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress.Women in the crowd can relax: Thompson’s Horrible Things are usually male, her victims in the crowd likewise. The first sketch sound clips an interview with 12-year-old Jacob Rees-Mogg, and if you ever doubted lip-sync as an art form, I offer you Thompson’s performance here as the very junior minister. As his every word damns the way this country’s ruling classes are raised, her hyper-expressive face and nanosecond-precise timing pass sharper commentary than a thousand satirical words ever could.There’s more where this came from: a collage of interviews laying bare the tawdry machismo of the whips’ office; a skit questioning the wholesomeness of Cliff Richard and his Summer Holiday. Occasionally, the theme is diluted, with a song about paint sample names, say. But there’s always another shudder of horrible around the corner, as when Thompson recruits a mime orchestra from the audience to accompany a recording of Frank Sinatra’s bizarre 1980 release Trilogy: Past Present Future, the final album of which is a sci-fi fantasia of the male ego unleashed, in which Ol’ Blue Eyes disappears entirely up his own Uranus.Those People review – a double act with raw passion and no filterRead moreRevenge is then wreaked on the men present in several interactive interludes, in which chaps are dragooned on stage to dance, be babies, be stabbed, be expelled from the room. I will never love members of the public looking ill-at-ease on stage, but if it must happen, let it happen in the hands of a comic as adroit as Thompson – who backs herself into uncomfortable corners too, now licking the floor, now lathering herself in shaving cream. By doing so, in this airing of some dank corners of our cultural memory, she posits laughter not as the best medicine, but the best exorcism.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 9-21 November.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)TheatreClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A rock star on her own terms’: why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White | The White Stripes | The Guardian
description: Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer
Author: Annie Zaleski
Headline: Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer
Content: Meg White in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Rideaux/Rex FeaturesView image in fullscreenMeg White in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Rideaux/Rex FeaturesThe White Stripes‘A rock star on her own terms’: why we’re still so fascinated by Meg WhiteRecent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummerAnnie ZaleskiMon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 2011, theWhite Stripesannouncedthey were no longer going to tour or release new music. The decision wasn’t based on “artistic differences” or “health issues”; instead, the decision was “mostly to preserve what is beautiful and special about the band and have it stay that way”.In the ensuing years, vocalist-guitarist Jack White cultivated a wildly successful solo career and continued working sporadically with his other bands, the Raconteurs and the Dead Weather. Drummer Meg White, meanwhile, retreated from music, preferring instead to be a private citizen. In recent years, she politely declined to speak for a 2023 Elle story and didn’t attend the White Stripes’ 2025 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.Daily Mail accused of stalking woman mistaken as White Stripes drummer Meg WhiteRead moreAs a culture, we’re fascinated by musicians who stay out of the spotlight. Over the years, journalists have tried to track down elusive artists such as Cleveland singer-songwriter Bill Fox (who actually gave several interviews last year) or Suburban Lawns’Su Tissue. We’re not entitled to know details of their personal lives, of course, which is why this fascination occasionally slides into pernicious territory – like the now-deletedDaily Mail articlethat recently attempted to find Meg but instead stalked the wrong person.Meg had an uneasy relationship with being a public figure during the White Stripes’ active existence. She was notoriously shy, once tellingNPRabout the advice a teacher gave her: “She wrote in my yearbook to speak softly and carry a big stick, you know? And I took to that heart.” The White Stripes alsocanceledtour dates in 2007 due to Meg’s “acute anxiety”, something Jackspokeabout candidly and empathetically later. “To go full-speed from a dead-halt is overwhelming, and we had to take a break.”Such vulnerability made Meg enormously relatable, someone you wanted to root for to succeed. But people also feel protective of her because she was often treated so poorly when the White Stripes were an active band. Meg started playing drums in 1997 at Jack’s behest – the first song the duo played together was David Bowie’s Moonage Daydream – skipping formal music lessons in favor of more unvarnished creativity.View image in fullscreenMeg White in 2004.Photograph: Jean Baptiste Lacroix/WireImageThis irked people who expected virtuosity. A now-archived2016 article– Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her – outlined the sexism in exhaustive detail, from Pitchfork calling her drumming “pancake-handed” to a 2007 Pearl Jam message board thread titled “Official Meg White can’t play thread.” (Both jabs are still online.) Long after the White Stripes ceased recording, the negativity persisted. In 2023, a journalistapologizedafter intense outcry to his offhand comment that “the tragedy of the White Stripes is how great they would’ve been with a half-decent drummer.”The observation is especially absurd because the White Stripes were great precisely because of her approach to drumming. She and Jack complemented each other perfectly; her combination of steely focus and serene nonchalance balanced his more outgoing presence. “Meg is the best part of this band,” JacktoldRolling Stone in 2005, adding: “When she started to play drums with me, just on a lark, it felt liberating and refreshing.”Indeed, Meg was a powerful player who propelled the White Stripes’ blues/punk/garage rock hybrids with a steady hand. Her thumping kickdrum propels The Hardest Button to Button like a thundering metronome; the garage-rock classics Fell In Love With a Girl and Hotel Yorba lift off due to her buoyant, ramshackle playing. Later-era singles like Icky Thump and Blue Orchid boast a heavier edge thanks in no small part to Meg’s seething, sizzling grooves.And, unlike other duos, the White Stripes didn’t hire additional musicians to flesh out their live sound. It was always Meg and Jack against the world – her forceful rhythmic backbone anchoring his wild-hair extroversion, whether a grimy guitar line, a soulful organ, antique piano part or even a lively marimba.Criticized at the time, the White Stripes’ Glastonbury 2005 performance looks like a revelation through a modern lens; Meg looks unflappable, even ecstatic, as she mouths along with the words and steers the set. On the pair’sominous coverof Dolly Parton’s Jolene, her light-touch cymbal hits generate tension for much of the song – until it explodes as she ferociously attacks her entire drumkit, mirroring the moment when the narrator collapses in anguish.“It will always be us two,” JacktoldRolling Stone in 2005. “I will never do the White Stripes with another drummer. She’ll never do it with another guitarist.”He’s kept his word: when the duo was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Jack didn’t perform in Meg’s absence. Instead, Twenty One Pilots whacked through Seven Nation Army, while Olivia Rodrigo and Feist picked through a delicate We’re Going To Be Friends. However, Meg sent a note of gratitude that Jack read; he also noted she helped write and shape the speech he gave. “A lot of punctuation corrections too,” he quipped. “She’s pretty good at that.”With this honor, Meg became just the third female drummer inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, after Gina Schock of the Go-Go’s and Velvet Underground’s Moe Tucker. Like those two artists, Meg reinforced the idea that you could be in a band, create your own style and carve out your own destiny. She didn’t wait around for permission to be an artist.Meg’s iconoclastic music career and drumming skills are finally receiving their due, in no small part because younger fans and musicians aren’t saddled by the same sexist cultural baggage. Speaking to Elle in 2023, Rodrigo noted Meg’s playing and the White Stripes themselves taught her “the value of simplicity in music … that a truly great song doesn’t need to have crazy production or layers of sound. It just needs to move you. You can sense her passion in every song she plays.” But in the end, Meg proved you could be a rock star on your own terms – both duringandafter your music career.This article was amended on 24 August 2026. The article titled Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her was published in 2016, not 2006 as an earlier version stated.Explore more on these topicsThe White StripesPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Parisians out!’ Why the French have had enough of French tourists | France | The Guardian
description: As holidaymakers descend on Brittany this summer, trebling the population of some villages and towns, local people are unimpressed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As holidaymakers descend on Brittany this summer, trebling the population of some villages and towns, local people are unimpressed
Content: A beach in Finistère, Brittany.Photograph: Kumar Sriskandan/AlamyView image in fullscreenA beach in Finistère, Brittany.Photograph: Kumar Sriskandan/AlamyPass notesFrance‘Parisians out!’ Why the French have had enough of French touristsAs holidaymakers descend on Brittany this summer, trebling the population of some villages and towns, local people are unimpressedMon 24 Aug 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:“Parisians out!”Age:It officially commenced at the start of August.Appearance:Scratched into cars and painted on walls, mainly.Where?In southern Finistère, specifically in the Bigouden area.InFrance, you mean?Yes, the western edge of Brittany.Why wouldn’t Parisians be allowed in Brittany?They are, but they’re not wholly welcome. Many residentswant Parisian tourists to go home.Why?Because they’re sick of them.When did this start?It’s said to have originated from a sharp rise in second homeowners from the French capitaldating back to the pandemic, but this summer it began with a “Parisians Out!” sign being displayed in the town of Plogoff.That’s not very nice.The mayor of Plogoff agreed. “We can defend our peace and quiet, our environment and our quality of life without rejecting or stigmatising those who come to our area,” he wrote.Did that put a lid on things?It did not. Some days later in the town of Plobannalec-Lesconil, a car was scratched with the words “No to Parisians”. Two more cars were similarly vandalised.How did the vandals know the cars belonged to Parisians?Cars registered in Paris have “75” in their number plates.That sounds like a bad idea.Ironically, the vandalised cars were allowned by local people who had moved to Paris. Later, graffiti saying “Refugees welcome, tourists go home!” was found on a wall in the area.Aren’t these places sort of dependent on tourism, from Paris and elsewhere?Yes, but the pressure on local infrastructure is apparently overwhelming. The population of some villages and towns in Finistère trebles in July and August.I can see how thatwould be maddening.Also, the heatwaves and wildfires led people to change their plans and take “coolcations” on the northerly Brittany coast, adding extra pressure.So the anger is confined to Brittany?Not at all. People are handing out“Parisians go home” leaflets on the Île de Ré, and threatening second homeowners in Corsica.Threatening?A dormant Corsican independence movement has been revived this summer, with second homeowners told: “Do not consider yourselves safe on our national territory.”That sort of language istotalement inacceptable.Agreed.Do say:“Between the excesses of tourism and the rights of local people, a difficult balance must be struck.”Don’t say:“Welcome to Bognor Regis, Parisians!”Explore more on these topicsFrancePass notesOvertourismEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content
