title: Our climate is changing rapidly – and our politicians sound increasingly surreal | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: On a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with reality, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: On a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with reality, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed’ …  a man stands in a parched field in London.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed’ …  a man stands in a parched field in London.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisOur climate is changing rapidly – and our politicians sound increasingly surrealZoe WilliamsOn a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with realityMon 24 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTShareAs it is August, and everyone with stronger opinions is currently on holiday, last week I went onAny Questions?, the BBC Radio 4 panel show. I had prepared beforehand with a friend whose life’s work it is to make sure people don’t say anything stupid on the radio (or TV), and we’d talked about everything – the strait of Hormuz and energy prices; bus fare caps and the relative price of eggs; racism in the press and in public life; the AI bubble and the next financial crash; how many bathrooms Harry and Meghan currently have in the US, and whether a property even exists in the UK with that amount of toileting hardware.Predictably, perhaps, the audience’s questions did not spread themselves neatly across the full suite of current affairs, though Harry and Meghan’s return did come up – it was more a matter of which question about the climate crisis best represented the fact that everyone wanted to talk about the climate crisis. The news had just dropped thatEl Niño would deliver us an unprecedentedly wet autumn, but that was unlikely to soothe the parched earth of the record-breakingly hot, dry summer. Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed.The question that best caught the mood was: “Have we left it too late to avert the crisis?” I said there was no such thing as too late, channelling the economist Ann Pettifor, one of the architects of the original Green New Deal, back in the 00s, when it looked as if some politicians, at least, were in the market for ideas. She argued that we had to proceed as though there was still hope, because the alternative – grim nihilism – was no basis for a cooperative, generative body politic, and however many degrees of warming we were facing, we’d need one of those. Isabel Hardman from the Spectator said that it was already too late for some things, and not for others. Things weren’t looking good for birch trees in the south and east of England, for instance. It was a sombre but not bitter point of difference.Then the Conservative MP, Nigel Huddleston, came in. When detached from the phrase “net zero”, he seems like a reasonable, personable guy. But they’re not allowed to detach. Conservatives are tribally required to say that transforming to a carbon-neutral future is too expensive at this time. Even while they can see the impact of fossil fuels all around them, even when sitting in front of 200 people who palpably believe that there is no such thing as too expensive, when the prize is a beautiful planet that you can live on, Tories have to hold the line.The purge of the net zero believers from the Conservative party has a brute logic; Kemi Badenoch has chosen this as a red line, the signal difference between herself and the government. She can’t very well hold together a loose coalition between those who cleave to this pillar of new Conservatism and those who don’t. But when you take that position, which must have sounded solid in a strategy meeting, and perform it in front of normal people, who wake up every day to a rapidly changing climate, it sounds unhinged. All the standard lines, about how the UK accounts for only 1% of emissions globally, and that we should leave all the transformation and future-proofing to China, dissolve on contact with reality.Someone in the audience gave the only sensible response, which was to make a timeless and highly legible gesture involving his hand and his head (I call it legible, there is some contention about whether it means “wanker” or “dickhead”). Obviously I started laughing because I’m only human, but he got told off by a member of the production team and I got a bit of a glare as well. It’s one thing to understand the exigencies of classic Westminster politics, it’s another to watch these rhetorical manoeuvres in real life, where they are too ridiculous to take seriously, but too serious to laugh off. For the climate, it may be too late and not too late; but we definitely don’t have time to carry on indulging this surrealism.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions | Michael Jacobs | The Guardian
description: Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price, says economist Michael Jacobs
Author: Michael Jacobs
Headline: Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price, says economist Michael Jacobs
Content: Climate activists gather in central London to protest against the development of the Rosebank oilfield, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClimate activists gather in central London to protest against the development of the Rosebank oilfield, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionFossil fuelsCan Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditionsMichael JacobsCarbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the priceMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareThe British government must soon decide whether it should give consentto two oil and gasfields, Rosebank in the North Atlantic and Jackdaw in the North Sea. Amid both insecurity of energy supplies and deadly evidence of the climate crisis, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, isfacing pressurefrom the oil and gas industry and unions on one side, and environmentalists on the other.Labour’s manifesto commitment not to approve new drilling licences offers little help, because the fields already have licences, granted by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and 2023. But last year,Edinburgh’s court of sessionruled that the environmental impact assessments on which this decision relied were unlawful. The Conservative government had, the court ruled, failed to include the emissions generated when the oil and gas from the fields is burned. The court allowed work to continue on the fields, but a new assessment had to be done and approval sought again.The issue facing the new energy and climate secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is whether the additional information on the fields’ global emissions alters the grounds for consent.Although invariably discussed together, the two fields are very different. Jackdaw is a small gasfield, with aproduction life of only 11 years. Its total carbon emissions will be onlyaround 24m tonnes. Annually this would equate to around 0.8% of the UK’s total emissions. The gas would be piped into the UK, so would be consumed domestically. As this would probably displace dirtier liquified natural gas (LNG) imported from the US, it would make a small contribution to the UK’s energy security and emissions reduction.By contrast, Rosebank is a large oilfield, with a 25-year life. During that time it would generate around250m tonnesof carbon emissions. The oil would be sent to the Netherlands for refining, since the UK no longer has the appropriate capacity – and very little, if any, is likely to be used in the UK. So it would not contribute to our energy security.There are good reasons, therefore, for the government to make different decisions on the two fields. Jackdaw can be justified (just) on energy security grounds. The UK needs gas over the coming decade, and there is a benefit to a little more of it being domestic. Jackdaw will stop generating emissions in 2037-2038, when the UK, and the world, will still be well above net zero.Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby HinsliffRead moreRosebank, by contrast, will still be producing oil in 2050, when the UK is legally obliged under theClimate Change Acttoachieve net zero emissions. Indeed, by 2050, the Paris agreement (which forms the bedrock of the UK’s international commitments) expects the entire world to be just adecade or so offachieving net zero emissions. For that reason, theInternational Energy Agency expectsglobal oil demand by that date to be lower than today and falling, if governments around the world follow their own stated climate policies.Jackdaw is frankly too small to have any meaningful impact on global supply and demand in the decade it will be producing. But because of its size and longevity, the same cannot be said of Rosebank, which between 2040 and 2050 will be making a material contribution to global oil supply just when the market should be starting to decline. The greater the supply, the lower the price, and the higher the demand. So Rosebank has implications for both global emissions and international climate change policy.Rosebank could be given consent while avoiding these consequences if the government required it to pay for some or all of its emissions to be captured and stored in disused oilfields or saline aquifers. Most of Rosebank’s emissions will occur when its oil is burned. So, making carbon capture and storage (CCS) a condition of its licence would effectively mean requiring it to pay to capture and store the equivalent volume of other producers’ emissions.Though controversial,CCS is a proven technology: one of Rosebank’s owners, Equinor, has been using CCS in its Norwegian Sleipner field since 1996, is reported to have storedover 20m tonnesof CO2without leakage. The UK government’s own CCS programme, operated by the North Sea Transition Authority,has now licensed 21CCS projects at different stages of development. But Rosebank is not one of them.The oil and gas industry has yet to acknowledge that its production can ultimately only beconsistent with net zero emissions if it uses CCS. Giving consent to the Rosebank field on condition that it pays for its emissions to be captured and stored – say, from 2035 onwards – is the only way to make it compatible with the UK government’s domestic and international climate change commitments. By joining the UK CCS programme, Rosebank would probably be eligible for government support.The additional costs of CCS might mean that Rosebank’s owners would decide not to go ahead with it. But this would merely demonstrate that the project cannot in practice be undertaken in a way that is consistent with the UK’s net zero commitments.It is also critical that for both Jackdaw and Rosebank the government insists onstrict methane limits. Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and both fields will have significant emissions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government should make two other announcements at the same time. The first is to secure thousands of jobs by accelerating the labour-intensive decommissioning of oil and gasfields in the North Sea. At the same time, the government should publish a net zero transition roadmap, explaining how the UK will “defossilise” its economy over the next 25 years.Rosebank’s and Jackdaw’s operators say they will create around3,500 jobs in development and around 880 in operation. These are not negligible, but they will not save the oil and gas industry or the wider economy of north-east Scotland. Between 2013 and 2023, jobs in the sectorfell by more than half, from 441,000 to 213,000. This has nothing to do with UK climate change policy, but is simply the inevitable consequence of the exhaustion of the British North Sea basin (around 90% of the UK’s oil and gashas now been extracted).With around1,700 wells due to be pluggedand abandoned in the next six years and 500 already overdue for removal, decommissioning is a huge task. It will create many more jobs than drilling would (it is estimatedthat decommissioning will generate up to 25,000 UK jobs over the next decade and deliver about £6.8bn in economic benefit).A net zero transition roadmap would cover both the anticipated technological pathways in energy, transport, industry and agriculture, and the implications for businesses and households. Such a roadmap would reassure firms, unions and consumers concerned about what the net zero goal really means, and deprive the media and opposition parties of the chance to speculate wildly about its costs.It would give investors much-needed certainty.France has already producedsuch a roadmap, and other countriesare also committedto doing so. Britain should join them.Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime ministerExplore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOpinionClimate crisisEnergyOil and gas companiesCarbon capture and storage (CCS)Energy industryGascommentShareReuse this content

title: Why is the John Lewis ‘uni essentials’ list so strange? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: It used to be that dorm rooms were chaotically messy, writes Emma Beddington. Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers?
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: It used to be that dorm rooms were chaotically messy, writes Emma Beddington. Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers?
Content: ‘How many clothes hangers do I need to bring?’Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘How many clothes hangers do I need to bring?’Photograph: Getty ImagesOpinionYoung peopleWhy is the John Lewis ‘uni essentials’ list so strange?Emma BeddingtonIt used to be that dorm rooms were chaotically messy. Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers?Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTShareOf all the questions this year’s freshers may be nervously asking themselves as they prepare for this next phase – did I pick the right course? Will I make friends? Is uni worth 30 grand when my future job prospects may be limited to dusting a datacentre? – one is particularly pressing: “How many clothes hangers do I need to bring?”Fret no longer, enquiring young minds: John Lewis has the answer on itspacking checklist for students. Thirty to 40, it claims, wildly, “consisting mostly of standard velvet or plastic hangers”. “Standard” velvet? I missed this memo.I found the list via the student news site the Tab, which posted a TikTok mocking J-Lew’s notions of what constitute “essentials”: a £495 Marc Jacobs bag, a £399 desk and an £80 spice rack carousel (I also spotted a £185 Ralph Lauren quarter-zip for those must-attend “man in finance” costume parties).In fairness, most of the stuff on there is fine, but the Stanley cups and shower squeegees conjure a slightly dispiriting picture of wellness-focused, sensible, hygienic youth. I know that’s their generation’s reputation, but it would be nice if parents could be persuaded not to stock up, instead letting them go rogue and fill their kitchens, bathrooms and bedrooms with chaotically impractical stuff they choose themselves. Isn’t that what early adulthood is all about?I’m optimistic, based on my own experiences: you needed a hazmat suit, not a shower squeegee, for my elder son’s student bathroom; the main feature of the younger’s kitchen was the Death-Star-sized air fryer he and his flatmates won at bingo.He’s back home, post-graduation, and the surviving uni purchases are all over the house: deflated duvets, half-melted spatulas, singed tea towels. I WhatsApped to ask if there was anything particularly good or bad. It was mostly fine, he replied (from his bedroom), although the colourful multipurpose pan I was influenced into buying in a moment of emotional weakness proved underwhelming. The real “door-opener”, apparently, was a kilo bag of Belgian chocolate chips I got him, so that is my freshers “essential” tip: social currency (and a delicious snack) for £18.99.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Marine Le Pen’s career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than ever | Mujtaba Rahman | The Guardian
description: No longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan Bardella, says Mujtaba Rahman of Europe at Eurasia Group
Author: Mujtaba Rahman
Headline: No longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan Bardella, says Mujtaba Rahman of Europe at Eurasia Group
Content: ‘The other candidates were wary of Jordan Bardella [left], but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.’Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The other candidates were wary of Jordan Bardella [left], but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.’Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionMarine Le PenMarine Le Pen’s career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than everMujtaba RahmanNo longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan BardellaMon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTShareFrance loves a battle-scarred survivor. Charles de Gaulle, François Mitterrand and Jacques Chirac clawed their way back from political failure to become presidents of the republic. There is a significant chance thatMarine Le Penwill be next.Now that the Paris appeal courthas unshackled herfrom an electoral ban for fraud, the far-right veteran has double appeal in the race for the French presidency next year. She will run, as always, as an outsider and a scourge of the political elites – despite continuously holding electoral office since 1998. She can also now pose as a “miraculous survivor”, a “mother courage” and “a battling granny”, as senior French political figures, including former ministers, described her to me during recent conversations in Paris.Le Pen will be a much more formidable candidate than her young understudy Jordan Bardella might have been. The other candidates were wary of Bardella, but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.Her party, theNational Rally(RN), has a new campaign slogan: “Renaissance”. The rebirth of Le Pen’s political career, the party says, foretells the rebirth of France.One might almost think Le Pen had been acquitted of fraud on 7 July.She was not. The judges essentially ruled that voters, not the courts, should decide who is president. They reduced Le Pen’s five-year ban from electoral politics, imposed by the Paris criminal court last year, to time already served.She is now a twice-convicted embezzler of more than €4m in EU funds. If her final appeal to France’s highest court is heard rapidly and rejected, she might have to campaign next spring wearing an electronic tag on her ankle.And yet. Two opinion polls since her reprieve suggest that she coulddefeat all imaginable opponentsin the two-candidate second round next year.Previous polls were almost as good for Bardella, but there were reasons to believe that he would not stay the course. The two-week-long second-round campaign traditionally stress-tests the capacity of the candidates not just to govern France but to represent it. Voters will wonder: do they have astature présidentielle? Bardella will be 31 in September. He has been an RN party apparatchik since he dropped out of college at the age of 19. Would voters have been able to imagine this talented but glib young man toe-to-toe with a Vladimir Putin or a Donald Trump?That question – presidential weight – is especially important for older voters. Of the 50 million registered French voters, 28% are over 65. Unlike younger people, they turn out in huge numbers.A recent Ifop poll showed Le Pen beating the former prime minister Édouard Philippe, the strongest of the many candidates looking to carry Emmanuel Macron’s centrist torch, by 54% to 46% in the second round. She had almost exactly the same lead among the over-65s. It is the first time any poll in any national election put the RN ahead with the “grey vote”.Bardella was also popular with older voters but his appeal to young and old was starting to fade. He comes from a working-class, Italian migrant family but had begun to show a Nicolas Sarkozy-like attraction to the high life, including, reportedly, a romance with anheiress from Italy’s remnant nobility.Le Pen was born into a wealthy family and political business but cultivates an image as a gruff-voiced people’s champion, a single grandmother living with her best friend,a breeder of catsand, above all, a survivor.There is, however, another issue that is crucial for older voters: economic stability. Le Pen’s feeble TV debate performances on the economyin 2017and 2022 helped Macron to defeat her.The RN’s economic policies remain an incoherent jumble of high social spending and low taxes, free markets and state interference. Bardella tried to shift the party towards a more traditional rightwing, low-tax policy and a more reformist approach to the EU, taking inspiration from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Le Pen’s return means a return to “Marinomics” and a policy ofwrecking the EU from the inside. With France€3.5tn in debtand permanently teetering on the brink of fiscal crisis, the prospect of a far-right government may disturb older and better-off voters.Le Pen will have an obvious riposte. Macron bamboozled you all twice with his clever people’s talk, she will say. Look where that got you: another €1tn in debt. Time to give a down-to-earth woman a chance. I could hardly do worse.But she could. Much, much worse.A President Le Pen or a President Bardella would take France and the EU into dangerous new territory. Bardella, at least, appeared aware of the difficulty of being so outlandishly anti-EU, and of trying to govern with slogans. Le Pen does not.A Le Pen presidency from next May is not a certainty. But it is, for the first time in seven decades of the family’s involvement in politics, a strong possibility. The comfort blanket for mainstream parties of right, left and centre – the implausibility of a 31-year-old slightly more pragmatic President Bardella – has been snatched away.Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director forEuropeat Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firmExplore more on these topicsMarine Le PenOpinionNational RallyFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: A music festival isn’t a music festival without children | Iman Amrani | The Guardian
description: Ignore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of events, says writer and producer Iman Amrani
Author: Iman Amrani
Headline: Ignore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of events, says writer and producer Iman Amrani
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onFestivalsThe hill I will die on: A music festival isn’t a music festival without childrenIman AmraniIgnore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of eventsMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTShareThe woman I used to be died the day I gave birth to twins. That life – full of spontaneous travel, impulsive decisions and a decorated social calendar – evaporated, giving way to a blank canvas of motherhood and two glorious little human beings. While I was inside that summer, many of my friends continued on their child-free paths. They posted pictures of themselves enjoying festivals, sleeping in tents with pop-up communities that I used to be a part of.So when the twins turned one last summer and we’d found our rhythm, I decided to take on the challenge ofsharing the magic of live music with them. It went better than I expected. Before their second birthday, we had danced at day festivals such as Situation Dance, put on by Femi Koleoso from Ezra Collective, camped out overnight in the Brecon Beacons for Green Man and been to the child-focused TOTFest.Some people think it’s wild, bordering on neglectful, to take children to festivals that also cater to adult punters. They tend to think that children and families need to be separated entirely from spaces where there is any drinking or adult fun happening. Mothers, especially, are used to being told that everything we could possibly enjoy ourselves is going to damage our children. Thankfully, wise women around me whose kids are now grown up have reminded me to ignore these pressures, and go with my maternal instincts.Taking young children to festivalsdoesrequire another level of research and responsibility. Ear defenders are packed; festivals more aligned with drugs and debauchery are avoided. But different worlds can coexist. Selecting the family camping area when you book is game-changing. The adult audiences get their late-night raving in, and the early risers include not just families, but the wellbeing crowd heading to yoga or for a swim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia TaitRead moreHaving families around often has a positive effect on an event. People operate more within the realm of moderation when there are kids present, and you have to be a real Scrooge to get upset at barefoot children with glitter on their faces having fun alongside their parents.I, for one, don’t want to spend the rest of my life solely listening to the Wiggles, and made the tactical decision early on to expose my babies to a wide range of sounds. We’ve got instruments at home and they’re fascinated by how it all works. They’ve taken to live music so easily, it’s a joy to watch them engage with something so human and far away from any screens.People often say that other countries in Europe are ahead of us in terms of being inclusive of families and children, but I’d say the UK really shines duringits festival season. My favourite ones are a microcosm of what coexisting can look like in the real world. I’ve found my village in the fields and car parks that host these events. My motherhood canvas is filling up with music, and I’ve found festivals are places where we can all get a bit of something that we want.Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producerExplore more on these topicsFestivalsThe hill I will die onParents and parentingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how | Jean Kaseya and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus | The Guardian
description: Ebola is a disease that spreads through communities, so we need to listen to communities if we want to halt its spread
Author: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
Headline: Ebola is a disease that spreads through communities, so we need to listen to communities if we want to halt its spread
Content: Vanny Birungi, a Red Cross volunteer, speaks to people in Bunia, DRC, during a public awareness campaign 10 days after the Ebola outbreak was officially declared.Photograph: M Sawasawa/APView image in fullscreenVanny Birungi, a Red Cross volunteer, speaks to people in Bunia, DRC, during a public awareness campaign 10 days after the Ebola outbreak was officially declared.Photograph: M Sawasawa/APOpinionGlobal healthAfter 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s howJean Kaseya andTedros Adhanom GhebreyesusEbola is a disease that spreads through communities, so we need to listen to communities if we want to halt its spreadSupported byAbout this contentMon 24 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTShareEach time we travel to theDemocratic Republic of the Congo(DRC), we go first to listen. In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas.Their message was direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They were right.Ebola spreads through communities – and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it.They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response will move faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.View image in fullscreenDr Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa CDC.Photograph: AFP/GettyThe government of the DRCdeclared its 17th Ebola outbreak 100 days agoafter confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus.Theoutbreak has since become the deadliest ever recorded, with about 2,500 deaths.Behind this unprecedented toll are families grieving and communities confronting Ebola alongside conflict, displacement and fragile access to care.At the centre of it all are the people who show up every day.Healthworkers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure areas.Some havecontracted Ebola in the line of duty; some have paid with their lives.Their service must be met with action: protection, training, reliable equipment, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to vaccination, testing and treatment. Their safety is central to stopping transmission.The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, theAfricaCentres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.Uganda has interrupted transmission anddeclared the end of its outbreak, proving the Bundibugyo Ebola virus can be stopped. Decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities broke the chains of transmission.Ebola outbreak: five big questionsRead moreThe emergency continues in the DRC. Cases are still being detected outside known contact lists. Each one points to a chain that has not yet been found. Every delay gives the virus another opportunity to spread.The next phase must reach the village.The DRC’s village-centred strategy takes the response to the places where transmission occurs. Surveillance, testing, treatment, vaccination, infection prevention and community engagement must operate together, close to affected families. Teams need the authority and resources to act quickly.This is how we stop Ebola at its source: identify infection early, isolate and care for patients safely, follow every contact and prevent the next transmission.Community leadership will determine whether this works. Women’s groups, young people, religious leaders, traditional healers, survivors and community health workers know where families seek care, how information moves and where trust is weakening. They can identify concerns early, challenge dangerous rumours and help response teams reach people who may otherwise remain invisible.Their knowledge must shape the response. When they raise concerns, they must see action.Trust is earned through delivery. A family that reports a suspected case needs safe transport and immediate care. A community that supports vaccination needs clear information about what the vaccine can do. Families who lose loved ones need dignity, compassion and support through safe burial procedures.View image in fullscreenTedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, who heads the World Health Organization.Photograph: EPAHealth facilities also require urgent protection. As of 18 August, 163 health workers have been infected and 47 have died in the DRC, whileUgandahas recorded four health worker infections. Every facility needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water and sanitation.An infection in a health facility places workers, patients and families at risk. A protected health facility becomes a centre for early detection, safe care and public confidence.Financing remains a decisive test. Governments and partners have made commitments that must now reach the response.National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, vaccination, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.Delayed financing costs lives; fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both.Cross-border coordination must remain strong. People move to trade, work, study, seek care and support families. Countries need rapid information-sharing, aligned surveillance and prepared health facilities along major routes.The first 100 days have made the priorities clear: find every case; follow every contact; protect every frontline worker; bring testing, treatment and vaccination closer to every affected community. Turn every pledge into action.Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, alongside neighbouring countries, communities and partners, to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.This outbreak can be ended. Uganda has shown what focused leadership and community action can achieve. The DRC can do the same.Dr Jean Kaseya isdirectorgeneral of theAfrica Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus isdirectorgeneral of the World Health OrganizationExplore more on these topicsGlobal healthOpinionEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaInfectious diseasesWorld Health OrganizationHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needs | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Moscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself alone
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Moscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself alone
Content: Andy Burnham in Mykhailivska Square, Kyiv, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in Mykhailivska Square, Kyiv, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersOpinionUkraineThe Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needsEditorialMoscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself aloneMon 24 Aug 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTShareThe events of the past few days on Europe’s borders may mark a turning point in Russia’s war on Ukraine. While the political skies in Kyiv havedarkenedfor Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the military picture looks brighter. Ukraine can already send swarms of drones against Russian oil facilities,e-commerce warehousesand airfields. Andy Burnham’sarrivalin Kyiv marks a step forward. Britain is releasing classified information on its components ofScalp, the French version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missile, enabling its assembly in Ukraine. This is more than another weapon for Kyiv. Britain is helping Ukraine become less dependent on the western armoury.Moscowsabre-rattles, but Britain should hold its nerve. Kyiv has been at the mercy of its allies, waiting to replenish weapons stockpiles and release sophisticated arms. Producing its own hi-tech armoury gives Ukraine greater freedom of action because western governments have let go. Two years ago it was different. Joe Biden waited untilNovember 2024before letting Ukraine strike deep into Russia with US weapons. Yet thresholds once deemed dangerously escalatory have since been crossed without provoking a Russia-Nato war. Kyiv is now being trusted with something more consequential: a measure of weapons independence.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy.Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/EPAIt needs this. Ukraine cannot overcome its manpower disadvantage by fighting Russia soldier for soldier for every kilometre of its vital eastern fortress belt, whereKyiv is losing ground. If Moscow can freely push ammunition, drones and equipment towards Donetsk, eventually something will give. Cruise missiles offer another strategy, making it harder and costlier for Russian forces to reach the front. Europe isthinkingdefensively too. Ukraine relies heavily on the US-made Patriots to down ballistic missiles, but global shortages of interceptors, a situation made worse by the US war with Iran, have left it exposed. With European help, Ukraine’s defence industry is developingan anti-ballistic systemintended to reduce that dependence. Kyiv is ramping up its own ballistic missiles. If both are successful, Ukraine would be better able both to strike and defend itself without first appealing to Washington.War is a terrible thing, but what is the alternative? Moscow offers little evidence that territorial success would satisfy it. Despite enormous casualties and painfully slow advances, Vladimir Putinrejectsproposals that fail to meet Russia’s broader conditions while expanding military power rather than preparing his people for compromise. Then there is the rise of the far right in Europe, large parts of which arepro-Russia. If Mr Putin thinks that the outlook for Russia’s position will improve politically over the next two or three years, he will bargain harder. Why accept merely the Donbas today if the coalition supporting Ukraine might be weaker tomorrow? That option disappears if either Russia’s war burden becomes intolerable or the west convincingly insulates its material help from political change.History offers lessons. InVladislav M Zubok’sCollapse: The Fall of the Soviet Union, Boris Yeltsin is startled to hear that Ukrainians, including millions of Russian speakers, want independence in 1991. Once convinced this is their democratic will, however, he accepts it. Russia, he says, will “recognise this new political reality”. Mr Putin starts from the same sense of historical intimacy and reaches the opposite conclusion: that Ukraine’s democratic choices cannot override Russia’s claim to a privileged role in its future. That is a revanchist error he ought to regret.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Tiananmen vigil convictions: Hong Kong too has been silenced. Others should speak out | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Two activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crime
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Two activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crime
Content: A candlelight vigil for victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre, at Victoria Park, Hong Kong, in 2019.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreenA candlelight vigil for victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre, at Victoria Park, Hong Kong, in 2019.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APOpinionHong KongThe Guardian view on the Tiananmen vigil convictions: Hong Kong too has been silenced. Others should speak outEditorialTwo activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crimeMon 24 Aug 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTShareFor decades,Hong Kongmourned when the mainland could not. Its huge annual Tiananmen vigil kept alive the memory of the 1989 pro-reform protests in Beijing, and of the massacre that suppressed them. Along with Macau, it was the only place in China where the anniversary could be publicly marked and the truth preserved.But the crackdown onthe 2019 uprising in Hong Konghas crushed the freedoms that the region once enjoyed. That year’s vigil was the last. On Friday, two leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which organised the commemoration,were convictedof incitement to subversion under the draconian national security law. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face up to 10 years in jail.A third defendant, the 74-year-old former legislator Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. All three have been imprisonedsince their arrestsin 2021. The court ruled that the alliance’s stated aim to “end one-party dictatorship” in itself constituted using unlawful means to overthrow the Chinese government – despite acknowledging that the group never used or advocated violence, or even set out a path to its goal.The convictions are shameful, but not surprising. They follow the jailing of the prominent pro-democracy activists known as the “Hong Kong 47” in late 2024 and the 20-year sentence handed to the media tycoon and activistJimmy Lai in February. Yet while this trial shows the authorities’ determination to eradicate Hong Kong’s previous freedoms, it also reflects the Communist party’s determination tocontrol and rewrite history across China.View image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesHundreds, perhaps thousands, of people were killed in the 1989 massacre. Xi Jinpingmade a rare referenceto the events last week, reaffirming the party’s “correct” response, in a speech paying tribute to the former leader Jiang Zemin. But the subject remains one of the most taboo in a country long adept at erasing uncomfortable truths – so sensitive that even words such as “remember” and “today” arecensored on social mediaon the anniversary. This June, the Tiananmen Mothers group of bereaved relatives, who have long mournedunder heavy police escort, were barred fromvisiting their loved ones’ graveson the date of the killings.Against such brutal edicts, memory appears fragile. Most younger people on the mainland have no idea of what happened. Yet late last year, previously unseen footagesuddenly emergedof the court martial of a general who defied the order to use force against demonstrators. The video was posted on YouTube – which is blocked in China – andsheds new lighton events. General Xu Qinxian, who was jailed and lived under heavy restrictions until his death in 2021, said that a commander imposing the order might become “a sinner in history”. Whoever leaked the footage, and whatever their reasons for doing so, it is clear that some still resist the national amnesia.Remembrance and mourning are not crimes. In a message to Andy Burnham, Ms Chow, a barrister who studied law in the UK, warned that Britain had a “non-delegable duty to adopt a more robust stance” to China. She was right. The UK was the other signatory of the treaty that supposedlypreservedHong Kong’s relative autonomy until 2047. For years in the annual vigils, Ms Chow, Mr Lee and other courageous Hong Kong people stood up for those on the mainland who had been silenced. Others should now stand up and speak for them as they pay the price for that solidarity.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: We need public records on the delivery of social housing  | Social housing | The Guardian
description: Letter: Marco Scalvini on why it’s necessary to know what was promised by developers and local authorities, what arrived and what it costs to live in social housing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Marco Scalvini on why it’s necessary to know what was promised by developers and local authorities, what arrived and what it costs to live in social housing
Content: New social housing in Kingsbury, London. ‘A home is counted as affordable on the day planning permission is granted and is rarely examined again.’Photograph: Arcaid Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenNew social housing in Kingsbury, London. ‘A home is counted as affordable on the day planning permission is granted and is rarely examined again.’Photograph: Arcaid Images/AlamySocial housingLettersWe need public records on the delivery of social housingMarco Scalvinion why it’s necessary to know what was promised by developers and local authorities, what arrived and what it costs to live in social housingMon 24 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTShareYour editorial on London’s social housing (16 August) makes a persuasive case for treating social housing as economic infrastructure. However, infrastructure is normally monitored and social housing is not, either when it is delivered or across the years in which it is meant to remain affordable. A home is counted as affordable on the day that planning permission is granted and is rarely examined again, through completion, tenure change and the service charges that can make it unaffordable within months of occupation, asyour reporting on shared ownership has shown.Southwark, like almost every local authority, publishes every pound of the financial contributions developers pay, yet offers no scheme-level account of whether the promised social rented homes were built. The consequences showed at Elephant and Castle, whereresidents needed three years of freedom of information battlesto force out the viability evidence behind an affordable housing commitment that ended at 82 social rented homes in place of more than a thousand. By the time it came out, the estate was gone, and a record that arrives after demolition can only count the losses. On the Old Kent Road, wherethe council plans around 20,000 new homesandonly a few thousand are yet built or under way, the record could still be kept in time to shape what is delivered.You close with Nye Bevan’s idea of housing as an essential service like the NHS, and the comparison is instructive. The NHS publishes waiting lists and inspection results, and is held to them, whereas housing has no equivalent, whoever the landlord is. If social homes are economic infrastructure, they deserve public, dated records of what was promised, what arrived and what it costs to live in them.Marco ScalviniLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Let’s focus on what people with special needs can do, rather than what they can’t | Young people | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s recommendation to boost internship opportunities for young people with special needs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s recommendation to boost internship opportunities for young people with special needs
Content: Alan Milburn meets one of the participants in an internship project at the Magna science centre in Sheffield.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlan Milburn meets one of the participants in an internship project at the Magna science centre in Sheffield.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianYoung peopleLettersLet’s focus on what people with special needs can do, rather than what they can’tReaders respond to Alan Milburn’s recommendation to boost internship opportunities for young people with special needsMon 24 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTShareAs a retired special school headteacher, I warmly welcome Alan Milburn’s proposal to expand supported internships for young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Turbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says Milburn, 16 August). For too long society has concentrated on what these young people cannot do rather than what they can, with the right support and opportunity.I often meet former students who, once established in a workplace, have not only held down jobs but progressed to positions of greater responsibility.If Milburn’s proposals help shift the question from “What can’t this young person do?” to “What could they do with the right support?”, they deserve wholehearted backing.Young peoplewith special needs do not need diminished expectations. They do deserve the opportunity to show what they can contribute.Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, WiltshireAlan Milburn should pay more attention to the £2.5bn ofnational insurance contribution (NIC) exemptionsfor employers taking on young workers under 21 and apprentices under 25. Only the second is mentioned in passing in his interim report. Neither is included in its total spending on employment for young people. Adding these to the Department for Work and Pensions employment service costs would have very significantly reduced the 25 to 1 ratio of benefits to employment that has been so much publicised in the media.Take-up rates for these reliefs introduced in 2015 do not appear to exist. HMRC-commissionedsurveysrevealed that over half the 340,000 employers claiming young workers NIC exemptions were not aware that they were.Milburn could switch the resources to specific funding of jobs and apprenticeships to provide better, more visible incentives. This could lead to more than the “modest impact” of the only partly known funding at present.Adrian SinfieldEdinburghIf my experience of just one young person with special needs being employed by a major hotel group is anything to go by, we should be emphasising the value that these young people bring to the workplace and what an incredible asset they can be. A young woman was waitressing at breakfast in a high-end hotel recently. She was very good at her job, really efficient with such a smile and great spirit. She clearly loved her job. None of the surly service you sometimes get from someone who feels the job is “below” them.We had a chat and she told me that she was neurodiverse and all about the project that supported her into this job. Chatting with her made me feel that employers were missing out on employing some of their best staff if they don’t get involved with projects providing supported internships. As these young people are so highly motivated, they return the investment in bucket loads.Joy McLaughlanLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: What comes in the wake of Woke 1.0? | Inequality | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Nesrine Malik’s article highlighting a shift away from US society’s progressive and inclusive zeitgeist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Nesrine Malik’s article highlighting a shift away from US society’s progressive and inclusive zeitgeist
Content: #MeToo badges on sale in Los Angeles during a protest in 2017.Photograph: Lucy Nicholson/ReutersView image in fullscreen#MeToo badges on sale in Los Angeles during a protest in 2017.Photograph: Lucy Nicholson/ReutersInequalityLettersWhat comes in the wake of Woke 1.0?Readers respond to Nesrine Malik’s article about the shift away from US society’s progressive and inclusive zeitgeistMon 24 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareRegarding Nesrine Malik’s article (Here is the news from the US: Woke 1.0 is over. But what did progressives do wrong?, 18 August), the mistake of Woke 1.0 was to believe that a self-evident truth was, well, a self-evident truth. I grew up in a divided society in which it was crystal clear, at least to my community, that we were second-class citizens. Nothing ever seemed to change and in the end we fought a war over it. Today attitudes are a lot different, but new truths are universally embedded.What we learned was that the self-evident truth of “first-class” citizens was that their position was one established long ago by right and might. Against that sense of rightness, you cannot appeal to another truth that is diametrically opposed. I raised boys and girls in a progressive, liberal home. It was some surprise to me that my boys were not onboard with Woke 1.0. Their truth was Jordan Peterson’s “equality of access, not equality of outcome”, and a belief that their own privilege as middle-class, intelligent white males was good luck to be defended.Phrases such as “toxic masculinity” and “check your privilege” were heard as an attack, and qualifiers like “not all men” and “I don’t mean you” as insincere.It is not all doom and gloom. We chip away, parents and siblings, and even in the pushback in defence of Woke 1.0 at home, we feel the softening. I think that is where the hope lies in the next phase of progressiveness – the changing of minds in the home and among friends, one self-evident truth at a time. That is not to deny the need for the public political 2.0 movement that will inevitably arise, but to acknowledge that its roots will be in smaller truths and smaller conversations. So you can start now, and with hope.Name and address supplied“Defund the police” is one of the most tone-deaf expressions I’ve ever heard. Safety is high on the human hierarchy of needs. Most Americans associate policing with safety. Something like “community policing” would resonate with most Americans and pique curiosity in how police and citizens can work together.This is only one example of how liberals snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. We need to forget ideological purity and instead formulate simple, easily understood positions that point towards positive solutions to real problems. We have to be more than “not them”.Bert LoveShrub Oak, New Yorkstate, USNesrine Malik asks what harm progressives did. I think CS Lewis summed it up nicely: “Of all tyrannies, a tyranny sincerely exercised for the good of its victims may be the most oppressive. It would be better to live under robber barons than under omnipotent moral busybodies. The robber baron’s cruelty may sometimes sleep, his cupidity may at some point be satiated; but those who torment us for our own good will torment us without end for they do so with the approval of their own conscience.”David ForsterPenzance, CornwallHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: French Sunday and the Italian month off | France | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: The antidote to a French Monday | August on holiday | School dinners | Dance-hall don’ts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: The antidote to a French Monday | August on holiday | School dinners | Dance-hall don’ts
Content: ‘In rural France [on Mondays] 80% of businesses, restaurants and public bodies remain closed all day.’Photograph: Pauline Cutler/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘In rural France [on Mondays] 80% of businesses, restaurants and public bodies remain closed all day.’Photograph: Pauline Cutler/AlamyBrief lettersFranceLettersFrench Sunday and the Italian month offThe antidote to a French Monday | August on holiday | School dinners | Dance-hall don’tsMon 24 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareAs I write this, I’m enjoying my French Sunday (Polly Hudson, 23 August) with a croissant from the local bakery – open, of course – and a coffee. I’ll meet friends for lunch in a local riverside restaurant, then travel a few miles to a wonderful cafe, for even more coffee and their homemade cakes. Relaxing? Of course it is. It’s a much-needed antidote to a French Monday, particularly in rural France, where 80% of businesses, restaurants and public bodies remain closed all day in order to recover from the excesses of a “do nothing” Sunday.Roslyn LockhartMontmorillon, FranceI enjoyed James Mackay’s article onvilleggiatura, the Italian tradition of taking August off, which is shown to help rather than hinder economic output (17 August). As he says, though, the point is “reclaiming life from the totalising logic of the market”. For an expansion of this idea, I recommend the work of Amintore Fanfani, Luigino Bruni and Stefano Zamagni, who deserve to be better known in Britain. Like Pope Leo, they put human dignity and flourishing at the centre of economics.Catherine McLoughlinLondonMany problems have an easy solution that is wrong, but I suspect that including food standards in Ofsted results would fix this one very fast (Most English secondary schools are breaking healthy food rules, finds report, 24 August).Brian FishLeedsIn Elgin in the 1960s, if you were caught snogging in the Two Red Shoes dance hall, a spotlight would be shone on you to kill the moment (Letters, 20 August).Mary McMurranLancasterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Glaring weakness in goal remains but early signs Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea should be fun | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The failure to replace Robert Sánchez remains a mystery but the new-look front three should buy time for the new manager’s principles to bed in
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The failure to replace Robert Sánchez remains a mystery but the new-look front three should buy time for the new manager’s principles to bed in
Content: Xabi Alonso can only have been impressed by Cole Palmer and his forward line, but Robert Sánchez remains a weak link.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenXabi Alonso can only have been impressed by Cole Palmer and his forward line, but Robert Sánchez remains a weak link.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesChelseaAnalysisGlaring weakness in goal remains but early signs Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea should be funJonathan Wilsonat Craven CottageThe failure to replace Robert Sánchez remains a mystery but the new-look front three should buy time for the new manager’s principles to bed inMon 24 Aug 2026 18.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTShareAfter a weekend on whichpretty much every potential challengerto Arsenal haddemonstrated their flaws, there was a sense, perhaps even a need, for Chelsea to emerge as a serious contender – if only to prevent the title race becoming a procession. And while they were far from flawless, there were at least some indications that they could mount some kind of challenge.They looked extremely dangerous in the final third, and Cole Palmer was involved in all threeChelseagoals, perhaps benefiting from a first summer off in three years. But they were rather less impressive through midfield or at the back, despite Josh Acheampong’s all-action performance, while goalkeeper remains the problem it has been since Thibaut Courtois left.Chelsea’s front three dazzle as they edge out Fulham in derby thrillerRead moreIt could easily have gone wrong: in the final quarter-hour; Antonee Robinson lofted an effort wide with Robert Sánchez off his line and Ryan Sessegnon smacked a shot from a narrow angle straight at the Spanish keeper. But neither opportunity was taken and so Chelsea got Xabi Alonso’s reign off to a winning start.At this stage, performances and learning the system are probably the most important thing, but if there is to be some sort of dart at the title, results matter if only to keep Chelsea somewhere near the race until the point at which Alonso’s principles are absorbed and they do find something close to top form.Perhaps what’s most striking, though, ishow different the approach isto Enzo Maresca’s. Where Maresca prioritised control to often stultifying effect, Alonso’s game is based on rapid turnovers and transition. It’ll probably settle down as his systems become deeper rooted but there was a sense of recklessness at times to their play. It was harum-scarum, end-to-end, thrilling stuff, which is all very well to watch, and may even come as a relief afterthe sterility of Marescaandthe shambles of Liam Rosenior, but may not be great for consistency or sustained runs of form.Alonso could hardly have dreamed of a quicker start, João Pedro putting Chelsea ahead after 31 seconds, matching the record for the quickest goal scored in the reign of a Premier League manager, David Unsworth’s goal – also against Fulham – inDavid Moyes’s first game in charge of Evertonin March 2002. João Pedro had scored eight goals in eight pre-season games; and this a player Maresca told not to focus on scoring goals shortly before he went on a run of seven games without a shot. That was a first indication of a forward line starting to show signs of an impressive understanding. All three combined for the third goal, Morgan Rogers flicking on for João Pedro who held the ball up for the overlapping Palmer to slip his shot cleverly between Bernd Leno’s legs.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro (second from left), Cole Palmer (second from right) and Morgan Rogers (right) combined impressively on their first outing as Chelsea’s front three.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAlonso’s first go at finding a pattern amid the legions of players assembled by BlueCo involved a midfield made up of two players who, despite being at Chelsea together for the past three years, had never previously been paired in the centre: Roméo Lavia and Reece James. It was not entirely by choice: Moisés Caicedo was left out as a precaution while Enzo Fernández remained on the bench until the 65th minute asManchester City continue their pursuit of him. And it didn’t entirely work. It may look a defensively robust pairing but there were long spells when Fulham had control of midfield.A feature of Alonso’s approach, and one of the reasons it takes time and commitment to learn – qualities that were notably lacking at Real Madrid – is that players can emerge in unexpected positions. Which doesn’t entirely explain how the right-sided centre-back Maxence Lacroix found himself running on to Palmer’s pass in theFulhambox but, having got there, he demonstrated great poise to skip around Jorge Cuenca and cut the ball back for Rogers to score his first Chelsea goal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet for all that was new and positive, and for all that was raw and unintentionally exciting, there wasone glaring and inexplicably familiar failingfor Chelsea: in goal. Sánchez’s positioning seemed very strange for Fulham’s first goal, drilled in at his near post by Josh King (who also benefited from a bizarrely ineffectual attempt to track from Rogers), and while it was a far less glaring error, he pushed Timothy Castagne’s shot straight to Gonzalo García for Fulham’s second.Although Sánchez doesn’t perhaps quite deserve the negative reputation he has among certain Chelsea fans, he did make a league-high five errors leading to goals in 2024-25 and three last season. It remains mystifying that a clubthat signs wide forwards by the dozencontinues to refuse to invest in a top-class goalkeeper. That may yet hold Chelsea back.Generally, though, Alonso can be satisfied with his start: a win against Chelsea’s local rivals, an impressive display from Acheampong, a number of fluent interactions from his front three and plenty of signs of his system beginning to take hold, with a few obvious improvements to be made. And from the point of view of fans and casual observers, it looks like it should be fun.Explore more on these topicsChelseaXabi AlonsoFulhamPremier LeagueanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Post-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and awe | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Possession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season began
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Possession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season began
Content: Ipswich, Hull and Brentford all thrived at the weekend despite a lack of possession.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty and Tom Jenkins)View image in fullscreenIpswich, Hull and Brentford all thrived at the weekend despite a lack of possession.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty and Tom Jenkins)Premier LeagueAnalysisPost-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and aweBarney RonayPossession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season beganMon 24 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTShareThere has been something oddly narcotic and moreish about the drip‑drip of fresh Pep Guardiola content either side of the start of the newPremier Leagueseason. Eras come and go. Everything dies, baby, that’s a fact. But four‑part Amazon Prime documentaries make angels of us all.So we have continued to feast on the Pep-at-City visuals: dead jeopardy, reheated beefs, the uplifting team talks of a departed manager to the departed players of a departed team, and moments that often feel far more gripping than the daily churn of what we must, out of habit, call the real world.Liverpool are still haunted by the mess of last summer | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThe thought occurred watching all this: has the Premier League found its Tupac? Is Pep just going to keep on doing this, dropping new material, fresh hits, posthumous platinum albums? A bald, thin charismatic man who keeps on releasing his lost tapes. We have exactly the thing, sir. Is he even actually dead?Probably this won’t happen. But a profound absence is still a profound presence at moments like these. The ghosts continue to pull the strings. This weekend was the first of the new Premier League season. More significantly, it was also the first of the post‑Pep era.And this has been a genuine era, 10 years in the game and an entire tactical culture shift in the making. Unsurprisingly, there was an odd sense of lightness across those nine fixtures on Friday through to Sunday, of old bonds cast aside, even a little giddiness. Suddenly dad isn’t home. The chair by the door is empty. Let’s all just rip it up a bit, shall we?This relies on a slightly out‑of‑date notion of what Guardiola‑ism became in its later years. But the fact is, something interesting did happen in those Friday‑to‑Sunday games. Think of pure Pep-ball and what are you seeing? Possession. Cold, high‑craft control. This is a coach who famously said: “My desire is to have 100% possession,” after a 5-1 thrashing of Arsenal in Munich during which Thiago Alcântara complete 122 passes.View image in fullscreenManchester City manager Enzo Maresca acknowledges the fans before City’s opener against Bournemouth.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesAdmittedly, Guardiola was speaking out of frustration that day, talking more about not losing the ball at key moments, possession as defence. But these ideas did have a profound mimetic effect in England. During Guardiola’s decade atManchester Citythe team that had the least possession in the Premier League would win, on average, only 30%-35% of games, a figure that fell as low as 28% in 2021‑22 but which had begun to pick up in the last two seasons as even City’s own version of Pep‑ball became more mixed and next‑gen.But this weekend the opposite thing happened. In six of nine games played from Friday to Sunday one team took significantly more possession while failing to win. Liverpool had 60% possession plus 27 shots but still just scrambled a draw and looked, frankly, pretty wild. Manchester United had 71% possession and were well beaten by Hull. Tottenham had 60 % possession and lost 3-0. Nottingham Forest had 56% and lost. Sunderland had 62%, Crystal Palace 58%, and both lost.There were three exceptions to this, all outliers in their own way. Manchester City had 66% possession and won at home against Bournemouth, but spent 84 minutes looking like they were losing. Brighton had 73% possession and beat an Aston Villa team that had made a collective decision to play with their eyes closed and their legs on the wrong way round. Arsenal dominated every metric against a promoted Coventry team that looked, frankly, a little spooked by their first sight of that fresh Everest.Graphic showing teams with less of the ball won an unusually high proportion of Premier League games in matchweek oneSo, a tiny sample size. It may mean absolutely nothing. It could get flipped on its head before we hit September. Also, it is important to note that pure possession stats have rarely dictated with any certainty who will win a game. The top teams always tend to have most of the ball, thus skewing the overall stats.Otherwise, possession has been a far less reliable guide to victory than, say, expected goals, which speaks clearly to the effectiveness of a system. Whereas simply keeping the ball is often a sign of the opposite of good health, of football as a collective anxiety attack, out there playing with your worry beads, tramping a horseshoe shape into the grass while your opponents mass for the decisive blitzkrieg.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.But it wasn’t just the possession numbers that were notable this weekend. The rhythms of the matches were striking. All three Sunday games featured nine or 10 substitutes in the last 40 minutes or so, and a sense of two separate halves, of finishers brought into play, of a broken, episodic tactical to‑and‑fro in response to shifts in the scoreline and the flow. The World Cup also had that pattern. Maybe this is what football is now.Mainly there was a striking level of targeted physicality, rehearsed blitz-transitions, groups of players running suddenly forward quickly in formation at certain triggering events. Anthony Elanga’s opener for Newcastle captured this best: 12 seconds, two passes, 70 metres covered in a single perfectly straight line, no off‑the‑cuff inventions or what you might call conventional “creativity”, but a perfect moment of planned collective intelligence and breathtaking athleticism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis was the pattern elsewhere too, games defined by rapid breaks, by powerful players sourced for their ability to win duels and to carry the ball, and a weekend that felt like another ratcheting up in the Premier League’s journey into hyper‑physicality.Graphic showing sprints and distance covered beat possession for correlation with winning in match week oneIsn’t it a trend? Is this the next stage in the league’s narrow but furiously intense evolution? There are several managers in new jobs who have reputations for the game of sprints, blitz‑ball: most notably Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle and Roberto De Zerbi at what was, on Saturday, the least De Zerbi‑ish of Spurs, a Spurs that seemed to have absorbed only the mouse part – play dead, hide, roll over – of that fast‑breaking cat‑and‑mouse football.There are two things worth saying about this. This is not a rejection of Guardiolaism and positional play. Keeping the ball was always about preparing for the moments when you don’t have it. Guardiola’s later Manchester City team would often win by direct means.But pure possession can also be boringly risk-averse, a kind of footballing atrophy where everyone just sits quivering on the touchline like a swarm of beached jellyfish at dusk. The spectacle is more gripping when the emphasis is on those transitions either side of the passing patterns.More specifically, it is also an interesting development for Pep’s successor at City, Enzo Maresca, Coolio to his Tupac, whose methods are still very much pure Pep origins, based in control of the ball and rigid positionism, like the last soldier still fighting the second world war from inside a bush on Iwo Jima in 1976.View image in fullscreenNewcastle’s Anthony Elanga celebrates his superb strike against Liverpool.Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/ShutterstockIs Maresca ready for this? Is he even ahead of it? He gave a televised interview at the weekend where he spoke about the tension between control and risk, possession and creativity, and where he defined players being encouraged to run into unexpected positions as “chaos”. On Monday morning there were headlines describing the Premier League weekend in those terms. But this isn’t chaos. We’ve seen chaos. We’ve seen attackshipson fire off the shoulder of Orion, jinking wingers,dogs of war, hitting the space, Lee Chapman, Rod Wallace and Eric Cantona making heavy metal music with two bass guitars and anantiqueviola. You want chaos. We can give you chaos.What the Premier League brought at the weekend, the quick breaks, the freedom to attack at selected moments, was more a kind of hyper-managed shock and awe, targeted speed and physicality born out of calculated risk, numbers, data, heavy briefings.It was also exciting to watch, which is no bad thing in the world’s most tightly contested, space‑averse league. No doubt there will be tightening, a reaction to the reaction, instant counter‑moves and contingency planning. August can also be odd and silly season-ish, the dog days of a World Cup summer. But it did at times feel as if we were in a post‑something moment. If not quite post‑Pep, whose influence will continue to loom, a tactical Machiavelli with plenty of tapes still left in the vault.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeaguePep GuardiolaManchester CityanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Brydon Carse dropped by England as investigation begins into handcuffs incident | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week after footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby emerged
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Brydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week after footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby emerged
Content: Brydon Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker in the 2025-26 Ashes.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker in the 2025-26 Ashes.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamBrydon Carse dropped by England as investigation begins into handcuffs incidentBowler spoken to by police outside bar in DerbyCarse replaced in squad for second Test by Sonny BakerAli MartinMon 24 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week while the footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby city centre is investigated by the sport’s disciplinary body.Carse was filmed by a member of the public while he was detained briefly on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in the early hours of Sunday morning. The 31-year-old fast bowler had been celebrating victory against Derbyshire in the County Championship with his Durham teammates.Brydon Carse handcuffed by police outside nightclub prompting ECB investigationRead moreThe former England captain Ben Stokes and the fast bowler Matthew Potts were also present at the scene, with Carse said to have been in handcuffs for “a few minutes” before he agreed to move on and was let go without charge.Though not officially on England duty at the time – he was in the squad for the first Test in Leeds last week but was then sent to play for Durham – Carse is centrally contracted. The matter is now being looked into by theCricketRegulator – the sport’s disciplinary body – regarding a possible disrepute charge.In the meantime, and in light of a string of drink-related incidents that have plagued the England men’s team over the past nine months, Carse has been dropped from the Test squad. While he was not expected to play unless there was an injury, Carse has been replaced by Hampshire’s Sonny Baker.A statement from the England and Wales Cricket Board on Monday read: “Following a referral from theECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby.“Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained. Brydon will be replaced in the squad for this match by Sonny Baker.”According to sources, the footage of Carse came after he had been denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time. He had left the building following “an exchange of words” with another member of the public who spilled a drink on him. Durham, though not his direct employers, are not said to be pursuing the matter, nor are Potts or Stokes considered to have done anything wrong.Carse had been due to travel to London on Monday, with England’s 16‑man squad reconvening after the three-day innings victory secured at Headingley last Friday. They go into two training days at Lord’s before the match starts on Thursday.The issue presents Joe Root with an early off-field headache at the start of his second spell as Test captain, having made one of his first acts theremoval of the team’s midnight curfew. Root has now brought forward by a day his pre-match press conference to meet the issue head on.Questions about the team’s relationship with alcohol are inevitable, likewise those about his authority. The Carse situation came in the same week that Root backed his players to be “grown up” and “good role models and good human beings”.The decision to drop Carse while an investigation takes place follows a precedent set this summer.
