Stokes and Gus Atkinson both missed the second Test against New Zealand at the Oval in June when the Cricket Regulator looked into alate‑night incident in a bar in Chelseaafter victory in the series opener at Lord’s.The midnight curfew was in place on that occasion, even if it was later argued the precise details of it had not been well communicated. Atkinson had been involved in a physical altercation with a Saracens rugby player – he was not the aggressor, as per the ECB – while Stokes was simply present at the same venue.The ECB chose a different path on the eve of the Australia tour last winter, however, when Harry Brook waspunched by a nightclub bouncerthe night before the Yorkshireman captained a one-day international in Wellington, New Zealand. Brook was given a clandestine fine at the time, something which came to light only at the end of the Ashes.In between Brook’s altercation and the story being broken by the Daily Telegraph came the team’snotorious mid-Ashes break in Noosa, when opener Ben Duckett was filmed inebriated outside a backpackers bar and the footage emerged on social media before the Boxing Day Test.Duckett was cleared to play.Carse was backed heavily by Stokes during that 4-1 defeat, playing all five Tests and finishing as England’s leading wicket-taker, albeit conceding runs with it. A hand injury delayed his start to the English summer – and scuppered an intended spell at the Indian Premier League – but he had returned to fitness during the Hundred.While England were intending to stick with Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue this week as they target a first Test series win in 18 months, Carse was deemed first reserve. The retirement of Stokes in June and the new four‑pronged pace strategy should, in theory, mean opportunities down the line, unless this latest late‑night incident has affected his place in the pecking order.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamECBEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York pleads no contest after arrest at Ohio trailer park | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: The San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has pleaded no contest to two criminal charges after being arrested in Ohio over the weekend
Author: Tom Lutz
Headline: The San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has pleaded no contest to two criminal charges after being arrested in Ohio over the weekend
Content: Jed York also owns a stake in Leeds United.Photograph: Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJed York also owns a stake in Leeds United.Photograph: Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty ImagesSan Francisco 49ersSan Francisco 49ers owner Jed York pleads no contest after arrest at Ohio trailer park46-year-old charged with possessing criminal toolsYork fined and sentenced to two days in jail49ers CEO also owns stake in Leeds UnitedTom LutzMon 24 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheSan Francisco 49ersowner Jed York has pleaded no contest to two criminal charges after being arrested at an Ohio trailer park over the weekend.KRON4 News in San Franciscoreported that York was initially arrested on suspicion of engaging in prostitution but that count was amended to a charge of disorderly conduct. He was also charged with possessing criminal tools.A no contest plea is not an admission of guilt but the defendant in question does accept the punishment for the alleged crimes in question. York was sentenced to a day in jail for each count to be served concurrently and was released on Monday morning. He was also fined a total of $1,150 and ordered to complete an online course. The arrest report does not specify what the criminal tools were in York’s case.According to the New York Post, court documents say York responded to an advert on a website and “arranged to have sexual activity with [a] female in exchange for $140.” York was arrested later arrested at a trailer park in East Palestine, Ohio, on Sunday morning. The East Palestine Police Department and the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force were involved in the arrest. York, 46, was born and raised in Youngstown, a 30-minute drive from East Palestine and still has a home in the area.York is the nephew of former 49ers majority owner Edward J DeBartolo Jr. York took day to day control of the 49ers in 2008 when he became the team’s CEO. After acquiring his mother’s shares, he became the team’s principal owner in 2024.“As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time,” the 49ers said in a statement. TheNFLsaid in a statement that it is “aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy.”Since York took over as CEO, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls but lost each time.He also owns stakes in the Premier League’sLeeds Unitedand Scotland’s Rangers through 49ers Enterprises. He filed for divorce from his wife, Danielle, in May.Explore more on these topicsSan Francisco 49ersNFLSan FranciscoWest CoastUS sportsLeeds UnitedRangersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cycling chiefs criticised for response to Fin Tarling’s death: ‘This simply cannot happen’ | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Richard Plugge, the manager of the former Tour de France winner, Jonas Vingegaard, has criticised cycling’s governing body, the UCI, for a lack of action following the death of Fin Tarling
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Richard Plugge, the manager of the former Tour de France winner, Jonas Vingegaard, has criticised cycling’s governing body, the UCI, for a lack of action following the death of Fin Tarling
Content: Finlay Tarling competes in a race in France in May this year.Photograph: Abaca Press/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling competes in a race in France in May this year.Photograph: Abaca Press/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.CyclingCycling chiefs criticised for response to Fin Tarling’s death: ‘This simply cannot happen’Richard Plugge criticises UCI for its lack of action‘Riders must be certain they can race on a safe course’Jeremy WhittleMon 24 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard Plugge, the manager of the two-time Tour de France winner, Jonas Vingegaard, has criticised cycling’s governing body, the UCI, for a lack of action following the death of the teenage rider Fin Tarling 10 days ago and said cycling’s leading teams should take responsibility for ensuring safety in races.“Neither UCI president David Lappartient, nor anyone else, stands up and says: ‘Wait a minute, we really need to think about how we are going to prevent this from happening in the future,’” Plugge, the manager of the Vingegaard-led Visma-Lease a bike team, told the cycling website WielerFlits.Cyclists criticise ‘catastrophic’ safety measures after Finlay Tarling’s deathRead more“Maybe we as teams need to take responsibility for safety in races ourselves again. The lack of anger about what has happened is very disappointing to me.”The 19-year-old Tarling was killed during the Volta a Portugal when he was descending mid-race in pursuit of the peloton and collided with a non-race vehicle that was coming towards him on the race route, despite the road closure.“This boy encounters a car on a descent,” Plugge said of Tarling. “Can you imagine this happening during Formula One? That a car is suddenly driving on the track in the opposite direction? This actually does happen in a cycling race.“We are just carrying on. What disappoints me is that everyone says it is terrible, but then immediately a ‘but’ follows. We need to skip everything after the ‘but’. This simply cannot happen.”Jonathan Vaughters, the manager of the EF Education-EasyPost team, has called for a reduction in the number of races on the professional racing calendar.“The problem is lack of standards and oversight and the need to keep too many races that do not meet professional standards on the calendar,” he said.“There are many races running on too small a budget to be hosting a professional-level race. We don’t need 600 days of racing. How about 100 days of racing, all of which are safe?”While a formal investigation into Tarling’s death is now under way, neither the UCI nor the PortugueseCyclingFederation (FPC) have been willing to comment any further, particularly on media statements made by the Portuguese police (GNR) which confirmed that Tarling had been isolated and racing without a police escort.The FPC said: “As the organiser of the Volta a Portugal, we believe it would be neither appropriate nor responsible for us to speculate on matters that are currently being investigated by the competent authorities.”The UCI said: “As the circumstances surrounding the incident are still being established, we will not be commenting further at this stage.”Unlike Europe’s three Grand Tours, in France, Italy and Spain, the Portuguese race, like many other smaller events, operates a rolling road closure, which relies on secure policing at the front and back of the race convoy.Rolling road closures were highlighted again last week when the Australian rider Maeve Plouffe said that she hadnearly been hit by a carwhile racing in the Tour of Britain Women.“There is a hole in the system of rolling road closures,” the Association of Professional Cyclists president and former professional Adam Hansen told the Guardian. “We have to fix this.”Hansen added: “The most dangerous moments I had in a race did not result in a major incident. It was pure luck that I did not die sometimes. The organisers just think if nothing happened, it was fine.”Plugge argued that the serial failures to prioritise athlete safety meant that changes to the structure of many races had now become inevitable.“If cycling from A to B on public roads over 200km is no longer feasible, then we must ride laps of 15, 20, or 25km, provided those routes can be 100% secured. The riders must be certain that they can race on a safe course.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Project Magic’: RFL in talks with NRL over radical changes to investment deal | RFL | The Guardian
description: The Rugby Football League is to discuss a £50m loan package with the NRL after a £35m investment deal was rejected
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Rugby Football League is to discuss a £50m loan package with the NRL after a £35m investment deal was rejected
Content: Super League clubs voted last week to reject an NRL investment offer.Photograph: Richard Walker/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSuper League clubs voted last week to reject an NRL investment offer.Photograph: Richard Walker/ProSports/ShutterstockRFL‘Project Magic’: RFL in talks with NRL over radical changes to investment dealSuper League clubs rejected £35m deal last weekThe 14 owners due to discuss plans at meetingExclusive byMatt HughesMon 24 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rugby Football League is exploring radically different terms to the funding deal initially offered by Australia’s National Rugby League with talks under way over seeking a £50m loan package to replace the guaranteed investment of £35m that was rejected last week.The Guardian has seen details of an alternative vision produced by Rugby League Commercial in a document entitled Project Magic, which the 14 Super League clubs owners will discuss at a meeting on Tuesday .Leeds deliver timely Super League showcase while NRL investment hangs in balanceRead moreNigel Wood, the RFL chief executive, is understood to have circulated the document to the Super League owners last Wednesday, the day before they voted to reject the NRL’s offer. Discussions between the two competitions over investment from Australia have been ongoing since meetings in Las Vegas in January, with theNRLchief executive, Peter V’Landys, due to visit the UK next week in the hope of finalising the deal.The NRL offer would have seen it invest £7m a year for five years in return for a 10% stake in Super League, with the money to be distributed to the clubs. Instead of selling a stake in Super League, the Project Magic document details the RFL’s desire to seek from the NRL a £50m payment-in-kind loan, which it would use “to fund central growth initiatives and accelerate global expansion”.In another significant departure, the £50m would be retained centrally by the RFL rather than distributed to the clubs, which may prove a sticking point for many. The Project Magic document details what the RFL describes as a 10-year plan to grow the sport, and includes ambitious targets such as expanding Super League to 18 or 20 clubs, launching a joint direct‑to-consumer streaming platform with the NRL for non-domestic markets and creating a fully professional women’s competition.The RFL’s plans for investing the £50m are also outlined in detail, with £13.5m to be spent on improving the clubs’ commercial capabilities, £10m on the player pathway and £5m on broadcasting services.An RFL source said that the loan proposal is no longer its preferred option, but it is being considered significant enough for the clubs to discuss on Tuesday.While the Super League clubs were broadly united in rejecting the NRL’s initial offer, agreeing on a way forward may prove more difficult.Many of the competition’s bigger clubs such as Wigan, Warrington and the champions Hull KR are strongly in favour of partnering with the NRL, whereas smaller clubs like Wakefield are more sceptical amid concerns they could be left behind.Although the RFL appears to be advocating demanding an increase of almost 50% in funding from the NRL, it is unclear whether the Super League clubs will support the proposal, with many preferring a smaller cash injection to a centrally managed loan.One source with knowledge of the discussions described Project Magic as an attempt by Wood to retain control and influence at the RFL if the NRL deal closes.NRL sources have described its position as a “take it or leave it” however, and it is far from certain it would be willing to offer a £50m loan.Moreover, there are further significant obstacles to the deal being completed, as the NRL is demanding significant governance reforms, including the creation of an independent commission to run the sport in the UK, which would further reduce the influence of the RFL.Explore more on these topicsRFLNRLRugby leagueAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: The men claiming to defend women’s sports are throwing sex toys at female athletes | WNBA | The Guardian
description: The WNBA has attracted grifters who care little for basketball – and whose latest stunt exposes the hollowness of their supposed concern
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The WNBA has attracted grifters who care little for basketball – and whose latest stunt exposes the hollowness of their supposed concern
Content: Chicago Sky’s game against the Golden State Valkyries last week was disrupted.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChicago Sky’s game against the Golden State Valkyries last week was disrupted.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesWNBAThe men claiming to defend women’s sports are throwing sex toys at female athletesThe WNBA has attracted grifters who care little for basketball – and whose latest stunt exposes the hollowness of their supposed concernDave SchillingMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIregret to inform you that yet another dildo has hit a WNBA court. The Chicago Sky v Golden State Valkyries game was sullied bysex toys being chucked on to the playing surface on Friday. Aren’t we tired of all this yet? Toparaphrase the Sky’s Natasha Cloud, it takes a lot of effort to bother with such a juvenile act.This is yet another controversy for theWNBA, a league that up until a few years ago, most media observers ignored. The WNBA is full of incredibly talented players and has a rich history, but most sports fans treated all but ignored it for the majority of its 30-year existence. But when Caitlin Clark went pro, the league surged. Ratings, attendance, and interest exploded. But not all attention is good attention.Buzzer-beaters and besties: the rivalries and friendships that make the WNBARead moreClark has been polarizing from the start, owing to the fact that she’s a white superstar in a league that has historically been dominated by Black players. That alone makes her a prime candidatefor culture warriors to weigh in. But now, the level of debate around the league has somehow become worse. Clark’s teammate, Sophie Cunningham, chose this fraught moment to declare she’sagainst trans women playing in girls’ and women’s sports. Never mind that the league has never had a trans player assigned male at birth and this is all just a hypothetical scenario she’s concerned about. Cunningham is better at getting attention thanscoring points.Protests outside Fever gamesare often covered on the news more than the games inside the arena, which is hardly the kind of attention the WNBA has been looking for. A league that has long prided itself on its LGBTQ fans and players is now at the center of transphobic controversy. And then, it started raining dildos.The Sky-Valkyries game is not the first time sex toys have been thrown on to the court at a WNBA game – the dismal incidents started last season. It’s not even theonly league where this has happened. Regardless, the timing is pointed. The WNBA is not just a sports league – it’s also a furious petri dish for the opinions of people who often don’t even like women’s basketball. Agroup of crypto traders took responsibilityfor previous incidents and the most recent one in Chicago, declaring their support for Cunningham’s stance against trans women playing in the WNBA (which again, has not happened). You’d think they’d have come up with a new stunt, but apparently, good ideas are in short supply these days (they tried the same stunt last season to promote a meme coin, and there appears to be plenty of self-promotion behind these recent ones too). And if the group – and many of the anti-trans brigade who have descended on the WNBA – truly cared about women’s sports, perhaps funding scholarships and teams for young female athletes would be a more constructive way of going about it.With outlets like Fox News forced to cover the league and hucksters like ex-NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom coming outto glom onto the controversy, the WNBA seems to be drowning in the kind of press no one wants. There’s along history of athletes speaking up about their political and cultural opinions, but this seems especially dire when a women’s basketball player is actively speaking out against a community that has historically supported the sport. The WNBA finds itself in a culture war ignited by one of its own players, and the absurd spectacle of young men throwing sex toys at female athletes in the name of protecting women’s sports is just another front in that conflict. The “stick to sports” mantra that was so popular during the first Trump administration has become a punchline every time a dildo gets thrown on a basketball court.The sex toy incidents are just the physical manifestation of what Cunningham has done to her league – a needless plea for attention that serves no one but the person making the fuss. This was not a subject the WNBA was dealing with until she said something. It’s now something the WNBA can’t get away from. If women’s basketball is to maintain its recent growth it needs to continue producing stars like Clark, four-time MVP A’ja Wilson andthe ridiculously talented Olivia Miles. What it doesn’t need is players who court controversy for their own personal gain. Cunningham was barely on most fans’ radars until shebecame a meme, an honor usually reserved for such cultural luminaries as The Rizzler and the Real Housewives of Beverly Hills. Good for her, I guess. No doubt her post-career podcast will be thrilling. But where does she leave the WNBA? Drowning in the aftermath of childish pranks, it seems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNo doubt there will be further moronic stunts this season, especially during the high visibility period of the WNBA playoffs and finals. The league can’t stipulate the terms of players’ speech. It can only ban those young men who disrupt games (and it is only young men who have been apprehended for the stunts so far), although there seems to be an endless supply of them. If the WNBA is going to sustain itself and bring in more genuine fans (as opposed to people solely interested in the league because they want to make a political point), it will need to address all of this in some meaningful way. The bond it has built with many of the LGBTQ fans who have helped sustain and build the league is being torched, with the help of one of its own players. And now outside agitators have joined the party.Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 4: Brighton | Brighton & Hove Albion Women | The Guardian
description: Dario Vidosic has added nous and potential in a bid to build on a season that saw the club get to a first FA Cup final
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Dario Vidosic has added nous and potential in a bid to build on a season that saw the club get to a first FA Cup final
Content: Brighton were one of only three teams to beat the champions Manchester City last season. Photograph: Steve Bardens/Getty ImagesDario Vidosic has added nous and potential in a bid to build on a season that saw the club get to a first FA Cup finalBySophie DowneyMon 24 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:6th (NB: this is not necessarily Sophie Downey’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:7thProspectsAfirst FA Cup finalwas a historic moment for Brighton. Despitelosing to Manchester Cityat Wembley, it will have filled Dario Vidosic and his team with the belief that they are on the right track.It has been a summer of relative stability on the south coast. While there are seven new faces, departures have been limited to four. The arrivals of Lia Wälti and Gabby George bring vast experience and increased defensive acumen to the ranks while the Republic of Ireland’s Emily Murphy and Poland’s Nadia Krezyman are young attacking talents who have started to make a name for themselves.Brighton’s Emilie Joramo: ‘I feel like I’m now in the place I want to be’Read moreBrighton’s inconsistency was their downfall last season. They were seriously hampered by the lack of an out-and-out centre-forward after the anterior cruciate ligament injury suffered by the Arsenal loanee and England Euros hero Michelle Agyemang. Kiko Seike finished as their highest scorer in the league with eight and she was their only representative in the Women’s Super League’s top 20 for goals and assists. That problem remains unsolved and will surely be a focus for the remainder of the transfer window.The conclusion of their season certainly gave Brighton something to build on over the summer. They secured an impressive league victoryover Cityanda draw against Arsenaland will hope to outdo the latter when they host Renée Slegers’s sideat Crawley in their opener on 6 September. That on paper is the toughest of Brighton’s opening four fixtures.A graph showing where Brighton have finished in the WSL over the past five seasons: 7th in 2022, 11th in 2023, 9th in 2024, 5th in 2025, 7th in 2026Off-field picturePinterest has become the first solo sponsor of the women’s team with a four-year partnership. The deal pivots around the concept of ‘matchday style’, bringing to life the way fans show support for their team. Plans continue for the construction ofEurope’s first purpose-built women’s football stadium. Located next to the Amex Stadium, the hope is it will open for the start of the 2030-2031 campaign.The managerNow entering his third season, Vidosic is the second-longest serving manager in the WSL, a period that has brought much-needed stability to the club and allowed the Croatian-born Australian time to fully implement his aggressive pressing and possession-based style.He has been on a journey, developing an out-of-possession style to help his team deal with some of the bigger clubs in the WSL The 39-year-old has never hidden from his desire to bring silverware to Brighton and last season’s FA Cup final will have given him a taste of the steps required to realise that ambition.Star signingThe acquisition of Wälti remains one of the biggest coups of the summer. The 33-year-old Switzerland captain returns to England after a year in Italy with Juventus, bringing with her a wealth of experienceand, from her seven years with Arsenal, a WSL title and a Champions League winners’ medal. Wälti’s technical ability is second-to-none, as is a level of intelligence that allows her to dictate play from the middle of the park. She leads by example and guided Switzerland to the quarter-finals at Euro 2025. If Wälti can stay injury-free, she could play a significant role this season.View image in fullscreenLia Wälti should bring quality and know-how to Brighton.Photograph: Neil Holmes/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockStat attackBrighton had a finishing problem in 2025-26. Not in terms of hitting the target – no other side had as strong a shot accuracy – but only three teams converted a lower proportion of their on-target efforts. If the Seagulls can fire towards the corners of the goal rather than close to the goalkeeper, they could fly this season.A graphic showing that last season Brighton had the highest percentage of shots on target in the league, but the fourth-worst conversion of shots on target to goalsSet for a breakthroughSophie Peskett has already made history when in 2021, aged 18, she became Ipswich’s first professional player. The winger spent the best part of seven years at Ipswich, making 127 appearances and helping them earn promotion to the WSL 2 twice. Now 23, it would have been a big decision for her to leave, but Brighton seems like a sensible next step. A nifty player with an eye for goal, Peskett will prove useful to Brighton’s attacking output.What they say …“Brighton is not a team that has to hide. In the last couple of years, they’ve been able to hurt the big teams in many moments, and they reached the FA Cup final last season as well. We’re not going to be favourites in every single game, but that’s a nice position to be in.”– Lia WältiWhere are they playing their home games?Brighton will continue to play most of their home games at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium although four of their six opening home fixtures will be at the Amex. The club have added an Amex 4-Match Pack to their ticketing options, priced at £45 for adults. The club have also launched ‘Built For Her’, their dedicated women’s football membership option that offers a bundle of exclusive perks as they look to build their fanbase before the stadium move.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Brighton & Hove Albion WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: giant hail forces stage three abandonment in Pyrenees | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: A torrential hailstorm in ⁠the French Pyrenees forced the ⁠abandonment of ⁠the ​third stage of the Vuelta a ⁠España
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A torrential hailstorm in ⁠the French Pyrenees forced the ⁠abandonment of ⁠the ​third stage of the Vuelta a ⁠España
Content: Wout van Aert of Team Visma heads to a hotel for cover after the abandonment of stage three.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWout van Aert of Team Visma heads to a hotel for cover after the abandonment of stage three.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: giant hail forces stage three abandonment in PyreneesHuge hailstones prompt organisers to act 15km from endRiders seen heading into hotel on route to take coverReutersMon 24 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the ⁠third stage of theVuelta a Españaon Monday.With 15 kilometres (9.32 miles) remaining of the 174km route ⁠from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the ​skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began ⁠bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead ⁠of the peloton when the elements intervened as the race leader and favourite ​Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating ‌to the peloton ‌to pull off the course.View image in fullscreenA view of the finish line following the stage cancellation.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesBedraggled riders were then seen getting off their ‌bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.“For the security of the riders, stage three has been cancelled due to hail and severe weather,” race organisers said shortly afterwards. “There will be no winner and no podium ceremony.”Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from the Belgian rider ‌Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with the British rider Matt Brennan 10sec back.Earlier it had been warm and sunny ​on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta ⁠for the first time, was always near the front of ​the pack with ​the Slovenian’s team setting the pace.His expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul ​of the ‌weather in an ​anticlimactic finish. Pogacar ​will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though, with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaTadej PogacarCyclingSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Balding making serious tilt at prestigious British Flat trainers’ crown | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Balding says victory is ‘very unlikely’ but there is a good chance he will improve on second-place finishes achieved in 2021 and 2024
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Balding says victory is ‘very unlikely’ but there is a good chance he will improve on second-place finishes achieved in 2021 and 2024
Content: Plage De Havre, ridden by PJ McDonald (yellow cap), was one of Andrew Balding’s winners at the York Ebor festival.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PAView image in fullscreenPlage De Havre, ridden by PJ McDonald (yellow cap), was one of Andrew Balding’s winners at the York Ebor festival.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PATalking HorsesHorse racingAndrew Balding making serious tilt at prestigious British Flat trainers’ crownBalding says victory is ‘very unlikely’ but there is a good chance he will improve on second-place finishes achieved in 2021 and 2024Greg WoodMon 24 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British Flat trainers’ championship winners’ club is among the most exclusive in the sport, with just a dozen new members through its doors in the past 50 years. Aidan O’Brien, John Gosden, Richard Hannon Jr and Charlie Appleby, meanwhile, are the only trainers to win a first title outright this century.Becoming the fifth seems to be the last thing on Andrew Balding’s mind, however, despite an exceptional week at York’s Ebor festival that took his prize-money total for the season past £7m, his domestic Group One tally since 10 July to four and left him just under £700,000 behind O’Brien in the title race.Love Me Tender can deliver a slice of history as Mullins looks for fourth Ebor winRead more“Our luck will run out at some stage,” Balding said on Racing TV’s Luck On Sunday over the weekend, “but we are enjoying it while we can. The trainers’ championship is the least important thing in my opinion, if the right races are abroad then that’s where they should go.“It’s a big climb anyway and Aidan will win £2m more before the end of the year, so it’s very unlikely anyway.”It is true that a good deal would need to fall into place for Balding to improve on his second-place finishes in 2024 and 2021, behind O’Brien and Charlie Appleby respectively. “It’s a big climb anyway,” though, is hardly the language of an ambitious and ultra-competitive player in any sport – and you do not build and maintain a 250-horse stable in the results-driven world of Flat racing if you are anything but.Balding, as he is the first to admit, enjoyed a huge slice of racing luck when he inherited the trainer’s licence at one of the sport’s finest and most historic yards from his father, Ian, in 2003.Park House Stables, near Watership Down in Hampshire, was founded by John Porter, the most successful trainer of the Victorian era, in the 1860s, and was home to 23 Classic winners – including three Triple Crown winners – between 1868 and 1900.Porter was champion trainer in 1899, while Ian Balding, who died on 2 January this year, was a second champion at the yard in 1971 when he prepared the brilliant Mill Reef to win the Derby, the King George and the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe.A rich inheritance in any walk of life can be easily squandered, but Andrew Balding has instead built the operation to an entirely new level over the past 23 years. As a result, he not only has the proven Group One quality required to mount a serious challenge for the title – he has the numbers, too.John Gosden, in 2023, was the last title-winning trainer based in Britain. He saddled 130 winners from 600 runners for a total of £7.21m in prize money, including seven Group One winners, beating O’Brien’s total of £6.46m – from just 21 winners in all, eight in Group Ones – by £750,000.View image in fullscreenAndrew Balding receives a trophy from Queen Camilla after winning the Juddmonte International Stakes on the first day of the Ebor festival at York.Photograph: Chris Jackson/PAMostahdaf’s wins in the Prince of Wales’s Stakes and International Stakes made him the stable’s biggest individual winner by far, with £1.13m all by himself. But the top 10 earners combined picked up a total of £4.05m, and Gosden ran no fewer than 210 individual horses over the year. It was sheer force of numbers that ultimately got him over the line.Balding, with £7.06m this season, is already within sight of Gosden’s winning total three years ago. O’Brien, though, has already banked £7.77m and is on course to eclipse his personal record of £8.12m in the 2025 championship.But whether he will add “another £2m” is debatable. O’Brien has won the St Leger for the past three seasons and has the top two – Christmas Day and Pierre Bonnard – in the ante-post betting for the Doncaster Classic next month, so we can probably give him that. He is also likely to field the favourite in most – or perhaps all – of Britain’s five Group Ones for juveniles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut O’Brien is not omnipotent (though admittedly there are times when it can feel that way). He has never won all five of the juvenile Group Ones in a single season (and while he was a nose away from doing so in 2017, when Laurens pipped September in the Fillies’ Mile, that remains the only time he has landed four).Among the remaining all-aged Group One prizes, Balding’s Falmouth Stakes winner, Blue Bolt, is favourite for the Sun Chariot Stakes and third-favourite for the QEII on Champions Day. And both John Gosden’s Ombudsman and the winner last year, Calandagan, are in front of O’Brien’s Constitution River in the betting for the Champion Stakes, the biggest prize left on the schedule and a race where Balding’s Kalpana, the King George winner, could yet emerge as a contender.But it was quantity, rather than Group Ones, that made the difference for Gosden three years ago and Balding has already sent out 218 individual horses this year.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowMusselburgh: 2.15Vegasmile2.45Aodhan3.15Only Dream Big3.45Furhaan (nb)4.15Coconut Bay4.45Jojo RabbitLingfield: 2.30Havana Touch3.00Thai Baht3.30Let’s Go Hugo4.00Musical Soldier (nap)4.30Dialstone5.02Sovereign BrightStratford-upon-Avon: 5.10Diamond Grace5.40French Diablo6.15Beorma6.45Getmyfriend7.15Youdecide7.45Roccana RoseWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Fifteen of those have already contributed at least £50,000 to the total and there will be useful prizes for horses of that calibre all over the country as the turf campaign concludes. Balding’s three handicap winners at York last week picked up nearly £200,000, and there is even a sprinkling of £40,000 and £30,000 races on the all-weather in November and December to consider too if the race were to get really tight.Balding is still a long-shot for a first trainers’ title, but nothing like as big an outsider as he was this time last week. While the right races for a horse such as Item, the International Stakes winner, might well be elsewhere, there are hordes of talented horses in the stable, with plenty of targets to choose from in the months ahead.Balding played an impressively straight bat to the championship talk on Sunday but having worked so hard, this year and since 2003, to get to this point, is a title tilt truly “the least important thing” on his mind? Or will his famous meticulousness with the programme book go into overdrive in the final weeks of the campaign?Explore more on these topicsHorse racingTalking HorsesHorse racing tipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mercedes’ Wolff wary that Norris and Hamilton are genuine F1 title contenders | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Toto Wolff said the title race could tighten still further and the Mercedes team principal revealed Kimi Antonelli will take grid penalties at the next round in Monza
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Toto Wolff said the title race could tighten still further and the Mercedes team principal revealed Kimi Antonelli will take grid penalties at the next round in Monza
Content: Lando Norris’s win on Sunday took him to 159 points, 83 behind Kimi Antonelli. George Russell and Lewis Hamilton are on 183.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLando Norris’s win on Sunday took him to 159 points, 83 behind Kimi Antonelli. George Russell and Lewis Hamilton are on 183.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/Abaca/ShutterstockFormula One 2026Mercedes’ Wolff wary that Norris and Hamilton are genuine F1 title contendersMercedes team principal: ‘It could become tighter’Title leader Antonelli will take grid penalties in MonzaGiles Richardsin ZandvoortMon 24 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMcLaren’s Lando Norris and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton are genuine contenders for the Formula One world championship, according to the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, who watched Norris take a decisivewin at the Dutch Grand Prix.With Mercedes’s early-season dominance looking to have been all but erased, Wolff noted that there would be no quick fix for the team who could not develop at the same rate as their rivals because they had opted to use their budget differently.Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podiumRead moreNorris won the race at Zandvoort for McLaren with the team having brought several car upgrades to the meeting, beating the Mercedes of the championship leader Kimi Antonelli and George Russell into second and third respectively.Ferrarihave also moved closer to Mercedes, who won eight of the opening 12 meetings including all of the first six.Antonelli leads Hamilton, who was fourth in Zandvoort, and Russell by 59 points in the championship and Norris by 83. However, Wolff expected the fight to become tougher in the title run‑in, with 11 races remaining.Wolff said that he and Mercedes are “absolutely conscious of the threat” adding: “It’s not only Norris, it’s also Ferrari, even if you have a gap of 50 points to lose, that’s something you need to be worried about. This is going to be tough. It could become tighter, we need to do the optimal job every single weekend, every single session, every single weekend.”Norris’s win at Zandvoort was his second in a row this season, while Ferrari have also taken two, one apiece for Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc. Both teams have deployed an extensive series of upgrades, while Mercedes have brought only one major development thus far, at the Canadian GP.The teams all operate under the same budget cap and, as it stands, Mercedes are opting not to use their allocation in the same way as their rivals, who have front-loaded their upgrades early in the season.“We haven’t got the money to put developments on account,” Wolff said. “We are trying to evenly split that through the season based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimising the championship points. We just can do what we can do. That’s why it is a development race. So the ride has been a bit tougher than at the beginning of the year.”Mercedes are not expected to bring another major upgrade until the grand prix in Malaysia, branded as the Bahrain GP, in October with three races still to come before then. Ferrari are understood to be bringing their extensive engine upgrade to the next round in two weekends’ time at Monza, where the Scuderia hope to make a major step forward. Wolff confirmed that Antonelli will take a new engine at his home race in Italy and with it the attendant grid penalties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth Antonelli and Russell observed after the race in the Netherlands that they thought theMcLarenwas now the quickest car, but Norris maintained that the Mercedes was still the class of the field. “We certainly have a car now capable of beating them,” Norris said.“We didn’t win [in the sprint race] but I worked a lot on my driving. I want to believe more than everyone else and we turned things around on Sunday. So we certainly have a very similar car all in all to Mercedes but I think they have a better all‑round performing car than we do.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Toto WolffMercedes GPLando NorrisLewis HamiltonMcLarenFerrarinewsShareReuse this content

title: Largest review of its kind confirms benefits of tai chi and other Chinese exercises  | Health | The Guardian
description: Analysis finds ‘high certainty evidence’ of their effectiveness for the 1.7bn people worldwide with musculoskeletal conditions
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Analysis finds ‘high certainty evidence’ of their effectiveness for the 1.7bn people worldwide with musculoskeletal conditions
Content: Tai chi was found to significantly ease chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness while boosting bone mineral density in people with osteopenia and osteoporosis.Photograph: MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTai chi was found to significantly ease chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness while boosting bone mineral density in people with osteopenia and osteoporosis.Photograph: MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesHealthLargest review of its kind confirms benefits of tai chi and other Chinese exercisesAnalysis finds ‘high certainty evidence’ of their effectiveness for the 1.7bn people worldwide with musculoskeletal conditionsAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 24 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTraditional Chinese exercises such as tai chi can offer wide-ranging benefits for people with musculoskeletal disorders, improving physical function, pain, mental health, sleep quality and bone mineral density, according to the largest review of its kind.More than 1.7bn people have musculoskeletal conditions worldwide. While prevalence varies by age and diagnosis, people of all ages in every country and every continent are affected.Musculoskeletal conditions significantly limit mobility and dexterity, leading to early retirement from work, lower levels of wellbeing and reduced ability to participate in society. They are also the leading contributor to disability worldwide, with low back pain being the singleleading cause of disability in 160 countries.My first time doing tai chi: ‘It feels like my brain is solving a Rubik’s Cube’Read moreThere wasalready evidenceindicating traditional Chinese exercises were associated with beneficial health outcomes in people with musculoskeletal disorders, but much of it was fragmented and contained inconsistencies.The overarching review of pooled data analyses of systematic reviews by researchers at hospitals and universities in China,published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, drew on 92 data syntheses from 1,744 randomised controlled clinical trials.It found “high certainty evidence” for the effectiveness of traditional Chinese exercise – such as tai chi, qigong, baduanjin, wuqinxi and yijinjing – for a range of health outcomes for people with musculoskeletal disorders.These included improving movement in knee osteoarthritis, mental health associated with neck pain and knee osteoarthritis, and sleep quality associated with fibromyalgia.Tai chi, in particular, significantly eased chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness in several conditions while increasing bone mineral density in participants with osteopenia or osteoporosis,the research found.Maximum benefits were achieved when people did these exercises for longer than six months, at least three times a week, clocking up a total of at least 150 minutes a week.“This comprehensive [umbrella review] provides a definitive, high-level evidence synthesis supporting [traditional Chinese exercises] as effective interventions for a range of musculoskeletal conditions],” the researchers concluded.“The evidence, particularly for tai chi, reaches high certainty for improving key outcomes such as physical function in knee osteoarthritis, mental health in neck pain, sleep in fibromyalgia and bone density in osteoporosis.”The findings suggested traditional Chinese exercises should be included in clinical guidelines and rehabilitation programmes worldwide, the researchers added.“[These] exercises represent a safe, accessible, and cost-effective strategy that can complement conventional therapies, reduce pharmacological reliance, and empower patients in self-management.”While the prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions increases with age, younger people are also affected, often during their peak income-earning years.And with global population growth and ageing, the number of people living with musculoskeletal conditions and associated health problems is rapidly increasing.“For healthcare systems and policymakers, promoting the adoption of traditional Chinese exercises, particularly in community and primary care settings, could be a strategic component of public health initiatives aimed at healthy ageing and chronic disease prevention,” the researchers said.Explore more on these topicsHealthHealth & wellbeingMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting | US supreme court | The Guardian
description: Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms
Author: David Smith
Headline: Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms
Content: Donald Trump, left, and mail-in ballots.Composite: REX/Shutterstock/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump, left, and mail-in ballots.Composite: REX/Shutterstock/Getty ImagesUS supreme courtUS supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in votingJustices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midtermsDavid SmithMon 24 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS supreme courtsided withDonald Trumpon Mondayin his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it remains unclear if his administration can take action ahead of themidterm electionsin November.Justices on the court voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction from June that a judge in Massachusettsplacedon an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in placeand the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,” the majority wrote in an unsigned order. “On that score, time will tell.”The three liberal justices dissented. In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”.DoJ urges supreme court to allow Trump order targeting mail-in votingRead moreTrump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure.In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections.Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued over Trump’s March order, saying the US constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. They argued that imposing sweeping changes so close to the election risked disenfranchising voters and disrupting preparations already under way.A judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, sided with the plaintiff states – nearly half the country – and ruled that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states administer federal elections. She also questioned whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship lists.An appeals court upheld her decision. Talwani later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect.The justice department had argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature because the administration had not yet taken concrete actions that harmed them and they therefore lacked legal standing to sue. The administration said the Massachusetts injunction prevented it from finalising and implementing policies intended to promote “election integrity” before November.Republican-led states backed the administration before the supreme court, arguing that states would have an opportunity to provide input on the final lists of eligible voters.The supreme court’s conservative majority has now lifted the first injunction, allowing the administration to move forward while litigation continues.Letitia James, New York’s attorney general, called the court’s decision a “painful setback” but said her office was exploring all legal options. “It won’t be the final word,” she said.Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said his state is also planning a legal challenge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country,” Newsom said in a statement. “California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.”Voting right activists condemned the ruling. Derrick Johnson, the president of the NAACP, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever, guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it, and we have to protect the rights we do have within it.US Postal Service rule tightens mail-in voting despite court orders blocking changesRead more“Those in power know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election, and so they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote. Trump’s order has nothing to do with election integrity. It has everything to do with maintaining power at all costs.”The wrangling over how US voters can cast their ballots comes less than 100 days until November’s midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in the US Senate and House of Representatives.Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024,accordingto the States United Democracy Center, alongside one in five registered Republicans.About 30% of all ballots were cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10m mail ballots cast.Trump’s executive order forms part of a wider effort to reshape the electoral system. He has repeatedly made false claims of widespread fraud in American elections, including his defeat by Joe Biden in 2020, and has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Save America Act, a contentious package of voting restrictions.Explore more on these topicsUS supreme courtDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026US voting rightsUS politicsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission
Content: A spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAPrince HarryPrince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abusesSpokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ missionCaroline DaviesMon 24 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee ofAfrican Parks, whichadmitted last yearthat human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.Ina 2024 reportpublished by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.After the review, African Parkspublished a statementacknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people,had called on Harryto step down as a member of the board.Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 yearsPrince Harryhas served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, withreports she has been in talksabout a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reportsthat the deal was off.The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryAfricaCongo-BrazzavilleMonarchyWildlifeHuman rightsCharitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Households in Great Britain ‘could owe energy suppliers £7bn by end of year’ | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: After higher prices for winter kick in, energy debt unpaid for more than 30 days likely to rise, says Energy UK
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: After higher prices for winter kick in, energy debt unpaid for more than 30 days likely to rise, says Energy UK
Content: Domestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDomestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesEnergy industryHouseholds in Great Britain ‘could owe energy suppliers £7bn by end of year’After higher prices for winter kick in, energy debt unpaid for more than 30 days likely to rise, says Energy UKJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouseholds in Great Britain could owe their energy suppliers as much as £7bn by the end of the year after higher gas and electricity prices forecast for the winter kick in, an industry group is warning.Domestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June as the Middle East conflict continued to stoke rising gas market prices.The amount of energy debt left unpaid for longer than 30 days is likely to accelerate to £7bn by the end of the year, according to the trade association Energy UK, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices isexpected to climb to a three-year high.Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?Read moreThe regulator is expected to confirm later this week a 4% increase on the energy price cap for millions of households from October as “too many households continue to feel the strain of high energy bills”, the group’s chief executive, Dhara Vyas, said.She urged Andy Burnham’s government last week to consider a “targeted and more permanent” solution to the rise in energy bills – including a social discount tariff – rather than rely on “stopgap, ad hoc or emergency measures”.The increase will more than wipe out the impact of the new prime minister’s promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from October, which aimed togive voters “some breathing space”by shrinking bills by an average of about £45 a year.“The current arrangements fail to provide the help needed and work out more costly,” Vyas said. “A social discount will address the fuel poverty gap and provide the right amount of support to the right households at the right time – reflecting that needs vary across different customers.”The forecast energy price cap rise means that over the final three months of 2026 the typical household faces a gas and electricity billequivalent to £1,729 a year, forecasters at Cornwall Insight predict.The consultancy expects electricity rates to rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.57p, and gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.90p for households that pay via direct debit. However, the actual bill for a household will depend on how much each consumes.The average bill under the price cap was calculated assuming lower annual energy use than in previous years, because the high cost of energy has forced many households to use less gas and electricity as debt levels rise. Using the previous methodology, the price cap would be forecast to rise to £1,940.69 from October – the highest level since the summer of 2023.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAhead of the new cap, Energy UK told journalists that the rising cost of sourcing gas from the global wholesale market was the single largest contributing factor to the expected rise, although the expense of upgrading Great Britain’s energy networks was also playing a larger role in setting energy costs.The trade group’s debt estimates are about £1bn higher than the official figures reported byOfgem, which counts unpaid bills only once they are 90 days overdue. Although it uses a lower debt figure publicly, it spreads the cost of unpaid bills across all consumers using the higher estimates. This currently adds about £50 a year, or about 3% extra, to a typical annual bill.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnergy billsOfgemGasConsumer affairsHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fix that little spot’: Danish PM hits back at unsolicited beauty tip from cosmetic surgeon | Denmark | The Guardian
description: Mette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises women to embrace self-acceptance
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Mette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises women to embrace self-acceptance
Content: Mette Frederiksen with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. She says a cosmetic surgeon got in touch with her while she was away offering to help her with her appearance.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenMette Frederiksen with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. She says a cosmetic surgeon got in touch with her while she was away offering to help her with her appearance.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPADenmark‘Fix that little spot’: Danish PM hits back at unsolicited beauty tip from cosmetic surgeonMette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises  women to embrace self-acceptanceDeborah ColeMon 24 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSick of getting unsolicited beauty tips on social media, the Danish prime minister,Mette Frederiksen, rebuffed a male cosmetic surgeon’s offer to “fix” her and advised women in similar situations to embrace self-acceptance.Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, posted on Instagram that she had just returned from a trip toUkraine, where she was subjected to air raid sirens, when she found a message proposing some help with her appearance.She included ascreenshot of the exchangein which the doctor, who was not identified, said he could “fix that little spot on your nose”.Her retort was swift and pointed: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body – I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!”Frederiksen, who has led the EU and Nato member country since 2019 and is one of Europe’s longest-serving heads of government, said being a woman in the public eye meant regular exposure to such unwanted and superficial scrutiny.“I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” the 48-year-old wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”Frederiksen’s global profile has grown this year as she stood up to US president’srepeated claims on Greenland, a semi-autonomous Danish territory. She is also a staunch supporter ofUkraineagainst the Russian onslaught.In a moment of striking candour, Frederiksen admitted annoyance with pushy beauty advice while offering her own guidance how to deal with it.She said she did not volunteer opinions about other people’s looks and said that “I’m perfectly fine with my body – as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”Frederiksen said she was fine to stay in conversation with the public on a range of topics but encouraged Danes to set the bar higher with their chosen subject matter.“If you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful,” she said. “Not my nose.”Although the mean-spirited suggestions made her feel “indignant”, she said, “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDenmarkEuropeUkraineBeautyWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: World’s oceans hit hottest temperature on record in August | Oceans | The Guardian
description: Average sea surface temperature outside polar regions was 21.1C on Saturday, latest data finds
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Average sea surface temperature outside polar regions was 21.1C on Saturday, latest data finds
Content: Hotter oceans will exacerbate extreme weather, scientists warned.Photograph: Denys Bilytskyi/AlamyView image in fullscreenHotter oceans will exacerbate extreme weather, scientists warned.Photograph: Denys Bilytskyi/AlamyOceansWorld’s oceans hit hottest temperature on record in AugustAverage sea surface temperature outside polar regions was 21.1C on Saturday, latest data findsDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorMon 24 Aug 2026 08.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s oceans were hotter than ever previously recorded on Saturday, according to the latest data.The average surface temperature was 21.1C, with therising marine heata stark indicator of the climate crisis. More than 90% of the heat trapped by carbon dioxide from fossil fuel burning enters the oceans.Hotter oceans exacerbate the sea level rise and extreme storms that threaten billions of people, as well as driving marine heatwaves that decimate sea life and undermine coastal livelihoods, scientists warned.Daily global sea surface temperature records brokenThe northern hemisphere summer has already been hit by record-breakingheatwaves,droughtandwildfiresin Europe andNorth America, andintense rain and typhoons in Asia.The ocean heat spike is being intensified by a fast developingEl Niño event, which is set to be the hottest in at least a century. El Niño events are natural climate variations that raise global temperature and change weather patterns, with serious impacts around the world. The new El Niño has already deliveredlow monsoon rain in India, majorwildfires in Indonesiaandheightened fire concerns in Australia.The new ocean heat record being set in August is especially remarkable as global sea temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the austral summer. The southern hemisphere has significantly more ocean area than the northern.“The record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Dr Samantha Burgess, at the European Union’sCopernicus Climate Change Service(C3S), which produced the new data. “El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming. The consequences are already visible: the number of marine heatwave days globally has more than tripled since the early 1990s.”Warmer oceans contribute to sea level rise because of thermal expansion of the water, increasing flooding risks for coastal communities and low-lying island nations. Higher ocean temperatures also supercharge extreme weather events, because warmer seas transfer more energy and water vapour to the atmosphere, intensifying rainfall and storms.Most of the planet-heating CO2from fossil fuel burning and forest destruction is absorbed by the oceans. However, a hotter ocean is less efficient at absorbing CO2. This is potentially weakening one of the planet’s most important natural buffers against global heating, the scientists said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Two key actions are needed to address this record ocean warming,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature. “Fossil fuel emissions need to be rapidly reduced. Meanwhile, it is essential that countries protect marine and coastal ecosystems. Kelp beds, mangroves and marshes absorb carbon and coral reefs protect against storms and provide habitat. More than 190 governments have committed to protect and conserve at least 30% of the planet by 2030, and now is the time to turn that commitment into effective, durable conservation on the ground.”Thedata, from the C3S, covers the oceans outside the polar regions. The Arctic is the fastest-heating region on the planet. The records stretch back to 1979, when satellites began delivering the highest quality date.The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts – including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. title: No fridge, no fans, just blocks of ice: improvising to survive in Pakistan’s searing heat | Global development | The Guardian
description: With limited electricity and poor ventilation, many families in Nasirabad have little to shield them from temperatures of up to 50C
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With limited electricity and poor ventilation, many families in Nasirabad have little to shield them from temperatures of up to 50C
Content: In Balochistan province, where many lack electricity, ice is the only means of keeping water cool during hot months.Photograph: Fida Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn Balochistan province, where many lack electricity, ice is the only means of keeping water cool during hot months.Photograph: Fida Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal developmentNo fridge, no fans, just blocks of ice: improvising to survive in Pakistan’s searing heatWith limited electricity and poor ventilation, many families in Nasirabad have little to shield them from temperatures of up to 50CSupported byAbout this contentHazaran Rahim Dad and Changeez Nazir in Nasirabad, PakistanMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the first light reaches Nasirabad, a queue of men, women and children has already formed outside the town’s ice factory, with their buckets, sacks and plastic containers. Among those hoping to buy some ice to help their families endure another scorching day is 12-year-old Taimoor, in his school uniform. He says it is his most important task of the day.“If I do not bring the ice, how will we endure the heat at home?” he says. “And how will we drink water that feels as though it is boiling?”Once he collects his share, Taimoor hurries home to drop it off before setting out again for school, with a small portion of the ice in a plastic container to keep him cool on the journey.By 8am, the sun is hot and he is wetting his face with the meltwater.View image in fullscreenTaimoor collects ice to take home to his mother before going to school.Photograph: Changeez NazirHis mother is pregnant with her second child. Having experienced two miscarriages, she is afraid that walking to the factory herself and carrying ice through the heat could endanger her pregnancy.As temperatures have been rising across this region ofPakistan, protection from the heat depends on what individuals can find, buy or improvise.Surrounded by mountains and date-palm orchards, Nasirabad is a small town about 25 miles (40km) from Turbat in Kech district, in the province of Balochistan. Most people live in mud-built houses. Residents say electricity is available for about three hours a day, and that the voltage is often too weak to operate a fridge reliably.Those who can afford solar panels use them to power fans and, in some cases, fridges during daylight hours. For everyone else, their only defence is the ice they collect each morning.The intensity of heat in Nasirabad places the town near the frontline of a much wider warming trend.Ina heatwave warning in May 2026, the Pakistan Meteorological Department included Turbat in the regions expected to face temperatures reaching between 46C and 50C.Extreme heat has become a defining feature in Asia, with the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) suggesting the continentis warming nearly twiceas fast as the global average.Globally, the 11 yearsup to 2025 were the11hottest ever recorded, according to the WMO.In Nasirabad, these planetary trends are experienced through the temperature of a glass of water, the length of a queue and whether a family can afford to keep a fan running.View image in fullscreenMohammad Haider’s ice factory sells out as people struggle to cope with the heat.Photograph: Changeez NazirMohammad Haider owns Nasirabad’s ice factory, which he says was established by his late father in 1992. Every morning at about 7am, workers raise the metal shutter and within two hours, all 400 blocks produced overnight are usually sold.Haider’s factory has effectively become Nasirabad’s cooling centre, although its limited production cannot meet the needs of everyone who depends on it. He says almost all the ice is bought to cool drinking water. Demand is so high that some residents queue up only to leave empty-handed.“It saddens me when people cannot get ice before it runs out,” he says. “They then have to spend the entire day drinking warm water.”In the evening, Haider says, residents often gather outside, where he offers them cups of cold water without charge, while another batch freezes for the following morning.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose who miss the factory’s morning distribution sometimes buy ice from residents who bought more than they needed. A piece bought for 40 rupees (11p) may later be resold for 80 rupees, Haider says.Pakistanranked 147thin the 2024 Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative country index. Its relatively high vulnerability and low readiness scores indicate that exposure to climate hazards is compounded by limited institutional and economic capacity to respond.Each morning, 66-year-old widow Raj Bibi fills several bottles with water and carries them to a neighbour who owns a refrigerator powered by solar panels and allows her to store them inside. Bibi cannot afford ice or a solar system of her own. She returns in the evening to collect the cooled water, hoping it will remain drinkable through the night.View image in fullscreenRaj Bibi, 66, has to carry water to her neighbour’s house to cool in her fridge.Photograph: Hazaran Rahim Dad“The day passes in heat and suffocation,” she says. “There is no electricity to run a fan, and I cannot afford solar panels.”Even households with solar panels remain vulnerable. Many cannot afford the expensive batteries needed to store the electricity generated during the day. Families often carry bedding outside and sleep beneath the sky.The distinction between households is determined by who can afford each layer of adaptation – panels, batteries, refrigerators, water and ice – and those who cannot.The extreme heat has persisted through the summer. In its forecast for August, the Pakistan Meteorological Departmentpredicted very hot and dry conditionsacross Balochistan. In its warnings in May, it advised people to avoid unnecessary exposure to the sun, to remain hydrated and use water carefully. Farmers were urged to adjust their activities and protect livestock.But each precaution assumes a degree of choice that many people do not have.Taimoor cannot avoid the morning sun when his family depends on him to collect ice. Bibi has to walk to her neighbour’s house for water. Farmers cannot abandon the orchards that are their income. Women cannot avoid the heat of the cooking fires.View image in fullscreenWith no gas available, women in Nasirabad have to cook over burning wood, even during the intense heat.Photograph: Hazaran Rahim DadPakistan does have heatwave plans. The National Disaster Management Authority has issuedguidelines on preparing for extreme heat, and the Provincial Disaster Management Authority of Balochistan has a district plan for Kech. But residents in Nasirabad say they see little evidence of protections on the ground.
