Instead they rely on their own fragmented system: solar panels without batteries, neighbours sharing refrigerators, families sleeping outside and one factory producing 400 blocks of ice each night.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentPakistanExtreme heatSouth and central AsiaClimate crisisAccess to waterGlobal healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Wild beaver kits born in Norfolk for first time in more than 500 years | Animals | The Guardian
description: Pair are offspring of two beavers who mysteriously arrived in Pensthorpe nature reserve near Fakenham in December
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Pair are offspring of two beavers who mysteriously arrived in Pensthorpe nature reserve near Fakenham in December
Content: The two wild beaver kits captured on camera trap footage.Photograph: Pensthorpe Nature ReserveView image in fullscreenThe two wild beaver kits captured on camera trap footage.Photograph: Pensthorpe Nature ReserveAnimalsWild beaver kits born in Norfolk for first time in more than 500 yearsPair are offspring of two beavers who mysteriously arrived in Pensthorpe nature reserve near Fakenham in DecemberDonna FergusonMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWild beaver kits have been born inNorfolkfor the first time in more than 500 years.The pair of newborns are the offspring of two free-living beavers whomysteriously arrived in Pensthorpe nature reservenear Fakenham in December.This couple, who have built a lodge on the River Wensum, werethe first wild beavers recorded in Norfolksince the native species was hunted to extinction in England at the beginning of the 16th century.How they got to the Wensum remains a mystery. Although beavers have re-established themselves in the English countryside since 2015, the nearest population of wild beavers is thought to be more than 130 miles away, on the River Stour in Kent..Some suspect the breeding pair were illegally released by conservation activists, a practice known asbeaver bombingwhich Pensthorpe does not support, said the reserve’s manager, Richard Spowage.However, he welcomed the arrival of the “very playful” kits, which are thought to be about three months old. “It’s amazing,” he said.Viewing camera trap footage and discovering the kits had been born were moments of intense joy, he added.“We initially saw a single young one with a parent, just pottering around, doing little beaver things, chewing on little bits of branch and leaf. And then, in a later piece of footage, it went off … and suddenly it came running back, and a second kit was running after it.”Beaver kit seen in NorfolkThe kits appear to enjoy feeding on willow and water mint, but not everything on the menu in Norfolk has proved a hit. “One got stung by a nettle, we think, because it reacted really suddenly, jumped back and started shaking its face.”They are already becoming very independent, and have been learning how to dive into the river and tailslap its surface to make a big bang when they want to scare off a predator. “We’ve got footage of an adult tailslapping against an otter … and one of the little ones is able to do that now, too.”Although the beavers live in a secret, inaccessible location in the nature reserve, they may expand their territory and become more visible to visitors in the future, he said.The birth of the kits presents a conundrum, because they will have no mates to breed with in the future except their parents and siblings. “You can’t have just one family in the river system,” said Spowage. “You need a wider genetic pool.”The reserve is now crowdfunding so that it can apply to the government advisory body,Natural England, for permission to legally introduce more wild beavers into the Wensum, which feeds into the Norfolk Broads.It will be an expensive project, involving studies of the river system, staff training and discussions with multiple stakeholders, but Spowage is hoping all hurdles can be overcome so Norfolk’s first family of wild beavers can thrive: “If we can introduce other beavers, then they will interbreed and the population will expand properly.”Farmers have traditionally opposed beaver reintroduction in the UK over fears their dams could flood fields and damage crops. But during the heatwave, one farmertold the Guardianthat his best asset has been a family of beavers who have built a reservoir on his land that contains 3m litres of water.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritain experiencing a beaver baby boom as kits spotted across the countryRead more“What’s happening now is there are landowners suddenly realising that when they do have beavers, the beavers are holding back and managing water, which is valuable for farmland in our current climate,” said Spowage.Introducing more beavers into the Wensum would be a way for the government to lead on species recovery, he added, and would help to alleviate the frustration many conservationists feel about the speed and scale oflegal beaver releases in the UK.So far, the impact of the beavers on the reserve has been minimal: “They haven’t made any dams or built anything on the river. The only things they’ve been doing is clearing trees a bit and digging tiny little channels off to the sides of the river.”By thinning some of the nearby woodland, the beavers have opened up the reserve’s rich fen habitat, allowing more light to reach the forest floor and encouraging plant growth.“That means more food – not just for them, but for all wildlife … they’re doing things we were doing as humans in our management plan, but we were doing it quite poorly, and they are doing it really well.”Blue tits, great tits, blackcaps, water rails, jays, mallards, ducklings, foxes, otters and roe deer have all been recorded using or drinking from the shallow 30cm-wide river channels created by the beavers.Natural England spokesperson Matt Heard said: “We are working with Pensthorpe nature reserve,the Beaver Trustand other stakeholders to ensure the welfare of the animals, and to develop a plan of action.“Reintroducing beavers to our landscapes makes a huge difference to nature’s recovery and where releases are managed carefully, they can secure long-term environmental benefits.”Explore more on these topicsAnimalsNorfolkEnglandNatural EnglandConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific  | Deep-sea mining | The Guardian
description: US agency releases plan to lease millions of hectares of seabed off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam
Author: Mar-Vic Cagurangan
Headline: US agency releases plan to lease millions of hectares of seabed off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam
Content: Leaders in the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam have expressed opposition to US plans to auction deep sea mining leases.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyView image in fullscreenLeaders in the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam have expressed opposition to US plans to auction deep sea mining leases.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyDeep-sea miningUS territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the PacificUS agency releases plan to lease millions of hectares of seabed off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and GuamMar-Vic Caguranganin Hagatna, GuamSun 23 Aug 2026 21.34 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as theTrump administrationremains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.On Tuesday, the Marine Mineral Administration (MMA), an agency under the US department of the interior, released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28m hectares (69m acres) of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands andGuam.‘Severe’ stress on oceans as rate of sea level rise doubles in 10 years, UN warnsRead moreThe leases ​would allow companies to ‌explore the seabed and potentially extract ‌deposits of critical minerals – known as polymetallic nodules – that could be used in batteries, electronics and defence technologies. Many environmental ​groups have ​opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.The Northern Mariana Islands is a self-governing commonwealth of the United States, while Guam is an unincorporated territory of the US.The governor of the Northern Marianas, David Apatang, has said his government would approach the Trump administration’s proposal “with extreme caution”.Proposed lease areaApatang, while acknowledging the strategic importance of critical minerals, said it was necessary that “no activity, survey or otherwise, takes place without rigorous scientific baseline studies, complete transparency, and explicit protections for our marine resources”.He said his administration would “thoroughly examine the proposed terms over the next 60 days to ensure that the ecological integrity of our waters and the long-term wellbeing of the [Northern Marianas] are fully safeguarded”.The Guardian approached the Marine Mineral Administration for comment.In an earlier statement, the MMA said it had completed an environmental review of proposed commercial leases for critical minerals in the Marianas area. The MMA said it would consider comments from the governor.A statement from the office of the governor of Guam acknowledged the Trump administration’s focus on national security and strategic needs, but added: “National security cannot mean asking the people of the Pacific to accept environmental risks before those risks are fully understood.“We’re unequivocally opposed to the deep sea mining efforts in this region,” said Guam’s lieutenant governor, Joshua Tenorio.He told the Guardian: “The department of interior is giving assurances that mining activity is not going to commence with the awarding of these licences, [but] I think that this is a matter where we can’t really trust that because this has been rapidly evolving.”The proposed lease notice for deep sea exploration in the Marianas region came just weeks after the initiation of a leasing process for 12.4m hectares (31m acres) of American Samoa’s seafloor, with plans to award contracts in November.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds up a gold replica of a deep sea nodule given to him at a mining industry event earlier this month.Photograph: Eric Lee/Getty ImagesThe governor of American Samoa, Nikolau Pula, said his government remained opposed to deep sea mining, noting that untested extraction processes could harm the territory’s tuna industry, which fuels its economy.On 19 August, environmental groups in American Samoa and Hawaii launched legal proceedings against the US government to halt the proposed auction of seafloor permits around the islands, alleging that federal agencies failed to evaluate the destructive impact mineral extractions could have on marine ecosystems.In a Hawaii court, Fa’asao Ameika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawaii warned that the extraction machinery “can destroy nearly all life in its path” and “stirs up sediments that can introduce toxic substances into the food web and smother seafloor ecosystems”.“Even just exploring for seabed minerals introduces extremely loud noise into the marine environment that can harm marine mammals and other wildlife,” the complaint reads.The Marine Mineral Administration was approached about the concerns over the American Samoa leasing process.Explore more on these topicsDeep-sea miningGuamPacific islandsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing children | Snooker | The Guardian
description: Five-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Five-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse
Content: Graeme Dott arrives at the high court in Glasgow.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersView image in fullscreenGraeme Dott arrives at the high court in Glasgow.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersSnookerFormer world snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing childrenFive-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abusePress AssociationMon 24 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of sexually abusing two primary school age children. The 49-year-old subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse, with the girl targeted between 1993-96 and the boy between 2006-10.A five-day trial at the high court in Glasgow heard Dott exposed himself in front of both children, touched them inappropriately, and kissed them. On Monday, he was found guilty of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour towards them. In both cases the abuse happened in the Glasgow area.During the trial, jurors heard from one of Dott’s victims, a woman now in her 40s, who told the court Dott had sexually abused her on multiple separate occasions while she was a child. She said the abuse had started with Dott “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggyback.The woman also described an occasion when she said Dott suggested playing a “guessing game” where she had to guess what he was doing. She told the court she lay down and he exposed himself to her and then began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis. The woman told the court that Dott told her not to tell anyone he was sexually abusing her.The second victim, a man who is now in his late 20s, said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts. He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.“He would … come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court. “While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.”He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place. The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”. The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips and “push himself up against me”.Giving evidence last week, Dott had said there was “absolutely no way” he sexually abused two children. Under cross-examination by prosecutor Lindsey Dalziel, Dott denied being attracted to the girl when she was young, calling the idea “disgusting”.When Dalziel put it to Dott that he touched the first victim and told her what to do, he denied the allegation and called it “lies”. Speaking about the second victim, Dott said he was “never in my company” and denied all allegations of abuse.In her closing speech on Friday, Dalziel called on the jury to find Dott guilty of both charges. She said: “The Crown’s case is that Graeme Dott subjected vulnerable children to the worst kind of abuse with a course of conduct which relied on opportunity, for his own gratification.”Dott’s lawyer, Euan Dow, had invited jurors to clear his client of both charges. But Dott, who won the World Snooker Championshipin 2006, was found guilty on Monday following the trial which began on 18 August, with verdicts by majority.Judge Lord Harrower told him: “You have been convicted of charges involving sexual abuse of young children. I will refrain from passing comment further on any of these offences until I receive a background report from a social worker as I must in order to consider the full range of sentences open to me. You must register your name and address with the police so your name can be added to the sex offenders register.”He deferred sentence until 29 September at the high court in Edinburgh. Dott was remanded in custody.Explore more on these topicsSnookerScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies a year after son | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Gardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Gardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020
Content: Jo Gardiner and her son Sam in Chapultepec, Mexico City, taking part in Race Across the World.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenJo Gardiner and her son Sam in Chapultepec, Mexico City, taking part in Race Across the World.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PATelevision & radioRace Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies a year after sonGardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020Kevin Rawlinsonand agencyMon 24 Aug 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTributes have been paid to the Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner, who has died a year after her son and co-star Sam was killed in a car crash.The physiotherapist fromManchesterdied after “a long and courageous battle with cancer”, relatives said. She was 61 and is survived by her other son, Charlie.She and Sam competed in the second series of the BBC’s global travel competition, journeying across South America together in 2020.Relatives remembered her as “an intrepid adventurer” who was “brave, kind, witty and endlessly loving”.Her family said: “She had a rare gift for making everyone around her feel more alive. She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves. She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism. Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best.“To us, she was more than all of these things. She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure. We know how deeply Jo was loved, and we take comfort in knowing that her laughter, her courage, her kindness and her wonderfully outrageous spirit will live on in the many people whose lives she touched.”View image in fullscreen‘She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves,’ Gardiner’s family said.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe family asked that those who knew and loved her “do exactly what she would have wanted: tell the funny stories, raise a glass, have an adventure, laugh loudly and live life to the full.”They added: “She was one of a kind. There will never be another her.”Sam Gardiner died in June 2025 at the age of 24 after his car came off the road, rolled and landed on its side.The mother and son competed on Race Across the World because Jo wanted to have a travel adventure with Sam, who had ADHD. They competed against four other pairs of contestants racing from Mexico City down to Ushuaia in Argentina.A spokesperson for the programme said: “On behalf of the Studio Lambert production team, the BBC and the whole Race Across the World cast, we offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo’s son Charlie and her wider family and friends.“Millions of people remembered their transformative journey across Latin America in 2020 and we hold that memory in our hearts as we fondly recall Jo’s passion for life, her kindness, her strength and above all her utter devotion to Sam and her family.”Jo Gardiner had type 1 diabetes and was an ambassador for Diabetes UK. Her family has set up aJustGiving pagein her name and said all donations are to support the charity.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioReality TVManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Survivors of violent crime criticise MoJ for not explaining offender restriction zones | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Campaigners accuse ministers of trying to grab headlines with announcement before a working system is ready
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Campaigners accuse ministers of trying to grab headlines with announcement before a working system is ready
Content: Rhianon Bragg, who was stalked and held hostage at gunpoint by her ex-partner, said critical questions remained unanswered.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRhianon Bragg, who was stalked and held hostage at gunpoint by her ex-partner, said critical questions remained unanswered.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUK criminal justiceSurvivors of violent crime criticise MoJ for not explaining offender restriction zonesCampaigners accuse ministers of trying to grab headlines with announcement before a working system is readySteven MorrisMon 24 Aug 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSurvivors of violent crime and families of victims have criticised the UK government for announcing “world first” plans to introduce restriction zones for serious offenders freed from prison within a few weeks without spelling out how they would work.Key campaigners who have championed the idea of thezones, designed to “lock” offenders into specific areas, accusedthe government of seeking to grab headlinesrather than providing the detail that would reassure survivors and families.Rhianon Bragg, who has become a leading campaigner on domestic violenceafter she was stalked and held hostage at gunpoint by her ex-partner, said she was concerned that the announcement had come before a working system was ready.She said: “Victims can’t rely on headlines. I can’t imagine how anxious victims whose offenders may be being released are feeling right now. The announcement leaves critical questions unanswered.”The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said at the weekend that restriction zones would be introduced in October inEnglandand Wales and would mean serious sexual and violent offenders could be confined to areas of a few miles.Offenders would be tagged to keep tabs on their movement and victims would have a say in setting boundaries.The MoJ said it was the first measure of its kind in the world and was a “more rigorous” version of “exclusion zones”, which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim’s home or place of work.Bragg said she and fellow campaigners wanted more detail on which offenders would be included, how zones would be implemented, what would happen if an offender left their zone and whether agencies such as the Probation Service and the police had the capacity to manage the system.Announcing the scheme,the justice secretary, Alex Norris,said no victim should “fear the shadow of an abuser”.Bragg said: “Speaking from my own lived experience, if that is to be achieved then restriction zones need to be the other side of the country from the area the victim is in.”Bragg and fellow campaigners wrote to the government before the parliamentary recess asking for a meeting so that specifics could be discussed, but it has not taken place. She said: “We need more transparency. If the system’s not ready, victims will be put at risk.”The campaigner Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, whose best friend, Joanna Simpson,was killed by Simpson’s estranged husband, said: “A headline doesn’t help victims one jot. The lack of detail is a huge issue.“We have been asking them for two months to meet with us to discuss how they are going to implement it and which offenders are going to be eligible.“You’ve got thousands of victims out there today who are utterly terrified at a visceral level of their offenders coming out of prison and they don’t know if their offender is going to be subject to restriction zones or not.“It creates more uncertainty for them, more trauma for them. The MoJ needs to hurry up and engage properly with victims.”Barkworth-Nanton, who co-foundedthe Joanna Simpson Foundation, which campaigns on domestic abuse and homicide, agreed the size of the restriction zone was not relevant. “I don’t care whether it’s 2 miles, 5 miles, 10 miles, 15 miles. The important thing is twofold.“One is whatever that restriction zone is, probation needs to be confident that they can monitor them. And the second thing is it needs to be far away from the victim. So a 2-mile restriction zone, 5 miles away from the victim’s home is hopeless.”Joanna Simpson’s mother,Diana Parkes, a leading campaigner for restriction zones, said: “On the whole I’m happy but we want to hear what the total plan is.”Natalie Queiroz,who was repeatedly stabbed by her partner while she was eight months pregnantand is now a victims’ advocate in the West Midlands, said: “Restriction zones are a really positive solution and all credit goes to all those who campaigned hard for them.“However, I’m yet to be convinced of the breadth of their impact in reality. The MoJ have stated that they will be enforced for the most serious violent offenders as well as for serious sexual offenders. Many domestic abuse offenders who still pose a significant risk to their victim will not fall under this definition and hence will not have a restriction zone applied to them.”The MoJ said further details would be announced in due course. It said the government would work closely with victims’ groups and other stakeholders as the scheme was rolled out to ensure it was operating as intended.Queiroz added: “The effectiveness of restriction zones will rely heavily on them being properly monitored and any breaches being addressed without delay. There needs to be clear commitment to investment into the active monitoring of them.”Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceDomestic violenceRape and sexual assaultCrimeStalkingEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian-produced Gaza documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli directors of No Other Land to screen at Venice film festival | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the war
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Film directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the war
Content: NAZA, selected for the Venice film festival.Photograph: Venice Film Festival/APView image in fullscreenNAZA, selected for the Venice film festival.Photograph: Venice Film Festival/APMoviesGuardian-produced Gaza documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli directors of No Other Land to screen at Venice film festivalFilm directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with  Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the warAndrew PulverMon 24 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new documentary about Israel’s bombing campaign in Gaza, directed by Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, is to receive its world premiere at theVenice film festival.The film, called NAZA, has been produced with Jim Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind The Zone of Interest, and is the only documentary that will compete this year for Venice’s prestigious Golden Lion.Abraham and Szor are the two Israeli directors of the four behind No Other Land, whichwon the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.Announcing the news, the film-makers said: “Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.”The Guardian addedin a statementthat NAZA is an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.The documentary builds on original investigative reporting between 2023 and 2025 by Israeli-Palestinian publication+972, Hebrew-language outletLocal Calland the Guardian.No Other Land, which was directed by Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal alongside Abraham and Szor,was described as a “sombre, sobering work”by the Guardian’s chief film critic Peter Bradshaw.Shortly after No Other Land’s Oscar win,Ballal was attacked by Israeli settlers and briefly arrested, following whichthe Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciencesapologised after failing to name Ballal or the film in a statement of support.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsVenice film festivalFestivalsGazaPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: French police accused of rising use of violence to stop Channel crossings | France | The Guardian
description: NGO criticises ‘human cost’ of UK-funded crackdown on attempts to set off from French beaches in small boats
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: NGO criticises ‘human cost’ of UK-funded crackdown on attempts to set off from French beaches in small boats
Content: People wade through water to board a boat in Gravelines, northern France, in May.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople wade through water to board a boat in Gravelines, northern France, in May.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersFranceFrench police accused of rising use of violence to stop Channel crossingsNGO criticises ‘human cost’ of UK-funded crackdown on attempts to set off from French beaches in small boatsDiane TaylorMon 24 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople trying to cross the Channel to the UK have reported an increase in French police use of violence on beaches to prevent them from getting into dinghies, according to a French NGO.Utopia 56, which works on beaches from where migrants attempt Channel crossings, says so far this year 2,720 people have reported being victims of French police violence, compared with 1,954 over the same period last year, when crossings overall were much higher.The organisation says that due to increased enforcement activity on French beaches, for which the UK provides funding, crossings have become more dangerous and disorganised, putting more lives at risk. So far this year at least 21 people have died trying to cross the Channel to reach the UK.The NGO’s report alleges that the UK and French governments are “the architects of this chaos”. It calls for an overhaul of the European asylum system and the opening of safe routes, which it says would stop the boats and neutralise the smugglers.Under a £660m deal agreed earlier this year between the UK andFrance, the latter has deployed a riot squad to try to stop the boats. Reports of violence include beatings and use of teargas. According to Utopia 56, teargas canisters were deployed during the recent heatwave in sand dunes, posing a fire risk.The NGO has documented at least 10 families becoming separated on French beaches as a result of enforcement action. In one case documented on 27 July, a woman’s leg was run over by a French gendarmerie buggy racing across a beach to try to stop a group of migrants.The briefing, titled “Behind the figures: violent practices, the human cost of repression on the French coast”, has been produced in response to a Home Office announcementwidely reported on Fridayabout the success of increased enforcement to stop the boats.Crossings have decreased by more than 40% so far this year compared with the same period last year and the numbers crossing in July were the lowest recorded for the month since 2020.French police slash small boat as migrants clash with officersTheHome Officestated that between 27 April and 2 August, French officers prevented 185 boats and more than 4,300 people from crossing the Channel. It is not known how many of these people subsequently succeeded in making the crossing.The Utopia 56 report says: “People do not simply vanish after being intercepted, contrary to what one might believe upon reading the British government statement.”The Home Office said a large amount of equipment had been seized including boats, engines and lifejackets. According to Utopia 56, the seizure of lifejackets does not deter the smugglers but increases the chances that people will drown.“This is a policy driven by statistics, implemented with a single goal, stopping the boats, without any regard for the suffering it causes,” the report says. “These figures may appear to prove that the crackdown is working, but they fail to account for the consequences: women, men and children abandoned on beaches – and, above all, many falling victim to the excesses of the security operation and, consequently, to police violence.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”France’s interior ministry was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFranceImmigration and asylumHome OfficeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months | Americas | The Guardian
description: US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs
Content: On 23 August, the US Southern Command executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: U.S. Southern CommandView image in fullscreenOn 23 August, the US Southern Command executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: U.S. Southern CommandAmericasUS strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in monthsUS Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugsMaya Yangand agenciesMon 24 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking.On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom)announcedit “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added.Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”“This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added.A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light.Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikeshave done littleto stem the flow of drugs into the country.It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’sCaribbeancoast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense SecretaryPete Hegsethsaid during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador andColombia.The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have beencondemnedasextrajudicial killingsby the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations.According toa 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean.Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.Meanwhile, aninvestigationby the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found.“There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release.Other familiescontinue to grieveas they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes.“If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia.Explore more on these topicsAmericasDrugsCaribbeanDonald TrumpVenezuelaPete HegsethColombianewsShareReuse this content

title: UK graduate job vacancies plunge to lowest in a decade | Economics | The Guardian
description: Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, says recruitment website Adzuna
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, says recruitment website Adzuna
Content: The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago.Photograph: RichardBaker/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago.Photograph: RichardBaker/AlamyEconomicsUK graduate job vacancies plunge to lowest in a decadeJust 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, says recruitment website AdzunaBusiness live – latest updatesAlex DanielMon 24 Aug 2026 02.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGraduate job vacancies in the UK have sunk to their lowest level since they started being tracked a decade ago, according to a recruiting website.Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, Adzuna reported on Monday, down 45% compared with the same point last year and the lowest since the company started gathering the data in 2016.The number comes as 262,820 people prepare to go to university in September, a record high that underlines the tough conditions facing graduates entering the job market asentry-level roles are threatened by AI.UK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank findsRead moreAbout 1 million young people in the UK werenot in education, employment or training, otherwise known as Neets,in the first quarter of this year, according to the Office for National Statistics.Adzuna said sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies, adding that the figures suggested that a recovery reported during the spring had gone into reverse.Andrew Hunter, a co-founder of Adzuna, said: “July’s numbers are a step backwards, not a blip. The annual vacancy decline got worse for the first time since January, and (the number of) jobseekers per vacancy are now higher than they were a year ago.“The graduate job market also keeps setting new lows, which tells us employers still haven’t found a reason to open up hiring at that level.”The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago. In 2017, there were more than 55,000 graduate positions.More recently, employers have also reined in their hiring in the face ofincreases in national insurance contributions and the minimum wageannounced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in her last two budgets.The extra labour cost for businesses also comes as some companies areprioritising investment in automation and artificial intelligencetools rather than hiring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe trend has left some young peopleincreasingly demoralised. One report, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), said this summer that 16- to 21-year-olds were less confident about being successful than a decade ago and that some were “losing faith in their futures”.In July, Andy Burnham said he would try to boost youth employment withmore backing for technical education and apprenticeships.The only sectors showing increases in jobs for university leavers were travel, teaching and construction, Adzuna said.Hunter added: “It isn’t all bad news. Teaching, travel, and trade and construction are still adding roles, and manufacturing is now doing the same, too. But that’s a short list, and everyone outside of these sectors is having a harder time than they were three months ago.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsGraduate careersWork & careersUK unemployment and employment statisticsStudentsHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling chairs on Titanic’ with plan for new board | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Campaigners say proposal for £10bn rescue deal in bid to avoid nationalisation is a ‘cosy stitch-up’
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Campaigners say proposal for £10bn rescue deal in bid to avoid nationalisation is a ‘cosy stitch-up’
Content: Any Burnham has said there should be ‘greater public control’ of Thames Water.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAny Burnham has said there should be ‘greater public control’ of Thames Water.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockThames WaterThames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling chairs on Titanic’ with plan for new boardCampaigners say proposal for £10bn rescue deal in bid to avoid nationalisation is a ‘cosy stitch-up’Business live – latest updatesAlex DanielMon 24 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe group of creditors pursuing a rescue bid forThames Waterhave been accused of shuffling the deckchairs on the Titanic after proposing an overhaul of the stricken utility’s board.In a bid to stave off temporary nationalisation by Andy Burnham, the lenders said they would appoint Liz Barber, the former chief executive of YorkshireWater, and Clive Selley, the former chief executive of network operator Openreach, as directors if they are allowed to take formal control of the company.London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors holding £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has also lined up Dame Bernadette Kelly, the former permanent secretary of the Department for Transport.Thames Water plans to restart desalination plant – after drought has endedRead moreMike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter leading Thames’s overhaul, would become the new chair, replacing the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if Thames is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government. McTighe is the current chair of Openreach.He said: “The challenge at Thames Water is huge. If this recapitalisation plan is accepted, we will apply full dedication as a new board, working alongside the executive team to transform the business and build a culture in which the customers and local communities who depend on Thames Water come first.”The proposed appointments are designed to reassure the government that any commercial deal would bring with it a leadership overhaul, as Burnham’s team examines the possibility of taking the company back into public ownership.L&VW’s announcement was criticised by the public ownership campaign group We Own It. Cat Hobbs, the director at We Own It, said: “This is absolutely absurd. A cosy stitch-up that has nothing to do with the interests of the 16 million people who depend on Thames Water. This amounts to nothing more than a reshuffling of chairs on the deck of the Titanic.”Burnham has said there should be“greater public control”of Thames Water and previously told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation. This would probably come via placing the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary nationalisation.More recently the prime minister said he was “angry” after companies including Thames Waterwere given the green light to raise bills even higherearlier this month.He said the companies must not be allowed to treat bill payers like a “blank cheque”, an escalation of his warnings to utility companies that he is looking at options for more government control of the sector.The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water claiming the bill could come to £2bn.L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe consortium has hired the top litigation and disputes lawyers Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals.The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring Thames out of administration after a failed attempt tosell the utility to the US investment group KKRlast year.However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt in June when Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat,voicing concerns about the terms of the deal.McTighe said the 10-year plan to turn the water company around would “fix the foundations” at Thames. “It will take time to fix Thames Water, but we are committed to rebuilding trust with the customers and public Thames Water serves,” he said.Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell, said of the proposed new appointments: “The hope being that these are the sort of credible names which can inspire confidence in the company’s future in private hands.“Such an outcome would impose large losses on creditors, who are seeking to formally take ownership of the business, having already assumed de facto control, with plans to list it on the stock market as early as 2030.”Explore more on these topicsThames WaterWaterUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: The treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven? | US economy | The Guardian
description: The US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not working
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: The US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not working
Content: Scott Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/CNP/Andrew Thomas/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenScott Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/CNP/Andrew Thomas/ShutterstockUS economyAnalysisThe treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven?Eduardo PorterThe US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not workingMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTShareThe bond market is driving the Trump administration crazy. Last week, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced that the government wouldsharply rampup its purchase of treasury bonds, in an effort to raise their price and thus push down their yield, which amounts to the interest rate the government pays on its debt.It didn’t quite work as planned. Yields on treasurys fell after Bessent’s bond market intervention but soon bounced back. By Friday afternoon, the yield on the 10-year treasury was back nearwhere it wasbefore the secretary’s announcement. The yield on the 30-year bond was again trading around itshighest levelin 20 years or more.Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields since the upsurge in inflation in 2022 has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt, which has ballooned to arecord $40tn. This year interest payments will absorb 13.5% of all federal spending, more than defense and up from 5.2% in 2021.US treasury doubles debt buyback to steady bond market amid inflation fearsRead moreTo Trump’s chagrin, higher treasury yields – which set the benchmark for rates on mortgage loans and other long-term lending across the economy – are walloping his popularity, helping freeze the housing market and contributing to the growing realization that he has been adismal stewardof the economy.An irked president has called interest rates “ridiculous” and “artificially high”, and blamed the Federal Reserve for not cutting them. In one of his most recent signs of derangement, he lashed outagainst Switzerlandfor having lower interest rates than the US, pointing out that he had the “absolute right” to cut off all US business with the country. And he hinted at a novel approach to monetary policy, suggesting that “the ultimate interventionis our military”.But treasurys’ persistent weakness raises a more broadly unsettling prospect for the global economy: the end of the era in which the United States provided a more or less universally accepted safe, liquid asset for investors, companies and governments around the world to store their wealth.Between the turn of the century and the Great Recession, foreign central banks increased their holdings from about 20% to more than 30% of all treasurys outstanding, as they built reserves to ward against speculative attacks or tried to manage their exchange rates. Foreign investors also piled in. By 2008, over half of all treasury bonds were in the hands of foreigners.US government bonds were considered such a solid place to store money that their price would rise (and their yield would fall), any time a crisis struck, sending investors scurrying for safety. This was true even when, as during the collapse of the housing bubble in the US in 2007, the crisis was sparked by a mix of financial exuberance and inept policymaking in the United States.The pillars supporting the treasury markethave been weakeningfor some time, however. Foreign central banks – mainly in China and Japan – have sharplypared backtheir holdings. Private foreign investors have picked up some of the slack. By mid 2025, private foreign investors held $7tn in treasurys, almost twice as much as the $3.9tn held by foreign official entities. Still, the foreign share of treasury holdings has fallen by 10 percentage points over the last two decades or so, to about 40%.double quotation markThe main threat to treasurys’ status as the paramount store of value in the world comes from withinThe new buyers of treasurys come with new risks. Unlike foreign official entities, which hold the bonds to ensure financial stability, private investors seek returns. They will sell to make a buck. Their rising footprint has turned the treasury market into a more volatile place than it used to be.The main threat to treasurys’ status as the paramount store of value in the world, though, comes from within. The supply of treasury bonds has been growing at a fast clip in recent times, to fund a budget deficit that is now hovering at about 6% of GDP. Supply has outpaced demand. These days, US government debt no longer has the top rating from the big credit rating agencies andmust offer a higher yieldthan that of many other affluent nations.Add in the increasing mistrust of Trump’s reckless economic governance and you have the makings of a problem. In the Trump era, treasury bonds no longer rise as they used to in moments of high risk. When Trump unleashed his volley of tariffs against everybody on“Liberation Day”in April last year, investors dumped treasurys just as they would a lowly emerging market bond.Bessent knows this poses a problem for the government. Funding the deficit requires adding some $10bn a day, net, to the mountain of treasurys on the market. But it also poses a potential problem to investors and governments in the rest of the world. They all learned to trust treasurys as a bedrock asset in which to store their wealth, a perfect complement to the dollar as the main mode of exchange for trade and investment around the world. What will they do without it?Like Nato trying to convince Trump to stay or the World Trade Organization working to restore its relevance since the US left, financial leaders don’t yet know quite how to cope with the seemingly inevitable demise of the American safe haven. Indeed, treasurys maintain what is left of their status largely because it has not been easy for foreign countries and businesses to find somewhere else to keep their stash.But the search is on. Bessent will have to do more than repurchase a few billion worth of treasurys to overcome mistrust in America’s Loony Tunes leader and ensure that there is sufficient demand out there to match the massive supply coming down the pike.Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon SubstackExplore more on these topicsUS economyBondsUS interest ratesDonald TrumpFederal ReserveEconomicsTrump administrationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Fast-fashion giant Shein sets cut-price $27bn valuation for Hong Kong IPO | Shein | The Guardian
description: China-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprint
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: China-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprint
Content: Clothes from fast-fashion brand Shein hang at its office in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Silva/ReutersView image in fullscreenClothes from fast-fashion brand Shein hang at its office in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Silva/ReutersSheinFast-fashion giant Shein sets cut-price $27bn valuation for Hong Kong IPOChina-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprintBusiness live – latest updatesAlex DanielMon 24 Aug 2026 04.57 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShein, which built a fast-fashion empire onwhat seemed like impossibly low prices, has been forced to lower its own valuation in a cut-price stock market float, after falling into the red earlier this year.The online retailer will list on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September at a valuation of close to $27bn (£19.8bn), significantly down from a near-$100bn private market peak four years ago.It is one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings (IPO) of recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns. Shein then considered a £50bn float in London, but facedsimilar questions about its supply chainfrom campaigners, MPs and investors.EU introduces €3 customs charge on small parcels to curb cheap Chinese importsRead moreThe company moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts have said was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.In early 2025 itrefused to reassure British MPsthat its products do not include cotton produced in the Xinjiang region of China, which has been linked to forced Uyghur labour.Founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, the company runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world.But more recently it has faced questions over slowing growth and rising costs. It swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed an import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country.The company said the Iran war had caused delays to deliveries in some of its leading markets, while there was also less demand for its products because of the economic fallout from the conflict.Sheinsaidon Monday it would offer nearly 280m shares for between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 each. That would raise roughly £1.3bn for the company at the top end of the range, and give it a market valuation of just under £20bn. The final offer price will be set on the day before it starts trading on 1 September.The company’s European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users by the end of last year, making it one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside Amazon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShein partly benefits from sending goods directly to shoppers, including to the UK and US, fromChinaso they attract fewer taxes. The tactic has prompted calls for a change in tax rules.In November, the group opened itsfirst-ever physical outlet, a dedicated spacein the BHV department store in Paris. Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence.Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “Shein may still be one of the biggest names on the fast-fashion catwalk, but the IPO is going to be a harder sell, with plenty of investors questioning whether its low-cost formula still has the star power to deliver the growth they’re looking for.’’Explore more on these topicsSheinRetail industryChinaAsia PacificIPOsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: The comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?
Content: ‘I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy’…Russ Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy’…Russ Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe big interviewTV comedyInterview‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked awaySimon HattenstoneThe comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe electronic gates slide open to reveal a gorgeous Portuguese villa, a swimming pool and a beansprout of a man. “You’ve made me feel very important,” says Russ Abbot with a smile. “Come in!”It’s more than 30 years since Abbot, aged 78, dominated Saturday night TV with his sketches, songs and impersonations. He appealed to all sorts. Kids, parents and grandparents united around the TV – first for Russ Abbot’s Madhouse, which ran from 1980 to 1985, then The Russ Abbot Show, from 1986 to 1991. He was joined by the inimitable Bella Emberg and a cast of young comics, including Les Dennis, Dustin Gee and Michael Barrymore. But make no mistake, it was Abbot’s show and the 80s was his decade. At his peak, he attracted 18 million viewers an episode.When TV commissioners tired of his brand of sketch comedy, he did stints in the sitcoms Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine and played it straight in the moving TV drama September Song. There was a run of West End musical smashes – Fagin in Oliver!, Roger de Bris in The Producers, Alfred P Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Then, in 2016, he quietly retired. For the past seven years, he has split his time between Barbados and the Algarve, where I find him today.View image in fullscreenAbbot and Trish have been married for 60 years.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianAbbot introduces me to his wife, Trish, who has a smart silver bob and a northern accent. How long have you two been married, I ask her. “Sixty years,” she says quietly. “Not even the Train Robbers got that!” Trish, 80, giggles.We’re standing in a large, airy hall. On a table are figurines of Laurel and Hardy – Abbot’s heroes. Upstairs, I can make out lots of framed photos. He takes me on a tour. There are pics of him with the great entertainers of his era (Brucey, Elton, Tarby, Shaky) and the royals (Philip, Anne, Charles). We pass the silver discs from his brief period as Britain’s unlikeliest pop star (who can forget Atmosphere?). “That’s a certificate acknowledging the biggest box office in summer season history,” he says, like an accountant conducting an audit of his success. “And that’s whatshisname.” He squints at a picture. “Live Aid. Bob Geldof.”Pride of place is a photo of him dressed as Cooperman, with Tommy Cooper. Cooperman was one of Abbot’s more surreal mashup characters – Superman meets the brilliantly bumbling comic giant, who died on stage in 1984. He adored Cooper. “It was so funny at the funeral. All the faces were there. Max Bygraves, Eric Sykes, me. And when the cortege came in, we’d forgotten he’d got a younger brother who looked just like him. He walked in and we’re like: ‘Oh God! Another Tommy prank.’ When the curtain closed on the coffin, I thought: he’s going to come out in a minute because he was such a practical joker.”View image in fullscreenWith his band the Black Abbots, with whom he won Opportunity Knocks.Photograph: Anwar Hussein/AlamyHe pauses. Now he sounds emotional. “After the funeral, we were walking out paying our respects to his wife, Gwen, and she said to me: ‘He thought you were the cat’s whiskers!’ I filled up. Amazing.”More photos. Dennis and Gee, the double act who memorably impersonated Coronation Street’s Mavis Riley and Vera Duckworth on his show. Gee died in 1986, at 43. “So talented. Died too young.” We come to a picture of Abbot dressed as CU Jimmy, the incomprehensible, ranting Scottish stereotype that he’d struggle to get away with today. He says the character was based on his Scottish mother, whose accent got thicker the nearer the family got to Scotland for their holidays. He impersonates her – and she sounds as incoherent as Jimmy.Abbot’s mother, Elizabeth, was in domestic service to the Duke of Westminster at Eaton Hall in Cheshire when she met his father, Don Roberts, a tanker driver for Pratt’s Oil who went on to become an area manager. Young Russell Roberts was a bright lad who went to Chester Grammar. But he became obsessed with drumming, flunked his O-levels and left school at 16 to join a band called the Black Abbots. He supplemented his income with a job as a stagehand at the Royalty theatre in Chester, where the band had a residency.They soon became a comedy band, with Abbot dismounting the drums to tell daft jokes. The band won the talent show Opportunity Knocks six weeks in a row, became huge in the working men’s clubs, but never had a hit record. By 1973, Abbot was appearing on the TV standup comedy show The Comedians and his manager, Mike Hughes, didn’t think Russell Roberts had a ring to it. He suggested he become Russ Abbot. “He said: ‘Think about it, if your bill is in alphabetical order, you’ll always be top of the bill.’ He said: ‘Abba could top you, but that’s about it.’ That’s clever, isn’t it?”View image in fullscreenIn Russ Abbot’s Madhouse in the 1980s.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockBy the late 1970s, Abbot was well known as a comic and starred in the original Madhouse series with the more famous Freddie Starr. After 17 years as a Black Abbot, he left to go solo. Within months, Russ Abbot’s Madhouse started on ITV (The Russ Abbot Show would move during its run to the BBC) and he was a Saturday night fixture.We join Trish outside in the shade. She’s made us coffee and piled a plate with digestive biscuits. Did life change when he became a household name? “No.” He looks at her for confirmation. “Just in the sense we moved up the ladder homewise, didn’t we, Trish? So we started in the caravan. Trish’s dad had a win on the pools that paid for the caravan as a wedding present. Then my dad got us a place with £1-a-week rent. Two up, two down. Then we got a £10,000 bungalow and sold it for twice the price.”“Yep,” says Trish.‘Then we moved down south, we moved to Wentworth. We looked at this nice house …”“And that was it, yes,” says Trish.“We bought it, cash.”Were loads of women interested in you? “Not really, no,” he says. There’s a glint in his eye. “Oh, I suppose in my drumming days. Early.” The glint vanishes. “Actually, it was more the singers. Because I was just the drummer in the back.” He tells me how he met Trish. “She came to the stage door of the British Legion in Ellesmere Port as I was packing my drums up. We had a bass player in those days called Paul Dodd. He ended up a policeman. Trish says: ‘Is the bass player around?’ I said: ‘No, he’s gone, love.’ She said: ‘Oh, that’s a shame, I wanted to say hello to him.’”Did you fancy the bass player, I ask Trish.“Yeah.”So you got the wrong bloke?“Yeah, I got him instead.”“I said: come on, I’ll buy you a drink. Then I said: let me give you a lift home. She said: I only live across the road. I said: you can’t walk alone at this time of night. So I left with a kiss and a cuddle. And it all started from there, didn’t it, Trish?”Did she find him funny? “Oh no. Very normal. Lovely brothers, lovely mum and dad. Just normal, like the boy next door.” Did she like comedy? “Oh God, no!” Actually, she says, there was one occasion when he really made her laugh. “He opened the garden fete and chopped his nose off instead of cutting the ribbon.”Genuinely?“Yes, he was rushed to hospital. That’s what made me laugh.”“I had stitches all round my nose.”Trish is in stitches at the memory.“But that wasn’t intentionally funny,” Abbot protests.“No,” says Trish, still hooting. “But it was very funny, Russell. And we’ve laughed ever since.”He must have been stopped a lot over the years by fans. “No, not really,” he says. “It was always a nod and a wink and a smile. There’s one funny story. We went to the opening show of Miss Saigon.” Trish is already giggling. “We go into the VIP area. We sit there and Trish nudges me. All these heads are turning. And I say: ‘It’s all right! The lights will go down in a minute.’ I say: ‘Trish, it’s acompliment.’ And she nudges me again and says: ‘Look who’s sitting next to me!’ And it was Burt Lancaster. She fell about. Lovely story.”View image in fullscreenIn Cooperman getup, with his good friend Bella Emberg as Blunderwoman, in the late 1980s.Photograph: ITV/Rex/ShutterstockAbbot never considered himself a star. “I always think I’m playing that role of Russ Abbot. I go in the stage door as Russ Abbot and come out as Russell Roberts.” And he was too reserved to play the big I am. “I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy and I found them embarrassing. It’s like, now I’m retired, I’m not so shy and I can talk about it because it’s past.”Trish has always been his biggest fan, he says. Then he corrects himself. “Trish and my mum. She used to do handouts for the WI. I’d sign the autograph and she’d sign the back: ‘Russ’s mum!’ She loved it!” In her 70s, his mother got dementia. She went into a home, but Abbot didn’t realise how bad it had got until he arranged for her to come to a show. “Trish brought her up to the dressing room and Mum walked in and said: ‘What a pleasure to meet you. Thank you so much, I’ve been so entertained. It was absolutely marvellous, and now to meet you in person.’“I stood there and said: ‘Mum, it’s me,’ and she said: ‘I’ll have to go now, my family’s waiting for me.’ So Trish took her back. I slammed the dressing room door three times. It was terrible. It’s a terrible illness. She died about a year later. She was still a very elegant lady, very smartly dressed. She didn’t act like she had dementia. She just couldn’t remember who I was.”Abbot worked incredibly hard in his heyday. “In 1984, I worked 363 days.” Meanwhile, Trish was working incredibly hard, too, bringing up their four children. “Trish raised them all. I was always away, summer season tour or pantomime. Pantomimes, gosh! You’d get home Christmas Eve, put the presents under the tree, go to bed, have breakfast, watch the kids open the toys and then go back to do a matinee.”View image in fullscreenWith Les Dennis in The Russ Abbot Show, circa 1991.Photograph: TV Times/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesBut, he says, they were great times. He tells me of all the wonderful people he worked with. It sounds like an Oscar acceptance speech.Barry Cryerwrote much of his material, but there was a whole team involved and there is not an actor, producer, writer or manager he misses out.He was the ideas man, he says, rather than the wordsmith. “I loved it. All the nonsense.” He talks about the silly names they invented for characters. “My favourite was Miss Funnyfanny intead of Miss Moneypenny. I think that was my cousin Russell. I loved Basildon Bond because of the silliness of it.”Suddenly he’s quoting a 40-year-old monologue from a sketch featuring his James Bond parody. ‘My name’s Bond. Basildon Bond, licence to kill and drive a heavy-goods vehicle. I’d been away on holiday when I was summonsed back to headquarters to see my boss P … ‘Was it a good holiday Bond?’ I said: ‘Yes, thank you, sir, I went away for a bit of peace and quiet. I found a nice little piece. I just hope she keeps quiet.’ He said: ‘Don’t bother me with a silly little thing like that.’ I said: ‘It’s funny, that’s what she said.’”He quotes the monologue word-perfect, in all its anachronistic glory. For all the inappropriateness, there’s also an innocence to it, as there is to him. I notice he doesn’t swear and I ask if he’s religious. “Oh, I believe in God. I say my prayers every night.”Abbot fell out of fashion in the 1990s, as did virtually all the standup rooted in working men’s clubs and seaside summer seasons. Did he mind when his TV show got cancelled? “I wasn’t distressed or angry or anything. It came about when the head of entertainment gave an interview and said: ‘The BBC’s going to change. No more of this, no more of that,’ and somebody said: ‘Does that mean Russ Abbot?’ and he said yes, meaning the sketch shows. So then it became ‘BBC sacks Russ Abbot’, but that didn’t bother me. I thought: well, I’ve had a very good run. Also, I’d just cracked the West End, so I was doing everything I wanted to do without the stress of the TV shows.”Why did he fall out of fashion? “It was when the new wave came in. Alternative comedy. I thought, alternative comedy? What’s it alternative to? If the thing’s funny, it’s funny. Political correctness came in, and you can’t laugh at each other and you can’t laugh at yourself. At the same time, a lot of comedy started going blue and I thought: I’m not going down that road.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ve had a wonderful career,’ says Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSo much of his show’s humour was rooted in stereotyping and many of the jokes were at the expense of his great friend Emberg’s weight. Did he understand why that was no longer acceptable? “Yes. Some of the scripts I used to look at myself and wonder. I’d say: ‘Bella, have you read the script?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, I think it’s funny’. I’d say: ‘Are you sure?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, why?’ ‘I’m just asking your opinion,’ and she’d say: ‘I think it’s hilarious,’ and I’d say: ‘So do I!’” Did she ever get upset? “No, she never got upset once.” Emberg died in 2018 at 80. Of all the people he’s worked with, he says he misses her most.I loved it when Emberg as Blunderwoman lifted Abbot over her shoulders and carried him off. Even at his heaviest, he weighed only 12 and a half stone. Not much for a man over six foot tall. These days, Emberg would have had even less trouble. He’s lost two and a half stone. He knows Trish is worried, but he’s had every test going and nothing has been diagnosed. As for Trish, he says, she’s had two strokes in the past year, so they are taking it easy. Which doesn’t mean they’re not up to a round of golf. Abbot is a fine player and used to play off a handicap of 12, but he insists Trish is better than him. To be fair, so does she.Stories circulated that Abbot retired because he was embittered that comedy had changed and no straight roles were being offered to him. It’s true that he’s not a great fan of today’s comedy, he says, and he was disappointed when Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine were cancelled, but he insists the stories are nonsense. He actually retired because Hughes, his manager, was retiring and he thought it was a good time to call it quits and spend more time with Trish and have a social life.“I’ve seen something on YouTube saying ‘The tragedy of Russ Abbot’ and ‘He’s run away to Portugal’.” He smiles.“We just watched it once,” says Trish. “I said, don’t watch it, Russell.”It doesn’t look much of a tragedy to me, I say, glancing out at the cloudless sky, swimming pool and topiaried bushes.“Thank you,” Trish says.“I’ve had a wonderful career,” Abbot says.“Wonderful!”“He’s always said that,” Trish says.And now you’re enjoying a richly deserved retirement? “Absolutely,” he says.How would Trish feel if he decided to go back to work? Her eyes light up. “Happy,” she says. Why? “I’d like him to do something like Last of the Summer Wine. I think he does miss it, I’ve got to say.”Abbot gives her a look. “Yeah!” he says. “But not desperately, Trish.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
