title: Slayyyter live review – raucous show announces a new princess of sleaze-pop | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesse
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesse
Content: Slayyyter performing at Coachella on 10 April 2026.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty Images for CoachellaView image in fullscreenSlayyyter performing at Coachella on 10 April 2026.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty Images for CoachellaPop and rockReviewSlayyyter live review – raucous show announces a new princess of sleaze-popShrine Auditorium, Los AngelesThe cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesseEmma MaddenMon 24 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last timeSlayyytertoured, in 2023, she struggled to break even and had to fly home boxes of unsold merch. Back then, she was still largely the domain of Twitter gays: a subcultural figure to those who assessed music in terms of “flops” and “bops”.Then, midway through 2025, she released the electro-trashy Beat Up Chanel$, and suddenly caught everyone’s attention. With a career-defining Coachella set earlier this year, she had broken through into the mainstream alongside a class of flop-no-more artists –Zara Larsson,RayeandTinashe– who had spent years seeming cruelly shut out of its central sphere, only to break through with a surprise big hit. For these artists, and Slayyyter in particular, the urgency of a last chance had become as galvanizing as the urgency of a first.‘I didn’t think anyone would be into it’: Slayyyter turns midwest trash into pop goldRead moreFollowing what she described to the Switched on Pop podcast as the “financial failure” of her previous tour, Slayyyter’s fourth studio album, Wor$t Girl in America, became that final chance. She intended it to be the last album she’d ever record, trading the pinkish, delusional chic of her earlier work for Middle American sleaze. CloserBrittany Murphy, a song about depression and suicidal ideation, doubled as a meta-farewell to the chase for musical relevancy: “Do you notice all I’ve done? Do you know it’s all I want?”When she announced the accompanying North American leg of herWorst Girl in the World tour in March this year, it sold out in minutes. Her team immediately set to work on venue upgrades and added extra dates; tonight and tomorrow night at the Shrine inLos Angelessold out almost instantaneously, a venue that Slayyyter said midway through the set was a place she “always dreamed of playing”.At her first of these two packed Los Angeles shows, she finally got the answer she wanted to the question she posed on her album’s closer: a crowd screaming those lyrics back at her. Three songs into the set, she told them, seemingly unaware of the connection to Brittany Murphy, “This is all I’ve ever wanted.”She came out to devilish howls from the crowd, which almost drowned out her version of St Francis’s prayer. She walked, at first somberly, across the stage, which consisted of a tiny Missouri home, likely similar to the one she grew up in in St Louis; a lone carousel horse, a washing line full of Slayyyter-branded white tees, a crucifix poking out of the ground, and a high-exposure timelapse of a blue Missouri sky over a wheat field. As the sky turned from blue to gray and then lightning, Slayyyter detonated, bringing the energy of a hardcore show to a pop performance.Slayyyter’s production was distinct, self-contained and grand without losing its sense of scum. It was aHarmony Korine-like meeting of the baroque and Americana, finding beauty in a pack of Marlboro Reds and a gas-station T-shirt with a ganja leaf on it.Like the album, the set married pop and hard techno with Americana scuzz. While Slayyyter sang and screamed on the record through punkish distortion, with most of the music happening in the low end, live, you heard the clarity of her voice and just how incredible it was. When she sang, she belted in a single note with the heft of Dua Lipa, the hiccups of Chappell Roan, the girlish trails of Ariana Grande and the inferno of Courtney Love.She performed mostly with a rock band set-up: drummer, guitarist, bass; aproperlive show. Early in her career, when she came up among the first wave of hyperpop artists, she proved she could do it alone and make low budget look cool. Now, more impressively, she can make a much larger budget look cool, too.Trash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreEverything else was equally precise: the crowd work, the stage blocking, the hairography (and what hair!) were all on point. There was something deeply gratifying about hearing Slayyyter and seeing her vision so clearly, welcomed with such enthusiasm. It was particularly satisfying if you had followed her long enough to remember when the idea of this many people standing in a room to hear her sing would have seemed slightly delusional.The crowd had changed, too. Slayyyter had built a visual brand strong enough that the audience could wear it back to her. A great majority of the 5,000 in attendance came dressed in gas-station trucker caps, boxy thrifted tees, and oversized camo khakis. Everyone was mercifully at her feet while she fed the 5,000. When she sang bloghouse banger Old Technology, repeating the lyrics, “I’m doing drugs tonight,” a woman in the crowd with a bleach-blond skullet vomited into a bin.Rounding off the night with Beat Up Chanel$, Slayyyter stood beneath the blue Missouri sky as thousands screamed for her not to go. The prayer that opened the show had asked for grace in a world of suffering. Finally, she received a room full of people who knew exactly what she was trying to say. Her prayers had been answered.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockLos AngelesElectronic musiclive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movie | Horror films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise
Content: Cary Elwes in Saw.Photograph: Cinetext/Lions Gate/AllstarView image in fullscreenCary Elwes in Saw.Photograph: Cinetext/Lions Gate/AllstarMy feelgood movieHorror films‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchiseEmma MaddenMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas petsitting recently for a white suburban family, with the typical streaming habits therein. They had two kids; their most-watched shows, according to the history that showed up on the screen, were Bluey for the kids and The Office for the adults. When they came home from their weeklong trip, they would’ve found their watch history upheaved. The Bingos and Michael Scotts all erased by Saw I, Saw II, Saw III, Saw IV, Saw V, Saw VI, Saw 3D, Saw Spiral, Saw Jigsaw and, finally, my new favourite, Saw X.‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movieRead moreI was obsessed with the Saw franchise well before I ever saw it. At 11, as Jigsaw puppets became Halloween costumes, I went to bed each night convinced Jigsaw was going to scoop me up in a van because the word “hell”a popped into my head. By 13, I looked up every film on Wikipedia and read through each trap with terrified excitement. By 14, I drank my first can of Stella and typed Saw II into YouTube, watching it in 12 installments. It was utterly horrifying. And so, so, so much fun.I am now 31 and have seen every film so many times I could count on both hands – which Jigsaw would sever finger by finger – how many times I’ve seen them. Somewhere along the way, Saw became my feel-good film.The reasons why are mostly shallow and unsophisticated. It’s not like I care for the nonsensical storyline, or the dubstep editing, or the ham acting. No one’s exactly raving about Saw’s mise-en-scene. Its morality – the murderer keeps insisting he’s not actually murdering anyone – is deeply specious, and it’s never fully clear whether the film-makers are aware of this or not. But I obviously do not care. Just as I don’t care if a rollercoaster has any “worldbuilding”. I just want it to go whoosh and loop the loop.The one thing about Saw – other than its asinine-cop B-storylines – is that I’m guaranteed not to be bored. I just cannot tap out while watching a man in a revolving crucifix, his bones crushed one by one, or a woman cutting off her leg and extracting her bone marrow. Even typing that is making me squirm.When I first started watching these films, I looked away; now I stare them down blankly. I think watching horror is a bit like meditation, or doing planks. You go through waves of discomfort and the feeling that you can’t go on, but then you do. You subject yourself to something counterintuitive and unpleasant, and then you discover that you are still there at the end of it.It feels sort of embarrassing to dignify Saw with any kind of seriousness – and to say this in light of the films – but I’ve struggled with suicidal ideation my entire life. I think I am so benumbed that I am utterly beyond pain, but then I watch Saw and find myself wincing. As a suicidal person, I would undoubtedly qualify as one of Jigsaw’s “victims”. He would say that I don’t appreciate life.But when I watch Saw, I think:Thank God I’m not stuck at the bottom of a vat, with liquefied pig carcasses drowning me.Annoyingly, life is all about learning to let go: of others, of ego, of the flesh. Martyrs, a much better film in every way, takes those ideas seriously, treating suffering and transcendence as something profound and spiritual. But it’s no fun. Saw takes the sacrifice of life at its absolute stupidest and turns it into a game. No matter how much you think you want to die, you probably do have a bit of survival instinct left. “Live or die” is the Jigsaw villain’s catchphrase, and of course, living is much harder. It requires constant attention and struggle. But that’s the choice almost everyone makes.As I watch Saw, I put myself in the victims’ positions every single time: whatwouldI do if I had 60 seconds to cut into my eye or die? I’d rather not answer, but if I had to,hadto, I think I might choose to dig right in.If on another day I’d feel like throwing the scalpel down and just giving up, I’ll put on Saw once again, and remember what it costs to choose otherwise.Saw is available to rent digitally in the US and UK and on Stan and Binge in AustraliaIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsMy feelgood movieThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limbo | Movies | The Guardian
description: This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting
Content: Intriguing notes of absurdity … The Visitor.View image in fullscreenIntriguing notes of absurdity … The Visitor.MoviesReviewThe Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limboThis portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up driftingPhil HoadMon 24 Aug 2026 06.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt one point in this Nordic-Baltic homecoming film, Danielius (Darius Šilėnas) refuses an invite for beachfront karaoke, preferring to watch from behind a polythene partition. At another, a neighbour glimpses him exercising across the courtyard, through the window of the flat in an end-of-summer Lithuanian resort that Danielius is trying to sell. Having returned from Norway to settle up accounts, this prodigal son is often holding the world at arm’s length – and director Vytautas Katkus does his best to help him with this distanced technique in this quizzical and faintly existential drama.Little tangible is disclosed. Danielius is a thirtysomething father who skipped the funeral of his own dad the year before. Preparing the flat to go on the market, he walks the dog of his neighbour, Vismante (Vismantė Ruzgaitė), hangs speculatively at beach gatherings and falls asleep in pine forests. Ice-cream is eaten at every available opportunity. He’s not alienated exactly, but somewhat out of step. As he looks for new anchorage, even the film seems to question whether Danielius has sufficient main character energy: it periodically drifts to follow another resident, Tomas (Rokas Siaurusaitis), who is caring for his grandmother over the way.Given Katkus’s cinematography background, it’s not surprising that this smalltown ennui comes gracefully shot, with stray snippets of quirk, like the fairground diplodocus poking its head over the treetops as Danielius arrives. But with much of The Visitor’s long runtime devoted to simply surveilling this entropic purgatory and little else, it leaves it until late before openly broaching the matter of its protagonist’s diffidence. Is it because of guilt for returning too late? Or tied up with feelings about his own recent fatherhood? Or just common nostalgia about his old family life? All of the above, possibly.With the paternal issue apparently settled by a strange request over breakfast to Vismante’s father, Katkus – steadfast in his love of the mid-shot thus far – abandons his previous reserve. Where a character being gifted a red lifeguard beach inflatable prompted a diegetic burst of the Baywatch theme tune in the first half, the second half sees the film break with realism almost entirely for another seafront musical number. If not as stridently deadpan and stylised as the likes of Aki Kaurismäki, it brings gentler, intriguing notes of absurdism and human warmth to this seaside haven.The Visitor is at the ICA, London, from 21 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsLithuaniaNorwayEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Marching in the Dark review – rural Indian widows show stunning resilience as they battle poverty and taboos | Movies | The Guardian
description: Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront together
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront together
Content: Invisible suffering … Marching in the Dark.Photograph: SNG Film (Studio Nieuwe Gronden)View image in fullscreenInvisible suffering … Marching in the Dark.Photograph: SNG Film (Studio Nieuwe Gronden)MoviesReviewMarching in the Dark review – rural Indian widows show stunning resilience as they battle poverty and taboosKinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront togetherPhuong LeMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOut in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms.Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.Marching in the Dark is on True Story from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsIndiaFarmingSouth and central AsiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Breakout indie band Westside Cowboy on rejecting tech and loving imperfection: ‘We’re not hermits!’ | Music | The Guardian
description: Despite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Despite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?
Content: ‘We’re not cool’ … Reuben Haycocks, Jimmy Bradbury, Aoife Anson O’Connell and Paddy Murphy, AKA Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannView image in fullscreen‘We’re not cool’ … Reuben Haycocks, Jimmy Bradbury, Aoife Anson O’Connell and Paddy Murphy, AKA Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannMusicInterviewBreakout indie band Westside Cowboy on rejecting tech and loving imperfection: ‘We’re not hermits!’Daniel Dylan WrayDespite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Westside Cowboy played Later … With Jools Holland earlier this year, fellow guests Duran Duran offered some advice. “Nerves are just your mind telling you that you’re about to do something extraordinary,” Simon Le Bon told the band, who were “cacking their pants”. Le Bon’s words didn’t really help. “I was hoping for some real advice,” says vocalist and guitarist Reuben Haycocks, laughing. “Like, where do I look?”The Manchester band have had to learn the ropes quickly. By 2025, only two years after forming, they had won Glastonbury’s emerging talent competition, supported Geese on the year’s buzziest indie tour and signed to a major label.“We’d be lying if we said there wasn’t a little bit of pressure,” says vocalist and guitarist Jimmy Bradbury.Not that you can hear it on their hotly anticipated debut album, It Goes On. Recalling the likes of the Feelies, Parquet Courts and Courtney Barnett, the album touches upon the muscular end of indie-pop, a little midwestern emo and has a chugging drive inspired by the Velvet Underground. “We weren’t trying to make some career-defining thing,” says drummer Paddy Murphy, as we cram into their tour van backstage at Tramlines festival in Sheffield. “We love the way debut albums sound when a band feels hungry but still not quite settled. There’s unnecessary pressure on new bands to bottle everything on the first attempt. It doesn’t have to be that way. Just do whatever feels right.”Westside Cowboy: Pin Up Boys – videoWestside Cowboy are all aged 23 to 26, but – as their taste in music and resistance to the grind may indicate – share an old-school mindset. Most of them have brick phones, use MP3 players and collections of analogue gear, from radios to CD players and cassette decks. They’re even considering setting up a PO box address for fans to send letters to. “We’re not hermits,” insists Bradbury. “We still have laptops and send emails, but taking away that single-use device, like a phone, really helps free up headspace. These things are designed to be addictive, and it’s trying to find a way to control it, because you don’t have to buy into that.”It’s the same with their music. Bassist and vocalist Aoife Anson-O’Connell finds it “really stifling creatively and personally isolating” being locked perpetually on screens, while Haycocks’ previous band, he says, became frozen by the “option paralysis” of overusing technology. “It feels like the only way for people of our age, but we reject that. Starting this band, we thought we’d go for the most simple thing possible and that’s also seeped into our daily lives.”View image in fullscreen‘Britanicana is as pointless as all other genres’ … Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannOn stage later on, they play an explosive 4pm set to a rammed tent, contrasting sharp, noisy blasts of guitar with layered vocal harmonies. But back in the van, they are a modest and self-deprecating bunch. “We’re not doing anything revolutionary,” says Anson-O’Connell. Bradbury states: “We’re not cool.”All band members share songwriting duties; when Haycocks writes he tries to channel frontmen he feels possess more panache, such as Lou Reed or the Magnetic Fields’ Stephin Merritt (it might explain the American twang to his vocal delivery). “I’m not someone who feels at my coolest when I’m Reuben Haycocks,” he says. “There’s a certain level of bravado you need to try to write a song, so to get myself over the line, I’ll be X person for an hour – as I will never be able to reach that level of awesomeness.” This role play works for figuring out tone, too. One instruction Murphy gave to Bradbury when working out a guitar part was to imagine early rock’n’roller Link Wray “trying to scare kids”.Their love of folk, skiffle, Americana and early rock’n’roll led to them coining their own genre, Britanicana, to capture this hybrid. Now they call it a joke that got out of hand. “A very tongue-in-cheek thing,” says Murphy.“If people want to use Britanicana, be my guest,” Haycocks adds. “It’s as equally pointless as all other genres.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We’re really good. I don’t mean that arrogantly’: Yard Act on bullying, imposter syndrome and their heavy new albumRead moreAs much as Westside Cowboy feel like a band happily at home in the past, they’re just as invested in improving their own era. Alongside the indie bands Holly Head, Pushbike and Martial Arts, they run a night called No Band Is an Island, which programmes bands and leftwing political speakers to raise money for Medical Aid for Palestine. Although you won’t find explicitly political lyrics in their songs. “We are all political people,” offers Haycocks, who is wearing a T-shirt calling for animal liberation. “But we don’t think our music suits going on stage and shouting about politics because that’s not who we are, personally.”In hindsight, the fabulously slick Le Bon was probably never going to have much good advice for a band like this. Westside Cowboy’s own musical heroes are artists who have embraced imperfection. Haycocks scrolls through his MP3 player and finds Tom Waits’ Mule Variations. “It’s like, oh my God, how has he managed to write two of the most goofy songs in the world among five of the greatest?” he says, comparing the likes of Chocolate Jesus with Picture in a Frame.Bradbury jumps in: “You’ve got to have your duds!” Haycocks agrees, inadvertently summing up the band’s MO. “Duds are what make music human.”It Goes On is out now on IslandExplore more on these topicsMusicIndieinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: David Olusoga’s extraordinary new show: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’
Author: Nell Frizzell
Headline: The historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’
Content: David Olusoga presents A Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten Massacre.Photograph: Jon Parker Lee/Findmypast/PAView image in fullscreenDavid Olusoga presents A Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten Massacre.Photograph: Jon Parker Lee/Findmypast/PABest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioDavid Olusoga’s extraordinary new show: best podcasts of the weekThe historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’Nell FrizzellandHollie RichardsonMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekA Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten MassacreFrom the People’s History Museum, thisseriesis about the Peterloo massacre in Manchester, 1819, which the host David Olusoga calls the “ground zero of industrial capitalism”. Touching on systematic disenfranchisement (Manchester didn’t have a single MP) and state-sanctioned violence through the extraordinary story of survivor William Cheatham, it’s an invigorating if sobering listen.Nell FrizzellWidely available, episodes weeklyWriting FunnyAnalysing what makes something funny is the artistic equivalent of trying to peel a raw egg. And yet, funny people are fun to have in your ears. The Comedy Women in Print prize has anew podcast, presented by the award’s founder, Helen Lederer, and the author Chrissie Manby, in which they will tackle everything from a writer’s journey to writing comedy in dark times.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyWodcastView image in fullscreenElif Shafak, a guest on Wodcast.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesMabel Evans and Benjamin Aston turn their Word of the Day project into a very wholesomeseriesdescribed as “Desert Island Discs for words”. They ask guests to expand on the words that shape their lives, starting with Elif Shafak. Future guests include Stephen Fry and Tim Rice.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weeklyBig Little InterestsWhen I last worked in an office I watched videos of large boats misjudging their stopping distances and crashing into walls. Which is probably why I like the premise ofBig Little Interests: a podcast dedicated to the strange, funny hyper-fixations that make different comedians’ brains feel smooth and shiny. Episode one, with Steve Bugeja, features bull semen.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyCivilian Or SpyAs told by CNN’s Isabelle Chapman, this is the compellingstoryof how Russian-born American citizen Ilya Beloozerov was shot by the FBI outside a Super 8 hotel in 2024. With the relationship between the US and Russia as compelling today as during any cold war escapade of the 1970s, this investigation definitely has wider implications. Just don’t call it the new Serial.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat are you listening to at the moment? title: Betrayal by Luke Harding review – could Donald Trump be a Russian asset? | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind it
Author: Lawrence Freedman
Headline: A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind it
Content: Putin and Trump at an Anchorage airbase ahead of their Alaska summit in August 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPutin and Trump at an Anchorage airbase ahead of their Alaska summit in August 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewBetrayal by Luke Harding review – could Donald Trump be a Russian asset?A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind itLawrence FreedmanMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican presidents have struggled to get the measure ofVladimir Putin. When George W Bush met him in 2001, he reported that he had “looked the man in the eye”, got a “sense of his soul” and found him “trustworthy”. Barack Obama thought Putin was making a mistake with his interventions in Ukraine and Syria, but didn’t do much about it. Joe Biden backed Ukraine’s resistance to the Russian invasion, yet his fear that Putin would reach for the nuclear button if backed into a corner made him risk averse. He worried about the impact of the sort of long-range strikes against Russian territory that Kyiv is now launching on a daily basis.This caution frustrated Ukrainians to the point that they looked forward toDonald Trumpshaking things up after he won re-election. Be careful what you wish for: the returning president thought his rapport with Putin would be enough to get Russia to sign up to an immediate ceasefire. In Trump’s head it was President Zelenskyy, fighting a war he was bound to lose, who was the problem.This led to the betrayal that gives Guardian correspondent Luke Harding’s book its title. Instead of increasing the pressure on Moscow, the new administration set about abandoningUkraine. In the UN General Assembly, the US voted with the dregs of Russia’s supporters against a resolution condemning its aggression (even China abstained). Trump denounced his predecessor, Biden, for the support given to Ukraine, exaggerated its value (claiming it was $350bn when it was close to $70bn) and demanded privileged access to Ukraine’s mineral wealth as a form of repayment. Then came the greatest indignity of all as Zelenskyy was baited in the Oval Office, with JD Vance accusing him of disrespecting the president, after he had merely tried to correct falsehoods about how his country was coping with the war. He was ushered out of the White House and subjected to further denunciations. Intelligence was even cut off to Ukraine’s frontline forces for a short but critical period.double quotation markAs Zelenskyy was being ambushed in front of the world’s press, Harding was in Odessa, visiting a clinic that had been hit by a Russian droneTrump’s delusions about Putin persisted. Later that year he invited him to Alaska for a summit, where he was treated with extraordinary deference, in the mistaken belief that he was prepared to compromise. The only compromise Putin had in mind involved Ukraine handing over its territory without a fight. (Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, is still denying Russian claims that this was agreed in principle at the summit.) In any case, the meeting was a failure, with Trump left irritated by one of Putin’s long disquisitions on the history of Russian-Ukrainian relations. It ended before lunch.Harding demonstrates Trump’s betrayal less through accounts of negotiations and summits than in his reporting from Ukrainian cities under constant attack from the air. As Zelenskyy was being ambushed in front of the world’s press, Harding was in Odessa, visiting a clinic that had been hit by an Iranian-designed Russian Shahed drone. As she viewed the wreckage of the gutted children’s clinic in which she worked, Olena Palsh lamented: “We fashioned it with love. The work of five years was destroyed in an instant.” Harding tells many such stories of the suffering and devastation inflicted by Putin on a country he considers to be a natural part of Russia.In this way, he creates a sobering chronicle of a long and vicious conflict. He is skilled at describing the individuals caught up in events, including Ri Chol-nam, a North Korean soldier who was surprised to find himself fighting for Russia, and for whom the shame of being captured by the Ukrainians led to a suicide attempt. The wider context is also deftly conveyed, with chapters on how China is trying to make the most of the situation and how Putin seeks to intimidate Europeans, sabotaging internet cables on the seabed or flying drones into their airspace.The villains at the core of the book are undoubtedly Trump and Putin. Harding discusses the question of whether Trump might himself be a Russian asset. Is it just that he enjoys the company of tyrants and envies their supreme power, or do they have embarrassingkompromatthat he wants to ensure doesn’t see the light of day (though admittedly this is a man who seems to know no shame)? Harding concludes with a question in the subjunctive: “If Trumpwerea Russian agent, what exactly would he do differently?”Yet now Putin seems disappointed by Trump, for he has not delivered the Ukrainian surrender he sought. Which leads to a different question: given Trump’s readiness to accommodate Putin, how come the Russian leader has been unable to make the compromises that would have allowed him to close the deal? It’s a shame that Harding is no longer allowed into his old stomping ground of Moscow, where his contacts might have helped him to explore the biggest puzzle: why Putin persists with a futile and costly war he can’t win.Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest by Luke Harding is published by Guardian Faber (£20). title: The Disappearers by Marlon James review – a scorching exposé of homophobia in Jamaica | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queer
Author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
Headline: This Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queer
Content: Bleak and uncompromising … Marlon James.Photograph: Rahim Fortune/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBleak and uncompromising … Marlon James.Photograph: Rahim Fortune/The GuardianBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Disappearers by Marlon James review – a scorching exposé of homophobia in JamaicaThis Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queerYagnishsing DawoorMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Asense of sweep,” repliedMarlon James, when asked what moves him most in literature. “Sweep isn’t just about external journeys, but internal as well. It can be over years and decades, or across land and sea.” If that explanation is still hazy, pick up his mighty new novel, which is longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and is tirelessly – sometimes exhaustingly – grand and peripatetic. Mounting a grisly exposé of Jamaican homophobia, this polyphonic 640-page doorstopper is an emotionally bruising narrative that roves “uptown, downtown, ghetto and gully” through Aids-era Kingston with sidetrack excursions to 1950s England and a closing leap to 2000s United States.The novel’s defining event is a gruesome mob attack on eight queer men who have clandestinely come together to work on bringing John Herbert’s 1967 gay prison play, Fortune and Men’s Eyes, to the stage. The goal, in the words of director Havelock Titus, is to shatter “the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality”. “Because prison,” he explains, “is the ultimate male institution and yet masculine sexualities that could never happen outside in the normal world flourish in there all the time.”The spunk and sass of these men, their banter and squabbles as they feel each other out and ease into their roles, as well as their fears, insecurities and motivations for doing the play, are relayed by one of the actors: Eddy Porteous, a “white-ish” Belgian Jamaican college student from a well-heeled family. His diary entries over the course of the month preceding the assault make up the novel’s expositional first quarter, illuminating the interplay of class, race and colourism in the experience of Jamaican queerness.The narrative kicks into gear with the section on the attack. Now we are thrust, chillingly, into the minds of the perpetrators, among whom are a policeman, a self-loathing closet case, a deacon and a reggae singer named Streggeh Don whose hit, Batty Is Not Pussy, is the rallying-cry-cum-soundtrack for the splatterfest. Violence is James’s shtick and a hallmark of his fiction, from torture and sexual abjection in his subversive slavery epic, The Book of Night Women, and gang warfare in his Booker-winning novel,A Brief History of Seven Killings, to the near-ceaseless carnage in his ongoingDark Star fantasy trilogy. But here, far from the glib relish of which James has been accused throughout his writing career, one senses an unequivocal ethical purposefulness. “I think evil is a choice,” one survivor asserts, “and an ongoing one. Even in the midst of committing wickedness there are choices of how wicked one will be, which is made by the minute.” In order to grasp this statement in all its wounded, furious profundity – to see the outsize hate unleashed on these men as deeply volitional – the reader must bear witness not only from within the action, but also from within the consciousness of the perpetrators.One man has a branch shoved into his anus and dies. Another has both his eyes gouged out. All but Eddy, who had skipped rehearsal on that fateful night, are battered, gashed and maimed. Two of them will later vanish without a trace. Wrestling with survivor’s guilt, Eddy teams up with fellow actor Jordan to try to find them. More so than Eddy, it is Jordan who is the novel’s beating heart. A gleeful, foul-mouthed “sometime prostitute”, animated by the dangerous, liberatory ethos of American author John Rechy’s 1977 book The Sexual Outlaw, which he obsessively reads for affirmation, he is the Jamaican homophobe’s “battymonster” come to life.double quotation markFizzing with filth, snark and venom, the novel hawks and spits at conventionJordan and Eddy’s journeys into the promiscuous gay underground and the dark heart of heterosexual Jamaica are recounted in a series of interview transcripts, as the pair take turns speaking to a journalist from an American media outlet. Their frustrations gather further poignancy within the broader tragedy of the Aids epidemic engulfing Jamaica’s gay community: “This is what Aids is after all, isn’t it? One long set of disappearing acts. First is watching the friends and family disappear. Second act is when people try to disappear you. Third act is watching your body vanish from itself and wondering where the fuck you going, piece by piece, until all of you gone … If there is a fourth act it’s when everybody erase your name as if you were never born in the first place. Certainly no Christian church ever christened you.”The Disappearers is a bleak and uncompromising exploration of rage and survival; of trauma and its afterlife; of the terrible intimacy that binds victims to their perpetrators, and survivors to the dead, as well as revenge’s lure for those who are not given their due. Throughout, the narrative obsesses over the questions of whether meaning can emerge from the devastation of atrocity, and whether the void left by the missing is a mystery to be solved, or a limbo to be helplessly inhabited. What if the disappeared, done with being part of a world bent on eliminating them, didn’t want to be found? Fizzing with filth, snark and venom, the novel hawks and spits at convention, especially the politics of respectability that insists on restraint; it strafes down on homophobia with ruthless abandon. Few books have mapped the beleaguered realities of queer existence with such psychological depth, harrowing realism and searing condemnation.The formal design, however, is not without flaws. The overlong narrative sags in places, tarrying where it should speed along, and the intertextuality – most obviously the revenge plot’s debt to Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon – can veer into self-conscious pastiche. While the book’s conversation with the queer canon is richly rewarding (besides Herbert and Rechy, Gide, Genet, Vidal, Wilde, Baldwin and Holleran are some of the visiting spectres), I struggled with the fact that a significant chunk of the action is reported rather than dramatised. As well as the interview transcripts, we have letters from Havelock to a friend; some pivotal moments are thus experienced either at a temporal and affective remove, or inevitably somewhat summarised.Ultimately, these are redeemable shortcomings in an otherwise remarkable novel. James makes room for the contradictions of queer life, its intimacies, estrangements and hungers, in utterly indelible ways. His prose is a consistent triumph: bitter and hilarious, lyrical, bawdy, pugnacious and scorchingly, ravishingly queer. The Booker judges have described this novel as a “reckoning”; it is incontestably also a haunting.The Disappearers by Marlon James is published by Hamish Hamilton (£20). title: ‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta test | Games | The Guardian
description: Players will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Players will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?
Content: The shootfest returns … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenThe shootfest returns … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4.Photograph: ActivisionGames‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta testPlayers will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?Keith StuartMon 24 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a lot riding on this year’sCall of Duty, the inescapable first-person shootfest that’s been lobbing a grenade into the autumn release schedule since 2003. Previous instalment, Black Ops 7, performed poorly compared to previous titles, forcing Activision to post a semi-apology to fans. And that’s not the only challenge Modern Warfare 4 is facing: there’s a new indie shooter, Wardogs, promising a feel somewhere between classic CoD and Classic Battlefield. Then, lurking on the horizon, in mirror shades and an exotic sports car, is Grand Theft Auto 6, which is surely going to smash and grab all the attention (and money) from the market in mid-November.The good news is that, judging by the early access beta test that ran over the penultimate August weekend, we’re definitely getting what we expect from a Modern Warfare title: quasi-authentic boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. The weapons and general gunplay are highly effective, from default assault rifle, the Han 86 – a classic CoD beginner’s gun with decent fire rate and handling – to the bullet-spraying Nightshade SMG and the absolutely lethal KG-7 Vulcan sniper rifle. They all feel good to hold and fire, and there’s enough balance to let you experiment with slightly more offbeat numbers like the burst-fire Hyeon AR and the possibly overpowered Mar-9 marksman rifle.View image in fullscreenRefreshed armoury … Call of Duty Modern Warfare.Photograph: ActivisionAlso joining the refreshed armoury are an interesting array of field upgrades, the useful gadgets you open up as you play I tried the smoke wall which creates, well, a wall of smoke, hiding your movements (in theory) and I saw a few people deploying the razor-wire trap which slows enemies down while sapping their health. There are also new kill streaks (the special attacks you can trigger when you earn enough points in a match). Artillery Beacon lets you throw a beacon at a specific point which is then bombarded with missiles, and Wheelson is a remote control mini tank that clatters around the place firing a grenade launcher.A modest selection of small-ish maps was available for the weekend. Silkworm is a slab of South Korean cityscape, all minimarts and alleyways, while Transit 213 is a public transport depot with two parked buses at its centre and lots of generous sightlines for snipers. I found Cachette, a labyrinth of farm buildings, workshops and courtyards a little over-familiar, but Lotus, a larger harbourside map, brought in some interesting long-range combat. My favourite though, was the self-explanatory Rooftops, which takes place on the connected summits of two ageing New York high rises. Here, you fight through multi-levelled maintenance rooms and industrial laundries as well as out into open areas where water towers, exhaust fans and service ramps provide useful cover and mantling opportunities. There’s even a section of wooden scaffolding that offers a narrow shortcut over a vertigo-inducing chasm.View image in fullscreenThe TikTok of gaming? … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionThere are a bunch of new modes to accompany classics such as Team Deathmatch, Domination and Kill Confirmed. The key example is Kill Block, a ten v 10 gun fight taking place in a training camp that is reconfigured between rounds, providing hundreds of different layouts. There are trenches to crawl along, shipping containers to lie on and windows to camp behind. Like Search and Destroy, there are no respawns so it’s a fight to the death. The result is absolute carnage.How does it feel? Well, after the first day of the early access beta, gaming content creator Farzam referred to MW4 as the Tikok of gaming and it’s a good analogy. Everything happens fast and it just doesn’t stop happening; time-to-engagement (how long it takes from spawning to meeting your first enemy) is counted in microseconds, and if you blink, you’re dead. On every stretch of every map there is something to catch your attention, from exploding oxygen tanks to flickering video screens, and if you’re killed, hit a button and you’re instantaneously back in the game – no pause for breath, no time to think. You aren’t playing so much as doomscrolling an inescapable cognitive cacophony.Meanwhile, the omni-movement system introduced in Black Ops 6, which lets you jump, dive and skid along the floor in any direction, has been removed in favour of an ostensibly more naturalistic and controlled alternative. Is it really? Um, no. There is no friction at all in the landscape, so you can skid round corners and scale walls with superhero abandon. It’s fun and fluid, but it’s open to abuse: some players leap and twirl about the place as though performing in a particularly harrowing production of Swan Lake.For the first time in a CoD beta test, there’s a Campaign mission to try. Named Entrenched, it starts with … a trench, which you have to battle your way through against North Korean troops until you reach a power station. Then it’s a battle against time as you look to flood the reactor to prevent a catastrophic meltdown, before indulging in some parkour to escape the collapsing infrastructure. An average day at work for the CoD crew.I’m sure this beta test is going to give both the development team and the community plenty to think about. Ultimately, the game feels like what it is – a very modern Modern Warfare where your most effective weapons are lightning reflexes and superhuman concentration. I am too old for this shit, but I still thoroughly enjoyed it; diving round a corner and taking out two enemies in one burst remains as thrilling now as it was when the original Modern Warfare came out in 2007. There is a lot more competition out there now, though, and Call of Duty itself is starting to creak at the joints. The beta is yelling “I’ve still got it!” – but have the players? Money will be tight this autumn, and GTA 6 is standing at the bar, winking suggestively, beckoning us over.Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 is released on PC, PS5, Switch 2 and Xbox on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territory | Games | The Guardian
description: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Author: Bex April May
Headline: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Content: What if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesView image in fullscreenWhat if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesSummer games previewsGamesMy Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territoryDevelopers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limbBex April MayMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost stealth games cast you as a spy, an assassin or a master thief. My Arms Are Longer Now dispenses with most of the criminal person, to send in just one spectacularly badly behaved limb. It slithers across floors, winds around furniture, steals things and slaps anyone within reach – finally answering the question nobody asked: what if your own arm turned to crime?As TootGamesco-founder Matthew Jackson puts it: “You are the bad thing that happens to the people.”The idea began as a much simpler prototype made during a weekend game jam themed around the idea of lost and found. Jackson and fellow Toot co-founderMillie Holten, who met through Melbourne’s improv and sketch comedy community, wanted an idea that could be understood – and raise a laugh – in a single still image. A grotesquely extended arm proved to be just that.Since then, the game has been all about comedy. It has more than 40 speaking characters, voiced by Australian comedians who perform the written dialogue before improvising alternative takes. “It’s a vessel for jokes,” Jackson says. For almost a year, development largely involved trying to “cram jokes into the game”; only later did the team realise the physics of the increasingly sophisticated arm had become fun in their own right. Players can personalise its skin tone, hair and accessories, making it less somebody else’s disembodied crime spree than a freaky extension of their own body.The stealth here owes something toUntitled Goose Game: characters react to your crimes, but, Jackson says, “There are no fail states in the game.” A museum guard might smack the arm, or beg it to stop before they are fired. Anyone can be slapped, including an infant. While searching for a publisher, Jackson repeatedly asked: “Is someone going to come and tell us you can’t slap the baby?”Jackbox Games, thankfully, did not.View image in fullscreen‘A vessel for jokes’ … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesMaking that slap possible required rather more sophistication than the joke might suggest. The original game was flat and 2D, but Holten’s concept art showed the arm looping over tables, under chairs and around objects. Six months into development, the studio took the risky decision to rebuild in 3D. Working with developer Cherie Davidson, Jackson created a procedural, tube-like limb and a system that uses forced perspective to preserve the illustrated style while allowing the physical collisions the game needs.The work never quite ends. The team calls another session tinkering with the troublesome appendage “going into the armpit”.That labour is particularly demanding because comedy is finite. “You can hit a joke, and that joke’s done. You’ve burnt that,” Jackson says. Some publishers suggested adding more puzzles, but Toot feared they would obstruct the punchlines. Jackbox understood that it was meant to be “a good time, not a long time”, with players who do poke into every corner rewarded with optional interactions and voice lines.Jackson’s ultimate ambition for the game is appropriately simple: “I hope players say it was funny. That’s truly it.” And after three years in the armpit, 48 speaking characters, and one non-negotiable baby slap, Toot Games has gone to extraordinary lengths to reach gaming’s funny bone.My Arms Are Longer Now is in development forPC, with release planned for 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Goodbye Dandelion review – ode to a fabulous friendship with a 50-year age gap | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Maddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger one
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Maddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger one
Content: Sunny … Maddie Rice in Goodbye Dandelion.Photograph: Harry ElletsonView image in fullscreenSunny … Maddie Rice in Goodbye Dandelion.Photograph: Harry ElletsonEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewGoodbye Dandelion review – ode to a fabulous friendship with a 50-year age gapUnderbelly, EdinburghMaddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger oneMark FisherMon 24 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn unexpected theme on this year’s Edinburgh fringe is assisted dying. It is central to Morna Young’sAfter Party, about a matriarch who chooses to die after her 80th birthday, and Ben Harrison’s adaptation of Andrew O’Hagan’sMayflies, in which a terminally ill man travels to Dignitas. It is hinted at in Eilidh Loan’sCathy, about a woman adjusting to bereavement. And it is here again in this breezy storytelling show by sibling duo Maddie and Marcus Rice.The semi-fictional tale is about Maddie’s befriending of the 87-year-old Darcy O’Shea, an artist and piano teacher 50 years her senior, who is full of zest and vigour. As Maddie puts it, she is “unapologetically herself”, a woman living a life of happy self-reliance with limited tolerance for anyone else. A long-gone partner nicknamed her Dandelion because of her sticky-up hair, and it suits her personality.View image in fullscreenMarcus Rice at the piano plays songs and background music.Photograph: Harry ElletsonDarcy tells it as she sees it and does not mind shaming the younger woman for failing to change the things that weigh her down: life is too short not to plunge in headfirst.As a narrator, Maddie has a sunny disposition and relates the story with some wit. Lest she get maudlin, she has Marcus on hand as a counterbalance. Playing pretty waltzes on the piano throughout, he launches into songs that draw on the language of officialdom to comic effect. There is even some heartening audience participation.Knowing that death is coming can make plays on this theme feel like one long delaying tactic, especially here where the story has so little friction. Directed by Katie Pesskin, it is best – if briefest – on the impact the encounter has on Maddie and the way it propels her to make changes in her own life.At Underbelly, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreSpoken wordAssisted dyingEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ab-sol-utely incredible!’ The blockbuster ballet that says Pandora’s box unleashed AI | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: She was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her tale
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: She was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her tale
Content: ‘Dancers are heroes’ ... Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Chris HardyView image in fullscreen‘Dancers are heroes’ ... Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Chris HardyEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Ab-sol-utely incredible!’ The blockbuster ballet that says Pandora’s box unleashed AILyndsey WinshipShe was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her taleMon 24 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAszure Barton is taking herself back to the creation of Mere Mortals, remembering the creative buzz of the studio at San Francisco Ballet. “Sam was fiddling around making magic in one corner,” she says – that’s Sam Shepherd, AKA electronic musician Floating Points, who plays live in the show. Digital art duo Hamill Industries were there too, designing visuals for giant LED screens. “I was in a corner with the dancers,” says Barton. “Principals and apprentices, everyone working together. It was a really shared experience, which I loved.” In fact, it’s a “curiosity for real collaboration” that drives the Canadian-American choreographer. “If it was just about me,” she says, “the work wouldn’t be as powerful.”Mere Mortals, which opened in San Francisco in 2024, is finally getting a European premiere, at this year’s Edinburgh international festival. While Barton’s memories of making the show are all about human connection, the subject matter is quite the opposite: artificial intelligence. It’s inspired by the myth of Pandora’s box, but instead of a box unleashing the evils and sorrows of humanity, it is reimagined as a cautionary tale about AI.double quotation markI have to be in the back, bouncing up and down like I’m at a raveThe idea came from SF Ballet’s artistic director Tamara Rojo, who took over the company in 2022 after 26 years in the UK, notably as a principal dancer at the Royal Ballet and artistic director of English National Ballet. “She was very hands-off in terms of the work itself,” says Barton, but Rojo assembled a crack international team for her ambitious commission which garnered some rave reviews for the intensity of its scale, score and visual impact.View image in fullscreenDazzling … Wei Wang and San Francisco Ballet in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Alexander Reneff-OlsonBarton had worked with Rojo before, when she choreographed Fantastic Beings for English National Ballet in 2016, a dance full of endlessly inventive, quirky movement. Beyond that, the 50-year-old isn’t well known on this side of the Atlantic (Rojo has called her “completely underrated”), although she’s been choreographing for more than two decades with major companies all over the world, as well as for her own, Aszure Barton & Artists. She was mentored by the great Mikhail Baryshnikov at his Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York. What did she learn from him? “On day one, he said, ‘Never ask me for money’ and ‘I like your willingness to work your ass off.’”In the making of Mere Mortals, it turns out the richest conversations were not about the perils of AI, but the myth of Pandora, or “a myth that had been misconstrued”, says Barton. “A false story spread throughout history of this powerful being who didn’t have any agency and was toxic.”There’ll always be different tellings of Greek myths, but Pandora does seem to have had a bad rap. She was the first woman, an Eve-like figure, created from clay and given by Zeus to Epimetheus, unbeknownst to him, as a punishment for his brother Prometheus giving humans fire. “One of the things I was really driven by was the fact that she was an agent of change,” says Barton.As well as looking to a fictional figure from the past, however, Barton also used what was right in front of her in the present: the dancer in the lead role, Jennifer Stahl. “Ab-sol-utely incredible!” she says of Stahl, wide-eyed. “This stunning, powerful, amazing woman that I was getting to create with made my job very sweet.” Stahl, who has danced with SF Ballet for 20 years, will be returning to the Pandora role, having had a baby in between premieres.View image in fullscreenNot anti-AI … Aszure Barton.Photograph: Lindsey RalloIn the same way the inspiration for Pandora was right there in the studio, the show’s theme was all around her in San Francisco, the AI centre of the world. “You’re living the reality,” says Barton, “the systems and the chaos and the beauty, and I was really intuitively responding to that moment.” Barton uses lots of tech in her working life, not so much AI, more video, to endlessly document, analyse and deconstruct her way through the creative process. She calls choreography “the most magical Legoland for me”, but it always comes back to bodies. “I love dance because it’s so human and so beautiful. You can do some cool stuff with technology, but there’s nothing like sharing a space with a dancer.”She’s not anti-AI. Some choreographers use AI as a tool to interrupt their creative habits and find new ideas. “That’s cool,” says Barton, although her own creativity is sparked by interacting with dancers. “You never have choreographer’s block if you’re open to what’s right there in front of you,” she says. “Dancers are heroes. They don’t get credited enough for their input.”Barton hopes that all the fizzing creativity that went into making Mere Mortals is tangible to the audience. She wants them to be “showered with energy”. She can’t sit in her chair and watch it, she says. “I have to be in the back, bouncing up and down like I’m at a rave.” Between the dancers and the musicians (from the Royal Scottish National Orchestra) there are 87 performers in the show. “Masses of people sharing themselves, sharing this raw beauty,” says Barton. “It’s delicious.”Mere Mortals is atEdinburgh Playhouse, 28-30 August andSadler’s Wells, London, 9-12 September.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceEdinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Academy of St Martin in the Fields/Marquise Gilmore review – bassoon earns its spotlight in Thea Musgrave’s Out of the Darkness | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Amy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to Mozart
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Amy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to Mozart
Content: Lyrical … Amy Harman plays bassoon with the Academy of St Martin in the Fields at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenLyrical … Amy Harman plays bassoon with the Academy of St Martin in the Fields at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewAcademy of St Martin in the Fields/Marquise Gilmore review – bassoon earns its spotlight in Thea Musgrave’s Out of the DarknessRoyal Albert Hall, LondonAmy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to MozartFlora WillsonMon 24 Aug 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid this year’s crop of Proms premieres, one stood out a mile – long before any of us had heard a note of it. Out of the Darkness is a new bassoon concerto by the98-year-old Scottish composer Thea Musgrave, whose music was first heard at the Proms in 1960. Sixty-six years later, Musgrave is one of classical music’s most eminent elder stateswomen; hernext opera will make its debut next year. But bassoon concertos remain a rare breed.The first performance of Out of the Darkness emerged from a dark grumble of the Academy of St Martin in the Fields’ percussion and bass instruments, whichbassoonist Amy Harmananswered from the back of the stage, weaving a warm, baritonal vocalise through the orchestral duskiness. Only the solo violin line of ASMF’s director Benjamin Marquise Gilmore offered a lighter, brighter sound, until it was picked up by the rest of the violins. The musical material was all beguiling loops and phrases ending in question marks, Harman’s tone deliciously lyrical. Nothing was spelled out, except her journey around the orchestra, the bassoon gathering rhythmic vitality as she walked to join the trumpets, then double basses, finally arriving at the front – a soloist’s standard spot – in time for the disarmingly near-tonal final chord.View image in fullscreenSole music … Felix Klieser performs at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe remainder of the programme mixed Mozart and 20th-century British music. A fast, ultra-precise performance of Britten’s Simple Symphony was followed by a pleasant take on Mozart’s Horn Concerto No 3 in E flat major, K447 withFelix Klieserthe soloist. Klieser’s ability to play the instrument with his feet remains astonishing, but this surely should not be the most interesting feature of a performance. Harman returned to the stage post-premiere for Elgar’s charming Romance for bassoon and orchestra, allowing this period instrument ensemble a rare opportunity for voluptuous tone and a spot of Edwardian passion. In Mozart’s Symphony No 35 “Haffner”, K385, the ASMF were back on repertorial home turf, their playing neat, fleet-footed and tremendously classy. It was just a shame that the subtle drama of their approach could make only a limited impact in a space as cavernous as the Royal Albert Hall.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicAcademy of St Martin in the FieldsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Those People review – a double act with raw passion and no filter | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Are they besties, housemates or more than that? Lara Ciulli and Riana White keep the audience guessing in a gripping hour of comedy
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Are they besties, housemates or more than that? Lara Ciulli and Riana White keep the audience guessing in a gripping hour of comedy
Content: The bickering feels close to the bone … Lara Ciulli and Riana WhiteView image in fullscreenThe bickering feels close to the bone … Lara Ciulli and Riana WhiteEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThose People review – a double act with raw passion and no filterPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAre they besties, housemates or more than that? Lara Ciulli and Riana White keep the audience guessing in a gripping hour of comedyBrian LoganMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen years ago in this room, I remember the thrill of encounteringLizzie and Sarah Daykin’s duo Toby, which complicated the double-act dynamic with highly charged, is-it-real sibling rivalry. I felt the thrills again with this two-hander featuring Lara Ciulli and Riana White, which refracts sketch comedy (and dance, and confessional) through the lens of queer female friendship. Who knows whether Ciulli and White are lifelong besties, housemates, sometimes-almost lovers? But they defy you to believe otherwise, in a gripping and slippery hour that splays their intimacy, codependency, mutual resentment and few-holds-barred humour across the stage.In a show with a major movement component – they spend much of it all over one another – Those People begins with a mime, of two women crashing their car into a lake, then one rescuing the other. Being one another’s salvation is the subtext of much that follows, as we dip in and out of the malfunctioning relationships in their pasts: the partner who insisted on showing Ciulli his favourite porn scene; the ex who refused to return White’s Calvin Kleins. The latter abstracts into an underwear fever dream, then into a naked breakdance by scene-stealing Ciulli. “You’re being selfish,” protests Riana, stepping out of the show. “OK, and you’re being insecure,” retorts Lara.The bickering feels close to the bone; proximity to real life and its complexities (is this a friendship? Is it a romance?) is the draw here. So too is Ciulli’s charisma and self-delighted flirting with the audience, which is grounded, and just about tolerated, by White.Dan Tiernan: Quartz and All review – a furious comedy show about healing crystalsRead moreThe Wuthering Heights mickey-take is fun, but ancillary to the main event. A filmed ending feels a bit grafted on, and not only because it’s shot against London rather than Edinburgh backdrops. It’s lovely to look at, mind you: often the pleasure here – when the particular meaning of a sequence escapes your grasp – is in the striking stage-pictures, the lack of filter, the rawness of the confused passion on display. An arresting debut.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)TheatreDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSSO/Canellakis review – electrifying trio of women unleash the horror in Strauss’s Elektra  | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Making the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realised
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Making the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realised
Content: Exceptional clarity … conductor Karina Canellakis and BBCSSO in Strauss’s Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalView image in fullscreenExceptional clarity … conductor Karina Canellakis and BBCSSO in Strauss’s Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBBCSSO/Canellakis review – electrifying trio of women unleash the horror in Strauss’s ElektraUsher Hall, EdinburghMaking the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realisedMichael DownesMon 24 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristopher Nolan’s filmThe Odysseycarries a content warning for “strong violence and intense mythological horror”, but even its goriest scenesdo not matchthe mythological horror Richard Strauss produced nearly 120 years earlier inElektra, whose special effects are confined to the 111-piece orchestra. The heckelphones, basset horns and Wagner tubas Strauss adds to an already outsized band makes staging Elektra unfeasible for all but the best-resourced companies. But the extraordinary colours he draws from the orchestra and the storytelling he entrusts to it make concert performances particularly rewarding.View image in fullscreenOutstanding singing from Karen Cargill, Vida Miknevičiūtė and Ingela Brimberg … Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalThe BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra played Strauss’s most dissonant score with relish, responsive toKarina Canellakis’s efficient, economical gestures. Brutal climaxes were suitably overwhelming, but equally striking was the refined string sound in occasional moments of repose. Clarity was exceptional, as whips crackled, flutes fluttered and trombones groaned; balance almost always excellent.All the roles were superbly sung, even the tiniest. Lea Shaw and Emma Morwood were outstanding among the maidservants who launch the action; Lee Bisset,a notable Brunnhilde, shone as their Overseer. Men often receive short shrift in Strauss: here it’s more than an hour before one is heard. But Günther Groissböck’s resonant bass made Oreste’s nobility obvious from the first bar, even if Elektra took longer to cotton on, and tenor John Daszak introduced a note of camp entirely in keeping with the text’s contemptuous depiction of Aegisthus.The evening was dominated, however, by outstanding performances in the three female roles at the heart of the psychodrama.Karen Cargillcompellingly charted Klytämnestra’s breakdown, snarling and sneering without ever compromising vocal beauty. Vida Miknevičiūtė produced the concert’s most radiant singing in her touching portrayal of Chrysothemis, a woman who longs only for the normality of family life. In the notoriously demanding title role, meanwhile, Ingela Brimberg combined seemingly tireless vocal powers with attentiveness to every textual nuance.Everything was as impressively acted as it was sung: devising mise-en-scene without directorial input, singers deployed the small playing space with imagination and eloquence, highlighting the story’s horrors with a focus that even the most elaborate staging – or Hollywood movie – would struggle to match.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsClassical musicBBC Scottish Symphony Orchestralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: On Donetsk’s ‘life or death’ highway with the Khyzhak brigade – photo essay | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehicles
Author: Julia Kochetova
Headline: The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehicles
Content: The road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone nets.The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehiclesByJulia KochetovaMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Holy yeah! Yeaaaah! Done!”Booooooom.“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!” Dzhangofrom the Khyzhak brigade shouts in English. He has just shot down a Russian FPV drone.View image in fullscreenDzhango firing to shoot down a Russian FPV-drone.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenRussian waiting drone after being shot on the road by a mobile firing crewView image in fullscreenDzhango, a shooter, gets ready before the daily shiftView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenDzhango loads a magazine while brushing his teeth in the dugout before the daily shift. Inside the dugout of the mobile firing crew of Khyzhak brigadeView image in fullscreenYoung and Dzhango taking a break after the shift.A small moving target that wants to kill you is a challenge with an asterisk.I don’t manage to photograph the drone above us, but I’m glad that Dzhango shoots more accurately. The normal rule is for everyone else is to stay under cover and not stick your head out.View image in fullscreenThe remains of burned vehicles on the roadView image in fullscreenA ground robot returning from a logistic missionThe tasks of Dzhango’s mobile fire group are different – to stand watch and shoot down Russian drones.The H20 highway runs from the frontline city of Kramatorsk to the battlefield in Kostyantynivka in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The last road always becomes either the “road of life” or the “road of death”. Drone warfare is deadly simple – everything flies toward the road; any movement is a target. Us too.View image in fullscreenThe moon over the roadThe road is covered with scars: FPV drones, cluster munitions, artillery, glide bombs – a map of modern war. Pears on the ground are entangled with fibre-optic cable – this harvest will not be gathered. Anti-drone nets fall on to a highway strewn with burned-out ground robots, pickup trucks, and armoured vehicles. Donetsk is crumbling before my eyes.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenA Russian fibre optic drone flies above the mobile firing crew. Dzhango loads a magazine during the shiftThe fighters of the Khyzhak brigade are police patrol officers who joined up. The five of them share a dugout with Zhuzha, a dog that came to them in search of food and cuddles. A shower, a washbasin, a kitchen, even a plasma TV playing Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us – a parallel universe built underground. The peace sign on Jackson’s T-shirt contrasts with the sound of loading magazines.View image in fullscreenThe mobile firing unit of Khyzhak brigade on dutyView image in fullscreenSoldiers from Khyzhak brigade fire on a Russian drone during the rotation. Borya, a shooter on dutyView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSoldiers stop for a quick chat – they use scooters to drive between positionsAbove, the kill zone, which lives by its own rules: food and water are delivered by ground robots, via electric scooters, or through the sky while Ukrainian Vampire drones carry supply packages above.“We try as much as possible to shoot down whatever is flying toward us. We understand that it’s someone’s ground robot, or someone’s car, or even – someone’s life,”Dzhango tells me.He is 31, from Chernivtsi, which is more than 1,000km away.View image in fullscreenDzhango and Young during a shiftView image in fullscreenDzhango near the ruins of a homeIn the morning he talks to his family on a video call – on the screen there’s a beach, white sand, colourful umbrellas, his son – a parallel world. “What I miss most is my family, my child … living through the coolest moments of his childhood from a distance. His first baby teeth fell out! And I wanted to pull them out with a string, as my father did.”His son knows exactly what Dzhango’s job looks like and asks: “Bring me an FPV!”Dzhango does not bring FPVs home.His son’s birthday is tattooed on his right arm. On the left – a long scar and a tattoo: “Jump off the cliff and wings will grow.” It is a reminder of his father’s advice and of a police shift in Chernivtsi, when he was wounded – three bullets – and his 22-year-old colleague, Taisiia Tataryn, was killed. After a long rehabilitation, he joined the combat unit.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenYoung and Dzhango pass a burned-out scooter. A soldier was injured while driving on it and evacuated from the combat area.
