Fibre optic cable mixed with pears on the ground in Donetsk regionView image in fullscreenRemains of a shot-down Russian FPVEvery morning we walk the same streets and tree lines, but the landscape changes – fresh craters, fallen trees, smoke on the horizon. The remains of drones and munitions form a map of the area – here a Molniya, a Russian kamikaze drone, is stuck in a tree.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe body of a civilian covered with plastic sheeting near the road to Kostyantynivka. The body of a Ukrainian soldier – which was evacuated a few days laterHere – since the beginning of July – a dead civilian has been lying under a black plastic bag. A little further on – a soldier from a neighbouring unit, his body will be evacuated in a couple of days. In the tree line – a burned scooter, an FPV strike; a fighter from another unit was evacuated, but the soldiers will say that he died in hospital that night.View image in fullscreenSoldiers driving on a buggy at high speed, risking being spotted by a drone“Something’s flying!” – within seconds the guys start shooting.Dzhango’s comrade, 41-year-old Young, associates every successful shoot-down with adrenaline and a rush. He served almost eight years in the police and almost two years in the Khyzhak brigade.View image in fullscreenYoung, a shooter from Khyzhak brigade, on duty with the mobile firing crewView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenYoung collecting apricots next to the road. Young taking a breakOn his very first combat mission, two small fragments entered his body; he calls it luck. On the next one – an FPV drone hit the side window of his armoured vehicle – the shaped charge flew inside. “A flash behind me – out of the corner of my eye I see that something exploded inside. Sparks, smoke, you can’t see anything, it’s impossible to breathe,” he recalls.View image in fullscreenOne of his brothers-in-arms died instantly; a second was seriously wounded: “I guess the shaped charge passed through him, and then hit the floor where another fighter was sitting … And it exploded between his legs.”Now his task is to make sure another FPV does not reach his comrades’ vehicle.The only intact building among the erased skeletons of houses is the church.View image in fullscreenDzhango lighting a candle in a damaged churchView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHoly images inside the damaged church near the road to KostyantynivkaA blue eye looks out. Some of the saints are on the floor, others remain by the altar. Dzhango lights a candle – according to tradition, a candle is lit either for the health of the living or for the repose of those no longer here. Half an hour later, the artillery shelling will begin, and the church will come under fire. A week later I receive a short message: “The church burned down.”While waiting for the rotationout, we sit along the highway on scattered chairs and stools under the dense cover of the trees.View image in fullscreenTsygan from Khyzhak brigade is driving soldiers for rotation on the road towards Kostyantynivka, Donetsk regionView image in fullscreenSoldiers from Khyzhak brigade after the rotationDzhango plays Madonna’s Music from his phone, then Justin Timberlake’s Mirrors, and dances a little. From time to time he pauses – to stop and listen whether something is flying.Then he turns the music back on and sings along again.Even in abnormal circumstances, inside war – at least you can always choose the soundtrack.View image in fullscreenThe road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone netsView image in fullscreenA sunset over the road to KostyantynivkaThe next day Dzhango will write saying that they shot down another nine drones.And then – send a video of how another morning in the dugout began with “Good Morning, good morning to you” from the musical Singin’ in the Rain.“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!”, he said.Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayUkraineEuropeRussiaDrones (military)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffin | Photography | The Guardian
description: Bloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then men
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Bloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then men
Content: ‘It made me realise that life is very short’ … Lawrence, left, and Philipp, whose lives are recorded in Chronograph. All photographs: courtesy the artist and Mack.View image in fullscreen‘It made me realise that life is very short’ … Lawrence, left, and Philipp, whose lives are recorded in Chronograph. All photographs: courtesy the artist and Mack.Photography‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffinBloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then menTim JonzeMon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot many family photo albums open with images of the twin towers on fire. But for Nick Haymes, it made perfect sense. “When 9/11 happened,” he says, “I realised life was very short.” At the time, he was living in New York, trying to forge a career, while his friend, colleague and future wife Lina was dealing with the fallout of her previous marriage. “It made us realise we should probably get together and have a family. It was this huge historical event, but on a very micro level, it also shaped my relationship with my wife and children.”Chronograph is a photography book that runs from those terrorist attacks to the present day, tracing the journey of Haymes’s two sons, Philipp and Lawrence, as they grow from drooling babies into young men. We are given a ringside seat as arms get broken, beloved pets die and hairs start sprouting from armpits. The mundane side of life – verrucas, messy kitchens, Lina cleaning out an ear with a cotton bud – is captured in the same way as birthday parties and rites of passage.double quotation markLawrence would joke: ‘You photograph me when I’m crying rather than dealing with it’“Because we lived in this tiny, 800 sq ft apartment in Manhattan, you don’t miss a thing, all the ups and downs, all the mood swings,” says Haymes. “There was no door slamming, because there was nowhere to go!”View image in fullscreenIndeed, we are not spared from seeing the children at their least flattering: “We used to have a running joke where Lawrence would say: ‘You’re the only parent that would photograph me when I’m crying rather than deal with the issue straight away,’” admits Haymes, “but I like to think I was attentive. It was a funny balance because the camera was always around, but it seemed to work.”There are also multiple shots of the boys naked – not just running around the house as young children but as they transition into adulthood too. I suspect most teenagers would not be cool with this, but Haymes insists he had their approval. “They don’t have an issue,” he says. “I’ve been lucky enough to have some very nice photographers in my household at various times, so they’re aware of the creative process.” He shrugs: “There are bigger themes in the book than child nudity. That was just a part of our daily life.”Besides, when Philipp and Lawrence reach their teens – all bleached hair, tattoos and stubble – they work out an ingenious method of rebellion. Instead of sulking or turning away from the camera, Haymes says his kids smiled and put their thumbs up, knowing that the last thing their dad wanted was a posed family portrait. “That was basically their way of telling me to clear out of their lives,” he says.View image in fullscreenBorn in Stratford-upon-Avon, Haymes hoped to study art but ended up dropping out. “I took way too many drugs in my 20s and had a bit of a breakdown,” he says. After couch-surfing in London for a bit, he found work in a photo studio, eventually assisting Jürgen Teller. In 1999, he packed two cameras into a bag and decided to try his luck in New York. It was here he met Lina, a Jewish refugee who, as a teenager, had moved to the US with her parents from Ukraine – then part of the Soviet Union. She was working on a magazine and gave him a commission that allowed him to get a visa and stay.Haymes’s own difficult transition from youth to adulthood is perhaps what draws him to his subjects. Between Dog and Wolf captured his road trips across California and Oklahoma with a group of young skateboarders. Follow-up Gabe TM unfurled over many years hanging out with Gabe Nevins, the teenage star of Gus Van Sant’s Paranoid Park. Unexpectedly, Haymes found himself chronicling Nevins’s homelessness and addiction in the wake of making the movie. Dancing on the Fault Line, published in 2024, was another mammoth excursion, following teenager Love Bailey and her extended queer family right up to her decision to transition in her 30s.Haymes is still in touch with his previous subjects: he shot Bailey’s wedding; Gabe is living a “normal life” now in Oregon; the skaters have children of their own. Haymes doesn’t intend to foster such deep relationships with his subjects. “I always think, ‘Oh, I’ll just do a nice quick shoot.’ But then I get attached to everybody, they become part of my life. You can become a father figure to them, or a therapist maybe. That’s part of it, and that’s part of the educational process for me, just to be with people and understand them.”View image in fullscreenIt was during Covid that Haymes found the time to go through all his family negatives and work out what to do with them. “It moved me pretty heavily,” he says. “I also had to try to be as impartial as I could because I didn’t want it to be saccharine.”Did he know, as he took them, that the photos of his children would end up in a published book? “I suppose, as a photographer, yes. But I really did it for personal memory, and as a little self-analysis. To think about how I was as a parent. Also, I shoot on film and at the time, in the early 2000s, digital photography had kicked in so I was finding myself more and more unemployable. I thought, ‘OK, I am becoming a house husband.’ But I wanted to be a photographer still, so the family life around me is what I photographed.”Besides Lina and the boys, the other key figures in the book are Lina’s parents Nadia and Mikhail. “They werebigcharacters,” says Haymes. “I had to learn how to become a little more emotional and a little more warm and compassionate.”One striking image is of Mikhail sitting with wrapping paper on his head. He’s in a full tracksuit, giving off a slightly intimidatingPaulie Walnutsvibe. “He was a very loving person,” says Haymes, “but yeah, maybe a bit of a rogue. Whereas my mother-in-law had her issues and I think maybe undiagnosed bipolar disorder. She also became a victim of prescription medication in the US, and we had to deal with that. She was certainly a tough mother-in-law, but at some point you fall in love with her anyway.”There are some portentous images in the book. Scars on Mikhail’s stomach mirror Lina’s caesarean scars, although we can only guess why he’s been cut open. Then there is the pet hamster, who we see being held, adored and then grieved for as it rests in its cardboard coffin.View image in fullscreenThe book’s closing passages are extremely moving, as we see Nadia and Mikhail in hospital together, their conditions slowly deteriorating. “We were bringing two people to dialysis every day, which was two pretty gruelling years.” At some point, Haymes converted the home art gallery into a hospice.In the book, it appears as if the couple died at the same time. In reality it was a year apart and the couple had gone through a divorce by that point. “There are things that don’t need to be known,” says Haymes of the story his book tells. “Everybody has a family album, and through those you only remember certain parts.”Despite their divorce, Nadia and Mikhail were buried together in Los Angeles. “I’m not sure if Lina’s father is enjoying that right now, but that’s what happened,” says Haymes with a smile.He says he had been asked to make a photography book of his family for 15 years but it was only when the grandparents died that he realised the project was complete. “The book starts with death and ends with death,” he says. “It’s gone full circle.”Interspersed with beautiful, closeup images of flowers received at the funeral, we see Philipp and Lawrence standing by the graveside with the urn. “For them to be able to communicate those emotions and to speak at a service, for me that felt like, ‘OK, they’re on their own now. They’ve become men.’”He pauses, then laughs like only a father can. “Having said that,” he adds, “they’re still on my Uber account.”Chronograph(SPBH Editions, 2026) by Nick Haymes is published by Mack, £55Explore more on these topicsPhotographyFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: I worked for an infamous clothing brand – but it was one of the most positive workplaces of my life | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Despite its global reputation, my time there felt less sexy party, more wholesome summer camp. Then one day my boss told me a hard truth
Author: Wendy Syfret
Headline: Despite its global reputation, my time there felt less sexy party, more wholesome summer camp. Then one day my boss told me a hard truth
Content: ‘Memories of this time seem to exist in an endless summer, where it was always warm twilight at closing time’: Wendy Syfret with friends in Melbourne, circa 2010.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Memories of this time seem to exist in an endless summer, where it was always warm twilight at closing time’: Wendy Syfret with friends in Melbourne, circa 2010.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesA job that changed meAustralian lifestyleA job that changed me: I worked for an infamous clothing brand – but it was one of the most positive workplaces of my lifeDespite its global reputation, my time there felt less sexy party, more wholesome summer camp. Then one day my boss told me a hard truthWendy SyfretMon 24 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 20.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I tell people I spent a chunk of my early 20s working at a hipster clothing retailer infamous for salacious ads and sexual assault allegations, I’m usually met with scandalised interest. I imagine what they imagine: a harshly lit harem of flesh and vice, where young women were offered up on an altar of mid-priced T-shirts.We had our moments. An occasional visiting corporate lackey would inevitably grind up against one of us while checking a window display. A weekly caller would gasp and choke while asking if we sold women’s underwear. A co-worker inquired whether I’d be interested in going on dates with rich, interesting men for money. It was impossible to ignore the reputation of our store. But it was the 2010s, a strangely liminal time of sexual and social awakening. When we could roll our eyes at the problematic gender politics of our advertisements while never considering wearing a bra to work.But the truth is, despite the global reputation, our little store in Melbourne was one of the most positive workplaces of my life.The store was divided into two tribes: shop assistants – mostly doe-eyed art girls – and backstock workers – mostly charming burnout skaters. While the shop assistants got the most attention and lustful public glares, the weed-scented heart of the store was the backstock room.I was a rare breed: a shop assistant who transitioned to a backstock role, mostly because I couldn’t use a cash register properly.A job that changed me: After years of being a marriage celebrant, I became uneasy with the institutionRead moreDespite technically being a demotion, the move made me the envy of the shop assistants. In backstock we’d listen to music while folding T-shirts and debating Simpsons lore like greasy-haired scholars.After hours we drove around listening to music, slept in each other’s beds, held pizza parties, dated friends of friends, occasionally kissed and sometimes fell in love.Memories of this time seem to exist in an endless summer, where it was always warm twilight at closing time. Even when winter rain flooded through the roof and we mopped up dirty puddles with damaged clearance stock. It felt less like a sexy party and more like wholesome summer camp.Central to this group was our boss, who was barely 30 but held the role of paternal authority. He guided our rambling crew of bleary-eyed adult children through the basic requirements of our jobs.He ran a tight ship. We might have smelled like cheap wine but we worked hard, dutifully memorising our SKU codes and ensuring the dickheads of Melbourne were kept in a steady supply of lamé leggings.After about two years of this heavenly haze, he pulled me aside. Ensconced in piles of chunky acrylic knits, he broke the news: “You have to quit.”I was shocked. Yes, I was famously bad at my job. But his directive wasn’t based on my shirt-folding incompetence.The problem was I loved the job so much I’d never leave.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe knew I wanted to be a writer. Occasionally I’d pick up a passing freelance gig or have a submission accepted. But in the time I’d been working happily at the store, my career had made little progress.With this context, he made something clear that I’d been too afraid to admit to myself: this fantasy life was stopping me from beginning my real one.He pointed out that instead of being satisfied, I was satiated. I had just enough fun to keep me ticking along day after day. This was, he stressed, exactly the kind of job that could trap you.It was a tough lesson, and one I didn’t receive immediately. But slinking away, I reflected on how little I’d actually written. How many days were full of work I liked but hardly lived for.Within a month, I’d applied for an internship that would lead to the job that would shape the rest of my 20s and kickstart my life as a professional writer. It often made me stressed, angry and exhausted, but it also expanded my abilities and sense of self.Fifteen years and many jobs and careers later, I still return to that advice. It’s not that I don’t want to feel comfortable and happy. Rather, I’m aware of the sticky allure of “good enough”. A job, relationship, situation that isn’t actively bad, but isn’t what I truly want or deserve.Although, even now, nothing relaxes me like folding a T-shirt.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleA job that changed meRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A new start after 60: I became a grocer – and feel stronger physically and quieter mentally | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: Robert Solomon loves the early mornings, picking out the apples, tending to the broccoli and fussing up the dandelion greens. At 71, he says it’s the best job he’s had
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Robert Solomon loves the early mornings, picking out the apples, tending to the broccoli and fussing up the dandelion greens. At 71, he says it’s the best job he’s had
Content: ‘One of the big attractions is that it’s a low-fantasy job’ … Robert Solomon in Brooklyn, New York City.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘One of the big attractions is that it’s a low-fantasy job’ … Robert Solomon in Brooklyn, New York City.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianA new start after 60VegetablesA new start after 60: I became a grocer – and feel stronger physically and quieter mentallyRobert Solomon loves the early mornings, picking out the apples, tending to the broccoli and fussing up the dandelion greens. At 71, he says it’s the best job he’s hadPaula CocozzaMon 24 Aug 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Robert Solomon’s working hours were cut during the pandemic – he did building management and tech support for a nonprofit organisation – he got an extra job at a food cooperative, helping to stock the store. It was, he says, the most ordinary job, but that’s what made it special.That job ended with the pandemic, but in 2022 he left the nonprofit and hunted for grocery positions. Now, at 71, he is assistant buyer in produce (ie fruit and vegetables) at an independent market inNew York. “I love the opportunity to do physical, creative work with my body, hands and mind,” he says. “I’m working harder than I have since my 30s, and I love it.”Solomon’s favourite time of day is the morning. He often starts at 5.30am or 6am. “I put the rugs back on the floor and the carts out in the yard. And then I start stocking.” Certain products make him particularly happy.“I like fussing up the dandelion greens,” he says. (Though dandelions are often considered weeds, both leaves and roots are edible.) “I have a little bucket of water and I swish them around head first so they’re fresher again. We have to restock broccoli many times a day, and I like that.” When it’s in order, “it makes a sea of broccoli”. We are speaking on a video call, and Solomon lifts his phone to the camera to show waves of blue-green broccoli heads.“The work requires good attention,” he says.By “attention” he means his mind doesn’t wander too often. “One of the big attractions is that it’s a low-fantasy job. I spend most of my time working, not fantasising about what a wonderful job I’m doing and how I’ll get famous for it next year.“My political belief is that all work is important,” he says.Solomon grew up in Brooklyn, five miles from the shop. His mother was a musician turned director of a daycare centre, his father a professor of art history. “They were first-generation immigrants from Russia, and to them it was a step up to be doing something technical or managerial.” His father “probably” wanted Solomon to be a scientist.Solomon left school at 17. He had stints at night school but got his degree at 46“with independent study and life credits”. For most of his working life, he was “a house painter, handyman and cabinet maker”. After the degree he worked for a neighbour’s company that sold energy-efficient lighting solutions, and had two stints at the nonprofit.View image in fullscreenApples of his eye … Solomon handles the produce.Photograph: Tobias Everke/The GuardianThrough it all, he says, “I kept trying to change my job to a better job, and it just didn’t work for me.” At various times he aspired to become a computer programmer, an interfaith minister and a nurse practitioner. “In each case things went terribly wrong.”At an interview to be an emergency medical technician, having scored an A on the course, Solomon was asked if he would cross a picket line. “No way,” he said. “My mother would roll over in her grave.” He watched his application drop into the bin.Sometimes Solomon has a feeling his late parents would disapprove of his grocery job. But recently he’s remembered one of his mother’s sayings when he’d pitch a tantrum: “Stop running around like a chicken with your head cut off!”Solomon thought that impossible, but she explained that “when she was a girl, they had a little shop on the porch of their home. When my mother would get home, my grandfather would take a break, and if someone came in for a chicken, she would have to kill it.”Solomon doesn’t handle poultry, but in his produce work “all these things I learned from her that she didn’t mean to teach me are coming back. … She knew how to clean lettuce and she knew how to pick a good apple. I’m like: ‘That’s how I know all of this.’”Initially shop work was challenging. On the subway home, it was hard to stand up again. “But now it feels fine,” he says. “I feel quieter mentally. My knees hurt less. I feel stronger.“There are no guarantees on how long I will be able to work. But I think this is the best employment I’ve had. It’s an appreciation of good things.”Tell us: has your life taken a new direction after the age of 60?Explore more on these topicsVegetablesA new start after 60FruitFoodUS work & careersOlder peopleNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Which eco-friendly laundry detergents actually clean your clothes? I put 11 to the test | Homes | The Guardian
description: Our writer spent weeks putting capsules, sheets and liquid detergent through their paces to find the best for your clothes and the planet
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Our writer spent weeks putting capsules, sheets and liquid detergent through their paces to find the best for your clothes and the planet
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHomesReviewWhich eco-friendly laundry detergents actually clean your clothes? I put 11 to the testOur writer spent weeks putting capsules, sheets and liquid detergent through their paces to find the best for your clothes and the planetSustainable cleaning subscriptions that make life easierJane HoskynMon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNothing makes falling into bed more enjoyable than freshly laundered sheets, especially if they’ve just been dried in the sunshine. It’s a definite bonus, though, to know your clean bedding won’t bring you out in a rash or pollute your local river.Laundry detergent can be a troublesome product. A few years ago, I suffered a full-body rash after using pound-shop detergent on my sheets. I switched to a big-brand product and never had a reaction again, but there’s still the question of whether its ingredients may be causing environmental harm after they’ve gone down the drain.The sulphates, phosphonates and bleaches that many detergents use to remove stains and brighten fabric can cause lastingenvironmental damage, especially to aquatic life. I’m lucky enough to live next to the sea, and the output of my washing machine is unlikely to be doing it much good.Brands such as Smol, Ecover and Bio-D claim to be eco-friendly alternatives, but can they tackle dirty laundry as well as standard detergents – and are they as green as they say? To find out, I challenged 11 of them to clean my clothes, soften my sheets and remove stains, including makeup, raspberry juice and ground-in mud. Here are the ones that rose to the challenge, and those that were no more effective than using nice-smelling water.At a glanceBest laundry detergent overallSmolBio capsules, 24£6 at SmolBest budget laundry detergentEcoeggLaundry egg, 70 washes£9.99 at AmazonBest-smelling laundry detergentEcoverNon-bio laundry liquid, 1.43l£7.35 at AmazonBest laundry detergent for sensitive skinBio-DFragrance-free laundry liquid, 1l£5 at OcadoWhy you should trust meI’ve spent decades writing about products, from smartphones tohay fever remedies, so I’m professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically improve our lives by buying their stuff. Given how long I’ve been testingduvets,blankets,mattressesand theirtoppersand other washable homewares for the Filter, it’s about time I found the best way to launder them.How I testedView image in fullscreenMessy business: a towel was stained with everything from mud to ketchup to compare each detergent’s cleaning power.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianInevitably, there was a lot of washing. To fairly compare all these detergents on key variables, including stain removal, fabric softness and lasting fragrance, I spent three weeks running my washing machine twice a day. At about 5kg per load and 22 loads, that’s more than 100kg of soggy laundry in the name of Filter research.Before any socks could get washed, though, I had to choose and source my test detergents. I scoured ingredients lists and company information for evidence of ethical and environmental kudos, including certifications from bodies such asB Corp,Allergy UKand theVegan Society. I also looked for sustainable packaging, innovative ways to reduce weight and waste, and bottles that could be refilled without buying more plastic.My house is no science lab, but I did what I could to ensure that my testing was fair and thorough. I devoted one day each to 11 detergents across three weeks. Each time, I used the detergent to wash two sets of laundry in my standard front-loading Beko washing machine. One load was 2kg of clothes that included sweaty running kit, underwear and coloured T-shirts, washed at 20C. The larger 4kg load was washed at 40C and contained white items, including a duvet cover and a large white towel that was my stain-test guinea pig.Each morning, I daubed the poor towel with mucky substances, includingliquid foundation, tomato ketchup, cat food, garden mud and a juicy squashed raspberry. I photographed the blotches before and after washing, then used them to compare how the detergents removed dirt.Other factors were more subjective. I’m not a perfume-wearer, but I love a gently fresh fragrance from my laundry, as long as its source doesn’t bother my skin. I buried my nose in every load of laundry when it was fresh from the machine, and then again when it was dry. I put a couple of freshly laundered socks aside each time, then sniffed them again after a few days to see how well the scent had lingered.Price was important, too. Laundry detergent can get expensive, especially for families. I calculated the price per wash for a small (2kg) load, but also awarded value-for-money kudos to detergents that never needed a double dose.I was left with a little spare after testing, so I was able to donate the detergents toYellow Door, my local domestic abuse refuge.The best laundry detergentView image in fullscreenClean sweep: 11 eco-friendly detergents were tested on items from sweaty running kit to stubborn stains.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianBest laundry detergent overall:Smol bio capsulesSmolBio capsules, 24£6£6 at SmolWhat we loveExcellent cleaning power using fewer chemicals by weightWhat we don’t loveNot chemical free, and only available on subscriptionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£6 for 24 capsules at SmolAll I really want from a detergent is clean laundry and good eco credentials. Smol triumphs on the first of these key factors and does well on the second. With B Corp certification, it’s a solid eco choice. It doesn’t quite score five stars, though: Smol isn’t entirely free of hazardous ingredients, and you can only get it on subscription.Why we love itSmol’s subscription isn’t a contract, so you’re not tied into a payment trap, and you can order a one-off box (you just pay postage for the “free” nine-capsule introductory offer; mine was £1.99). Regular deliveries mean you won’t run out of detergent or ever need to lug it back from the shops, and you can skip or pause whenever you want.The detergent was my favourite by far. Smol’s capsulescontain chemicals, including some derived from fossil fuels, which is probably why Smol can say it uses“less chemicals”than big brands. It works, too: in the 40C stain test, Smol was the only detergent to remove any trace of the mud I’d ground into my towel. With my 20C load, my clothes emerged outstandingly bright and clean.Everything smelled delightful, and that was important for me. Smol doesn’t give its detergent’s fragrance a name, but says it’s “unique to Smol” and created using what the brand claims are ethically sourced essential oils, including orange, pine, elemi, lavender and patchouli. If you’re a fan of punchy fragrances, you may want to add fabric softener for extra scent, but I loved the gentle, soothing aroma that lasted for days.It’s a shame that …Smol’s concentrated formula is slightly lower on harmful chemicals rather than free of them, like a natural or plant-based detergent would be. The company is transparent about its ingredients, though (here’s the full list), and there are no parabens, phosphates or phthalates. It’s also a shame that you can’t buy Smol at the shops.Type:bio, non-bio or fragrance-free capsules (I tested non-bio)Size:24 capsulesMaximum loads:24Price per load:25pScent tested:standard Smol fragrance using orange, pine and other essential oilsSustainability:B Corp certified, concentrated formula, certified free of microplastics, 100% plastic-free packaging (sustainable FSC-approved cardboard)Certified cruelty-free?YesVegan?YesSmolBio capsules, 24£6£6 at SmolWhat we loveExcellent cleaning power using fewer chemicals by weightWhat we don’t loveNot chemical free, and only available on subscriptionBest budget laundry detergent:Ecoegg laundry eggEcoeggLaundry egg, 70 washesfrom£9.99£9.99 at Lakeland£9.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value and convenience; good eco-credentialsWhat we don’t loveNot the strongest on stainsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£9.99 for 70 washes at Lakeland£9.99 for 70 washes at AmazonThis refillable egg-shaped plastic cage looks like it should come filled with Maltesers for Easter. Instead, you fill it with the supplied “mineral pellets”, a mixture of tourmaline and detergent pellets, snap it shut and plonk it in with your laundry for up to 70 washes, all for less than a tenner. A full70-wash refillcosts an even more impressive £6.65.Why we love itThe 70-wash lifespan of each Ecoegg mineral pack is more than double that of most products in this test. If you live on your own and don’t roll around in mud too often, one Ecoegg could last all year. It’s also the most convenient detergent in my whole test: no liquid mess, no plasticky pods.There’s a sustainability claim baked into Ecoegg’s name, which is surprising for a product made from plastic and containing cleaning agents. The name is more than justified, though, not least because the egg itself is refillable and can be used for years. The mineral pellets are free of phosphonates, sulphates and parabens, and I didn’t suffer any skin trouble with the “fresh linen” fragrance pellets I tested, but if you’re particularly sensitive, there is afragrance-free editiontoo, which is approved by Allergy UK.My Ecoegg did a fine job of cleaning underwear, de-stinking running kit and leaving my bedsheets feeling soft and smelling fresh, which is impressive for a detergent that works out at 14p a wash for a small load.It’s a shame that …the detergent wasn’t powerful or sudsy enough to remove stains in one wash in my hard-water area. The makeup, mud and raspberry marks on my white towel remained noticeable.Type:non-bio mineral pelletsSize:1 eggMaximum loads:70 before it needs refillingPrice per load:14pScent tested:fresh linenSustainability:no phosphates or parabens,refill pelletsavailable, FSC-certified cardboard packaging, Allergy UK-approved fragrance-free rangeCertified cruelty-free?No, but claims to be cruelty-freeVegan?YesEcoeggLaundry egg, 70 washesfrom£9.99£9.99 at Lakeland£9.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value and convenience; good eco-credentialsWhat we don’t loveNot the strongest on stainsBest-smelling laundry detergent:Ecover non-bio laundry liquidEcoverNon-bio laundry liquid, 1.43lfrom£7.35£11.01 at Big Green Smile£7.35 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value; super sudsy; laundry smells divineWhat we don’t loveSulphates could cause sensitive skin reactionsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£11.01 for 1.43l at Big Green Smile£7.35 for 1.43l at AmazonAs well as ticking all the right aroma boxes, Ecover is also one of the best-value products I tested, especially as it’s so often available for less than its £10 RRP. Its cleaning performance is excellent, too, and its formula is lower in hazardous chemicals than its big-name rivals.Why we love itEcover’s 1.43l bottle is not bad value even at its full price, and in my washing test I found that a little goes a long way. Not only did one capful of this detergent create the most impressive suds of all the detergents in my test, despite me living in a hard water area, but it also rinsed away completely to leave my fabrics looking bright and smelling unbelievably good. Stain removal was well above average, with mud, cat food and ketchup all washing away – although raspberry and the makeup left shadowy marks.Ecover achieved these impressive results with a formula that uses rapidly biodegradable ingredients, excludes phosphates and optical brighteners, and largely avoids petrochemical ingredients derived from fossil fuels. Its fragrances, too, are 50% naturally derived – and the lavender and sandalwood variety was my favourite in the whole test. It’s not overpowering (some may find it too subtle, in fact), and it lifted my mood and lingered for days.It’s a shame that …Ecover contains sodium lauryl sulphate and laureth-7, which may trigger reactions in sensitive skin (I didn’t suffer any). Some organisations, including the UK-basedNaturewatch Foundation, have urged stockists and consumers to boycott Ecover after it was bought by SC Johnson, which tests on animals, but Ecover itself is stillcertified cruelty-free.Type:non-bio liquidSize:1.43lMaximum loads:40Price per load:from about 18pScent tested:lavender and sandalwoodSustainability:factory certified platinumzero wastebyTrue, bottles are made from 100% post-consumer recycled plastic (caps 50%),refillsavailableCertified cruelty-free?YesVegan?YesEcoverNon-bio laundry liquid, 1.43lfrom£7.35£11.01 at Big Green Smile£7.35 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value; super sudsy; laundry smells divineWhat we don’t loveSulphates could cause sensitive skin reactionsBest laundry detergent for sensitive skin:Bio-D fragrance-free laundry liquidBio-DFragrance-free laundry liquid, 1lfrom£5£5 at Ocado£6.35 at Abel & ColeWhat we loveKind to fabric and skin; cleans wellWhat we don’t loveWon’t shift stubborn stains, including mudView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£5 for 1l at Ocado£6.35 for 1l at Abel & ColeBio-D’s fragrance-free liquid is the only other detergent in my test to be accredited by Allergy UK. Despite being fragrance-free, it left my clothes and sheets smelling fresh. Its biodegradable formula is great for delicates, not least because it’s designed to be used at low temperatures, but like Ecoegg, it struggled to shift my stubborn stains.Why we love itI confess I was surprised by how well Bio-D’s naturally derived formula cleaned my laundry. The gentle liquid left my stinky running kit smelling and feeling wonderfully clean even at 20C, and it generated enough suds to be effective for hand-washing, too. My fabrics looked bright but didn’t feel as soft as with some of the other detergents. If you’re after softness and fragrance, Bio-D’slavender fabric conditioneris worth adding.It’s a shame that …my ground-in mud, makeup and raspberry stains sailed through almost untouched, so this may not be your first choice of detergent if you have to deal with lots of mucky school shirts.Type:non-bio liquidSize:1lMaximum loads:25Price per load:from about 20pScent tested:fragrance-freeSustainability:B Corp certified, bottles made from 100% post-consumer recycled plastic (except caps), solar-powered manufacture, fully traceable ingredients, refills available, Allergy UK-approved fragrance-free rangeCertified cruelty-free?YesVegan?YesBio-DFragrance-free laundry liquid, 1lfrom£5£5 at Ocado£6.35 at Abel & ColeWhat we loveKind to fabric and skin; cleans wellWhat we don’t loveWon’t shift stubborn stains, including mudThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Beautifully packaged and left my towel smelling sensational’: Eat Dirt non-bio laundry liquid.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianIneos non-bio laundry liquidIneosNon-bio laundry liquid, 1lfrom£6.98£6.98 at Asda£7 at TescoWhat we lovePlant-based; fruity fragrance; good cleaning powerWhat we don’t loveNot chemical-free as its “plant powered” tag suggestsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£6.98 for 1l at Asda£7 for 1l at TescoBest for:families who need reliable cleaning without a big price tagIneos is well priced for a detergent that beat most others in fading my dreaded raspberry stain. It also left my sweaty running kit smelling gorgeous after a mere 20C wash.Ineos is not quite what I’d call an eco detergent, but it does take a few steps in the right direction. Ineos contains some plant-based ingredients (just enough to warrant its claim of being “plant powered”) and omits phosphonates and optical brighteners, but the formula still contains synthetic ingredients, includingone that’s harmful to aquatic life.It didn’t make the final cut because …I would have liked the lovely fragrance to last longer than a day.Type:non-bio liquid;size:1l;maximum loads:33;price per load:from about 21p;scent tested:rhubarb and pomegranate;sustainability:some plant-based cleansing ingredients,bulk sizesavailable;certified cruelty-free?Yes;vegan?YesIneosNon-bio laundry liquid, 1lfrom£6.98£6.98 at Asda£7 at TescoWhat we lovePlant-based; fruity fragrance; good cleaning powerWhat we don’t loveNot chemical-free as its “plant powered” tag suggestsMethod concentrated laundry liquidMethodConcentrated laundry liquid, 33 washesfrom£5.79£8.50 at Big Green Smile£5.79 at AmazonWhat we loveGood value and works well on stainsWhat we don’t loveScent won’t suit everyone; not especially greenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£8.50 for 990ml at Big Green Smile£5.79 for 990ml at AmazonBest for:anyone who wants their detergent to act like a second perfumeMethod is Ecover’s sister product, and its eco credentials include recycled bottles, cruelty-free testing and a formula designed to work at lower temperatures. However, it contains many of the standard synthetic detergent ingredients.On the upside, it’s a capable cleaner with a strong, lasting floral scent that many will love. The bottle’s a bit dribbly, but once I managed to get the liquid into my washing machine, it made an excellent attempt at removing the raspberry stain in a single 40C cycle.It didn’t make the final cut because …owned by US conglomerate SC Johnson, Method is not a particularly eco-friendly choice thanks to ingredients including laureth-7, sulphates and optical brighteners.Type:bio liquid;size:990ml;maximum loads:up to 33;price per load:20p;scent tested:peony blush;sustainability:100% recycled plastic bottle (except cap);certified cruelty-free?Yes;vegan?YesMethodConcentrated laundry liquid, 33 washesfrom£5.79£8.50 at Big Green Smile£5.79 at AmazonWhat we loveGood value and works well on stainsWhat we don’t loveScent won’t suit everyone; not especially greenMiniml non-bio laundry liquidMinimlNon-bio laundry liquid, 1lfrom£5.59£5.59 at Big Green Smile£6.99 at RegnWhat we loveFully biodegradable; leaves clothes feeling softWhat we don’t loveNot strong enough to shift stubborn stainsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£5.59 for 1l at Big Green Smile£6.99 for 1l at RegnBest for:families, and children sensitive to cleaning chemicalsMiniml’s biodegradable formula contains almost entirely (99%+) plant-based ingredients – for example, a coconut-derived surfactant – and felt gentle on my skin and fabrics. It did a fine job of freshening up and softening my clothes and sheets, although it couldn’t rescue my longsuffering stained towel. I expect it would take a few more washes before the slightly faded marks stop being noticeable.It didn’t make the final cut because …the gentleness of Miniml makes it a great family choice, and it can even be used for hand-washing, but it may admit defeat against a muddy school kit.Type:non-bio liquid;size:1l;max loads:33;price per load:from about 17p;scent tested:dragon fruit and orchid;sustainability:biodegradable formula, bottles made from recycled plastic (except lids) and refill pouches and 5l bottles are free to return,refillshave aclosed-loop supply chainfor zero waste, factory runs on renewable energy, B Corp certification pending;certified cruelty-free?Yes;vegan?YesMinimlNon-bio laundry liquid, 1lfrom£5.59£5.59 at Big Green Smile£6.99 at RegnWhat we loveFully biodegradable; leaves clothes feeling softWhat we don’t loveNot strong enough to shift stubborn stainsFaith in Nature laundry liquidFaith in NatureLaundry liquid, 1lfrom£8.07£9.99 at Faith in Nature£8.07 at AmazonWhat we loveGentle on sensitive skin, B Corp certifiedWhat we don’t loveNot powerful on stains; squirting gets messyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£9.99 for 1l at Faith in Nature£8.07 for 1l at AmazonBest for:eco-conscious householders who want a full range of green cleaning productsFaith in Nature, which has B Corp certification, makes all sorts of plant-derived household cleaning products that can be refilled. As with Ecover, it contains laureth-7, which may trigger sensitive skin, but I didn’t suffer any reactions. It smelled delicious, felt soft and looked bright.As with many of the detergents made largely from plant-derived ingredients, though, Faith in Nature couldn’t remove my makeup and raspberry stains. I faded them slightly by spot-cleaning with a little of the detergent, but that still didn’t shift the marks completely. I think the lesson here is that if you want to wash with truly green detergent, don’t get makeup on your clothes.It didn’t make the final cut because …I just couldn’t work out how to squirt the liquid into my machine’s drawer without dribbling it all over my hands.Type:non-bio liquid;size:1l;maximum loads:30;price per load:about 33p;scent:aloe vera and rosemary;sustainability:B Corp certified, recycled plastic bottle, larger 5l and 20l bottles can be returned for free,refillsavailable;certified cruelty-free?Yes;vegan?YesFaith in NatureLaundry liquid, 1lfrom£8.07£9.99 at Faith in Nature£8.07 at AmazonWhat we loveGentle on sensitive skin, B Corp certifiedWhat we don’t loveNot powerful on stains; squirting gets messyEat Dirt non-bio laundry liquidEat DirtNon-bio laundry liquid, 1l£24.75£24.75 at Eat DirtWhat we loveSustainable ingredients; lovely scent and packagingWhat we don’t loveExpensive, especially if you don’t subscribeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£24.75 for 1l at Eat DirtBest for:anyone who’d like to display their detergent as well as use itNewcomer Eat Dirt is one of the most beautifully packaged products I’ve seen. Its one-litre tin is much easier to recycle than a plastic bottle, but I’d rather hang it on the wall or use it as a vase. It’s a glorious piece of visual design, although I did find it a pain to open.Once I managed to get a capful of liquid into my machine’s drawer, I was struck by its delicious smell. Its cleaning agents are reassuringly green too, although there are a few standard detergent ingredients, such as the preservative phenoxyethanol. It left my clothes looking clean and bright and feeling soft, and although it couldn’t shift the makeup and raspberry stains, it left my towel smelling sensational.It didn’t make the final cut because …Eat Dirt is expensive, especially if you only want a one-off rather than a monthly subscription. It’s aiming to be available in stores soon, though, and I’m hoping that will bring the price down.Type:non-bio liquid;size:1l;maximum loads:50;price per load:50p;scent tested:bitter orange;sustainability:mostly naturally sourced ingredients, recyclable tin, often delivered in secondhand boxes;certified cruelty-free?No, but claims to be cruelty-free;vegan?YesEat DirtNon-bio laundry liquid, 1l£24.75£24.75 at Eat DirtWhat we loveSustainable ingredients; lovely scent and packagingWhat we don’t loveExpensive, especially if you don’t subscribeNimble Cares laundry detergent sheetsNimble CaresLaundry detergent sheets, 30 sheetsfrom£19£19 at Nimble Cares£19.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLight and easy to use; kind to skin and fabricsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and not particularly powerfulView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£19 for 30 sheets at Nimble Cares£19.99 for 30 sheets at AmazonBest for:saving space and spills in your cleaning cupboardLaundry sheets are like slightly spongy pieces of A5 paper infused with detergent and designed to dissolve in your washing. They’re easy to use, and they’re much lighter than liquid or pods, so they score sustainability points for being less carbon-intensive to transport (although they are being shipped from China).I loved the lightweight logistics of Nimble Cares’ sheets, but I was slightly disappointed by their cleaning power. I used a whole sheet on my large load (half a sheet is recommended for small loads), and it still couldn’t shift the mud, makeup or raspberry. My fabrics did feel soft, though, and the use of allergen-free perfume is helpful if you have sensitive skin.It didn’t make the final cut because …even if you stick with the half-sheet recommendation for smaller loads, this is a pricey detergent. Nimble’s failure to publish information about its use of toxic chemicals falls short of theGood Shopping Guide’s ethical benchmark.Type: non-bio detergent sheets;size:30 sheets;maximum loads:60;price per load:from about 26p;scent tested:spring blossom;sustainability:mainly plant-based ingredients, no plastic in product or packaging, light weight reduces carbon footprint;certified cruelty-free?No, but claims to be cruelty-free;vegan?YesNimble CaresLaundry detergent sheets, 30 sheetsfrom£19£19 at Nimble Cares£19.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLight and easy to use; kind to skin and fabricsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and not particularly powerfulDr Beckmann Magic Leaves non-bioDr BeckmannMagic Leaves non-bio, 25 sheetsfrom£3.50£3.50 at Sainsbury’s£3.50 at AmazonWhat we loveGood on stains and great value for moneyWhat we don’t loveFormula is based on standard synthetic ingredientsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£3.50 for 25 sheets at Sainsbury’s£3.50 for 25 sheets at AmazonBest for:families regularly dealing with muddy school uniformsDr Beckmann describes its new sheets as “a great eco choice” because they have less packaging than powder or liquids, but their ingredients are pretty standard detergent fare, including sulphates, perfumes and chemicals that are “harmful to aquatic life with long lasting effects”.On cleaning power, though, Magic Leaves do well. The dissolved sheet fought a particularly winning battle with my ground-in mud – a weak spot for the eco-liquids – and left my whites looking bright. Its results didn’t outclass Smol’s, though, and Smol ticks far more sustainability and ethical boxes with B Corp and Leaping Bunny certifications and plastic-free packaging.It didn’t make the final cut because …despite the green claims, its ingredients are pretty standard laundry detergent fare. You’re hit by the familiar old laundry detergent smell the moment you open the packet.Type:non-bio sheets;size:25 sheets;maximum loads:up to 50;price per load:from about 7p;scent tested:fresh breeze;sustainability:biodegradable, lightweight packaging reduces transport emissions;certified cruelty-free?No;vegan?YesDr BeckmannMagic Leaves non-bio, 25 sheetsfrom£3.50£3.50 at Sainsbury’s£3.50 at AmazonWhat we loveGood on stains and great value for moneyWhat we don’t loveFormula is based on standard synthetic ingredientsWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenInside job: Ecoegg’s mineral tourmaline balls offer a different approach to conventional laundry detergent.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianHow can I tell if a laundry detergent is sustainable?Limit your sustainability expectations if you want clean laundry. “I don’t think any detergent can ever be completely sustainable, because there will always be an environmental impact somewhere along the line,” says Ross Osborne, sustainability director at cleaning supplies companyJangro. “The more honest question is whether one detergent is more sustainable than another.“You have to look at the whole picture. That includes the ingredients, how biodegradable they are, their potential effect on aquatic life, how much product is needed, the packaging, where it has been manufactured, how far it has travelled and whether it actually works.”In my testing, I was impressed to discover how well many of the detergents cleaned my laundry using non-synthetic and biodegradable cleaning agents. These include naturally derived surfactants (as used by Bio-D, Miniml and others) and the mineral tourmaline (as used by Ecoegg), plus essential oils for fragrance (as used by Smol).A vital factor is a detergent’s ability to clean at cool settings, says Lauren Hill, product manager at appliance manufacturerHaier. “Detergents designed for lower temperatures reduce the energy used during the washing cycle. Also consider concentrated formulas that contain less water and require smaller packaging, which reduces transport emissions.”Other steps in the right direction include plastic-free and refillable containers, recycled bottles (not just “recyclable”), and innovations such as lightweight laundry sheets, which can help reduce transport emissions. One of the most original sustainability measures I encountered during this test wasEat Dirt’s decision to often deliver its products in used boxes, eBay-style. That shows an imagination and lack of brand vanity I wish others would follow.Bio vs non-bio detergentsBio (biological) detergents may sound more environmentally treacherous than non-bio, but that’s not necessarily the case. It just means they contain enzymes (usually protease, amylase and lipase) that help break down common stains such as food, sweat and blood. Enzyme-based products can be an effective bleach-free way to clean around the house. As a cat owner, I swear by theNaturally Goneenzyme spray for getting rid of the dreaded “cat wee” whiffs.“Enzymes are a good example of a biodegradable cleaning agent that actually works,” says Osborne. “Different enzymes deal with different types of soiling. Proteases help break down protein-based stains, amylases work on starch and lipases tackle fats and oils. This helps a detergent clean effectively at a lower temperature rather than relying on hotter water or larger quantities of conventional chemistry.”Repeatedstudieshave found that enzymes can trigger reactions in people with eczema or sensitive skin, though, so if that applies to you or your kids, you may be better off sticking with non-bio detergents. Non-bio formulas can still rely on potentially hazardous surfactants such as sodium laureth sulphate, so look for naturally derived surfactants – such as the coconut-based ingredients cocamidopropyl betaine, lauramine oxide and cocos nucifera oil inMiniml– if your skin can’t tolerate bio formulas and you’re trying to shop sustainably.For more, read oureasy plastic-free kitchen swapsand thebest refillable beauty productsJane Hoskyn is a features journalist with three decades of experience rearranging bookshelves and “testing” gadgets while deadlines loom. She would always rather be running in the woods, which is probably why she needs to wash her clothes so oftenExplore more on these topicsHomesThe FilterEthical and green livingInteriorsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Courgette kraut and fermented pepper sauce: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s Czech pickle recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: In an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-round
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-round
Content: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s courgette kraut.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenŠárka Otevřel Camrdová’s courgette kraut.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodCourgette kraut and fermented pepper sauce: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s Czech pickle recipesIn an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-roundŠárka Otevřel CamrdováMon 24 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePreserving the abundance of summer produce is a wonderful way to extend the season long after the gardens have faded. Opening a jar in the colder months offers more than just something good to eat; it also holds joy, patience and memories. When winter comes knocking, we are ready with something sweet, sour or salty waiting on the shelf, reminding us that summer will return and the sun will shine again.Courgette krautWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThis kraut can be used much like traditional sauerkraut, though its flavour is milder and its texture more delicate. Sauteed with onions in a little butter or lard, it makes an excellent accompaniment to roast meats and sausages; it can also be added to potato pancakes or used as a filling for savoury pies and pastries.Prep5 minCook40 minFerment2 weeksMakes3-4x 650ml jars2kgcourgettes2tbsp (25g) granulated sugar1½tbsp (25g) salt65mldistilled white vinegar(8% acidity)1½tsp caraway seeds, crushedWash the unpeeled courgettes and pat them dry. Cut the courgettes in half lengthways, scrape out the seeds and shred or coarsely grate the flesh into a bowl.Mix the sugar, salt and vinegar, then pour this over the courgettes. Sprinkle in the caraway seeds, mix well and set aside for 15-30 minutes. Adjust the seasoning to taste, adding sugar or vinegar as required.Transfer the courgettes to sterilised jars, leaving a space of about 2cm between the veg and the rim of the jar, and making sure everything is completely covered in the liquid. Cover the jars tightly, place them on a rack or folded tea towel in a large pot, add warm water until it comes about three-quarters of the way up the sides of the jars, and keep at a steady at 85-90C (185-195F) for 15 minutes. Carefully lift out the jars, leave to cool completely, then store in a cool, dark place for about two weeks before use.Fermented bell pepper sauceWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenŠárka Otevřel Camrdová’s fermented bell pepper sauce.You can modify this recipe to suit your taste, by using different types of bell peppers, for example, or replacing some of the peppers with tomatoes, or adding other herbs and spices. You can also use this recipe to make your own hot sauce – just replace the bell peppers with chilli peppers. Fermented bell pepper sauce has a flavour that is reminiscent of the Balkan red pepper condimentajvar, which means you can use it in a similar way: as a sauce for grilled meat and kebabs, burgers or sandwiches; as a dip for different vegetable side dishes; as an accompaniment for bulgur and couscous; or spread it on toast.Prep15 minCook30 minFerment5 days+Makes3 x750ml bottles1lwater1tbsp (20g) salt6 red or orange bell peppers,halved lengthways, stalks, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh washed and cut into chunks3 sprigsflat-leaf parsley, or lovage1 onion,peeled and cut into wedges3-5garlic cloves,peeled and halved3-6 bay leaves(optional)To make the brine, put the water in a saucepan, bring to a boil, then leave to cool completely. Add the salt and stir until it’s all dissolved.Divide the pepper pieces between three sterilised jars, then add a parsley sprig, a few pieces of onion and garlic, and a bay leaf or two, if using, to each one. Leave at least a 3cm gap between the contents of the jar and the rim. Pour the brine over the vegetables – the pepper pieces should be completely covered to prevent contact with the air, so, if need be, use a sterilised fermentation weight to keep them in place. Leave some space between the salt solution and the rim of the jar to allow room for the formation of foam on the surface of the liquid.Close the jars with their lids, but do not tighten them. Put the jars on a tray or baking sheet and leave in a dark place at room temperature (preferably at 18-21C/65-70F) to ferment for five to seven days: the exact time will depend on the temperature of the room (a warmer temperature speeds up the fermentation process). Check and taste the contents of the jars regularly (always use an impeccably clean fork) – the peppers are ready when no more bubbles form or the foam dissipates, and they should now have a pleasantly sour and mildly spicy taste.Fine-strain the contents of the jars and collect the liquid. Discard the bay leaves. Puree the vegetables and herbs until thick and creamy, diluting the sauce, if need be, with some of the reserved liquid. Fill sterilised bottles with the sweet pepper sauce and use immediately or store in the fridge.These recipes are edited extracts from God is a Pickle: Recipes and Stories for Preserving the Seasons – A Culinary Journey Through the Czech Republic, byŠárka Otevřel Camrdová, published by Gestalten at £35. To order a copy for £31.50, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodEastern European food and drinkVegetablesPickling, fermenting and preservingSide dishesHerbs and spicesextractsShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos | Snacks | The Guardian
description: A fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alike
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alike
Content: Georgina Hayden’s charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Quick and easySnacksGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachosA fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alikeGeorgina HaydenMon 24 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCorn is a late-summer staple in our house, but its arrival often leaves me feeling a little blue (end of summer and all that). So, instead, I like to entertain more and make the most of the warm, light evenings. These nachos are a great snack for adults and kids alike (just adjust the chilli for younger palates), and a solid base that can be tweaked any which way. Have some lovely ripe tomatoes to hand? Chop them up and throw them in, too. Avocados at their peak? A side of guacamole would be a dream. Got a well-stocked spice cupboard? Add a little sweet smoked paprika and even some crushed coriander seeds to the fried beans. Make it to your liking and pantry, and enjoy with friends, ideally in the evening sun.Charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachosWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook20 minServes4-62 ears of corn, kernels cut off the core2 tbsp vegetable oil200g tinnedblack beans, drained and rinsed (net weight)½ tsp cumin seeds, lightly groundSea salt andblack pepper2 limes½ bunch coriander, finely chopped2jalapeños, or green chillies, stalks, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped200g tortilla chips75g grated mozzarella100g mature cheddar, gratedSouredcream, to servePut a large frying pan on a high heat, add the corn and fry for five to 10 minutes, until the kernels start to char. Transfer to a large bowl.Pour the vegetable oil into the pan, then add the black beans and ground cumin, and season well. Fry on a high heat for about five minutes, until the beans start to crisp up and pop a little, then tip into the bowl of charred corn.Finely grate in the zest of one of the limes, and squeeze in the juice of one and a half limes. Add most of the chopped coriander and chilli, then toss well. Tweak and adjust the seasoning to taste, adding more lime juice or salt as required.Meanwhile, heat the grill to high. Spread out the tortilla chips on a baking sheet or tray, and cover with both grated cheeses. Pop under the grill for a couple of minutes, until the cheese turns oozy – if if starts to catch, turn off the heat and leave it to finish melting in the residual heat.Transfer the cheesy nachos to a platter and dot with the corn salsa. Dot with the soured cream and finish with the remaining coriander and chillies scattered over the top.Explore more on these topicsSnacksQuick and easyFoodVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkSide dishesMexican food and drinkSummer food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Ernie the danger dog – who loves dicing with death | Dogs | The Guardian
description: He has chased a deer across a dual carriageway, eaten an entire tray of chocolate brownies and jumped head first into a canal. But despite all the worry he brings us, he is extraordinarily lovable
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: He has chased a deer across a dual carriageway, eaten an entire tray of chocolate brownies and jumped head first into a canal. But despite all the worry he brings us, he is extraordinarily lovable
Content: Roll with it … Ernie, pictured in May 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of Farryn StockView image in fullscreenRoll with it … Ernie, pictured in May 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of Farryn StockDogsThe pet I’ll never forget: Ernie the danger dog – who loves dicing with deathHe has chased a deer across a dual carriageway, eaten an entire tray of chocolate brownies and jumped head first into a canal. But despite all the worry he brings us, he is extraordinarily lovableFarryn StockMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErnie found his way into our hearts and home about nine years ago, when he strategically crawled into my lap during a family visit to meet a litter of puppies. While all the other beagle puppies ran wild, Ernie sat comfortably on me with his long, soft ears dangling down. We chose him because of his placid nature and named him Ernie after my mum’s late dad, who coincidentally also had short legs and a bit of a round belly.View image in fullscreenSofa so good … Ernie and Farryn in January 2026.Photograph: Courtesy of Farryn StockAfter a few weeks we realised that Ernie was anything but placid. His gentle temperament quickly morphed into an unruly and persistent need to find his way into danger.The most shocking incident happened one morning in November 2022. Ernie spotted a deer in the forest behind our house. He darted away from me and my mum, through the forest and towards a busy dual carriageway. Ignoring our screams, Ernie crossed the road, missing multiple lorries and cars, making his way to safety on a small patch of grass on the pavement. It was a miracle he had managed to avoid injury.Escaping death was a recurring theme. As a puppy he ate through an entire tray of freshly baked brownies, which we mistakenly left on the kitchen counter to cool. As chocolate is toxic to dogs, we were terrified that he had been poisoned but, indestructible as ever, he was fine. Since then he has also eaten a four-pack of raw chicken breasts; spring rolls, including the paper bag they came in; three Easter eggs with the foil on; and an entire six-pack of hot-cross buns.Last year, during what was supposed to be a relaxing weekend on a canal boat with my mum and her partner, Ernie decided to jump head first into the River Wey. Initially sinking in the fast currents, Ernie resurfaced a short while later and paddled his way to the bank, unaware of the panic he had once again caused.Despite all of this worry, and the ever-mounting vet bills (over £12,000 so far), the love Ernie has brought to our lives far surpasses any amount of stress he has caused. He has been with our family through three house moves, break-ups, job changes, birthdays, exams and just about everything in between.View image in fullscreenErnie last summer.Photograph: Courtesy of Farryn StockBeagles are known as good hunting dogs and Ernie’s hound instincts are what led him to finding a missing dog once in the woods. Out with our dog walker, they crossed paths with the owner of the missing dog, along with the search party she had gathered. Ernie managed to sniff out the lost dog by following its scent from a toy he’d been given, reuniting the dog with its owner.His craziness has started to ease in recent years, but he’s still as charming and gentle as ever. Just a simple walk can end up as an adventure with Ernie. There’s never a dull moment with him by my side.Explore more on these topicsDogsPetsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How can I convince NHS pensions that I am not dead? | Pensions | The Guardian
description: It has not paid me for months and I am in severe financial distress, and apart from my husband while I try to sort it out
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: It has not paid me for months and I am in severe financial distress, and apart from my husband while I try to sort it out
Content: A reader has been left with pressing financial problems by the NHS Business Services Authority, which runs the pensions scheme.Photograph: Joseph Gaul/AlamyView image in fullscreenA reader has been left with pressing financial problems by the NHS Business Services Authority, which runs the pensions scheme.Photograph: Joseph Gaul/AlamyConsumer championsPensionsHow can I convince NHS pensions that I am not dead?It has not paid me for months and I am in severe financial distress, and apart from my husband while I try to sort it outAnna TimsMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI stopped receiving myNHSpension in May and, when I rang to ask why, I was informed that I was deceased.I have repeatedly called to no avail and my emails have received auto-generated responses.The same thing happened last December and I was without my pension for four months, during which I had to borrow from my brother. That time, I was told that someone had changed my account details and my pension had been paid to the wrong person.The problem wassorted out after I sent identity verification, and now here I am again, only this time I’m apparently dead.My husband and I are under severe financial distressbecause of this error and are in dread of the end-of-month bills.IM,Cape TownYour plight has echoes of the Teachers’ Pensions fiasco in whichretired teachers had their income stoppedafter they were declared dead by the system.You worked in the NHS for 11 years before retiring to your native South Africa in 2015.The blunder has left you in such dire straits that you can no longer afford the international calls to the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), which administers the pension scheme, and you mention that you have had to live with a broken tooth for a month because you can’t cover the dentist’s fee.Last month you flew to the UK with money borrowed from a friend, to try to resolve the problem in person. It got you no further forward. Promised call-backs did not happen and you were told, two months after your first complaint, that your “death” needed to be referred to the fraud department.Days after your arrival in the UK, an email informed you that because of a system upgrade, NHSBSA would only be able to assist with general queries for eight days.A further week passed and you were informed that an investigation into your case was required and you would hear back within 30 days.It seems nothing had been done to resolve the problem during the months you had been kept waiting, and no action was taken to escalate it when you flew over. In the meantime, you are stuck indefinitely in the UK, apart from your elderly husband and sleeping on a friend’s sofa while you try to get answers.Three weeks after I contacted NHSBSA, it finally paid the arrears – by now three months’ worth – into your account and apologised for the distress and hardship you have been caused.An NHSBSA spokesperson said: “While we cannot go into the specific details of the case, an error was made in the records, which we have now corrected. We take our responsibility to members extremely seriously, and this case has shown us where we need to do better.”As for compensation, not least for the expenses you have been caused, it said it would discuss this with you.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsPensionsConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsPensions industryNHSShareReuse this content

title: New daily diabetes pill that helps with weight loss launches in UK pharmacies | Health | The Guardian
description: Foundayo will be available on private prescription, with pharmacists warning of counterfeit GLP-1 problem
Author: Hannah Devlin
Headline: Foundayo will be available on private prescription, with pharmacists warning of counterfeit GLP-1 problem
Content: Orforglipron, known as Foundayo, is a weight loss pill developed by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly.Photograph: Michael Siluk/AlamyView image in fullscreenOrforglipron, known as Foundayo, is a weight loss pill developed by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly.Photograph: Michael Siluk/AlamyHealthNew daily diabetes pill that helps with weight loss launches in UK pharmaciesFoundayo will be available on private prescription, with pharmacists warning of counterfeit GLP-1 problemHannah DevlinScience correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new daily pill that treats diabetes and helps with weight loss will be available in UK pharmacies from Monday.Pharmacists said the move would be welcome for people who cannot use weight-loss jabs, but also issued a warning over the growing problem of fake,unlicensed or counterfeit versions of GLP-1 tablets.Orforglipron, known as Foundayo and made by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly, was authorised by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) earlier this month. The UK is the first country in Europe to approve it, after approving another weight-loss pill in June.“The UK is the first country in Europe where Foundayo is now available,” said Khalil Asmar, the vice-president of cardiometabolic health at Lilly Northern Europe. “We’re pleased that this means there is another oral treatment option for eligible UK patients alongside licensed injectable treatments.”The drug will initially be available through private prescription, with Eli Lilly saying it is working with the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) on its assessment of Foundayo for a potential rollout on the health service in England.Th drug is licensed for people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or above, or those with a BMI of between 27 and 30 and at least one weight-related condition. It can also be used to improve blood sugar levels in patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The pill is taken once a day, at any time, with no food or water restrictions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK men with heart disease at higher risk of developing and dying from cancerRead moreHenry Gregg, the chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said: “This is another significant day with a second weight loss pill available from today in certain pharmacies. This is particularly significant for patients who cannot or do not want to take an injectable medicine and could make weight-loss treatment available to a wider range of patients.”However, there are concerns about the marketing of fake, unlicensed or counterfeit drugs, which can be easier to produce in pill form than injectables. Last year, the MHRA seized £250,000-worthof unlicensed weight-loss pens and ingredientsfrom a factory in Northampton, and Eli Lillyis suing various suppliersit accuses of participating in an illegal hidden market for its drugs.Patients are being urged to ensure that they access weight-loss treatments only through safe and regulated pharmacies.Gregg said: “There must now be a redoubling of efforts within government and the NHS to use pharmacies to make sure more eligible patients in clinical need can get weight loss treatments on the NHS, rather than the current postcode lottery that exists for weight management services via GPs.”The MHRA approved the first GLP-1 pill for weight loss, a tablet form of Wegovy, in June.Explore more on these topicsHealthDiabetesWeight-loss drugsDrugsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place’: Brescia, Lombardy’s hidden gem | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: The city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change that
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: The city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change that
Content: The winding alleys of the Carmine district in Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardainView image in fullscreenThe winding alleys of the Carmine district in Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardainItaly holidays‘Everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place’: Brescia, Lombardy’s hidden gemThe city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change thatKevin RushbyMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe have hardly begun walking before I spot the side alley, curving away from the main road in a patchwork of sunlit yellow walls, shuttered windows and shadowy archways. “What’s up there?” Elena, my guide to the city, pulls a wry smile. “That is Carmine. As a kid, I was warned not to go there.”I turn up the alley. There’s a lot of graffiti. Next to an anarchy symbol, someone has sprayed “morte al decoro” – death to decorum. I’m intrigued. We go further, finding a labyrinth of colourful streets filled with bars and restaurants, a few just opening up for the day.Like the bohemian quarter at its heart, Brescia is an Italian city that is easily missed: it’s near the Dolomites and Lake Garda, but not close enough to be a base for them. Tourists tend to speed past on their way to Milan or Verona. Fiercely proud of her city, Elena is on a mission to convince me it is worth a stop. “You’ll see. We’ve got everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place.”View image in fullscreenAndrea, manager of I Dù dela Contrada bar in Carmine, Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianHer confidence is matched by Andrea, the manager ofi Dù dela Contrada, a Carmine bar that we step into for a coffee.
