Quirky bric-a-brac is dotted around, the bar itself plastered with passport photos, donated by its many fans. “Twenty years ago, this was an area for prostitutes and thieves,” Andrea tells me. “Now it’s safer but still vibrant, and growing.”I tell him Elena’s mission and he nods. “She’s right, ask anyone.”“OK. Who shall I ask next?”“Piera at Ostería dei Mercanti. She’s a real character.”And so begins a magical day in the city where we wander, one person leading to the next, each encounter enriched by Elena’s deep knowledge of her home town.We find Piera sitting among a gaggle of friends, the table covered in coffee cups and one or two glasses of Brescia’s favourite aperitivo,pirlo. “The drinks here are special,” she tells me. “We’ve got the Franciacorta wine region on our doorstep. I came 17 years ago and knew instantly I would stay.”double quotation markWithin 20 minutes, I’m sitting outside eating the best pizza of my life – for breakfastShe sends us to meet her friend Maria. That means passing through the medieval square of the city, Piazza della Loggia, which is dominated by theTorre dell’Orologio, a magnificent clock that features two lifesize automatons, “the lunatics of time”, who have been bashing out the hours on a large bell since 1581. We can’t find Maria, but bump into her amiable friend Antimio, whoseLestro restaurantis both a homage to the 1970s and a laboratory where he experiments tirelessly, perfecting the pizza.Next thing, I’m in his kitchen getting a swift lesson in the mix of special flours, the best kneading methods, how to prep the cheeses … “I like to mix smoked scamorza and mozzarella, but my favourite isbagòss, a local speciality.” Within 20 minutes, I’m sitting outside, listening to the lunatics hammer out the hour and eating the best pizza of my life – for breakfast.View image in fullscreenPiazza della Loggia.Photograph: Bogdan Lazar/Getty Images/iStockphotoThus fortified, Antimio sends us around the corner to visit Roberto atBrescia’s sumptuous Teatro Grande. The theatre was founded in the 1660s and is considered one of Italy’s finest. The palatial cafe with its murals is a popular spot formerenda, the traditional afternoon cake stop, but the tour adds wonderful details, such as the way horses were steered on stage and how Puccini, chastened by the rejection of his new opera, Madama Butterfly, at Milan’s La Scala, brought it here in 1904 and won acclaim.Roberto’s tip is the church of San Cristo, but first we divert through Piazza Vittoria which Mussolini, at the peak of his power in 1932, had remodelled on fascist principles, kicking out residents to erect monuments to youth, energy and strength; in other words thuggish neo-classical blocks round a massive male nude statue. A decade later, Mussolini was back, this time as a German puppet, governing the republic of Salò, a rump state that included Brescia. In recent years, the piazza has been renovated, but the male nude remains warehoused, and the large capital letter “M” on one building does not refer to the fallen dictator.I’m beginning to understand why Elena believes Brescia is a microcosm of Italian history and culture. She now takes me back to the medieval Piazza della Loggia to point out something I had missed, a small pillar marking the spot where a bomb exploded in 1974, killing eight people. The political forces of the Mussolini era reached a terrible climax in the 1970s and 80s, theanni di piombi, “years of lead”, when fascist groups and the leftwing Red Brigades traded lethal bombings, kidnappings and assassinations. The extent of the carnage is revealed in hundreds of pavement plaques that lead up to Brescia’s medieval castle above the city, each plaque representing a victim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPiera at Osteria dei Mercanti: ‘I came 17 years ago and knew instantly I would stay.’Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianAfter this sombre digression, we cool off inChiesa di San Cristo, a 16th-century church known as “the Sistine Chapel of Brescia” for the luminous murals that cover every available space. A few doors down the lane isOsteria del Savio, a famous spot for local cuisine where we tuck intocasoncelli, a ravioli made with sage and butter, thenmalfatti, a local mountain gnocchi, while owner Michaela explains why there is a Roman column in the middle of her restaurant. “It actually goes down another 5 metres and my neighbours have the capital off it – they use it as a coffee table.”double quotation markChiesa di San Cristo is known as the Sistine Chapel of Brescia for the luminous murals that cover every available spaceFinding history hidden under columns is a Bresciano tradition. Back in the 1820s, archaeologists decided to dig under the top of a Roman column in a city garden that was being used as a picnic table. What they discovered was a vast temple complex and a bronze statue, the Winged Victory, that has been dated back to the first century BC.A short walk down the lane brings us to that spot, now a partly subterraneanarchaeological site. Other Roman artefacts are in the nearbySanta Giulia Museum, a warren of ancient buildings that could easily occupy a day, but we whip through because it is time to go and taste some wine.If Brescia keeps below the mass tourism radar, its wine district, the Franciacorta, is also a well-kept secret. Planted on volcanic soils south of Lake Iseo, these vineyards produce sparkling wine so good that the locals drink most of it.View image in fullscreenMonte Isola, an island on Lake Iseo.Photograph: Faber 1893/Getty ImagesI stay by the lake shore in Sulzano, a 30-minute drive from Brescia, then next day catch the ferry across to Monte Isola, an island in the lake. Ringed by mountains and a popular day trip for the Bresciani, the island still keeps its home-spun friendliness. At the fishing net shop, Paolo demonstrates the knots to make a net using a double-ended needle that “is the same tool they found in Pompeii”. Further on, in the small net factory, owner Daniela points to a photo of her grandmother mending nets, then tells me that most Serie A football nets are now made here. In the shop round the corner, they give me a taste of their local salami – they are very proud of that. But the climax, for me, is when I wander, unannounced, into the Archetti boatyard.This is the kind of place where royalty and billionaires buy handmade wooden boats, but Andrea and his dad have no time for airs and graces. They are craftsmen, proudly showing me works in progress. “Our ancestors were gondola-makers in Venice,” says Andrea. “In 1640, they came here and liked Brescia and its surrounding area so much, they stayed.” It was a decision, I admit to Elena, that I can heartily endorse.The trip was provided byVisit Brescia. Doubles atHotel Lenelin Bresciafrom€183, and atHotel Rivalagoin Sulzanofrom€209.Kevin Rushby travelled to Brescia by train, via Milan. title: Fairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets faster | Android | The Guardian
description: Dutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular design
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Dutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular design
Content: The Fairphone 6+ is a solid mid-range Android alternative.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Fairphone 6+ is a solid mid-range Android alternative.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.AndroidReviewFairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets fasterDutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular designSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 02.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFairphone’s topAndroidfor 2026 is a little faster with more memory while maintaining full compatibility with its previous phone, including its repairable and ethical chops.The Fairphone 6+ continues the Dutch cooperative’s mission to make consumer electronics longer lasting and more sustainable, containing 51% either recycled or ethically sourced materials while being fully repairable at home with just the one screwdriver included in the box.It is also the first model to expand beyond Europe, going on sale in the US directly from Fairphone. But the new Android costs £70 (€50) more than the launch price of its predecessor, available from £569 (€649/$650), competing directly with Google’s £499Pixel 10aand Apple’s £599iPhone 17e.View image in fullscreenThe new cobalt blue colour for the Fairphone 6+ is striking in person.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ is an almost exact clone of theFairphone 6, with the same plastic body, 120Hz OLED screen and fingerprint scanner in the power button. It also supports the sameexcellent modular accessoriesthat simply screw into the back of the phone to add a lanyard, handle or wallet.The new model is 2g heavier, but the biggest difference for the 6+ is an upgraded chip to the newer Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and an additional 4GB of memory for 12GB in total.The Gen 4 chip is about six to 10% faster in testing, which places it firmly in the mid-range category alongside the likes of theNothing Phone 4a Prowith the same chip. It won’t win any performance awards and is significantly slower than chips used in Apple, Samsung or Google’s latest smartphones, but it feels snappy enough in use and can be used for light gaming without issue.The battery life is very similar to the phone’s predecessor, lasting about a day and a half between charges with the screen actively used for about five hours across 5G and wifi, for messaging, note-taking, photos and browsing. Most will need to charge it nightly, which is a bit behind the curve. A full charge takes about 80 minutes using a 30W power adaptor (not included), hitting 50% in under half an hour.View image in fullscreenThe camera app has most of the features you need and will be familiar to users of other Androids or iPhones.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ also has the same dual-camera system as its predecessor with a 50-megapixel main and 13MP ultra-wide camera. It has improvedsince its debut last yearthrough software updates, which have fixed a few of the issues and inconsistencies. It can shoot pretty good photos with a bit of work and manages a reasonable 2x zoom. It isn’t the best in lower light conditions, though its new Super Night AI feature helps.SpecificationsScreen:6.31in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (431ppi)Processor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4RAM:12GBStorage:256GB + microSDOperating system:Android 16Camera:50MP + 13MP, 32MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4 and GNSSWater resistance:IP55 (splash/rain)Dimensions:156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mmWeight:193gGoogle’s Android 16 or e/OSView image in fullscreenFairphone’s minimalist Moments interface can be switched on to reduce distractions, allowing access to only a limited number of apps.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ ships with last year’s Android 16, not the latest Android 17, but will be supported with updates until 2033 at least, which is roughly the same as mainstream rivals.Fairphone’s software is generally clean and uncluttered with only an additional gallery app and the My Fairphone app for repair and diagnostics from the standard Android app loadout. It has Google’s Gemini in various bits, but no other AI additions to get in the way. It also features Fairphone’s“Moments” minimalist interface,activated by the big yellow switch on the side, for a less distracting smartphone experience.But for those who want an alternative to Google’s Android, the phone is available with the privacy-focused, open-source version of Android, without Google services,called /e/OS.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe power button with fingerprint scanner sits below the Moments switch and directly opposite the volume buttons.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery will maintain at least 80% of its original capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles and it can be replaced at home using a single screwdriver along withthe rest of the 12 modular components. Batteries cost£34.20, screens£77.00and the main camera£59.88. The phone was awarded10 out of 10 for repairabilityby specialists iFixit.The handset is made with51% recycled or fair materials, while Fairphonepublishes life cycle reportsfor its products.PriceThe Fairphone Gen 6+ costs£569(€649/$649.99) with Google Android or£598.63(€699.99/$699.99) with e/OS.For comparison, theGoogle Pixel 10acosts£499, theApple iPhone 17ecosts£599and theNothing Phone 4a Procosts£519.VerdictThe Fairphone 6+ continues to demonstrate that good, solid Android phones can be made fully repairable at home without specialist tools.It is only a small spec bump on the originalFairphone 6, which helps keep up with mainstream rivals without sacrificing parts compatibility, sustainability or ethical credentials. It is also available directly in the US for the first time. But that also means the 6+ shares the same flaws as its predecessor.The camera, battery life, performance and screen are all decent, if far from the best you can get for the money. However, those looking for a high-end smartphone experience best look elsewhere as the Fairphone can’t match a recent iPhone, Pixel or Galaxy S with similar levels of software support.That makes it hard to recommend to everyone. But for those who prioritise repairability and ethical ethos, this is the phone for you.Pros:choice of Android operating systems, modular accessories, repairable-at-home design, recycled and fair materials, microSD card slot, good screen, five-year warranty, software support to 2033Cons:mid-range performance, average battery life, fingerprint scanner can be tricky to press, average camera, cannot be submerged in water, no Android 17 yet.Explore more on these topicsAndroidSmartphonesMobile phonesSoftwareTelecomsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission
Content: A spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAPrince HarryPrince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abusesSpokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ missionCaroline DaviesMon 24 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee ofAfrican Parks, whichadmitted last yearthat human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.Ina 2024 reportpublished by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.After the review, African Parkspublished a statementacknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people,had called on Harryto step down as a member of the board.Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 yearsPrince Harryhas served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, withreports she has been in talksabout a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reportsthat the deal was off.The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryAfricaCongo-BrazzavilleMonarchyWildlifeHuman rightsCharitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people
Content: Nigerian millitary take part in a security drill in Nigeria as mass kidnappings become more common in some parts.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigerian millitary take part in a security drill in Nigeria as mass kidnappings become more common in some parts.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesNigeriaVideo shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnappingGunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older peopleReuters in MaidiguriMon 24 Aug 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn armed group has posted a video showing what ⁠residents said were about ⁠600 women, children and ​older people abducted in an attack on a mosque in Nigeria’s north-central Niger State last week.The video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp, ⁠showed large groups of people seated in a forested area surrounded by armed men. Several children could be heard crying in the background.Mass kidnappings for ransom have become commonin ⁠parts of north-western and north-central Nigeria, where heavily armed gangs frequently raid villages, schools and highways and hold them until ​paid large sums of money. The violence was previously focused in the north of the country, but gunmen have ‌increasingly moved south.How rampant violence made Nigeria an insecurity hotspot in the Sahel – mappedRead moreThe video surfaced two days after the latest kidnapping, when gunmen ‌attacked worshippers at the mosque in Dekara village during Friday prayers, taking people away in what residents said were simultaneous raids on several communities.In the video, a gunman speaking in Hausa addressed families of the captives and urged them to identify relatives among the people in the footage.“These are all your people. We are showing you this video so that you can identify your family members, your fathers, mothers, children ‌and relatives,” the gunman said.Reuters could not verify the exact date or the location where the video was filmed. However, no older version of the video was found posted ​online before Sunday.Four residents said they were able to confirm the identities of some of those seized.“The people in the video are from Dekara. I’ve identified 13 people that I know,” Ibrahim Abubakar said.Another resident, Abdulmutallib Muqaddas Dindi, said those who appeared in the video had been seized during the prayers. “We have ⁠identified our elders, relatives, and some of us have seen their wives and children ​in the video,” he said.Police ​and state authorities did not respond ​to requests for comment on Monday. Police had earlier confirmed an attack on worshippers in ​the area but said ‌they could not ​verify the number of people ​abducted.Jamilu Ibrahim, another resident, appealed to the federal and state authorities to secure the release of the captives, pointing out the number of mothers with infants and children among those shown in the footage.Explore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Children make up half of mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads  | Global development | The Guardian
description: West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected
Content: A child is vaccinated at a health centre in Quebo, Guinea-Bissau. There is a sense of urgency in the heath sector, with schools due to reopen in September.Photograph: Vincent Tremeau/UnicefView image in fullscreenA child is vaccinated at a health centre in Quebo, Guinea-Bissau. There is a sense of urgency in the heath sector, with schools due to reopen in September.Photograph: Vincent Tremeau/UnicefGlobal developmentChildren make up half of mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreadsWest African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetectedSupported byAbout this contentEromo Egbejulein CotonouMon 24 Aug 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than half of the mpox cases reported inGuinea-Bissauhave been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic.A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four.Ina statementon Thursday, Unicef warned that because the country’s health surveillance systems were fragile, the virus is probably spreading undetected, leaving even more children at risk.Sandra Martins, the country’s deputy representative for Unicef, said: “This is the first time mpox cases have been reported in Guinea-Bissau, making even a small outbreak a major public health event.”Mpox is an infectious viral disease that can be transmitted through close contact. There have been more than 2,000 mpox-related deaths among tens of thousands of cases recorded across east, central and west Africa since January 2024.Health workers say theCladevariants are consistent with viruses circulating in neighbouring countries, meaning that a risk of cross‑border transmission in the region remains strong. The vast majority of confirmed cases are in the Bissau autonomous sector, where the capital is, while one case is in the nearby Biombo area. No deaths have been reported to date.Dr Magda Robalo, a former health minister who led the country’s Covid-19 response, said that to eliminate the “biggest gaps in the health system right now”, increased surveillance would have to be prioritised and frontline capacity reinforced.“Even though the numbers are small, new cases have appeared intermittently over several weeks, which means transmission is ongoing,” said Robalo, who is also co-founder of the Institute for Global Health and Development and former director of communicable diseases for the World Health Organization.The outbreak comes as the country grapples with infrastructure challenges and the aftermath of the suspension oflast November’s presidential electionby the military, which remains in power. There wasno electricitythroughout Thursday in Bissau for instance because of petrol scarcity since the weekend.First malaria drug for babies is approved in ‘major public health milestone’Read moreMany public health laboratories in the region lack equipment to deal with epidemics but have institutional knowledge from handling other crises.In Guinea-Bissau, that is no different but there is also a sense of urgency, with primary schools scheduled to reopen across the country in September. After the outbreak was declared, community health workers immediately began a door-to-door public awareness campaign with megaphones and translated leaflets, supported by the health ministry and international agencies.These grassroots initiatives are seen as vital for building public trust in the public health sector. Earlier this year, the countrysuspended a controversial US-funded trialon hepatitis B vaccinations for newborns, citing ethical concerns and procedural flaws. The decision was lauded by many across the continent and has highlighted sensitivities around emergency health interventions.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentMpoxGuinea-BissauAfricaGlobal healthEpidemicsInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months | Americas | The Guardian
description: US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs
Content: On 23 August, the US Southern Command executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: U.S. Southern CommandView image in fullscreenOn 23 August, the US Southern Command executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the eastern Pacific.Photograph: U.S. Southern CommandAmericasUS strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in monthsUS Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugsMaya Yangand agenciesMon 24 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking.On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom)announcedit “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added.Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”“This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added.A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light.Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikeshave done littleto stem the flow of drugs into the country.It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’sCaribbeancoast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense SecretaryPete Hegsethsaid during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador andColombia.The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have beencondemnedasextrajudicial killingsby the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations.According toa 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean.Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.Meanwhile, aninvestigationby the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found.“There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release.Other familiescontinue to grieveas they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes.“If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia.Explore more on these topicsAmericasDrugsCaribbeanDonald TrumpVenezuelaPete HegsethColombianewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Move is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic ties
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Move is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic ties
Content: Manufacturing facility in Alliston, Ontario.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManufacturing facility in Alliston, Ontario.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTrump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelMove is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic tiesGaya GuptaMon 24 Aug 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpannounced a new 50%tariffon automobiles and crucial raw materials fromCanada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbors with historically strong economic ties.The US president said that the increased tariffs would start on 1 January 2027 on all cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel. He also derided the nation’s tariffs on American farmers, writing on social media thatCanadahas been “ripping off” the US “for years”.“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”In response,Mark Carneytold reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected.Mark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French languageRead more“It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” the Canadian prime minister said from Quebec.“But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” Carney continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.”He added that Canada would be ready to move forward with talks “when the Americans go to the negotiating table first with the right attitude toward our industry and a true partnership”.Trump’s announcement follows the last-minutecollapsethis weekend of a potential deal to lower tariffs on automobiles and other materials. After Trump imposed another 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports, including hockey equipment and electronics, Carney, rejected the latest deal between the two nations on Saturday.Carney said that the US “asked too much and they offered too little”, and he has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”.Canada and the US have been longtime partners, trading roughly $909bn, according to the office of the US trade representative. But Trump’s second presidential term and his aggressive trade policies have brought the era of “deep ties” between the two nations to a close, Carneysaidlast year, vowing to fight Trump’s sweeping tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaDonald TrumpMark CarneyAutomotive industryTariffsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French language | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Prime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from dispute
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Prime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from dispute
Content: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc at a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via APView image in fullscreenPrime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc at a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via APTrump tariffsMark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French languagePrime minister praised for rejecting US trade proposal as Trump shows little interest in retreating from disputeAre you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from youLeyland Ceccoin TorontoMon 24 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Carney said on Monday that while American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant … in Quebec, these are rights,” days after receiving widespread praise from political leaders for rejecting a US trade proposal that many perceived as weakening the country’s Francophone culture.The prime minister’s remarks came hours after the US president,Donald Trump, showed little interest in retreating from the spat, posting on social media that Canada had been “ripping off the United States of America for years” and threatening a swath of new, economically devastating tariffs on cars and trucks.Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week.Tariffson an array of Canadian products took effect over the weekend, affecting around 5% of Canada’s exports to the US, and Canada said it will retaliate in early September.On Monday, Carney toured a shipyard with Quebec’s premier, telling attendeesCanada“could not accept” a proposed trade deal that would have weakened French language protections after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, adding that his government “will not give what they have asked”.The prime minister’s decision to abandon trade talks with the US spurred declarations from political leaders and pundits in Canada that the country is now fully locked into an economic war with its longtime ally.Quebec, Canada’s predominantly French-speaking province, has long sought to protect its distinct identity, at times with laws thatclashed with the federal governmentand the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms.In recent years those rules have also frustrated US negotiators, who have framed them as trade irritants. Bill 96, for example, requires products sold in Quebec to have a French description and for trademarks using generic terms to be translated into French, while Bill 109 compels media services such as Netflix, Spotify and Apple to promote and prioritize French content for Quebec users.Quebec’s premier, Christine Fréchette, said Carney had made the right decision in walking away from talks that looked to cross a “red line” for Francophones.“Our culture, our language is central to our identity and it is important to exclude that from the negotiation table,” she told reporters over the weekend. “It’s something that is crucial for us and it won’t change, even though we are threatened with different tariffs, it won’t change. We will stay the way we are.”Polling from earlier in the month shows that dislike for Trump is highest in Quebec. Separatists in the provincehave seen a sharp decline in supportamid the economic wounds inflicted by the US.Last week, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the sovereigntist politician most likely to emerge victorious in upcoming provincial elections, said his party would delay a possible referendum into seceding from Canada until Trump is out of office. He wrote that deciding Quebec’s political fate “must not be hijacked by the upheaval of American politics, the outbursts of an unpredictable president or by a campaign of fear”.The Quebec Federation of Chambers of Commerce (FCCQ) called the tariffs a “worst-case scenario” for the province’s businesses.“Quebec, in fact, has been the most affected by these tariffs since the very beginning of this trade war,” Fréchette said. “In all our regions, businesses risk losing contracts. In fact, it has already begun.”On Monday, Trump’s top trade representative, Jamieson Greer, called reports that French language protections were up for debate a “a funny fake story”.“That is not true,” Greer told CNBC. “I like the Quebecois and I like that they speak French.” He said both he and his sons speak the language.He claimed the issue at stake was that Americans did not like Canada “forcing” streaming giants in the US to pay some of their profits to support Canadian content. Canada had already dropped that position, however, previously abandoning elements of digital services tax.“I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content. We think that’s a really valuable thing and we encourage countries to really put their own country first and put their national identity first.”Carney rejected that framing, telling reporters it was not “funny” and there was an “enormous spread” in perspectives.Also on Monday, Trump redoubled his efforts to wage economic war against his country’s longtime political, security and economic ally.“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trumpwrote on social media. Criticizing Canada’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers, Trump wrote: “Not sustainable, and not anymore!”The president, whofaces mounting domestic unease over his trade spatwith Canada, pledged to increase tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel beginning on 1 January . “We don’t need Canada, they need us!” he wrote, using capital letters.The move has provoked an increasingly predictable backlash from political leaders.The Conservative premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, told local media Trump can “kiss my ass”.“We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at him. He’s arrogant, he’s cocky, and you know, as Ronald Reagan said, if you come to a draw with a bully, what stops that bully from coming after you the next day and the next day. And that’s all Donald Trump is – is a bully,” said Ford. “Well, he’s going to have a rude awakening.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpTrump administrationTariffsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran vows to retaliate against countries that cooperate with fresh US sanctions | Iran | The Guardian
description: Test of US rhetoric will rest on whether nations such as India, China and Russia view economic threats as credible
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Test of US rhetoric will rest on whether nations such as India, China and Russia view economic threats as credible
Content: People walk past shops at a market area in Tehran on Monday. The White House believes the Iranian economy is once again on the brink of collapse.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople walk past shops at a market area in Tehran on Monday. The White House believes the Iranian economy is once again on the brink of collapse.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIranIran vows to retaliate against countries that cooperate with fresh US sanctionsTest of US rhetoric will rest on whether nations such as India, China and Russia view economic threats as crediblePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 24 Aug 2026 07.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTehran has vowed to retaliate against any country that cooperates with the USattempt to impose fresh sanctions against Iranin what the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has billed as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.In advance of the US announcement, the United Arab Emirates, Iran’s single biggest trading partner in the Middle East, announced it was ending all trade withIran, a move Tehran believes was coordinated between Washington and the UAE.The US has said it will impose sanctions on any country or entity trading with Iran – what are known as secondary sanctions.The test of the US rhetoric is likely to rest on whether countries such as India,Chinaand Russia believe continued trade with Iran would lead to credible US reprisals against their economies. China has for decades been the main importer of Iranian oil.In May, the US threatened sanctions against Chinese refiners and the banks funding them, but the Chinese commerce department directed Chinese firms to ignore US warnings over Iranian oil imports, saying the threats were illegitimate and deploying for the first time a government statute designed to render US sanctions ineffective in Chinese jurisdictions.The US had imposed sanctions on Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery Co in April but Washington largely backed off asDonald Trumprealised he was risking a wider trade and tariff war with China that the US was likely to lose.This time the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Lin Jian, again said China opposed unilateral sanctions that lacked basis in international law and China believed that military means, sanctions and pressure tactics were not the solution.Trump says he views strait of Hormuz as ‘American territory’Read moreHowever, unlike in May, Iran’s oil shipments to Asia have already all but ended due to the effectiveness of a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, driving the cost of those cargoes to the highest levels in years. Last week, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, admitted his country’s crude exports had “virtually stopped” due to the US blockade.The White House believes the Iranian economy is as a result once again on the brink of collapse due to hyperinflation and lack of foreign exchange income caused by the US blockade of oil exports.The rial was trading at 1.992 million per dollar on the unregulated market on Monday, down 4.5% since the US president announced a “crushing economic operation” against Tehran last week.“Iran is completely collapsing!!!” Trumppostedon social media in capital letters on Monday.View image in fullscreenA vessel in the strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/ReutersBut Iran has been under some kind of US economic maximum pressure campaign for more than 20 years and so far survived.Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tehran would respond with an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington proceeded with the proposed measures. He also warned Iran’s Gulf neighbours against joining the US sanctions campaign.“If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the strait of Hormuz,” Rezaei said, adding that Iran would also target other oil export routes from the Gulf.Shipping through the strait remained severely disrupted over the weekend, putting further pressure on global energy markets.Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, dismissed the expected sanctions as a sign of US desperation, arguing that the measures would fail to defeat Tehran. He said the US had shifted from military operations to what he described as “the same old plans”.Reza Nasri, an international lawyer with links to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “The announcement is not a measure against Iran. It is a claim of jurisdiction over the world, and every sovereign state on Earth is its real addressee. Iran is merely the occasion. The demand that no country allow its own banks, businesses, airports or ship registries to engage in lawful trade with another country is aimed at everyone else. Sovereignty itself is the target.”Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Repeating methods that have previously proven to fail will not produce any different results, except that it shows the extent to which America is hostile and spiteful towards each and every Iranian, because it knows very well that the effects of these sanctions will affect ordinary Iranian citizens.”He added: “Obliging or intimidating other countries to stop or limit their trade relations with another country means violating the most important foundation of international relations and the most fundamental pillar of the United Nations charter, which is respect for the national sovereignty of countries.”Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of west Asian studies at the University of Tehran, said: “There isn’t a single new sanction. Everything in Iran has been under primary and secondary sanctions since 2018. Since these sanctions failed to achieve the goals the US and Israel wanted, both sides turned to military action. The big fanfare about an ‘economic war’ is really just a public admission of a major step backward. After failing militarily, Washington is clearly stepping back to square one – the economy.”View image in fullscreenIranians walk past an anti-US billboard featuring Donald Trump in Tehran.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAHe said Iran had been signalling in recent weeks that US economic warfare was no longer an acceptable option for Tehran and it would prefer going to war rather than standing idly by in the face of the US implementing the blockade. He said this involved “Iranian calculations related to military capabilities, the American domestic situation, and the Iranian domestic situation”.Last Thursday Bessent claimed in an interview with CNBC that “the US will lead the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse with the toughest sanctions in history”.The Treasury secretary claimed “the US government is asking its allies and the rest of the world to stop trading with Iran”. He added that the US “will use all its power against anyone who does not comply with this demand”.“Either the countries are with us or against us,” Bessent said. “It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to decide, and we will destroy the economy of this regime.” Writing inthe Financial Timeson Sunday, he said: “Total financial isolation can obviate the need for American force while enlarging the sphere of freedom for our allies. Those who sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity will reinvigorate their own. They will deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy.”But China and Russia have so far shown no interest in succumbing to US pressure.By coincidence, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, flew to Tehran on Monday where he will explore the opportunity to revive talks on the stalled memorandum of understanding signed in June, but not implemented either by Iran or the US largely due to a dispute about whether the memorandum granted Iran interim control over shipping in the strait of Hormuz.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyInternational tradeDonald TrumpChinaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Fast-fashion giant Shein sets cut-price $27bn valuation for Hong Kong IPO | Shein | The Guardian
description: China-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprint
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: China-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprint
Content: Clothes from fast-fashion brand Shein hang at its office in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Silva/ReutersView image in fullscreenClothes from fast-fashion brand Shein hang at its office in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Silva/ReutersSheinFast-fashion giant Shein sets cut-price $27bn valuation for Hong Kong IPOChina-based retailer swung to $99m loss in first quarter and faces scrutiny over its environmental footprintBusiness live – latest updatesAlex DanielMon 24 Aug 2026 04.57 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShein, which built a fast-fashion empire onwhat seemed like impossibly low prices, has been forced to lower its own valuation in a cut-price stock market float, after falling into the red earlier this year.The online retailer will list on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September at a valuation of close to $27bn (£19.8bn), significantly down from a near-$100bn private market peak four years ago.It is one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings (IPO) of recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns. Shein then considered a £50bn float in London, but facedsimilar questions about its supply chainfrom campaigners, MPs and investors.EU introduces €3 customs charge on small parcels to curb cheap Chinese importsRead moreThe company moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts have said was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.In early 2025 itrefused to reassure British MPsthat its products do not include cotton produced in the Xinjiang region of China, which has been linked to forced Uyghur labour.Founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, the company runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world.But more recently it has faced questions over slowing growth and rising costs. It swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed an import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country.The company said the Iran war had caused delays to deliveries in some of its leading markets, while there was also less demand for its products because of the economic fallout from the conflict.Sheinsaidon Monday it would offer nearly 280m shares for between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 each. That would raise roughly £1.3bn for the company at the top end of the range, and give it a market valuation of just under £20bn. The final offer price will be set on the day before it starts trading on 1 September.The company’s European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users by the end of last year, making it one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside Amazon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShein partly benefits from sending goods directly to shoppers, including to the UK and US, fromChinaso they attract fewer taxes. The tactic has prompted calls for a change in tax rules.In November, the group opened itsfirst-ever physical outlet, a dedicated spacein the BHV department store in Paris. Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence.Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “Shein may still be one of the biggest names on the fast-fashion catwalk, but the IPO is going to be a harder sell, with plenty of investors questioning whether its low-cost formula still has the star power to deliver the growth they’re looking for.’’Explore more on these topicsSheinRetail industryChinaAsia PacificIPOsnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand to consider banning children under 16 from social media  | Social media | The Guardian
description: Prime minister Christopher Luxon’s party to introduce bill seeking the ban, citing harm to a generation of children
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prime minister Christopher Luxon’s party to introduce bill seeking the ban, citing harm to a generation of children
Content: New Zealand’s proposed social media ban for under-16s comes after Australia in December became the world’s first country to impose such a ban.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew Zealand’s proposed social media ban for under-16s comes after Australia in December became the world’s first country to impose such a ban.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesSocial mediaNew Zealand to consider banning children under 16 from social mediaPrime minister Christopher Luxon’s party to introduce bill seeking the ban, citing harm to a generation of childrenReutersMon 24 Aug 2026 01.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Zealand prime ministerChristopher Luxonhas said his party will introduce a bill in parliament that ⁠seeks to ban children ⁠under ​16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance.The bill would ⁠require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and ⁠digital identity documents.“We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of ​New Zealand children,” Luxon said ‌in a statement on Monday.“Social media ‌is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not ‌equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.”Four in five under-16s in Australia using social media despite ban, study showsRead moreIt was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners – the New Zealand First party – saying it would not support it.“We have been concerned with ‌the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country,” New Zealand First’s ​leader, Winston Peters, who is also the country’s foreign minister, said on X.In December, Australia became the world’s first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta’s Instagram ⁠and Facebook.That legislation had been a “colossal failure”, Peters said, adding that ​keeping children off ​social media should be the responsibility ​of parents.“I won’t pretend that it will be simple or ​that it ‌will be perfect,” Luxon ​said at an ​event.“We won’t get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it’s just way too important not to at least try.“Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaNew ZealandChristopher LuxonNew Zealand politicsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Victorian premier Ben Carroll pushes ahead with rail loop plan after hinting at pause  | Victorian politics | The Guardian
description: A day after suggesting other projects were more important to Victorians, Carroll says train line will go ahead but at a slightly reduced cost
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: A day after suggesting other projects were more important to Victorians, Carroll says train line will go ahead but at a slightly reduced cost
Content: Tunnelling between Glen Waverley and Burwood set to begin soon on the Suburban Rail Loop project.Illustration: Supplied by the Victorian governmentView image in fullscreenTunnelling between Glen Waverley and Burwood set to begin soon on the Suburban Rail Loop project.Illustration: Supplied by the Victorian governmentVictorian politicsVictorian premier Ben Carroll pushes ahead with rail loop plan after hinting at pauseA day after suggesting other projects were more important to Victorians, Carroll says train line will go ahead but at a slightly reduced costFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has made an about-face, committing to pushing ahead with the first stage of the Suburban Rail Loop while promising to reduce its total cost by about 6%.Carroll will on Tuesday announce changes to the scope of the first stage of the project, known as SRL East – a 26km stretch of tunnels between Cheltenham and Box Hill – estimated to save $1bn.He will also order an “independent, technical review” to identify a further $1bn in savings.No further contracts will be awarded until the review is complete but the government has stressed all current works will continue, with tunnelling between Burwood and Glen Waverley set to begin soon.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCarroll said the changes showed he “respects” taxpayer money.“The SRL will be built on time. Today’s changes mean it will be built under budget,” he said.Combined, the two measures would reduce the total cost of SRL East by 6% to about $32.3bn from a maximum $34.5bn contained in the project’s 2021 business and investment case.Carroll will also annouce that the Suburban Rail Loop Authority, the statutory agency responsible for planning and delivering the project, will be folded into the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority. The move was already under way prior to Carroll becoming premier four weeks ago.Since Carroll took on the Labor leadership, he hassought to differentiate himself from his predecessors, Jacinta Allan, and Daniel Andrews, who both championed the orbital train line.In his first week as premier, Carroll said he would not tear up the project’s contracts. But hewould not rule out redirecting billions of dollarsearmarked for the SRL to other projects,such as Melbourne Airport rail.Then, in radio appearances on Monday, he suggested projects other than SRL were more important to Victorians.“The Suburban Rail Loop, an orbital line, makes sense, but it cannot be crowding out everything else we need to do as a government,” Carroll told 3AW. “Airport Rail, Melton electrification, filling potholes and doing the job properly – these are the things Victorians want from their leader and their government.”On ABC RadioMelbourne, he said work on SRL would go ahead but there were “other projects that are so much more needed and urgent”.“There is a contract in place and that work will go ahead. But I am also having a very good look at how we fix up potholes, get on with Airport Rail, get on with Melton electrification,” Carroll said.Liberal plan to split Victorian appeals court attacked as ‘thought bubble’ that would politicise judiciaryRead moreThe changes to SRL East’s scope includes scrapping underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley, a second station entrance at Clayton and “complex” pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham. Amultilevel car park at Glen Waverley, which was meant to replace about 400 spots lost due to construction of the new station, will be scrapped.The SRL Community Projects Fund, designed to support local community groups with grants of between $10,000 and $80,000 while construction is under way, will also end at the completion of the current round.The government also said some future precinct works – totransform the areas around the new stations into housing hubs– will be scaled back.It has allocated $11.8bn to SRL East while the federal government has handed over $6bn, including$3.8bn in May’s federal budget. About $14.5bn worth of contracts have been signed.The state opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has said if the Coalition is elected in November, she will pause and review the project.Explore more on these topicsVictorian politicsMelbournenewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold, scientists warn | Bird flu | The Guardian
description: Virus has already caused catastrophic losses in seals in South America and sub-Antarctica, particularly among pups
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Virus has already caused catastrophic losses in seals in South America and sub-Antarctica, particularly among pups
Content: A fur seal on Kangaroo Island. A second suspected case of bird flu in the mammals has been found after the South Australian government confirmed the first case last week.Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fur seal on Kangaroo Island. A second suspected case of bird flu in the mammals has been found after the South Australian government confirmed the first case last week.Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty ImagesBird fluAustralia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold, scientists warnVirus has already caused catastrophic losses in seals in South America and sub-Antarctica, particularly among pupsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScientists have warned deadly H5 bird flu could cause “carnage” for Australia’s seal and sea lion populations after detection of the virus in long-nosed fur seals inSouth Australia.SAconfirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammalon Saturday after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.The state government announced a second suspected case on Monday in a dead long-nosed fur seal found on the Pages Islands, off Kangaroo Island, with results from CSIRO testing pending.John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said he feared the virus would quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.”H5 bird flu has already affectedpinnipedsin South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups.In 2023, H5N1 killed more than 17,000 southern elephant seal pups in Argentina and drone surveys detectedmore than 13,000 dead southern elephant seal pupson Australia’s Heard Island in 2025 and 2026.Bird flu has devastated wildlife around the world. What Australian birds are most at risk?Read more“In South America, we’ve seen huge infection rates in sea lions and fur seals,” said Jane Younger, an Antarctic disease ecologist at the University of Tasmania.“Then across the Southern Ocean we’ve seen really big mortality rates in southern elephant seals and Antarctic fur seals.“In some places, the numbers are just astronomical.”Three types of pinnipeds breed in Australian waters: the long-nosed fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the endangered Australian sea lion. The Australian government hasrated all as being at very high riskfrom H5 bird flu.Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though one recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000 – with about three-quarters of the population found in South Australia and the remainder in Western Australia.Thousands of little penguins being vaccinated against H5 bird flu in Victoria – videoThe long-nosed fur seal suspected of having bird flu was found on the Pages Islands where, the SA government reported last week,there had been mass deaths among greater crested terns.The islands are home to one of Australia’s largest breeding colonies of Australian sea lions, with long-nosed fur seals known to visit the area.Younger said while there was some uncertainty about how Australia’s seals and sea lions would fare, the mortality rates seen in South America and the Southern Ocean “make me very worried”.“There’s only 12,000 Australian sea lions in existence,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“For some of these other species like elephant seals, we’ve seen many more than that killed by this virus.“Hopefully it doesn’t wipe out the species, but that’s a possibility.”Younger said seals and sea lionswere vulnerableto H5N1 because they gathered in large colonies that overlapped with seabirds infected with the virus. The environment itself, including the water and beaches, could also be contaminated with the virus.H5N1 can be transmitted from birds to seals or between seals.“At the moment there’s mass mortalities in birds and that infection will cause contamination of the environment,” said Rachael Gray, a pinniped specialist at the University of Sydney’s School of Veterinary Science.“Once you get mammals infected, it’s likely you will see mammal-to-mammal transmission, which is obviously of concern because that facilitates more rapid spread between [members of] a species.”While there are no registered vaccines for treating H5 bird flu in mammals, the United States has undertaken experimental trials on a small number of seals.The SA government said last week it was investigating potential opportunities to vaccinate high-priority at-risk mammals, such as Australian sea lions at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island.A crested tern with a suspected case of bird flu, filmed at Portland, VictoriaThe Australian Marine Conservation Society said the arrival of bird flu in SA followed significant environmental harm caused by the algal bloom.Alexia Wellbelove, the society’s campaigns director, said some species such as sea lions were in poorer condition because their food sources had been affected “meaning they are likely more vulnerable”.Wellbelove said the organisation had been calling for increased funding to target other threats to the species, such as fishing.“With reported mass mortality of terns and now the death of a long-nosed fur seal on the Pages [Islands] it is now highly likely that this vital population of Australian sea lions has also been exposed to the virus,” she said.Explore more on these topicsBird fluSouth AustraliaMammalsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese seeks to quell datacentre disquiet as climate expert warns ‘we’ve got one shot to get the rules right’ | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power use
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power use
Content: Anthony Albanese will tell national cabinet his government will legislate next year to ensure the benefits of AI and datacentres are shared among states.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese will tell national cabinet his government will legislate next year to ensure the benefits of AI and datacentres are shared among states.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian politicsAlbanese seeks to quell datacentre disquiet as climate expert warns ‘we’ve got one shot to get the rules right’Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power useFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandPetra StockMon 24 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Albanese will seek to use Wednesday’s high-stakes talks with premiers to quell growing unhappiness aboutnational controls on datacentre developments, promising new approval laws will complement state rules.Faced with growing opposition from conservative governments in Queensland and the Northern Territory, Albanese will tell national cabinet he plans a major piece of legislation next year to ensure the economic benefits of AI are shared widely.With potential to be one of the major reforms of Labor’s second term, the new law will set tough copyright rules for AI businesses and impose standards for security, safety and skills development.The meeting on Wednesday will come after the latest forecast from the Australian Energy Market Operator showing datacentre power use is projected to increase seven-fold over the next decade.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe industry’s rapid growth, driven by increasing reliance on AI and cloud computing, remained one of the most significant causes of growth in electricity demand, according to Aemo’s annual Electricity Statement of Opportunities.In addition to 165 datacentres already operating around the country, a further 225 are in development, the report showed, reflecting a substantial increase in new proposals compared to 2025, Aemo said on Tuesday.Datacentre electricity demand was expected to grow from 5 to 34 terawatt hours by 2035-36, the report said, growing from 3% of overall consumption to 13%.AEMO said high datacentre growth could see consumption reach 52 TWh – a 10-fold increase over the decade.But there were high levels of uncertainty, with more than a third of projects listed in 2025 since cancelled, and operating facilities taking years to ramp to full capacity.Daniel Westerman, Aemo’s chief executive, said record levels of new generation and storage coming online had improved the outlook for reliability, even with the expected retirement of coal power stations.“The reliability outlook has improved, supported by record levels of new generation and storage, and a strong pipeline of projects expected over the next decade.”Report supporting Australia’s teen social media ban appears to contain AI hallucinations, Senate hearsRead moreThe Climate Council chief executive, Amanda McKenzie, said datacentres were set “to devour an enormous share of Australia’s electricity in the coming years”.“We’ve got one shot to get the rules right now and ensure that datacentre growth doesn’t strain our grid and push up pollution.”Albanese will use national cabinet to strike agreement on a plan to legislate nationally consistent minimum obligations for datacentres, requiring them not to push up energy prices, meet their own infrastructure costs and minimise water use.The rules will also require developers to minimise the effect of new datacentres on local communities, ensuring they are appropriately sized and appropriately located, away from homes, schools and potential housing or agricultural sites.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProjects approved for development before the new rules come into place will only be subject to existing state and territory laws.Last month, the prime minister promised“the strongest possible protection”for Australian creatives against misuse of their work by artificial intelligence models. He said it would be “theft” if writers, artists and musicians didn’t have control of their work or receive payment for its use in training large AI models.Combining the elements into a single piece of legislation signals the government’s ambition on AI, but could also heighten the political risk of getting the bill through parliament ahead of the next election.Queensland premier David Crisafulli and the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, have signalled opposition to federal rules requiring datacentres to be powered by renewable projects at the exclusion of coal and gas.Albanese is expected to seek broad consensus, but could be challenged by the increasingly outspoken Liberal-National and Country Liberal party leaders.He will also discuss state opposition to the national gun buy-back, which only has support from New South Wales and the ACT so far. Action to curb violence against women and the growing H1 bird flu crisis are also on the agenda.Anger about Western Australia’s favourable GST share will also flare. In Perth on Monday, Albanese said he would not change the deal, which costs taxpayers more than $6bn a year.“There will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements while I’m prime minister,” he said.Promising Australia would do more to unlock frontier AI development in the future, Albanese will tell a Business Council event on Tuesday the government was determined to succeed.“It will advance our national sovereignty. And it is essential for our national security, business productivity, science, innovation and resilience.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAI (artificial intelligence)Anthony AlbaneseComputingLabor partynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to use Ukraine battlefield data to train AI to protect sensitive sites | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure
Content: A pilot project will use AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement at a UK defence site.Photograph: Andrew Brookes/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenA pilot project will use AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement at a UK defence site.Photograph: Andrew Brookes/Getty Images/Image SourceDefence policyUK to use Ukraine battlefield data to train AI to protect sensitive sitesLondon and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructureJessica ElgotandAisha DownMon 24 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack.
