It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement.The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure.The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.Palestine Action said at the time that it had targeted RAF Voyager aircraft used for transport and refuelling, and that “activists have interrupted Britain’s direct participation in the commission of genocide and war crimes across the Middle East”.Private companies will be able to access the data once approved by the MoD on a secure platform, though the data sharing is likely to raise alarm among privacy campaigners.Pilot projects have already been approved with three British AI companies – Sintela, Mind Foundry and Skyral. Sintela, a Bristol-based company that specialises in fibre-optic sensors, recently struck a $35m (£26m) deal with the Trump administration to provide surveillance on the US-Mexico border.The partnership with the Ukrainian AI lab means new UK security systems can be trained on operational drone datasets, strike mission footage and flight profiles, likely to include Russian sabotage attempts against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.The cache of four years’ worth of military data contains a far deeper picture than models outside Ukraine have previously been trained on, which had been mostly restricted to open-source data.The government eventually hopes to use the AI models to predict quickly when infrastructure such as railways, the power grid or military bases might be coming under threat or stress from hostile actors.That would primarily come from the laying of fibre-optic cables that are able to identify unique movements of people or vehicles around sensitive sites. Ministry of Defence sources said that would specifically include when a site might be targeted by protesters – not just hostile states.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it would be an opportunity for British companies to combine their AI expertise with Ukraine’s battlefield data, which would “accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home”.Other potential projects could include new AI chips to power drones, robotics and automated weapons systems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSteven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said technologies to detect movement from sensors in fibre-optic cables had been around for decades and that it was unclear if data from Ukraine would refine their capabilities.“I haven’t heard anything that is very convincing, but there is a plausible scenario where they could see something that could be predicted easily and isn’t in any publicly known dataset,” he said.Ukraine, however, has a lot of other data that may be valuable, especially related to new threats that countries in westernEuropemight face in the short to medium term.“What’s valuable is something we’re seeing today which other countries will be worrying about in the future,” Murdoch said. “Anything to do with drones, for example.”The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Ukraine was “pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion”.“By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security,” he said.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyUK security and counter-terrorismAI (artificial intelligence)UkraineComputingEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: giant hail forces stage three abandonment in Pyrenees | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: A torrential hailstorm in ⁠the French Pyrenees forced the ⁠abandonment of ⁠the ​third stage of the Vuelta a ⁠España
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A torrential hailstorm in ⁠the French Pyrenees forced the ⁠abandonment of ⁠the ​third stage of the Vuelta a ⁠España
Content: Wout van Aert of Team Visma heads to a hotel for cover after the abandonment of stage three.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWout van Aert of Team Visma heads to a hotel for cover after the abandonment of stage three.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: giant hail forces stage three abandonment in PyreneesHuge hailstones prompt organisers to act 15km from endRiders seen heading into hotel on route to take coverReutersMon 24 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the ⁠third stage of theVuelta a Españaon Monday.With 15 kilometres (9.32 miles) remaining of the 174km route ⁠from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the ​skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began ⁠bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead ⁠of the peloton when the elements intervened as the race leader and favourite ​Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating ‌to the peloton ‌to pull off the course.View image in fullscreenA view of the finish line following the stage cancellation.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesBedraggled riders were then seen getting off their ‌bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.“For the security of the riders, stage three has been cancelled due to hail and severe weather,” race organisers said shortly afterwards. “There will be no winner and no podium ceremony.”Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from the Belgian rider ‌Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with the British rider Matt Brennan 10sec back.Earlier it had been warm and sunny ​on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta ⁠for the first time, was always near the front of ​the pack with ​the Slovenian’s team setting the pace.His expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul ​of the ‌weather in an ​anticlimactic finish. Pogacar ​will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though, with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaTadej PogacarCyclingSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fix that little spot’: Danish PM hits back at unsolicited beauty tip from cosmetic surgeon | Denmark | The Guardian
description: Mette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises women to embrace self-acceptance
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Mette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises women to embrace self-acceptance
Content: Mette Frederiksen with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. She says a cosmetic surgeon got in touch with her while she was away offering to help her with her appearance.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenMette Frederiksen with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. She says a cosmetic surgeon got in touch with her while she was away offering to help her with her appearance.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPADenmark‘Fix that little spot’: Danish PM hits back at unsolicited beauty tip from cosmetic surgeonMette Frederiksen, who received message on returning from Ukraine, advises  women to embrace self-acceptanceDeborah ColeMon 24 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSick of getting unsolicited beauty tips on social media, the Danish prime minister,Mette Frederiksen, rebuffed a male cosmetic surgeon’s offer to “fix” her and advised women in similar situations to embrace self-acceptance.Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, posted on Instagram that she had just returned from a trip toUkraine, where she was subjected to air raid sirens, when she found a message proposing some help with her appearance.She included ascreenshot of the exchangein which the doctor, who was not identified, said he could “fix that little spot on your nose”.Her retort was swift and pointed: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body – I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!”Frederiksen, who has led the EU and Nato member country since 2019 and is one of Europe’s longest-serving heads of government, said being a woman in the public eye meant regular exposure to such unwanted and superficial scrutiny.“I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” the 48-year-old wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”Frederiksen’s global profile has grown this year as she stood up to US president’srepeated claims on Greenland, a semi-autonomous Danish territory. She is also a staunch supporter ofUkraineagainst the Russian onslaught.In a moment of striking candour, Frederiksen admitted annoyance with pushy beauty advice while offering her own guidance how to deal with it.She said she did not volunteer opinions about other people’s looks and said that “I’m perfectly fine with my body – as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”Frederiksen said she was fine to stay in conversation with the public on a range of topics but encouraged Danes to set the bar higher with their chosen subject matter.“If you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful,” she said. “Not my nose.”Although the mean-spirited suggestions made her feel “indignant”, she said, “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDenmarkEuropeUkraineBeautyWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham says UK with Ukraine ‘all the way’ despite ‘outrageous threats’ from Russia – Europe live | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Coalition of the Willing condemns Russian strikes on Ukraine, pledges to work on ‘constraining Russia’s war chest’
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: Coalition of the Willing condemns Russian strikes on Ukraine, pledges to work on ‘constraining Russia’s war chest’
Content: 12.46 EDTClosing summaryBritish prime minister Andy Burnham said that the UK will help Ukraine make its own long-range missiles by sharing classified technical information for British components.Burnham, who was in Kyiv alongside other international leaders for Ukraine’s Independence Day, said defence firm MBDA will release details on UK-made parts for the SCALP missile to Ukraine to help the country assemble the weapons.Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said ⁠there ⁠will be ​a “diplomatic track” with Russia discussing ⁠Moscow’s stepped-up attacks in the ⁠Black Sea ​that have ‌curbed ‌Ukraine’s export capabilities.Ukraine ‌will also strengthen its air defences in the region, he told ‌reporters.Zelenskyy urged Ukraine’s allies to ⁠deliver an ⁠air ​defence package ahead of ⁠the winter, with Russia expected to renew ⁠its strikes on ​his country’s ‌energy ‌infrastructure,Reuters reported. Addressing a Coalition ‌of the Willing meeting in Kyiv,Zelenskyy also asked Ukraine’s partners to help ‌cover a funding gap of 27 ​billion euros for its defencesector needs in ⁠2026.Britain’sAndy Burnhamhas urged Ukraine’s allies to provide more Patriot interceptor missiles to Kyiv, saying the country “needs more help to protect its people right now,”PA agency reported. Speaking in Kyiv as he chaired his first meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, the prime minister saidthe coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocksand help others dig into their stocks”.The Coalition of the Willing met online today, co-chaired by Britain’sAndy Burnhamfrom Kyiv.Poland’s foreign ministerRadosław Sikorskiposted a snap from the meeting, saying France’sEmmanuel Macron, Ukraine’sVolodymyr Zelenskyyand Italy’sGiorgia Melonialso spoke during the call.As European leaders gathered in Kyiv to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day, less than 100 miles (150 kilometres) north, the city of Chernihiv was attacked by Russian forces.Across three waves of attacks, a Russian drone struck an apartment building, injuring 18, the Chernihiv city councilposted on Telegram. Two of the injured were children.Ukraine’s southern Odesa region came under a large-scale Russian missile and drone attack on Monday, with food storage facilities and energy infrastructure among the targets, regional authorities reported.Eighteen people, including two children, were injured in a Russian drone strike on Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, according to Ukraine’s Emergency Service.Ukraine’s southern Odesa region came under a large-scale Russian missile and drone attack on Monday, with food storage facilities and energy infrastructure among the targets, regional authorities reported.Eighteen people, including two children, were injured in a Russian drone strike on Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, according to Ukraine’s Emergency Service.Share

title: Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US
Content: Andy Burnham (left) and Volodymyr Zelensky during a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (left) and Volodymyr Zelensky during a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/PAAndy BurnhamAnalysisBurnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for UkraineLuke HardingandDan Sabbaghin Pavlohrad, UkraineAs well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the USMon 24 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTShareSince moving into Downing Street in July,Andy Burnham– a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.The occasionwas the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots.In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France have been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.Burnham hands secret missile technology to Ukraine – The LatestRead moreIt was now handing over British blueprints for key components, Burnham said, so Ukraine could eventually make its own version with France.More Storm Shadows could go some way to dealing with Ukraine’s biggest problem: thewave of ballistic missiles fired by Russia that rain down on Kyivand other cities most nights. As of now, Ukraine has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting them down. The Trump administration is disinclined to provide more.Graph of the number of civilians killed by Russia in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasionThe British cruise missiles carry a larger payload than the long-range drones favoured by Kyiv. They could be used to destroy enemy ballistic missile launch systems, which can be quickly moved, and are dotted around sites in western Russia. Depending on their range, they could also disable military runways and aerodromes.But nobody expects production to start soon. In the meantime, the Kremlin has responded with characteristic belligerence. Vladimir Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow would destroy any Ukrainian Storm Shadow factories, and accused London of taking part in the war and adding “fuel to the fire” though it is France that is helping with building them.Last week Russia threatened “consequences” over the supply of British drones to Kyiv andwithdrew its ambassador from London. It is unclear how Putin might escalate further. He has already sent assassins to poison Russian dissidents on UK territory including the murder in 2006 of Alexander Litvinenko, killed with radioactive tea.Burnham appears unmoved by what he dubbed “outrageous” Russian threats, an encouraging sign for Kyiv. On Monday he pointed out that it was Putin who “started the fire” with his illegal and unprovoked invasion, and assured Zelenskyy of his “personal commitment” to Kyiv’s existential cause.Ukraine has warmly welcomed the Storm Shadow initiative. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian he hoped manufacturing could begin in “months, not years”. “We have proved many times we can do impossible things in producing weaponry,” he said, adding that the missile strengthened Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Moscow.Of Burnham’s visit, he added: “For us, it’s hugely symbolic and important. It illustrates that for the UK Ukraine remains a top priority. You are an important bridge and have rectified the situation whenever we have a crisis in our relations with the US. Your king is a valuable diplomatic tool and puts in a good word for us with Trump.”The trip also signalled to allies that the UK will continue to play a leading role in the coalition of the willing after the departure of Keir Starmer. Co-hosting a coalition meeting for the first time, Burnham said Europe would do everything it could to source more Patriotic interceptors for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has asked for 300 to help the country survive the coming winter.Burnham’s speech made clear that he regards Ukraine’s struggle as Britain’s too – at a time when the US has in effect given up on its attempts to broker a peace deal, and has halted direct military aid. “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security but the frontline in keeping Europe safe,” he said. “The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”Ukrainian leaders and soldiers are grateful for British diplomatic and moral support, though they know that London’s military power is limited. Storm Shadow is deemed to have been one of the UK’s most useful contributions but stockpiles were modest.Ukraine’s focus has been on developing its own long-range drones and cruise missiles, such as Fire Point’s Flamingo, which have been used to strike refineries and warehouses deep inside Russia. The goal is to attack Russia with 1,000 drones and some missiles a day this year, not when Storm Shadow production lines are ready.But the deal that Burnham has agreed with Zelenskyy is an important renewal of goodwill. At some point Zelenskyy will probably need the help of European allies whenever the White House re-engages with the peace process. Burnham may become an important interlocutor with Trump, and today’s trip is from Ukraine’s perspective an encouraging start.Betrayal by Luke Harding (Guardian Faber, £20) is published on Thursday. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyRussiaDefence policyVladimir PutinEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China
Content: Scott Bessent said the objective was to ‘sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone’.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenScott Bessent said the objective was to ‘sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone’.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranUS threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to IranWashington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to ChinaJulian BorgerSenior international correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties withIran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.It is unclear, however, how far theTrump administrationis prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.Iran, meanwhile,vowed retaliationagainst any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign.Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks.The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed.Hardliners appeared to strengthen their grip on government in Tehran and responded by declaring the closure of the strait of Hormuz, attacking ships that ignored its declaration. Trump imposed a counter-blockage on Iranian oil exports through the strait, leading to an impasse that has had profound effects on the global economy.Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, however, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth ⁠told reporters on Monday.In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyTrump administrationIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Immense drop-off’ in support contributing to care leaver deaths in England, review says  | Social care | The Guardian
description: Death rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on  isolation of those leaving care
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Death rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on isolation of those leaving care
Content: Suicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher than in the general population.Photograph: Lucy Lambriex/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSuicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher than in the general population.Photograph: Lucy Lambriex/Getty ImagesSocial care‘Immense drop-off’ in support contributing to care leaver deaths in England, review saysDeath rate three to four times higher than among general population blamed on isolation of those leaving care‘He was left on his own’: the care-leaver lives lost to a system that abandons them at 18Jessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfound isolation contributed to the deaths of more than 100 care leavers inEnglandin a year, with a dramatic drop-off in support from social services at 18 leading to catastrophic consequences, a review has found.A government-commissioned report into the early deaths of young people who left care described the problem as a national tragedy and said many were left on their own “at the height of vulnerability” before they died.Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, said: “Care leavers have been left so isolated, so lonely, and that is the core of the problem. Both adult and children’s social care need to be humanised and need to focus on building those enduring, loving connections. This is a stain on society because all of us have failed.”The review, led by the social work leader Clare Chamberlain and the broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, looked at the deaths of 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 in 2025.It found that the death rate among this group was three to four times higher than among the general population, and suicide rates among female care leavers were potentially 15 times higher.In total, 36% of the care leavers probably died by taking their own lives, including 24 women. One-fifth of the deaths were at age 18, which the review said highlighted the “immense drop-off in support services” when care leavers reach adulthood.John-Baptiste, whogrew up in the care system, said the review was the “most emotional and triggering piece of work I’ve ever had to do”.He said: “I remember being in a meeting at 17 where my foster parents said: ‘If we’re not getting paid, we don’t want to look after him.’ Why do services change when children reach 18 and should they have to change?“I think there is certainly a case for a 0-25 service. If 112 deaths doesn’t compel us to try and reform things quickly, there’s a big problem in our society.”Among the deaths examined were care leavers in custody, mothers whose children had been removed, people undergoing gender transition, young asylum seekers, murder victims and people who died from medical conditions.One case was that of David (not his real name), who died in the summer of 2025 from a lack of insulin after he lost access to the children’s diabetes nurse who had been helping him keep track of his condition since he entered the care system at 14.The care leavers’ hub he socialised in was closed for refurbishment and his personal adviser was on leave. After his death, his body wasn’t found for two weeks. The review found that when he turned 19, many of the connections he had made “fell away and he was left on his own”.Young people leaving care are assigned a personal adviser to help them transition into independent adulthood up to the age of 21. The review found many of these advisers “hardly knew” the young people they were working with and were only required to see them once every two months. It said many were untrained, ill-equipped and “avoided the emotional side of the transition”.It called for a “major national review of the knowledge and skills” of the workforce tasked with monitoring care leavers, including better mental health expertise.The review found that young people were often attracted to the “lure of living alone and being free of constraints” but were unprepared for the significant drop in support, which “no amount of transition planning will compensate”.In response to the review, the government said it was investing £25m in connected housing options for care leavers, which would include supported housing and shared housing for groups of care-experienced people.MacAlister said this was part of the government’s strategy to make “loving, trusted relationships around care-experienced people the central focus of the care system”.Since December 2023, local authorities must report the deaths of care leavers through a serious incident notification system. MacAlister said “the same thing happening over and over again” compelled him to commission the review.He said it should be a call to action not just for the government and the social care sector. “We need more foster carers, we need mentors for care leavers, we need neighbours to show an interest in a young care-experienced person who might have got their first tenancy and to extend the hand of friendship,” he said.“This is about connections and relationships, and you can’t pay people to do that – it has to be grown organically and nurtured over time.”Explore more on these topicsSocial careYoung peopleEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes | Housing | The Guardian
description: About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership
Content: Andy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesHousingBurnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homesAbout 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownershipKiran StaceyPolicy editorMon 24 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.He saidwhen launching his campaignto become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year | EditorialRead moreThe Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnhamhas promisedwill be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”Ministers drop plan to relax affordable housing rules after negative responseRead moreOfficials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”The plans contrast withthose announced by Reform UKon Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.Explore more on these topicsHousingSocial housingAndy BurnhamLabourAngela RaynernewsShareReuse this content

title: Man arrested on suspicion of arson after fire at car park used by Gatwick passengers | England | The Guardian
description: Blaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday night
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Blaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday night
Content: The blaze erupted at the Caldyne business park, a third-party parking site used by people flying from Gatwick airport.Photograph: Eddie MitchellView image in fullscreenThe blaze erupted at the Caldyne business park, a third-party parking site used by people flying from Gatwick airport.Photograph: Eddie MitchellEnglandMan arrested on suspicion of arson after fire at car park used by Gatwick passengersBlaze near Crawley destroyed 140 vehicles, damaged nearby businesses and led to power cuts on Saturday nightHarry CockburnMon 24 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire tore through a car park used by people flying from Gatwick airport, destroying about 140 vehicles.The blaze erupted at Caldyne business park near Crawley, about eight miles from the airport just after 9pm on Saturday. Images showed vehicles on fire and enormous plumes of smoke rising close to overhead power lines.As well as causing misery for those returning from summer holidays to find their cars destroyed, the fire led to power cuts at more than 2,000 businesses and homes.Emergency services described extinguishing the blaze as a “significant and complex” operation, with eight fire engines and water carriers deployed to bring it under control.UK Power Networks, which operates the electricity network across south-east England, had to isolate an overhead power cable while crews worked below.A spokesperson for West Sussex fire and rescue service said: “Approximately 140 vehicles were damaged, and a number of the vehicles involved in this fire were parked at a site used for holiday parking. Any affected consumers are advised to contact their operator directly.”There were no casualties, it said.The fire also caused significant damage to two breakdown and recovery businesses and a banger racing team.The Bears banger racing team said ina fundraiserthat they had lost everything.Autocovery and K&L Automotive had also previously donated abandoned vehicles to fire stations across West Sussex for training purposes,according to local reports.Sussex police said a 67-year-old man arrested on suspicion of arson had been bailed pending further inquiries.“Power was shut off to the immediate area, affecting a number of businesses and homes, and nearby roads were closed as a precaution,” a spokesperson said.“Emergency services remain on scene at this time and the public are advised to avoid the area.”A London Gatwick spokesperson said: “We are aware of a fire at an unaffiliated third-party car parking site, which occurred on Saturday evening, and understand how concerning and distressing this will be for any passengers whose vehicles may have been affected.“We are advising any passengers who are concerned that their vehicle might have been affected to contact their parking operator directly.“The parking company is not endorsed or operated by London Gatwick.”Police said anyone with information about the incident was asked to report it online or call 101, quoting serial number 1504.Explore more on these topicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Twelve people arrested after A66 crash that killed seven including two police officers | UK news | The Guardian
description: Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation of events leading to deadly collision
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation of events leading to deadly collision
Content: PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died in a collision between a police vehicle and a car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland police/PAView image in fullscreenPC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died in a collision between a police vehicle and a car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland police/PAUK newsTwelve people arrested after A66 crash that killed seven including two police officersNine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation into events leading to deadly collisionRaphael Boyd,Hannah Al-OthmanandRobert BoothMon 24 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwelve people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including being involved with organised crime as part of the investigation into events leading to a crash on the A66 that killed two police officers and five others.Cleveland police confirmed that nine men and three women were detained by officers investigating the events that led up to PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough dying when a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough collided with their marked armed response vehicle. All five men who were in the second car, aged between 17 and 23, were pronounced dead at the scene.Police said some of those arrested as part of the A66 investigation, whose ages range from 19 to 61, were suspected of various offences.Four people were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and four on suspicion of possessing a firearm, while four of the suspects were also accused of possessing class A and B drugs with intent to supply.Police have said the five men killed in the crash may have had links to “serious and organised criminal activity”, adding that four of those killed in the car that hit the police vehicle had previous convictions.The fatal crash sparked a wave of concern about a social media trend for posting videos of dangerous, high-speed driving, which the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday called “truly reprehensible”.Cleveland police said there was currently “no evidence that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning was for the purposes of TikTok”, but Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, wants assurances from the tech companies and from the online communications regulator Ofcom “that this content is being proactively sought and removed”.At least one of those killed in Saturday’s crash had previously posted reckless driving footage online.The Guardian on Monday found a video on YouTube seen 2.5m times showing a Honda being driven at dangerous speed through a council estate and then down a narrow country road. Google, which owns YouTube, terminated the account after being asked for comment.The arrests have come as part of a “wide-scale investigation into the criminality which took place” in the hours leading up to the crash, which has involved the help of officers and staff from Durham, Northumbria and North Yorkshire police forces.As part of the investigation a Volvo XC60, believed to be associated with the activities of the passengers of the Volkswagen Passat, had been identified and recovered, police said.Assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said his force had engaged in “a fast-moving and complex investigation, with significant links to serious and organised criminal activity” and claimed the “events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect”.He said: “We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice. Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organised crime.“Officers and staff across Cleveland have shown incredible resilience in continuing their work in the face of tragedy. Two of their colleagues lost their lives while serving the people of Cleveland and, while the impact will be felt by our people for a long time to come, they have continued to act with the utmost professionalism.“I am also extremely grateful for the support we have received, and continue to receive, from the public of Cleveland and our wider police family.”Earlier on BBC Radio 5 Live, defence minister, Luke Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies “step up”.“I think we all need to give the police time,” he said. “But there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content.”Earlier this month,five young men were killed in Irelandand four other people injured after the car the men were travelling in was driven the wrong way down the M9 motorway.More than £500,000 has been raised for the families of the two officers who died, while floral tributes have also been left beside the A66 close to the site of Saturday’s crash.One said: “Behind every uniform is a person with a life, family, friends and people whose lives they have touched along the way.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform would evict social housing tenants over unkempt gardens | Social housing | The Guardian
description: Plan part of a wider policy to remove foreign nationals from social homes and prioritise young British-born couples
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Plan part of a wider policy to remove foreign nationals from social homes and prioritise young British-born couples
Content: Reform UK has promised to oversee a boom in social home building.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenReform UK has promised to oversee a boom in social home building.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianSocial housingReform would evict social housing tenants over unkempt gardensPlan part of a wider policy to remove foreign nationals from social homes and prioritise young British-born couplesKiran StaceyPolicy editorMon 24 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTFirst published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial housing tenants will be evicted if they fail to keep their gardens well maintained under a Reform UK government, the party has announced.Lee Anderson, the party’s chair, said that if Reform came to power it would insist that those in social rented homes would be required to keep their properties decorated and gardens looked after.The plan is part of awider policythat would throw out any foreign national from their existing social home, and prioritise young married couples who were born in Britain for new housing.Anderson told a press conference on Monday: “If you go back in time and look what actually happened … the people that rented council homes had to be married under a Labour, socialist government.Reform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing listRead more“They had to look after their property. They had to keep it well maintained. The gardens done and decorated, and they were inspected on a regular basis by officers from the council.”He added: “What is wrong with expecting people who live in subsidised housing, paid for, subsidised, by the hard-working British taxpayer … to keep their house to a reasonable standard?”The policy is part of a promise by Reform to oversee a boom in social housebuilding, whether through council or housing associations.Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, said on Monday that Reform would change the law to make sure certain types of people got access to this new housing, with British-born working couples with children getting the highest priority.Tice and Anderson said that for the purposes of the policy, people who were born abroad to British parents who were temporarily overseas would count as British-born. Those born abroad to foreign parents who have lived in the UK as British citizens for almost their entire lives, however, would not.“We have no problem importing British-born people first,” Anderson said.Tice, who is divorced and is getting remarried later this year, said his policy was deliberately designed to promote marriage.“Marriage is a great thing, and in a sense, when people get married, we all hope that it’s going to be for life,” he said. “Sometimes it is, and sometimes it doesn’t work out, but I don’t think it’s wrong to be ambitious and to promote marriage.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe party’s plans to boost social housebuilding rest largely on allowing housing associations, which have built the bulk of social homes since the Thatcher government, to borrow more.Tory plan to ban foreign nationals from social housing condemned as ‘divisive’Read moreTice argued that if associations were allowed to increase the accounting value of the homes they own, they could borrow more and use that money to build.Industry insiders, however, warned that such a plan could push many cash-strapped associations into worse financial problems.Andy Hulme, the chief executive of Hyde, one of the country’s biggest housing associations, said: “As long-term charitable organisations that are closely regulated, social housing providers need to balance borrowing against the affordability of repayments.“These proposals would radically change housing associations’ debt levels, which could lead many to violate their banking agreements and likely tip some into default.”Explore more on these topicsSocial housingCommunitiesHousingReform UKImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Massachusetts woman suspected of killing police officer husband found dead | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home
Content: A ring camera showing Karen Solomon.Photograph: Worcester Police DepartmentView image in fullscreenA ring camera showing Karen Solomon.Photograph: Worcester Police DepartmentMassachusettsMassachusetts woman suspected of killing police officer husband found deadKaren Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their homeAssociated PressMon 24 Aug 2026 19.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Monday, six days after she disappeared from herMassachusettshome, authorities said.Karen Solomon, an advocate who called for improvements and greater awareness of police mental health issues, had disappeared after Worcester police officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home just before 5.30am on 18 August. Officials had named Karen Solomon a suspect and said she was believed to be armed.“We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred,” the Worcester police chief, Paul Saucier, said at a news conference Monday.Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman’s corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon.A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it.On 19 August, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple’s home and found her husband’s body.Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said.Worcester county district attorney Joseph Early Jr said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband’s death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.Arrest warrant issued for wife of Massachusetts officer found dead at homeRead morePolice handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple’s Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6km) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs.Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First Help, which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books – Hearts Beneath the Badge and The Price They Pay – about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders.In a 2020 interview on the Dr Phil show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives.In a statement read by Saucier during Monday’s news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers.“The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless,” the family said. “The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as “a tremendous human being” who was like family.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Move is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic ties
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Move is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic ties
Content: Manufacturing facility in Alliston, Ontario.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManufacturing facility in Alliston, Ontario.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTrump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelMove is latest deterioration in trade relations between neighbors with historically strong economic tiesGaya GuptaMon 24 Aug 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpannounced a new 50%tariffon automobiles and crucial raw materials fromCanada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbors with historically strong economic ties.The US president said that the increased tariffs would start on 1 January 2027 on all cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel. He also derided the nation’s tariffs on American farmers, writing on social media thatCanadahas been “ripping off” the US “for years”.“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”In response,Mark Carneytold reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected.Mark Carney says Canada can’t accept US trade deal that would weaken French languageRead more“It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” the Canadian prime minister said from Quebec.“But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” Carney continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.”He added that Canada would be ready to move forward with talks “when the Americans go to the negotiating table first with the right attitude toward our industry and a true partnership”.Trump’s announcement follows the last-minutecollapsethis weekend of a potential deal to lower tariffs on automobiles and other materials. After Trump imposed another 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports, including hockey equipment and electronics, Carney, rejected the latest deal between the two nations on Saturday.Carney said that the US “asked too much and they offered too little”, and he has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”.Canada and the US have been longtime partners, trading roughly $909bn, according to the office of the US trade representative. But Trump’s second presidential term and his aggressive trade policies have brought the era of “deep ties” between the two nations to a close, Carneysaidlast year, vowing to fight Trump’s sweeping tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaDonald TrumpMark CarneyAutomotive industryTariffsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Top US firms that backed Voting Rights Act donate to groups working to undermine it | US politics | The Guardian
description: Watchdog data shared with Guardian shows contributions to Republican Attorneys General Association and others
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Watchdog data shared with Guardian shows contributions to Republican Attorneys General Association and others
Content: People wait to vote in Columbia, South Carolina, in May 2026.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople wait to vote in Columbia, South Carolina, in May 2026.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesUS politicsTop US firms that backed Voting Rights Act donate to groups working to undermine itWatchdog data shared with Guardian shows contributions to Republican Attorneys General Association and othersLauren ArataniMon 24 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver a dozen US companies that signed a 2021letterurging Congress to strengthen theVoting Rights Actcontinue to contribute to state political groups that are actively working to undermine the legislation, according to a campaign finance watchdog.Researchers at the Center for Political Accountability (CPA), a nonpartisan organization that tracks financial disclosures, found that companies – including Airbnb, DoorDash, Target and Zillow – that signed the letter are contributing to groups known as 527 organizations that prop up key state races, according to data provided exclusively to the Guardian.Four longtime donors to these groups, Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, had either stopped contributing entirely or lowered their contributions to Republican and Democratic groups for the 2022 midterms, but have resumed contributions for the current election cycle.The January 6 insurrection created a brief reckoning among corporate leaders, many of whom criticizedDonald Trump’s role in inciting the violence. The Republican Attorneys General Association (Raga), a 527 organization, was under scrutiny after reports revealed the groupsent outrobocalls to people encouraging them to attend a “Stop the Steal” rally in front of Congress on 6 January 2021 – which preceded the insurrection. Raga leaders later said they had no knowledge of the robocalls.But the companies have resumed their donations to Raga and, in some cases, have become new contributors to the group. Google’s contribution went from $100,400 in the 2018 election down to $50,000 in 2022. So far this election, the company has donated $325,000 to Raga.Bar chart of tech company contributions to Republican attorneys general racesThe donations reflect a broader U-turn trend seen among many in corporate America who were publicly critical of Trump and Republicans after the January 6 insurrection and then did anabout-faceas soon as he was elected back into office.The 527 organizations are classified as tax-exempt political groupsoverseen bythe Internal Revenue Service (IRS). They often fly under the radar compared to political action committees (Pacs) that are overseen by the Federal Election Commission, but political experts say these 527 groups have enormous influence on the state level by supporting key swing races – and public corporations tend to be their dominant funders.Compared with their counterparts in Washington, who are often stalled in gridlock, state leaders and legislators often have greater influence in advancing policies that ultimately have a national impact.Aipac-linked Super Pacs spend millions in California to thwart progressive candidateRead moreState attorneys general have been key in fighting cases in front of the US supreme court that overturn decades of precedent. The court gave a Republican attorney general from Alabama a huge victory when itruledin her favor in Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization – the case that overturned Roe v Wade and gave states the power to legislate abortion access.Earlier this summer, the court gave a win to a Republican Louisiana attorney general when it ruled in her favor in Louisiana v Callais thatoverturnedkey components of the Voting Rights Act.Raga praised the ruling, saying in a Maystatementthat “no group of elected officials make a bigger impact than Republican AGs”.For groups largely operating at the state level, what may be considered a small amount of cash in a federal campaign can make a major impact in key state races.“A $100,000 contribution that ends up impacting a handful of state races can flip a state legislature, can flip an AG’s office,” said Jeanne Hanna, CPA’s vice-president of research. “It’s a trickle-up effect on state, and then federal policy, for a much smaller price tag. So while the numbers may not be as big and as flashy, the impact can be even more significant.”Overall, Republican 527 groups are outraising their Democratic counterparts this election cycle, with a large chunk of their donations coming from public companies. Major Republican state groups have raised $240m in the 2026 election cycle so far, while Democratic groups have raised $197m.These groups include Raga and the Republican Governors Association (RGA) that have been key in supporting figures including the former Texas attorney general Ken Paxton, Texas governor Greg Abbott and Georgia governor Brian Kemp.A third powerful group, the Republican State Leadership Committee (RSLC), which focuses on competitive legislative races, has raised a total of $55m this election cycle so far. It is unclear how much of that comes from corporate contributions as the organization has not filed specific contributor data for part of this election cycle, according to CPA.Bar chart showing the trend of Republicans out-raising Democrats in corporate donationsSince 2010, public corporations and trade associations have contributed $1bn out of the $2.5bn raised by the 527 organizations that assist governor, attorneys general and legislative races, according to the CPA. Historically, 62% of all corporate contributions go to Republican groups, while 38% go to Democratic groups.For the 2026 election cycle so far, corporation contributions made up 39% of all of Raga’s fundraising and 33% of RGA fundraising, totaling $63m to the two groups so far. In comparison, corporate contributions to their Democratic counterparts totaled $54m and made up about a third of total fundraising.Overall contributions to Republican and Democratic groups are already surpassing fundraising that was seen at this point of the election cycle in 2022, withRepublicansoverall raising 33% more and Democrats raising 22% more than the last midterm election.This tracks with the boost in corporate political contributions to Super Pacs that largely focus on congressional races. Corporate support for Super Pacs has totaled $517m so far this year, accounting for nearly a third of all corporate political spending since 2010, according toPublic Citizen.Hanna said corporate contributions to these political groups continue to be routine, even though their influence on policy has changed over the last decade.With $200m to spend on the midterms, crypto hopes to repeat its 2024 success: ‘It’s the most critical time’Read more“These groups have been around for a long time, and they were electing officeholders who were not nearly as political, not nearly as partisan as they are now,” Hanna said. “The role of the state AGs, even the role of state legislatures in some ways, has changed really dramatically in a pretty short span of time in recent years. The sort of reflexive giving that companies are engaged in for access and sort of elbow rubbing is having a different kind of impact.”Hanna said it is possible that some companies may be concerned that scaling back political donations could lead to retaliation in the future. But the donations are not as risk-free as companies may believe them to be.The groups are helping to elect officials “who are undermining not only the broader environment that companies need to be successful, but also the commitments that these companies are making to their employees, to their consumer base, to their investors”, said Bruce Freed, the president and co-founder of CPA. “You need to have consistency. There has to be an alignment between company policies, where their contributions go and what they enable.”In a researchprimerreleased by CPA and the Wharton School earlier this month, corporate ethics experts said corporate boards should have more active oversight over political spending. Companies should also adopt policies that require regular reporting of political spending and ensure that the political groups are disclosing how they intend to use their raised funds.“We’re pretty agnostic about whether or not companies spend,” Hanna said. “All we ask is that they increase their due diligence, to have more awareness of where the money actually ends up and ensure it aligns with their values.”Explore more on these topicsUS politicsUS political financingRepublicansUS voting rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven? | US economy | The Guardian
description: The US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not working
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: The US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not working
Content: Scott Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/CNP/Andrew Thomas/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenScott Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/CNP/Andrew Thomas/ShutterstockUS economyAnalysisThe treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven?Eduardo PorterThe US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not workingMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTShareThe bond market is driving the Trump administration crazy. Last week, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced that the government wouldsharply rampup its purchase of treasury bonds, in an effort to raise their price and thus push down their yield, which amounts to the interest rate the government pays on its debt.It didn’t quite work as planned. Yields on treasurys fell after Bessent’s bond market intervention but soon bounced back. By Friday afternoon, the yield on the 10-year treasury was back nearwhere it wasbefore the secretary’s announcement. The yield on the 30-year bond was again trading around itshighest levelin 20 years or more.Bessent’s desperation is hardly surprising. The rise in treasury yields since the upsurge in inflation in 2022 has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt, which has ballooned to arecord $40tn. This year interest payments will absorb 13.5% of all federal spending, more than defense and up from 5.2% in 2021.US treasury doubles debt buyback to steady bond market amid inflation fearsRead moreTo Trump’s chagrin, higher treasury yields – which set the benchmark for rates on mortgage loans and other long-term lending across the economy – are walloping his popularity, helping freeze the housing market and contributing to the growing realization that he has been adismal stewardof the economy.An irked president has called interest rates “ridiculous” and “artificially high”, and blamed the Federal Reserve for not cutting them. In one of his most recent signs of derangement, he lashed outagainst Switzerlandfor having lower interest rates than the US, pointing out that he had the “absolute right” to cut off all US business with the country. And he hinted at a novel approach to monetary policy, suggesting that “the ultimate interventionis our military”.But treasurys’ persistent weakness raises a more broadly unsettling prospect for the global economy: the end of the era in which the United States provided a more or less universally accepted safe, liquid asset for investors, companies and governments around the world to store their wealth.Between the turn of the century and the Great Recession, foreign central banks increased their holdings from about 20% to more than 30% of all treasurys outstanding, as they built reserves to ward against speculative attacks or tried to manage their exchange rates. Foreign investors also piled in. By 2008, over half of all treasury bonds were in the hands of foreigners.US government bonds were considered such a solid place to store money that their price would rise (and their yield would fall), any time a crisis struck, sending investors scurrying for safety. This was true even when, as during the collapse of the housing bubble in the US in 2007, the crisis was sparked by a mix of financial exuberance and inept policymaking in the United States.The pillars supporting the treasury markethave been weakeningfor some time, however. Foreign central banks – mainly in China and Japan – have sharplypared backtheir holdings. Private foreign investors have picked up some of the slack. By mid 2025, private foreign investors held $7tn in treasurys, almost twice as much as the $3.9tn held by foreign official entities. Still, the foreign share of treasury holdings has fallen by 10 percentage points over the last two decades or so, to about 40%.double quotation markThe main threat to treasurys’ status as the paramount store of value in the world comes from withinThe new buyers of treasurys come with new risks. Unlike foreign official entities, which hold the bonds to ensure financial stability, private investors seek returns. They will sell to make a buck. Their rising footprint has turned the treasury market into a more volatile place than it used to be.The main threat to treasurys’ status as the paramount store of value in the world, though, comes from within. The supply of treasury bonds has been growing at a fast clip in recent times, to fund a budget deficit that is now hovering at about 6% of GDP. Supply has outpaced demand. These days, US government debt no longer has the top rating from the big credit rating agencies andmust offer a higher yieldthan that of many other affluent nations.Add in the increasing mistrust of Trump’s reckless economic governance and you have the makings of a problem. In the Trump era, treasury bonds no longer rise as they used to in moments of high risk. When Trump unleashed his volley of tariffs against everybody on“Liberation Day”in April last year, investors dumped treasurys just as they would a lowly emerging market bond.Bessent knows this poses a problem for the government. Funding the deficit requires adding some $10bn a day, net, to the mountain of treasurys on the market. But it also poses a potential problem to investors and governments in the rest of the world. They all learned to trust treasurys as a bedrock asset in which to store their wealth, a perfect complement to the dollar as the main mode of exchange for trade and investment around the world. What will they do without it?Like Nato trying to convince Trump to stay or the World Trade Organization working to restore its relevance since the US left, financial leaders don’t yet know quite how to cope with the seemingly inevitable demise of the American safe haven. Indeed, treasurys maintain what is left of their status largely because it has not been easy for foreign countries and businesses to find somewhere else to keep their stash.But the search is on. Bessent will have to do more than repurchase a few billion worth of treasurys to overcome mistrust in America’s Loony Tunes leader and ensure that there is sufficient demand out there to match the massive supply coming down the pike.Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon SubstackExplore more on these topicsUS economyBondsUS interest ratesDonald TrumpFederal ReserveEconomicsTrump administrationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Post-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and awe | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Possession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season began
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Possession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season began
Content: Ipswich, Hull and Brentford all thrived at the weekend despite a lack of possession.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty and Tom Jenkins)View image in fullscreenIpswich, Hull and Brentford all thrived at the weekend despite a lack of possession.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty and Tom Jenkins)Premier LeagueAnalysisPost-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and aweBarney RonayPossession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season beganMon 24 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTShareThere has been something oddly narcotic and moreish about the drip‑drip of fresh Pep Guardiola content either side of the start of the newPremier Leagueseason. Eras come and go. Everything dies, baby, that’s a fact. But four‑part Amazon Prime documentaries make angels of us all.So we have continued to feast on the Pep-at-City visuals: dead jeopardy, reheated beefs, the uplifting team talks of a departed manager to the departed players of a departed team, and moments that often feel far more gripping than the daily churn of what we must, out of habit, call the real world.Liverpool are still haunted by the mess of last summer | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThe thought occurred watching all this: has the Premier League found its Tupac? Is Pep just going to keep on doing this, dropping new material, fresh hits, posthumous platinum albums? A bald, thin charismatic man who keeps on releasing his lost tapes. We have exactly the thing, sir. Is he even actually dead?Probably this won’t happen. But a profound absence is still a profound presence at moments like these. The ghosts continue to pull the strings. This weekend was the first of the new Premier League season. More significantly, it was also the first of the post‑Pep era.And this has been a genuine era, 10 years in the game and an entire tactical culture shift in the making. Unsurprisingly, there was an odd sense of lightness across those nine fixtures on Friday through to Sunday, of old bonds cast aside, even a little giddiness. Suddenly dad isn’t home. The chair by the door is empty. Let’s all just rip it up a bit, shall we?This relies on a slightly out‑of‑date notion of what Guardiola‑ism became in its later years. But the fact is, something interesting did happen in those Friday‑to‑Sunday games. Think of pure Pep-ball and what are you seeing? Possession. Cold, high‑craft control. This is a coach who famously said: “My desire is to have 100% possession,” after a 5-1 thrashing of Arsenal in Munich during which Thiago Alcântara complete 122 passes.View image in fullscreenManchester City manager Enzo Maresca acknowledges the fans before City’s opener against Bournemouth.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesAdmittedly, Guardiola was speaking out of frustration that day, talking more about not losing the ball at key moments, possession as defence. But these ideas did have a profound mimetic effect in England. During Guardiola’s decade atManchester Citythe team that had the least possession in the Premier League would win, on average, only 30%-35% of games, a figure that fell as low as 28% in 2021‑22 but which had begun to pick up in the last two seasons as even City’s own version of Pep‑ball became more mixed and next‑gen.But this weekend the opposite thing happened. In six of nine games played from Friday to Sunday one team took significantly more possession while failing to win. Liverpool had 60% possession plus 27 shots but still just scrambled a draw and looked, frankly, pretty wild. Manchester United had 71% possession and were well beaten by Hull. Tottenham had 60 % possession and lost 3-0. Nottingham Forest had 56% and lost. Sunderland had 62%, Crystal Palace 58%, and both lost.There were three exceptions to this, all outliers in their own way. Manchester City had 66% possession and won at home against Bournemouth, but spent 84 minutes looking like they were losing. Brighton had 73% possession and beat an Aston Villa team that had made a collective decision to play with their eyes closed and their legs on the wrong way round.
