title: Julián Álvarez walks alone at Atlético in transfer saga with no end – and no winners | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Barcelona target left exposed after draw with Villarreal as supporters vented their fury at his ‘dream’ to leave
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Barcelona target left exposed after draw with Villarreal as supporters vented their fury at his ‘dream’ to leave
Content: Julián Álvarez was the target of fan frustration at the Metropolitano as he seeks a move away from Atlético.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJulián Álvarez was the target of fan frustration at the Metropolitano as he seeks a move away from Atlético.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesLa LigaJulián Álvarez walks alone at Atlético in transfer saga with no end – and no winnersBarcelona target left exposed after draw with Villarreal as supporters vented their fury at his ‘dream’ to leaveSid LoweMon 24 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJulián Álvarez entered a long, dark tunnel on his own. “We’re stronger together,” Giuliano Simeone said but that wasn’t the way it went. At the end of their first home game of the season, a 2-2 draw with Villarreal, all of Atlético Madrid’s players gathered by the centre circle, shook hands with their opponents and each other, then headed towards the south end of the Metropolitano.Almostall of them did, anyway:one was left behind. Somebody in a suit had a quiet word then the press officer came, pointing in the other direction. So, while his teammates turned to the supporters who had turned on him, the man wearing No 19 went west, to the exit.Álvarez walked alone. Head down in silence, as he had been all afternoon and beyond, he set off slowly across the pitch accompanied only by his thoughts and the whistles that followed him. Not offered a hand to shake or a nod of acknowledgment, he stepped past the Atlético badge on the touchline where the mouth of the tunnel opens. Either side, supporters hung over the void, whistling and shouting. Way off to his left, Atlético’s other players paused, seemingly waiting for him to slip out of sight before approaching the stand, but none turned back. A scarf was thrown, landing at Álvarez’s feet and left lying there. And then he disappeared into the dark, a portrait of the place he is in.No one was waiting for him on the other side. Álvarez went up the stairs, past a couple of security guards and turned left to an empty dressing room, not lifting his gaze and not invited to either. Four minutes would pass before his teammates came up the stairs together. But at least it was quiet now, for a little while. The noise had been loud; no one could recall supporters turning on their own player quite like this. Atlético’s fans, stillhisfans, had whistled him when his name was read out, whistled him when he had warmed up, whistled him when he came on wearing red and white there for the first time since April and since he declared it his “dream” to leave, and they had whistled him out of there too, for good.Good?“Unhappily, this situation isn’t comfortable for anyone,” Jan Oblak said, and amid the damage done, the mutual accusations, the hurt pride and spited faces, nor is it easy to see a solution. The situation, in short, is this: Julián Álvarez wants to leave forBarcelona. Barcelona want to sign him. But he has a contract until June 2030, a €500m buyout clause, and Atlético won’t sell him. And definitely not tothem. And so, here they are.Stuck.View image in fullscreenJulián Álvarez trudges off the pitch alone as his Atlético Madrid teammates applaud the fans.Photograph: Manu Reino/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockThe first time Álvarez hinted he may not continue was after facing Tottenham in the Champions League last March. The timing seemed odd then: it hadn’t been an easy season, the feeling that something was wrong growing and about to be confirmed, but he had just scored twice andAtlético had won 5-2. It seemed odder still when he chose the moments after Argentina beat Austria at the World Cupto announce he wanted to go. “It’s not the time to talk about this but nor can I hide,” he said. “I spoke with the people I needed to [at Atlético] and the best thing for everyone is a transfer. I want to fulfil my dream.”There had been a “bid”that wasn’t really a bid at all from Real Madrid but the dream was Barcelona and they were the ones who had been speaking to Álvarez, planning how to make it happen. Which was one of the reasons why Atlético were so determined it wouldn’t, deciding to take a stand instead, make this a cause. This was not about him wanting to go, or not only, but about thewayit had been done.From New York, Joan Laporta claimed that Barcelona had made an “important” offer. “If Atlético are prepared to accept, fantastic,” he said, but they weren’t and they didn’t think much of the offer either. Atlético’s chief executive, Miguel Ángel Gil Marín, insisted they would not sell at any price: they had told Álvarez, his agent and Barcelona that. “I know Joan: he’s always acting up for the media, fans, his own personal circus,” Gil Marín said. “I told him: ‘Leave it, please. We don’t want to sell and won’t sell, stop insisting’. He loves to play the part but he knows perfectly well that Julián won’t play for Barcelona next season.”José Mourinho marks Real Madrid return with late drama and touch of humilityRead moreBarcelona insisted that they had approached a potential transfer the right way, with “respect”, but Atlético reported them to the RFEF (Spanish Football Federation) and refused to budge, a statement made, territory defended. This had become a point of principle, examples to be made of them. The noise though refused to go away. When Álvarez arrived for pre-season, still wanting out, he cut an isolated figure. If every silence and furrowed brow was analysed to death, it was true that there was an absence about him. This weekend Jorge Valdano took a line from Julio Cortázar to explain it: “When someone says they’re going, they’re already gone.”Even if they’re not going. While Atlético quietly investigated other options, Gil Marín gave a statement again insisting that Álvarez was staying. “We can’t allow other clubs and media to dictate our policy and disrespect us,” he said. “We have values.” He attacked Álvarez’s agent too, saying that Alvarez had been poorly advised. To which Fernando Hidalgo – whose version hasAtléticopromising that if Álvarez publicly said he wanted to go, taking responsibility, they would allow him to – replied with a post: “Never ask a liar to explain why he lied; he would only have to lie again.”As for the head coach, watching his superiors take the lead, he was ready to put Álvarez back in the team. “You can’t be clearer than the club’s been. It’s like when the judge says: ‘Denied!’” Diego Simeone said. As if it was that simple, the case so easily dismissed. While Atlético said they would “look after” him, while accusing Barcelona and Hidalgo lifted some blame from his shoulders, Álvarez’s return instead underlined that coming back from this might be even harder than anticipated, redemption more of a reach than imagined.View image in fullscreenDiego Simeone left Julián Álvarez (bottom right) on the bench to start with.Photograph: Sheng Cheng/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSunday did not suggest a solution, a moment for the healing to start. Instead, it felt unsustainable, the case eclipsing all else, pressure building to find a proper conclusion. This was a fun match, but it was all about one man, the bad guy, and the verdict against him – and that affects everyone, maybe no winners any more. After the game there was a moment when, hands raised in front of him, the press officer asked journalists if there were any more questions, pausing to add …about the game …and the hands went down again. Before it, every photographer gathered in front of the bench as Álvarez took up his place to the left of Juan Musso and José María Gimenez, staring at the floor, the only movement his clenching jaw, while 60,000 people whistled his name. That, it turned out, was just the beginning.Quick GuideLa Liga resultsShowRayo Vallecano 1-1 Alavés, Real Betis 1-0 Real Sociedad, Espanyol 1-2 Real Madrid, Valencia 0-0 Celta Vigo, Athletic Club 1-3 Sevilla, Elche 0-5 Barcelona, Getafe 1-0 Racing de Santander, Atlético Madrid 2-2 VillarrealWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.When he went to warm up on 51 minutes, they whistled again. From the south end, there were chants of “Fuck Barcelona! Fuck Catalonia!” They sang: “Weare Atlético”. And “Atlético yes, mercenaries no!” Another one ran: “Tell him to go, once and for fucking all!” (To which Álvarez might have thought:yeah, that’s what I’m trying to do). As Atlético’s players came to the touchline after their first goal, the fitness coach said Álvarez was about to go on. “Careful, eh,” Marc Pubill replied. The noise when he did was deafening and didn’t relent. There weren’t many touches but with every one the angry volume rose, the rejection not receding all the way to the final whistle, which was not the final whistle at all: that too was for Álvarez. With eight days left in the window, it could still have been a good riddance, but … if it’s not?“Julián is with us in the team and for as long as he is, we’re going to support him,” Oblak said. “All I know is that if Atlético want to win titles we have to be together, we need strikers and we need important strikers,” Simeone noted, admitting he had apologised to Ademola Lookman for making him play there in the absence of Álvarez and the injured Alex Sørloth. Theydohave strikers, the coach said the second time he turned to that line, but they would have to “take care” of them, the coach confirming that the club had told him it was their decision that he shouldn’t greet the fans, not Julián’s.Yet if it had been designed to protect Álvarez and if this statement had too, absolvinghimof having chosen to turn his back onthem, it also exposed him. Leaving first without the others, none joining him, served as an expression of his isolation, hisothering, of how broken the situation had become. “Together we’re stronger, that’s always characterised us, madeAtlético Madriddifferent. He is our player so we will die for him on the pitch,” Giuliano Simeone said, but when the time came, Álvarez went alone.PosTeamPGDPts1Sevilla2362Alaves2343Atletico Madrid2244Barcelona1535Espanyol2236Real Madrid1137Real Betis1138Getafe2-239Villarreal20210Deportivo La Coruna10111Celta Vigo10112Valencia10113Racing Santander2-1114Rayo Vallecano2-1115Elche2-5116Osasuna00017Real Sociedad1-1018Athletic Bilbao1-2019Malaga1-2020Levante1-30Explore more on these topicsLa LigaAtlético MadridBarcelonaEuropean club footballTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh tipped to approach James Hird for Bombers AFL role | AFL | The Guardian
description: James Hird was overlooked for the Essendon job, but Bombers legend Matthew Lloyd thinks new coach Mark McVeigh would still be keen to have him on the staff
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: James Hird was overlooked for the Essendon job, but Bombers legend Matthew Lloyd thinks new coach Mark McVeigh would still be keen to have him on the staff
Content: Mark McVeigh has left the Sydney Swans to take over as head coach at Essendon, where James Hird may still return as assistant.Photograph: Daniel Pockett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark McVeigh has left the Sydney Swans to take over as head coach at Essendon, where James Hird may still return as assistant.Photograph: Daniel Pockett/Getty ImagesAFLNew Essendon coach Mark McVeigh tipped to approach James Hird for Bombers AFL roleMcVeigh leaves Sydney Swans to take on role at crisis clubHird was McVeigh’s assistant when interim GWS coach in 2022Australian Associated PressMon 24 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEssendon great Matthew Lloyd is certain that new AFL coach Mark McVeigh would love to have James Hird on his staff. McVeigh and Bombers president Andrew Welsh will front the media on Tuesday, a day after the appointment was confirmed.On Sunday night, Hird himself had revealed that McVeigh had won the role. Hird’s bid to return to Essendon for a second term as senior coach continues to sharply divide opinion.Banned Sydney Swans players not welcome at Brownlows as AFL delays inquiry until police probe concludesRead moreWelsh said in the Monday announcement that McVeigh was the “clear standout” candidate, ahead of Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide coaching director Murray Davis.The Bombers are in crisis, finishing bottom this season with the worst win-loss record in club history. There is talk of a pending board challenge and former captain Zach Merrett appears certain to again seek a trade to Hawthorn, a year after his stunning bid was denied by Essendon.But Lloyd, who played alongside Hird, McVeigh and Welsh at Essendon, predicted the new coach would most likely put the feelers out to his old teammate.“All I will say is, Mark would love to have James Hird as part of his staff,” Lloyd told the Nine Network. “He [Hird] may say ‘you are kidding, there’s no way I’m coming, after being overlooked’. But Mark would certainly be open to it.”View image in fullscreenJames Hird is still being linked to a role at Essendon.Photograph: Morgan Hancock/Getty ImagesHird was an assistant to McVeigh when he was interim GWS senior coach in 2022. McVeigh has been an assistant coach at Sydney since 2023.Lloyd added that he will not return to the club as part of McVeigh’s football department, saying the new coach knows he will be unavailable next year.He also pleaded with Essendon to support McVeigh properly and spend big on their football staff. Lloyd referred to the unfortunate slogan that the club had for the 2013 season, the year they were punished heavily for their drugs debacle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFrom the Pocket: AFL WeeklyJonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL storiesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe fallout from that saga continues to bedevil Essendon and is a key reason why they are struggling so badly. Hird was suspended as coach for his role in the scandal and then returned, before resigning in 2015.There has been a growing push for him to come back as coach, but the support in and around the club for Hird is far from unanimous.“Where is the best development coach out there, in the land? Go after them, because I don’t think they have that,” Lloyd said. “There used to be a slogan, ‘whatever it takes’ – that’s where they need to be now. They can’t afford to have this one go wrong.”Explore more on these topicsAFLEssendonAustralian rules footballAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fulham 2-3 Chelsea: Premier League – as it happened | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Cole Palmer capped a majestic performance with the decisive third goal as Chelsea edged Fulham in a brilliant game
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: Cole Palmer capped a majestic performance with the decisive third goal as Chelsea edged Fulham in a brilliant game
Content: 5h ago17.07 EDTJacob SteinbergThis was a crash course for Xabi Alonso in life atChelsea.His new side thrilled in possession at Craven Cottage. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers combined to devastating effect and there was even an assist for the new £52m centre-back, Maxence Lacroix.At times the only issue was the two No 10s both laying claim to the ice cold celebration. Palmer had a point to prove after missing out on England’s World Cup squad and Rogers scored on his debut after his £117m move from Aston Villa. Yet victory in Alonso’s first competitive game as Chelsea’s manager was far from straightforward. He saw that he needs a better goalkeeper than Robert Sánchez and will worry about his side’s lack of smarts.Fulham, who will hope this bright start under Alvaro Arbeloa shows there is life after Marco Silva, were unfortunate not to rescue a point.Chelsea’s front three dazzle as they edge out Fulham in derby thrillerRead moreShare

title: ‘Project Magic’: RFL in talks with NRL over radical changes to investment deal | RFL | The Guardian
description: The Rugby Football League is to discuss a £50m loan package with the NRL after a £35m investment deal was rejected
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Rugby Football League is to discuss a £50m loan package with the NRL after a £35m investment deal was rejected
Content: Super League clubs voted last week to reject an NRL investment offer.Photograph: Richard Walker/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSuper League clubs voted last week to reject an NRL investment offer.Photograph: Richard Walker/ProSports/ShutterstockRFL‘Project Magic’: RFL in talks with NRL over radical changes to investment dealSuper League clubs rejected £35m deal last weekThe 14 owners due to discuss plans at meetingExclusive byMatt HughesMon 24 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rugby Football League is exploring radically different terms to the funding deal initially offered by Australia’s National Rugby League with talks under way over seeking a £50m loan package to replace the guaranteed investment of £35m that was rejected last week.The Guardian has seen details of an alternative vision produced by Rugby League Commercial in a document entitled Project Magic, which the 14 Super League clubs owners will discuss at a meeting on Tuesday .Leeds deliver timely Super League showcase while NRL investment hangs in balanceRead moreNigel Wood, the RFL chief executive, is understood to have circulated the document to the Super League owners last Wednesday, the day before they voted to reject the NRL’s offer. Discussions between the two competitions over investment from Australia have been ongoing since meetings in Las Vegas in January, with theNRLchief executive, Peter V’Landys, due to visit the UK next week in the hope of finalising the deal.The NRL offer would have seen it invest £7m a year for five years in return for a 10% stake in Super League, with the money to be distributed to the clubs. Instead of selling a stake in Super League, the Project Magic document details the RFL’s desire to seek from the NRL a £50m payment-in-kind loan, which it would use “to fund central growth initiatives and accelerate global expansion”.In another significant departure, the £50m would be retained centrally by the RFL rather than distributed to the clubs, which may prove a sticking point for many. The Project Magic document details what the RFL describes as a 10-year plan to grow the sport, and includes ambitious targets such as expanding Super League to 18 or 20 clubs, launching a joint direct‑to-consumer streaming platform with the NRL for non-domestic markets and creating a fully professional women’s competition.The RFL’s plans for investing the £50m are also outlined in detail, with £13.5m to be spent on improving the clubs’ commercial capabilities, £10m on the player pathway and £5m on broadcasting services.An RFL source said that the loan proposal is no longer its preferred option, but it is being considered significant enough for the clubs to discuss on Tuesday.While the Super League clubs were broadly united in rejecting the NRL’s initial offer, agreeing on a way forward may prove more difficult.Many of the competition’s bigger clubs such as Wigan, Warrington and the champions Hull KR are strongly in favour of partnering with the NRL, whereas smaller clubs like Wakefield are more sceptical amid concerns they could be left behind.Although the RFL appears to be advocating demanding an increase of almost 50% in funding from the NRL, it is unclear whether the Super League clubs will support the proposal, with many preferring a smaller cash injection to a centrally managed loan.One source with knowledge of the discussions described Project Magic as an attempt by Wood to retain control and influence at the RFL if the NRL deal closes.NRL sources have described its position as a “take it or leave it” however, and it is far from certain it would be willing to offer a £50m loan.Moreover, there are further significant obstacles to the deal being completed, as the NRL is demanding significant governance reforms, including the creation of an independent commission to run the sport in the UK, which would further reduce the influence of the RFL.Explore more on these topicsRFLNRLRugby leagueAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brydon Carse dropped by England as investigation begins into handcuffs incident | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week after footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby emerged
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Brydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week after footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby emerged
Content: Brydon Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker in the 2025-26 Ashes.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker in the 2025-26 Ashes.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamBrydon Carse dropped by England as investigation begins into handcuffs incidentBowler spoken to by police outside bar in DerbyCarse replaced in squad for second Test by Sonny BakerAli MartinMon 24 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week while the footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby city centre is investigated by the sport’s disciplinary body.Carse was filmed by a member of the public while he was detained briefly on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in the early hours of Sunday morning. The 31-year-old fast bowler had been celebrating victory against Derbyshire in the County Championship with his Durham teammates.Brydon Carse handcuffed by police outside nightclub prompting ECB investigationRead moreThe former England captain Ben Stokes and the fast bowler Matthew Potts were also present at the scene, with Carse said to have been in handcuffs for “a few minutes” before he agreed to move on and was let go without charge.Though not officially on England duty at the time – he was in the squad for the first Test in Leeds last week but was then sent to play for Durham – Carse is centrally contracted. The matter is now being looked into by theCricketRegulator – the sport’s disciplinary body – regarding a possible disrepute charge.In the meantime, and in light of a string of drink-related incidents that have plagued the England men’s team over the past nine months, Carse has been dropped from the Test squad. While he was not expected to play unless there was an injury, Carse has been replaced by Hampshire’s Sonny Baker.A statement from the England and Wales Cricket Board on Monday read: “Following a referral from theECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby.“Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained. Brydon will be replaced in the squad for this match by Sonny Baker.”According to sources, the footage of Carse came after he had been denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time. He had left the building following “an exchange of words” with another member of the public who spilled a drink on him. Durham, though not his direct employers, are not said to be pursuing the matter, nor are Potts or Stokes considered to have done anything wrong.Carse had been due to travel to London on Monday, with England’s 16‑man squad reconvening after the three-day innings victory secured at Headingley last Friday. They go into two training days at Lord’s before the match starts on Thursday.The issue presents Joe Root with an early off-field headache at the start of his second spell as Test captain, having made one of his first acts theremoval of the team’s midnight curfew. Root has now brought forward by a day his pre-match press conference to meet the issue head on.Questions about the team’s relationship with alcohol are inevitable, likewise those about his authority. The Carse situation came in the same week that Root backed his players to be “grown up” and “good role models and good human beings”.The decision to drop Carse while an investigation takes place follows a precedent set this summer. Stokes and Gus Atkinson both missed the second Test against New Zealand at the Oval in June when the Cricket Regulator looked into alate‑night incident in a bar in Chelseaafter victory in the series opener at Lord’s.The midnight curfew was in place on that occasion, even if it was later argued the precise details of it had not been well communicated. Atkinson had been involved in a physical altercation with a Saracens rugby player – he was not the aggressor, as per the ECB – while Stokes was simply present at the same venue.The ECB chose a different path on the eve of the Australia tour last winter, however, when Harry Brook waspunched by a nightclub bouncerthe night before the Yorkshireman captained a one-day international in Wellington, New Zealand. Brook was given a clandestine fine at the time, something which came to light only at the end of the Ashes.In between Brook’s altercation and the story being broken by the Daily Telegraph came the team’snotorious mid-Ashes break in Noosa, when opener Ben Duckett was filmed inebriated outside a backpackers bar and the footage emerged on social media before the Boxing Day Test.Duckett was cleared to play.Carse was backed heavily by Stokes during that 4-1 defeat, playing all five Tests and finishing as England’s leading wicket-taker, albeit conceding runs with it. A hand injury delayed his start to the English summer – and scuppered an intended spell at the Indian Premier League – but he had returned to fitness during the Hundred.While England were intending to stick with Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue this week as they target a first Test series win in 18 months, Carse was deemed first reserve. The retirement of Stokes in June and the new four‑pronged pace strategy should, in theory, mean opportunities down the line, unless this latest late‑night incident has affected his place in the pecking order.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamECBEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing children | Snooker | The Guardian
description: Five-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Five-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse
Content: Graeme Dott arrives at the high court in Glasgow.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersView image in fullscreenGraeme Dott arrives at the high court in Glasgow.Photograph: Lesley Martin/ReutersSnookerFormer world snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing childrenFive-day trial at high court in Glasgow heard Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abusePress AssociationMon 24 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of sexually abusing two primary school age children. The 49-year-old subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse, with the girl targeted between 1993-96 and the boy between 2006-10.A five-day trial at the high court in Glasgow heard Dott exposed himself in front of both children, touched them inappropriately, and kissed them. On Monday, he was found guilty of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour towards them. In both cases the abuse happened in the Glasgow area.During the trial, jurors heard from one of Dott’s victims, a woman now in her 40s, who told the court Dott had sexually abused her on multiple separate occasions while she was a child. She said the abuse had started with Dott “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggyback.The woman also described an occasion when she said Dott suggested playing a “guessing game” where she had to guess what he was doing. She told the court she lay down and he exposed himself to her and then began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis. The woman told the court that Dott told her not to tell anyone he was sexually abusing her.The second victim, a man who is now in his late 20s, said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts. He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.“He would … come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court. “While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.”He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place. The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”. The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips and “push himself up against me”.Giving evidence last week, Dott had said there was “absolutely no way” he sexually abused two children. Under cross-examination by prosecutor Lindsey Dalziel, Dott denied being attracted to the girl when she was young, calling the idea “disgusting”.When Dalziel put it to Dott that he touched the first victim and told her what to do, he denied the allegation and called it “lies”. Speaking about the second victim, Dott said he was “never in my company” and denied all allegations of abuse.In her closing speech on Friday, Dalziel called on the jury to find Dott guilty of both charges. She said: “The Crown’s case is that Graeme Dott subjected vulnerable children to the worst kind of abuse with a course of conduct which relied on opportunity, for his own gratification.”Dott’s lawyer, Euan Dow, had invited jurors to clear his client of both charges. But Dott, who won the World Snooker Championshipin 2006, was found guilty on Monday following the trial which began on 18 August, with verdicts by majority.Judge Lord Harrower told him: “You have been convicted of charges involving sexual abuse of young children. I will refrain from passing comment further on any of these offences until I receive a background report from a social worker as I must in order to consider the full range of sentences open to me. You must register your name and address with the police so your name can be added to the sex offenders register.”He deferred sentence until 29 September at the high court in Edinburgh. Dott was remanded in custody.Explore more on these topicsSnookerScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Big decisions pay off as Coco Gauff gears up for US Open with Cincinnati title | Coco Gauff | The Guardian
description: The American closed out one of the smoothest tournaments of her career, thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula in the final to win 6-2, 6-4
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The American closed out one of the smoothest tournaments of her career, thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula in the final to win 6-2, 6-4
Content: Coco Gauff watches the fireworks after receiving the Rookwood trophy for winning the women's title at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Scott Stuart/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCoco Gauff watches the fireworks after receiving the Rookwood trophy for winning the women's title at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Scott Stuart/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockCoco GauffBig decisions pay off as Coco Gauff gears up for US Open with Cincinnati titleAmerican beats compatriot Jessica Pegula 6-2, 6-4Gauff claims first title of season, her second in CincinnatiTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiMon 24 Aug 2026 00.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne year ago,Coco Gauffdeparted the Cincinnati Open with her career at a crossroads. On serve, she had capitulated, offering up countless double faults in most matches, and she had lost confidence in her progress and game. She believed she had to make drastic changes to her team before it was too late.It has taken an enormous amount of resilience, patience and toil, but this week Gauff began to feel the consequences of those efforts as she closed out one of the ­smoothest tournaments of her career with her best performance of the season, thoroughly outplaying the third seed ­Jessica Pegula to win 6-2, 6-4 and clinch the Cincinnati Open title for the second time.Arthur Fils wins first Masters title after beating Frances Tiafoe in Cincinnati finalRead moreThis tournament marked Gauff’s fifth WTA 1000 semi-final of the season and her third final. Gauff has enjoyed a fairly consistent past five months on the tour but the 22-year-old had yet to finish any tournament this season without a defeat. Victory in Cincinnati marks her first title of the season and fourth career WTA 1000 title.This win is particularly significant considering Gauff’s desperation a year ago. She served 16 double faults and made 62 unforced errors in her quarter-final loss to Jasmine Paolini at the 2025 tournament. After a summer of dire service issues, that defeat prompted Gauff to take the drastic decision of hiring Gavin ­MacMillan, a biomechanics expert, to completely reshape her serve.She began the transformation at the most difficult moment last year, the week before the US Open, and the challenge of making such a ­significant change on the eve of her most important tournament of the year was only exacerbated by the massive ­scrutiny that accompanied it. During her second-round match against Donna Vekic at the US Open last year,Gauff cried on the court.There have been so many more challenges, and double faults, over the past year but Gauff has finally found confidence with her serve and it has had a transformative effect on her game. “I think it was a long ­journey, but I’m happy,” she said. “I’ve obviously got more years of ­tennis to play, but I think last year I was just frustrated with my game, and I felt like I was declining, and it’s not something any player wants to feel.“You always want to feel like you’re getting better. So last year I was in a weird predicament, I made ­sudden decisions that most people probably wouldn’t do before a slam, but I think it’s worth it. And ­obviously, I feel like it’s night and day, the player I am from last year to now.”View image in fullscreenCoco Gauff advances to the net in the final at the Lindner Family Tennis Center.Photograph: Scott Stuart/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAfter losing her first set of the ­tournament against Liudmila ­Samsonova, the fourth-seeded Gauff rolled into the final having won the subsequent 10 sets during her time on the tour. Gauff has become well known for her tendency to fight through dramatic, tense three-set tussles, so the ease with which she moved through the draw in ­Cincinnati was striking.“A lot of my supporters are like: ‘I can’t take these three-set wins’ and my mom’s ­showing her heart rate going up and down,” said Gauff, laughing. “So hopefully I gave my team a little bit of a break this week. I can’t say the same for New York. It’s a grand slam, but I definitely was thinking about it. For the sake of my own mind and body, I was trying to get these done in two sets.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRather than desperately trying to manage her serve and minimise the amount of second serves she had to hit, Gauff now has the freedom to attack her serve. She played a spectacular match in the final, repeatedly cranking up her first serve above 120mph and she confidently forced herself inside the baseline whenever Pegula dropped the ball short. Her peerless defensive skills, meanwhile, drove Pegula crazy throughout.“It’s just so hard when you play somebody that moves … I mean, she’s the best mover on tour, I think by far,” Pegula said. “Just the way that she’s able to defend out of the corners is better than anybody else, and that’s truly her strength. So when she’s doing that and able to move forward and able to serve well and return well, it becomes very difficult.”Although Pegula’s tournament ended with a tough loss, she put together a spectacular run of her own, beating Sorana Cirstea, Amanda Anisimova and then the defending champion Iga Swiatek in consecutive three-set battles to reach the final, the latter being her best win of the year.As with Gauff and the Toronto champion Swiatek, Pegula heads to the US Open as one of the in-form players, where she will be desperate to turn her excellent results into a maiden grand slam title on home soil. As has been the case in the women’s game for much of the past few years, the competition for the title between the top players will be intense.Explore more on these topicsCoco GauffTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese seeks to quell datacentre disquiet as climate expert warns ‘we’ve got one shot to get the rules right’ | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power use
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power use
Content: Anthony Albanese will tell national cabinet his government will legislate next year to ensure the benefits of AI and datacentres are shared among states.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese will tell national cabinet his government will legislate next year to ensure the benefits of AI and datacentres are shared among states.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian politicsAlbanese seeks to quell datacentre disquiet as climate expert warns ‘we’ve got one shot to get the rules right’Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power useFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandPetra StockMon 24 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Albanese will seek to use Wednesday’s high-stakes talks with premiers to quell growing unhappiness aboutnational controls on datacentre developments, promising new approval laws will complement state rules.Faced with growing opposition from conservative governments in Queensland and the Northern Territory, Albanese will tell national cabinet he plans a major piece of legislation next year to ensure the economic benefits of AI are shared widely.With potential to be one of the major reforms of Labor’s second term, the new law will set tough copyright rules for AI businesses and impose standards for security, safety and skills development.The meeting on Wednesday will come after the latest forecast from the Australian Energy Market Operator showing datacentre power use is projected to increase seven-fold over the next decade.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe industry’s rapid growth, driven by increasing reliance on AI and cloud computing, remained one of the most significant causes of growth in electricity demand, according to Aemo’s annual Electricity Statement of Opportunities.In addition to 165 datacentres already operating around the country, a further 225 are in development, the report showed, reflecting a substantial increase in new proposals compared to 2025, Aemo said on Tuesday.Datacentre electricity demand was expected to grow from 5 to 34 terawatt hours by 2035-36, the report said, growing from 3% of overall consumption to 13%.AEMO said high datacentre growth could see consumption reach 52 TWh – a 10-fold increase over the decade.But there were high levels of uncertainty, with more than a third of projects listed in 2025 since cancelled, and operating facilities taking years to ramp to full capacity.Daniel Westerman, Aemo’s chief executive, said record levels of new generation and storage coming online had improved the outlook for reliability, even with the expected retirement of coal power stations.“The reliability outlook has improved, supported by record levels of new generation and storage, and a strong pipeline of projects expected over the next decade.”Report supporting Australia’s teen social media ban appears to contain AI hallucinations, Senate hearsRead moreThe Climate Council chief executive, Amanda McKenzie, said datacentres were set “to devour an enormous share of Australia’s electricity in the coming years”.“We’ve got one shot to get the rules right now and ensure that datacentre growth doesn’t strain our grid and push up pollution.”Albanese will use national cabinet to strike agreement on a plan to legislate nationally consistent minimum obligations for datacentres, requiring them not to push up energy prices, meet their own infrastructure costs and minimise water use.The rules will also require developers to minimise the effect of new datacentres on local communities, ensuring they are appropriately sized and appropriately located, away from homes, schools and potential housing or agricultural sites.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProjects approved for development before the new rules come into place will only be subject to existing state and territory laws.Last month, the prime minister promised“the strongest possible protection”for Australian creatives against misuse of their work by artificial intelligence models. He said it would be “theft” if writers, artists and musicians didn’t have control of their work or receive payment for its use in training large AI models.Combining the elements into a single piece of legislation signals the government’s ambition on AI, but could also heighten the political risk of getting the bill through parliament ahead of the next election.Queensland premier David Crisafulli and the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, have signalled opposition to federal rules requiring datacentres to be powered by renewable projects at the exclusion of coal and gas.Albanese is expected to seek broad consensus, but could be challenged by the increasingly outspoken Liberal-National and Country Liberal party leaders.He will also discuss state opposition to the national gun buy-back, which only has support from New South Wales and the ACT so far. Action to curb violence against women and the growing H1 bird flu crisis are also on the agenda.Anger about Western Australia’s favourable GST share will also flare. In Perth on Monday, Albanese said he would not change the deal, which costs taxpayers more than $6bn a year.“There will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements while I’m prime minister,” he said.Promising Australia would do more to unlock frontier AI development in the future, Albanese will tell a Business Council event on Tuesday the government was determined to succeed.“It will advance our national sovereignty. And it is essential for our national security, business productivity, science, innovation and resilience.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAI (artificial intelligence)Anthony AlbaneseComputingLabor partynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta test | Games | The Guardian
description: Players will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Players will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?
Content: The shootfest returns … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenThe shootfest returns … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4.Photograph: ActivisionGames‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta testPlayers will get what they expect from the new CoD title: boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. But what’s with all the distractions?Keith StuartMon 24 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a lot riding on this year’sCall of Duty, the inescapable first-person shootfest that’s been lobbing a grenade into the autumn release schedule since 2003. Previous instalment, Black Ops 7, performed poorly compared to previous titles, forcing Activision to post a semi-apology to fans. And that’s not the only challenge Modern Warfare 4 is facing: there’s a new indie shooter, Wardogs, promising a feel somewhere between classic CoD and Classic Battlefield. Then, lurking on the horizon, in mirror shades and an exotic sports car, is Grand Theft Auto 6, which is surely going to smash and grab all the attention (and money) from the market in mid-November.The good news is that, judging by the early access beta test that ran over the penultimate August weekend, we’re definitely getting what we expect from a Modern Warfare title: quasi-authentic boots-on-the-ground military action with a slight tactical edge. The weapons and general gunplay are highly effective, from default assault rifle, the Han 86 – a classic CoD beginner’s gun with decent fire rate and handling – to the bullet-spraying Nightshade SMG and the absolutely lethal KG-7 Vulcan sniper rifle. They all feel good to hold and fire, and there’s enough balance to let you experiment with slightly more offbeat numbers like the burst-fire Hyeon AR and the possibly overpowered Mar-9 marksman rifle.View image in fullscreenRefreshed armoury … Call of Duty Modern Warfare.Photograph: ActivisionAlso joining the refreshed armoury are an interesting array of field upgrades, the useful gadgets you open up as you play I tried the smoke wall which creates, well, a wall of smoke, hiding your movements (in theory) and I saw a few people deploying the razor-wire trap which slows enemies down while sapping their health. There are also new kill streaks (the special attacks you can trigger when you earn enough points in a match). Artillery Beacon lets you throw a beacon at a specific point which is then bombarded with missiles, and Wheelson is a remote control mini tank that clatters around the place firing a grenade launcher.A modest selection of small-ish maps was available for the weekend. Silkworm is a slab of South Korean cityscape, all minimarts and alleyways, while Transit 213 is a public transport depot with two parked buses at its centre and lots of generous sightlines for snipers. I found Cachette, a labyrinth of farm buildings, workshops and courtyards a little over-familiar, but Lotus, a larger harbourside map, brought in some interesting long-range combat. My favourite though, was the self-explanatory Rooftops, which takes place on the connected summits of two ageing New York high rises. Here, you fight through multi-levelled maintenance rooms and industrial laundries as well as out into open areas where water towers, exhaust fans and service ramps provide useful cover and mantling opportunities. There’s even a section of wooden scaffolding that offers a narrow shortcut over a vertigo-inducing chasm.View image in fullscreenThe TikTok of gaming? … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionThere are a bunch of new modes to accompany classics such as Team Deathmatch, Domination and Kill Confirmed. The key example is Kill Block, a ten v 10 gun fight taking place in a training camp that is reconfigured between rounds, providing hundreds of different layouts. There are trenches to crawl along, shipping containers to lie on and windows to camp behind. Like Search and Destroy, there are no respawns so it’s a fight to the death. The result is absolute carnage.How does it feel? Well, after the first day of the early access beta, gaming content creator Farzam referred to MW4 as the Tikok of gaming and it’s a good analogy. Everything happens fast and it just doesn’t stop happening; time-to-engagement (how long it takes from spawning to meeting your first enemy) is counted in microseconds, and if you blink, you’re dead. On every stretch of every map there is something to catch your attention, from exploding oxygen tanks to flickering video screens, and if you’re killed, hit a button and you’re instantaneously back in the game – no pause for breath, no time to think. You aren’t playing so much as doomscrolling an inescapable cognitive cacophony.Meanwhile, the omni-movement system introduced in Black Ops 6, which lets you jump, dive and skid along the floor in any direction, has been removed in favour of an ostensibly more naturalistic and controlled alternative. Is it really? Um, no. There is no friction at all in the landscape, so you can skid round corners and scale walls with superhero abandon. It’s fun and fluid, but it’s open to abuse: some players leap and twirl about the place as though performing in a particularly harrowing production of Swan Lake.For the first time in a CoD beta test, there’s a Campaign mission to try. Named Entrenched, it starts with … a trench, which you have to battle your way through against North Korean troops until you reach a power station. Then it’s a battle against time as you look to flood the reactor to prevent a catastrophic meltdown, before indulging in some parkour to escape the collapsing infrastructure. An average day at work for the CoD crew.I’m sure this beta test is going to give both the development team and the community plenty to think about. Ultimately, the game feels like what it is – a very modern Modern Warfare where your most effective weapons are lightning reflexes and superhuman concentration. I am too old for this shit, but I still thoroughly enjoyed it; diving round a corner and taking out two enemies in one burst remains as thrilling now as it was when the original Modern Warfare came out in 2007. There is a lot more competition out there now, though, and Call of Duty itself is starting to creak at the joints. The beta is yelling “I’ve still got it!” – but have the players? Money will be tight this autumn, and GTA 6 is standing at the bar, winking suggestively, beckoning us over.Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 is released on PC, PS5, Switch 2 and Xbox on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territory | Games | The Guardian
description: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Author: Bex April May
Headline: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Content: What if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesView image in fullscreenWhat if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesSummer games previewsGamesMy Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territoryDevelopers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limbBex April MayMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost stealth games cast you as a spy, an assassin or a master thief. My Arms Are Longer Now dispenses with most of the criminal person, to send in just one spectacularly badly behaved limb. It slithers across floors, winds around furniture, steals things and slaps anyone within reach – finally answering the question nobody asked: what if your own arm turned to crime?As TootGamesco-founder Matthew Jackson puts it: “You are the bad thing that happens to the people.”The idea began as a much simpler prototype made during a weekend game jam themed around the idea of lost and found. Jackson and fellow Toot co-founderMillie Holten, who met through Melbourne’s improv and sketch comedy community, wanted an idea that could be understood – and raise a laugh – in a single still image. A grotesquely extended arm proved to be just that.Since then, the game has been all about comedy. It has more than 40 speaking characters, voiced by Australian comedians who perform the written dialogue before improvising alternative takes. “It’s a vessel for jokes,” Jackson says. For almost a year, development largely involved trying to “cram jokes into the game”; only later did the team realise the physics of the increasingly sophisticated arm had become fun in their own right. Players can personalise its skin tone, hair and accessories, making it less somebody else’s disembodied crime spree than a freaky extension of their own body.The stealth here owes something toUntitled Goose Game: characters react to your crimes, but, Jackson says, “There are no fail states in the game.” A museum guard might smack the arm, or beg it to stop before they are fired. Anyone can be slapped, including an infant. While searching for a publisher, Jackson repeatedly asked: “Is someone going to come and tell us you can’t slap the baby?”Jackbox Games, thankfully, did not.View image in fullscreen‘A vessel for jokes’ … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesMaking that slap possible required rather more sophistication than the joke might suggest. The original game was flat and 2D, but Holten’s concept art showed the arm looping over tables, under chairs and around objects. Six months into development, the studio took the risky decision to rebuild in 3D. Working with developer Cherie Davidson, Jackson created a procedural, tube-like limb and a system that uses forced perspective to preserve the illustrated style while allowing the physical collisions the game needs.The work never quite ends. The team calls another session tinkering with the troublesome appendage “going into the armpit”.That labour is particularly demanding because comedy is finite. “You can hit a joke, and that joke’s done. You’ve burnt that,” Jackson says. Some publishers suggested adding more puzzles, but Toot feared they would obstruct the punchlines. Jackbox understood that it was meant to be “a good time, not a long time”, with players who do poke into every corner rewarded with optional interactions and voice lines.Jackson’s ultimate ambition for the game is appropriately simple: “I hope players say it was funny. That’s truly it.” And after three years in the armpit, 48 speaking characters, and one non-negotiable baby slap, Toot Games has gone to extraordinary lengths to reach gaming’s funny bone.My Arms Are Longer Now is in development forPC, with release planned for 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets faster | Android | The Guardian
description: Dutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular design
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Dutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular design
Content: The Fairphone 6+ is a solid mid-range Android alternative.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Fairphone 6+ is a solid mid-range Android alternative.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.AndroidReviewFairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets fasterDutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular designSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 02.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFairphone’s topAndroidfor 2026 is a little faster with more memory while maintaining full compatibility with its previous phone, including its repairable and ethical chops.The Fairphone 6+ continues the Dutch cooperative’s mission to make consumer electronics longer lasting and more sustainable, containing 51% either recycled or ethically sourced materials while being fully repairable at home with just the one screwdriver included in the box.It is also the first model to expand beyond Europe, going on sale in the US directly from Fairphone. But the new Android costs £70 (€50) more than the launch price of its predecessor, available from £569 (€649/$650), competing directly with Google’s £499Pixel 10aand Apple’s £599iPhone 17e.View image in fullscreenThe new cobalt blue colour for the Fairphone 6+ is striking in person.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ is an almost exact clone of theFairphone 6, with the same plastic body, 120Hz OLED screen and fingerprint scanner in the power button. It also supports the sameexcellent modular accessoriesthat simply screw into the back of the phone to add a lanyard, handle or wallet.The new model is 2g heavier, but the biggest difference for the 6+ is an upgraded chip to the newer Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and an additional 4GB of memory for 12GB in total.The Gen 4 chip is about six to 10% faster in testing, which places it firmly in the mid-range category alongside the likes of theNothing Phone 4a Prowith the same chip. It won’t win any performance awards and is significantly slower than chips used in Apple, Samsung or Google’s latest smartphones, but it feels snappy enough in use and can be used for light gaming without issue.The battery life is very similar to the phone’s predecessor, lasting about a day and a half between charges with the screen actively used for about five hours across 5G and wifi, for messaging, note-taking, photos and browsing. Most will need to charge it nightly, which is a bit behind the curve. A full charge takes about 80 minutes using a 30W power adaptor (not included), hitting 50% in under half an hour.View image in fullscreenThe camera app has most of the features you need and will be familiar to users of other Androids or iPhones.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ also has the same dual-camera system as its predecessor with a 50-megapixel main and 13MP ultra-wide camera. It has improvedsince its debut last yearthrough software updates, which have fixed a few of the issues and inconsistencies. It can shoot pretty good photos with a bit of work and manages a reasonable 2x zoom. It isn’t the best in lower light conditions, though its new Super Night AI feature helps.SpecificationsScreen:6.31in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (431ppi)Processor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4RAM:12GBStorage:256GB + microSDOperating system:Android 16Camera:50MP + 13MP, 32MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4 and GNSSWater resistance:IP55 (splash/rain)Dimensions:156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mmWeight:193gGoogle’s Android 16 or e/OSView image in fullscreenFairphone’s minimalist Moments interface can be switched on to reduce distractions, allowing access to only a limited number of apps.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6+ ships with last year’s Android 16, not the latest Android 17, but will be supported with updates until 2033 at least, which is roughly the same as mainstream rivals.Fairphone’s software is generally clean and uncluttered with only an additional gallery app and the My Fairphone app for repair and diagnostics from the standard Android app loadout. It has Google’s Gemini in various bits, but no other AI additions to get in the way. It also features Fairphone’s“Moments” minimalist interface,activated by the big yellow switch on the side, for a less distracting smartphone experience.But for those who want an alternative to Google’s Android, the phone is available with the privacy-focused, open-source version of Android, without Google services,called /e/OS.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe power button with fingerprint scanner sits below the Moments switch and directly opposite the volume buttons.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery will maintain at least 80% of its original capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles and it can be replaced at home using a single screwdriver along withthe rest of the 12 modular components. Batteries cost£34.20, screens£77.00and the main camera£59.88. The phone was awarded10 out of 10 for repairabilityby specialists iFixit.The handset is made with51% recycled or fair materials, while Fairphonepublishes life cycle reportsfor its products.PriceThe Fairphone Gen 6+ costs£569(€649/$649.99) with Google Android or£598.63(€699.99/$699.99) with e/OS.For comparison, theGoogle Pixel 10acosts£499, theApple iPhone 17ecosts£599and theNothing Phone 4a Procosts£519.VerdictThe Fairphone 6+ continues to demonstrate that good, solid Android phones can be made fully repairable at home without specialist tools.It is only a small spec bump on the originalFairphone 6, which helps keep up with mainstream rivals without sacrificing parts compatibility, sustainability or ethical credentials. It is also available directly in the US for the first time. But that also means the 6+ shares the same flaws as its predecessor.The camera, battery life, performance and screen are all decent, if far from the best you can get for the money. However, those looking for a high-end smartphone experience best look elsewhere as the Fairphone can’t match a recent iPhone, Pixel or Galaxy S with similar levels of software support.That makes it hard to recommend to everyone. But for those who prioritise repairability and ethical ethos, this is the phone for you.Pros:choice of Android operating systems, modular accessories, repairable-at-home design, recycled and fair materials, microSD card slot, good screen, five-year warranty, software support to 2033Cons:mid-range performance, average battery life, fingerprint scanner can be tricky to press, average camera, cannot be submerged in water, no Android 17 yet.Explore more on these topicsAndroidSmartphonesMobile phonesSoftwareTelecomsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’? | Dana Frank | The Guardian
description: The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left
Content: ‘The Times is shoring up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party.’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreen‘The Times is shoring up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party.’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APOpinionNew York TimesWhy does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’?Dana FrankThe newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the leftMon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTShare“El-Sayed and Stevens Project Party Unity After Divisive Race,”announcedthe New York Times on 5 August, the day the progressive Abdul El-Sayed beat out his centrist Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in the Michigan senatorial primary. “Divisive” is now the Times’s favorite attack word, deployed repeatedly to disparage and try to undermine the astonishing recent advances by progressive candidates.Four days after that first story, the Times againlanded“divisive” under “Obama and El-Sayed Discuss Unity After Ugly Michigan Primary.” El-Sayed, it asserted, had “narrowly prevailed in a divisive primary after campaigning on a progressive and anti-establishment platform”.On 12 August, the Timesreported thatDavid Crowley, who narrowly beat out Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, “promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany”, his Republican opponent. Other stories slip it in more subtly. That same day, in a piece about representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez allegedly distancing herself from “Woke 1.0”, the TimescitedMiddlebury College professor Erik Bleich, who “pointed to the calls to defund the police as a divisive goal”.By disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s leadRead more“Polarizing”, a close cousin to “divisive”, appears regularly, too. The Times especially likes to apply it to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. Areporter insistedin October 2025, for example: “As Mamdani’s campaign upends New York politics, no single stance has polarized New Yorkers as passionately as his pro-Palestinian activism and caustic criticism of Israel.”Perhaps most outrageous was the Times’s choice ofheadlinefor a recent review of David Zirin’s new book about Howard Zinn: “America’s Most Divisive Historian Gets a New Biography.” How, exactly, was Zinn “divisive”? And who are those other historians who are also divisive, just not as bad? Neither Adam Hochschild, in his review, nor Zirin, in his biography, nor any discussion of I’ve ever seen in 40 years as a practicing US historian (and co-author, along with Robin DG Kelley, of a book with Zinn), talk about Zinn that way.The Times’s choice to cast Zinn as divisive out of the blue, on top of its repeated usage of the word since the midwest primaries, suggests there’s a conscious campaign underway to utilize the concept however it can.Overall, the Times’ repeated charge of “divisive”, along with “polarizing”, implies a previous and virtuous whole that is currently being destroyed by the left. It assumes voters agree that in the face of deep fear of Trump and his allies, we have to stick together, and that progressive candidatescan’t beat Republicansin the midterms.But the Times’s mythical unified country never existed. The United States has always been riven by race, class, gender, religion, immigration status and much more. And vigorous debate has always been at the core of truly democratic politics.For the Times, “unity” is a stand-in for the powers-that-be in the Democratic party and “their preferred strategy of running moderate campaigns that won’t offend aging incumbents, never-Trump Republicans, and the multimillionaire-and-up donor class,” as the editors of Hammer & Hope Magazinerecently put it.The mealy-mouthed, centrist candidates the party’s leadership has chosen in the name of unity have repeatedly alienated or failed to energize voters, especially African Americans.Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not? | Nesrine MalikRead moreThe Times does on occasion employ “divisive” todescribe far-right Republicans, such as with Florida governor Ron DeSantis. But that, in turn, colors its usage against the left, which, implicitly, is behaving fanatically and dangerously, too. As the paperclaimedon 16 August, after the midwest primaries, “Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment.”Note, moreover, the recent actions by “moderate” Democrats the New York Times has apparentlynotdeemed divisive: James Carville, the political consultant, whocalled Democratic socialists“a pack of fools” on Fox News, or Abigail Spanberger, the governor of Virginia, who in Mayvetoed a billgranting collective bargaining rights to public workers, betraying the union base that had elected her.In Michigan, it’sIslamophobiathat’s in fact “divisive”, not the Muslim candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who, along with many of the other candidates the Times calls divisive, is not coincidentally a person of color.By charging progressives – and especially democratic socialists – with divisiveness, theNew York Timesis doing everything it can to shore up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party, and the rest of us fall into line to vote however they like.But it’s the Times that’s trying to divide us, as we form ever broader, ever more dynamic and ever more effective coalitions to challenge the masters it serves.Dana Frank is professor of history emerita at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Her newest book, Balancing Acts: How a Japanese Immigrant Built a Life in the Face of Racial Danger – Until Federal Agents Arrived, will be out from Beacon Press in April 2027This article was amended on 24 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly referred to Abdul El-Sayed as a democratic socialist.Explore more on these topicsNew York TimesOpinionUS politicsNewspapersUS press and publishingNewspapers & magazinesDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: ICE’s tactics look increasingly like torture | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Plans for gloves that can deliver electric shocks underline the homeland security department’s sadistic practices
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Plans for gloves that can deliver electric shocks underline the homeland security department’s sadistic practices
Content: ‘According to an investigation by theGuardian, at least 10 immigrant detainees have been subjected to force feeding and involuntary medical procedures.’Photograph: Erin Hooley/APView image in fullscreen‘According to an investigation by theGuardian, at least 10 immigrant detainees have been subjected to force feeding and involuntary medical procedures.’Photograph: Erin Hooley/APOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)ICE’s tactics look increasingly like tortureJudith LevinePlans for gloves that can deliver electric shocks underline the homeland security department’s sadistic practicesMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTShareOn 11 August, the Associated Pressreportedthat the Homeland Security Agency will spend up to $20m to equip its agents with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to the skin of a person deemed uncooperative. The “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices”– branded Glove, for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter – will be supplied by their manufacturer, Compliant Technologies, through ano-bid contract.News of the acquisition inspired the editorial cartoonist Ann Telnaes to publish acartoonof anICEagent wearing the glove, underneath which are a branding iron, an iron maiden, a rack, and other compliance technologies. AKA, instruments of torture.Indeed,Amnesty Internationalreports that portable, convenient electric shock devices made for law enforcement like the glove can be, and have been, used for torture. Once called weapons, they’re nowmarketed as “humane”. They are the former. A prisoner in Kentuckydied of a heart attackafter 27 successive shocks, directly following 13 Taser hits.ICE tactics, already sadistic, are looking increasingly like torture. TheGeneva conventionsdefine torture as the infliction of severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, by an agent of the state acting in their official capacity, to obtain intelligence or confession or to intimidate, coerce, or punish a prisoner or detainee.More than 90%of detainees are held in privately-owned immigration detention facilities, but their employees are contractual agents of the federal government.According to an investigation by theGuardian, at least 10 immigrant detainees have been subjected to force-feeding and involuntary medical procedures. The detainees are on hunger strikes in protest of the appalling conditions of their incarceration, including, ironically, inedible food and denial of necessary medical treatment. One of the victims, a Kurdish film-maker,describedbeing held in solitary confinement, tackled, shackled, and force fed twice daily for eight months. HSAanticipates hunger strike managementwill cost $169,000 in fiscal 2026.To force-feed a person, a tube is inserted into their mouth or nose and pushed down into their stomach. Then liquid food or medicine is poured into the tube through a funnel. The person gags, chokes, and often vomits; when they struggle – a natural response – they are usually restrained. “What they’re doing qualifies as torture,” a doctor told theGuardian, expressing a contention widely held by medical professionals,ethicists and human rights experts.Don’t call them ICE detention centers. Call them camps | John WashingtonRead moreSome of the torture is outsourced. The administration is sending asylum seekers back to the countries from which they fled under threat of imprisonment, torture or execution – and where they face torture or death on return. The UShas built a gulagof collaborating third countries where deportees may be locked up indefinitely or deported to the home countries they fled. Forced return, or refoulement, of refugees and asylees – which is also the result of Trump’s recent revocations of temporary protective status for many foreign nationals – is banned under theUN Convention Against Torture, which the US signed.And then there is the malign neglect. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has released detainees into the cold without adequate money or clothing. At least two – a Haitian woman,Daphy Michael,and a blind Rohingya man,Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a refugee from Myanmar – have frozen to death. Medical examiners are calling both deaths homicides. (DHS saysICE and border patrol had “nothing to do” with the deaths.)Children, too, are being deliberately abandoned. In a bid to force them to release confidential information about their clients, the administration iswithholdingpayments from the organizations that provide legal representation to unaccompanied migrant children. About 25,000 kids, some of them unable to speak English – or speak at all – have been left to fend for themselves in court. Such representation is mandated under a section of the 2008 federal anti-trafficking law, which Project 2025’s Homeland Security chapterrecommends repealing.Speaking toMSNOW, Lindsay Toczylowski, an attorney at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, said that since her agency’s payments were cut off on 31 July, colleagues “witnessed a seven-year-old child taking a final order to leave the United States this week, without a lawyer”, she said. Where will that child go? Who, if anyone, will look after him? What permanent damage will befall him?The number of infants and toddlers in custody has dramatically increased under the Trump administration, according to theMarshall Project, to 25 children under the age of three on an average day. That is “probably the most harmful time of their lives” to experience such trauma, said the cofounder of the executive committee of theAmerican Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health. “Our immigration system is breaking children.”Is this torture? Maybe not technically. It is surely child abuse, which is illegal under US criminal law andinternational human rights law– and immoral under any religious or ethical code.“The fact is, being in detention is a choice,” HSA deputy assistant secretary Lauren Bissaidin response to distraught parents’ reports of children sickening nearly to death at the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley. “We encourage all parents to take control of their departure by using the CBP Home app and receiving a free flight home and $2,600.” FAQs on the app’swebsitesuggest that this “option” is not exactly voluntary either. “Illegal aliens” are informed that should they decline to take the deal, “ICE will continue to prioritize your removal.”When Maga’s power fades, we cannot abandon those ICE killed | Moira DoneganRead moreRoutine practicesof current immigration detention such as prolonged solitary confinement, beatings, andsleep deprivationare widely defined as torture. An argument can also been made – andadvocateshave made it – that even those aspects of the mass deportation policy that do not conform with the legal definition of torture are designed to create so much misery that immigrants will leave on their own or not come in the first place. During Trump’s first term, the administration unapologeticallyjustifiedits “zero tolerance” family separation at the border as a deterrent to would-be immigrant parents.These tactics, even when carried out in diffuse and intermittent ways, fit the general definition of torture precisely: the infliction of pain and suffering by the state to compel a person to do something they fiercely do not want to do.The deportation machine is in high gear. In July, the New YorkTimesreported that ICE had arrested 10,000 people in five days, having doubled its daily quota to the 2,000. The abuses inside detention facilities are bound to increase too.At the same time,NPRreported on Thursday, the already teetering system through which ICE detainees could report abuse without fear of recrimination “has collapsed”, and there’s nowhere else to turn, since virtually all other government oversight has been demolished.Civil liberties and immigrant rights lawyers are flooding the federal courts with lawsuits and petitions for interdiction of these sadistic practices. But any charge of torture is unlikely to get far. The constitution’s eighth amendment prohibits cruel and unusual punishment, and harm by police or prison guards can be redressed through state civil rights laws. But torture is effectively condoned in the US; federalanti-torturestatute applies only to acts committed outside US borders.The slim avenues to legal recourse and the refusal of transparency or accountability by the perpetrators of de jure and de facto torture are driving detainees to desperate measures like hunger strikes. They are “risking their lives to protest inhumane conditions and legal rights violations”, reports NPR. Self-deportation or self-starvation. That is not a choice.Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack isToday in FascismExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)OpinionTrump administrationTortureUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Michael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than good, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
