Headline: Michael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than good, says the Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: GCSE students taking an exam at a school in Kent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGCSE students taking an exam at a school in Kent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionGCSEsHow can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a startPolly ToynbeeMichael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than goodMon 24 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareGCSE results day was marked with the usual front pages filled with pictures of beaming students. What you didn’t see was the invisiblethird of 16-year-oldsin England who failed their maths and English GCSEs, the obstacle to their future.That’s 360,000failedin a system designed by Michael Gove as education minister to mark out winners from losers. It’s a cast of mind shared by many in his party who still yearn for the11-plus, which consigned a random number of children to failure before they’d hardly begun. A few councils still do it.Once failed, this one-third must resit English and maths to do any other course: colleges cannot provide them with a blessed start from failed schooling, as they are refused funds for any student not taking repeated resits. Onlyabout 17%of the wretched resitters ever pass. Quite apart from the despair, David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, points to the waste: of the far-too-few 16 teaching hours a week for students on post-16 study courses, resitters must be taught seven hours of hated English and maths that most of them will fail. That leaves just nine hours for the vocational courses they choose. No wonder UCL research shows the damage done: self-confidence is lost, many drop out altogether. That doesn’t happen in Wales and Northern Ireland,where resits are not mandatory for continuing study.Labour gets it. Both the previous education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, and the current,Lucy Powell, well understand the damage done by this Gove-devised torment: finally compulsory resits will end in 2028. Instead, those who fail can take a new “stepping stone” qualification in functional maths and English, proving adequate literacy and numeracy skills.But an ideological dispute remains among Powell’s advisers. They will still make every 16-year-old take English and maths GCSE in the first place, even if they will probably fail. Many only need the stepping-stone qualification anyway. This doesn’t sit well with Andy Burnham spreading his successfulGreater Manchester baccalaureate(MBacc) nationally, ascheme that offersvocational courses suited to local employersalongside academic subjects from age 14, to keep them engaged and avoiding Neet status: not in education, employment or training.But ideological purists think dividing them early between GCSE groups and stepping-stone groups sets up a two-tier discrimination, downgrading some who might have passed a full GCSE. But with a million Neets, the key priority must be making school encouraging, not rejecting.Gove sticks to his Gradgrind resits. He calls Burnham’s approach “bring back stupid”, anti-intellectual and hostile to ambition. But had he invested in nursery education, where destinies are most surely set, there might be fewer 16-year-olds with failing grades to bully now. New researchreported by the Institute for Fiscal Studiesshows how entering childcare one year earlier gives an average 10% improved maths score by age 14 to 15, and a 28% higher score for those with a mother without qualifications.The good news is that Labour’s emphasis on skills has been infectious, with asurge in applications to technical courses, well beyond the current demographic bulge, while university applications still rise by 3%. Alan Milburn’s commission to solve the crisis of1 million Neetshas real policy steam behind it to urge more skills training.But further education (FE) has a lot of catching up to do. There are many ways England has not just neglected but discriminated against non-academic education. Despite recent extra funding for colleges, this stilldoesn’t cover the entire costof any extra student accepted, an additional 25,000 are expected to enrol this autumn,and colleges lack space and staff after colossal cuts in the Tory years: over-19s adult education fellfrom £5bn in 2002 to £1.5bn in 2025.Recent extra money for pay “only stopped the gap getting wider”, Hughes says, when FE staff are paid£10,500 lessthan school teachers, and are in short supply when construction and engineering jobs pay so much more. Why, he asks, do colleges pay VAT costing £200m, while schools are reimbursed?The spur of Labour’s new growth and skills levy is incentivising employers to take on beginners with short courses. But as applications quadrupled for degree apprenticeships, more sought-after than Oxbridge places for earning while learning,places have halved.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy do university students get maintenance loans, but FE students can’t? “Because too many will never earn enough to pay them back,” says Hughes bluntly. Worse still, Neets on benefits are barred from full-time courses, which is perverse.Needless barriers need fixing. Neets who need driving licences for jobs and apprenticeships, essential from care to plumbing, find the waiting time for a driving test is21 weeksor more.Burnham’s eloquence on valuing “the hard hat as much as the academic cap” earns Gove’s contempt, but it has raised FE spirits. Talking to college heads, they see that Labour knows what to do. As ever, the problem is overcoming Britain’s forever low esteem for technical education. It will take heavy lifting to shift mentalities towardsencouraging that third of 16-year-olds instead of tormenting them.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGCSEsOpinionFurther educationExamsHigher educationSchoolsMichael GoveLucy PowellcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Routine’ medical treatments are not risk free. Patients should ask questions before consenting  | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: The distinction has become blurred between something being medically available and actually being medically useful
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: The distinction has become blurred between something being medically available and actually being medically useful
Content: ‘If you have ever had a course (or three) of antibiotics “just in case”, you are in the 40% of the global population that leave the doctor’s office with an antibiotic prescription. Of these prescriptions, nearly 60% are unnecessary.’Photograph: Liudmila Dutko/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If you have ever had a course (or three) of antibiotics “just in case”, you are in the 40% of the global population that leave the doctor’s office with an antibiotic prescription. Of these prescriptions, nearly 60% are unnecessary.’Photograph: Liudmila Dutko/AlamyOpinionHealth‘Routine’ medical treatments are not risk free. Patients should ask questions before consentingRanjana SrivastavaThe distinction has become blurred between something being medically available and actually being medically usefulMon 24 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTShareWhen a friend finally arranges the chat we were meant to have some weeks ago, she apologises profusely for the lack of contact. I tell her she doesn’t need to mollify me but it turns out she is the one in need of sympathy. Her husband had gone into hospital for what was termed a routine procedure. While waiting to collect him, my friend suddenly heard the overhead announcement of a code, announcing a patient in extremis.“Something told me it was him.”The surgery had unleashed a bacterial shower, rendering him septic on the operating table.Fortunately, he was in a hospital with an intensive care unit, where he found himself for days receiving life-sustaining treatment. He recovered but I could still feel her palpable fear at the prospect of losing her husband on an ordinary day.In this case, the procedure was necessary. But just that week, another friend had undergone a gastroscopy to re-examine a gastric ulcer. Afterwards, she reported that the gastroscopy had been fine but the colonoscopy was “pristine”.“Why did you need a colonoscopy?” I asked.“They just did it.”“Do you know why?”‘I guess it was routine.’I didn’t press the point but these two accounts had me reflecting on how doctors and patients think about interventions.How much preventive health screening should I be getting?Read moreFor clinicians, routine simply describes familiarity and frequency. A routine procedure can be safe or low-risk but not no-risk. But patients might hear routine as reassurance that nothing serious can happen. These are two very different propositions.Takecolonoscopy, for instance.With the rising incidence of bowel cancer, this is the gold standard test for early detection and improved survival. But the fact that it is familiar doesn’t mean it is benign.Bowel preparation can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. The procedure can result in bleeding and, rarely, perforation and sedation carries its own risks. All the risks are increased in elderly people. Many colonoscopies won’t find disease and some that find a minor abnormality trigger additional procedures not strictly needed.Even a small risk of complications multiplied by millions of colonoscopies produces a substantial number of people who are harmed.If you have ever had a course (or three) of antibiotics “just in case”, you are in the 40% of the global population that leave the doctor’s office with an antibiotic prescription. Of these prescriptions,nearly 60% are unnecessary.Antibiotics are not a procedure but they are an extremely common intervention with potent downstream effects on a complex ecosystem.Apart from the “routine” side effects of rash, nausea, altered taste and diarrhoea, a dreaded result of antibiotic overexposure is the altered gut microbiome that predisposes to C difficile infection. And 70% of people who develop this obstinate diarrhoeal condition have receivedantibiotics in the past 12 weeks.double quotation markUnnecessary care compromises necessary careAntibiotic resistance is another concern. If more than a million people each year die from the direct result ofdrug-resistant infections, no antibiotic prescription can be labelled routine.Useful yes, routine no.When I was an error-prone medical student, the emergency department was the place to be when it came to practising IV insertion. After all, everyone “needed” an IV – and “routine” bloods to boot – even before they met a real doctor who could assess their need.Alas, little has changed in 25 years. By way of apology to those hapless patients, today I sound like a complete bore, peeking under every sleeve and bandage at every bedside.“Why is there an IV?”The commonest answer? “It was already in.”IV insertion is the most common invasive procedure performed in hospitals today –a billion such procedures a year, many done unquestioningly though the problems are well documented, from the pain of serial attempts (just ask my cancer patients) and local irritation to serious infection.Somewhere along the line, as healthcare discoveries grew more abundant and doctors felt increasingly well equipped, the idea that each intervention has its own toxicity slipped into the background. The distinction blurred between something being medically available and medically useful.A cynical take is to blame financial incentives but as a public hospital doctor, I see other forces at play: fragmented care, diagnostic uncertainty, unrealistic expectations and a lack of time offset by a battery of tests.Unnecessary care harms the recipient but it carries a second, quieter cost. Unnecessary care compromises necessary care.My most disadvantaged patients rarely know how to advocate for themselves; they only know to wait in line. If your child is injured in a sporting accident and a scan is weeks away or you need an urgent colonoscopy but it’s many months away, there is a reason. Healthcare is a finite resource; money, time and doctors’ attention devoted to low-value care are diverted from people with genuine need.The lesson for patients is that there are routine procedures and necessary procedures but no risk-free procedures. So, if you are a patient,please ask more questions. Why do I need it? What are the alternatives? What happens if I don’t have it?Doctors, meanwhile, should remember that familiarity does not equal harmlessness. Truly informed consent means telling patients honestly about how routine procedures can go awry.Good medicine isn’t necessarily more medicine or less medicine. It is the right medicine, for the right patient, at the right time.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionAntibioticscommentShareReuse this content

title: Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions | Michael Jacobs | The Guardian
description: Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price, says economist Michael Jacobs
Author: Michael Jacobs
Headline: Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price, says economist Michael Jacobs
Content: Climate activists gather in central London to protest against the development of the Rosebank oilfield, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClimate activists gather in central London to protest against the development of the Rosebank oilfield, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionFossil fuelsCan Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditionsMichael JacobsCarbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the priceMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareThe British government must soon decide whether it should give consentto two oil and gasfields, Rosebank in the North Atlantic and Jackdaw in the North Sea. Amid both insecurity of energy supplies and deadly evidence of the climate crisis, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, isfacing pressurefrom the oil and gas industry and unions on one side, and environmentalists on the other.Labour’s manifesto commitment not to approve new drilling licences offers little help, because the fields already have licences, granted by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and 2023. But last year,Edinburgh’s court of sessionruled that the environmental impact assessments on which this decision relied were unlawful. The Conservative government had, the court ruled, failed to include the emissions generated when the oil and gas from the fields is burned. The court allowed work to continue on the fields, but a new assessment had to be done and approval sought again.The issue facing the new energy and climate secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is whether the additional information on the fields’ global emissions alters the grounds for consent.Although invariably discussed together, the two fields are very different. Jackdaw is a small gasfield, with aproduction life of only 11 years. Its total carbon emissions will be onlyaround 24m tonnes. Annually this would equate to around 0.8% of the UK’s total emissions. The gas would be piped into the UK, so would be consumed domestically. As this would probably displace dirtier liquified natural gas (LNG) imported from the US, it would make a small contribution to the UK’s energy security and emissions reduction.By contrast, Rosebank is a large oilfield, with a 25-year life. During that time it would generate around250m tonnesof carbon emissions. The oil would be sent to the Netherlands for refining, since the UK no longer has the appropriate capacity – and very little, if any, is likely to be used in the UK. So it would not contribute to our energy security.There are good reasons, therefore, for the government to make different decisions on the two fields. Jackdaw can be justified (just) on energy security grounds. The UK needs gas over the coming decade, and there is a benefit to a little more of it being domestic. Jackdaw will stop generating emissions in 2037-2038, when the UK, and the world, will still be well above net zero.Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby HinsliffRead moreRosebank, by contrast, will still be producing oil in 2050, when the UK is legally obliged under theClimate Change Acttoachieve net zero emissions. Indeed, by 2050, the Paris agreement (which forms the bedrock of the UK’s international commitments) expects the entire world to be just adecade or so offachieving net zero emissions. For that reason, theInternational Energy Agency expectsglobal oil demand by that date to be lower than today and falling, if governments around the world follow their own stated climate policies.Jackdaw is frankly too small to have any meaningful impact on global supply and demand in the decade it will be producing. But because of its size and longevity, the same cannot be said of Rosebank, which between 2040 and 2050 will be making a material contribution to global oil supply just when the market should be starting to decline. The greater the supply, the lower the price, and the higher the demand. So Rosebank has implications for both global emissions and international climate change policy.Rosebank could be given consent while avoiding these consequences if the government required it to pay for some or all of its emissions to be captured and stored in disused oilfields or saline aquifers. Most of Rosebank’s emissions will occur when its oil is burned. So, making carbon capture and storage (CCS) a condition of its licence would effectively mean requiring it to pay to capture and store the equivalent volume of other producers’ emissions.Though controversial,CCS is a proven technology: one of Rosebank’s owners, Equinor, has been using CCS in its Norwegian Sleipner field since 1996, is reported to have storedover 20m tonnesof CO2without leakage. The UK government’s own CCS programme, operated by the North Sea Transition Authority,has now licensed 21CCS projects at different stages of development. But Rosebank is not one of them.The oil and gas industry has yet to acknowledge that its production can ultimately only beconsistent with net zero emissions if it uses CCS. Giving consent to the Rosebank field on condition that it pays for its emissions to be captured and stored – say, from 2035 onwards – is the only way to make it compatible with the UK government’s domestic and international climate change commitments. By joining the UK CCS programme, Rosebank would probably be eligible for government support.The additional costs of CCS might mean that Rosebank’s owners would decide not to go ahead with it. But this would merely demonstrate that the project cannot in practice be undertaken in a way that is consistent with the UK’s net zero commitments.It is also critical that for both Jackdaw and Rosebank the government insists onstrict methane limits. Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and both fields will have significant emissions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government should make two other announcements at the same time. The first is to secure thousands of jobs by accelerating the labour-intensive decommissioning of oil and gasfields in the North Sea. At the same time, the government should publish a net zero transition roadmap, explaining how the UK will “defossilise” its economy over the next 25 years.Rosebank’s and Jackdaw’s operators say they will create around3,500 jobs in development and around 880 in operation. These are not negligible, but they will not save the oil and gas industry or the wider economy of north-east Scotland. Between 2013 and 2023, jobs in the sectorfell by more than half, from 441,000 to 213,000. This has nothing to do with UK climate change policy, but is simply the inevitable consequence of the exhaustion of the British North Sea basin (around 90% of the UK’s oil and gashas now been extracted).With around1,700 wells due to be pluggedand abandoned in the next six years and 500 already overdue for removal, decommissioning is a huge task. It will create many more jobs than drilling would (it is estimatedthat decommissioning will generate up to 25,000 UK jobs over the next decade and deliver about £6.8bn in economic benefit).A net zero transition roadmap would cover both the anticipated technological pathways in energy, transport, industry and agriculture, and the implications for businesses and households. Such a roadmap would reassure firms, unions and consumers concerned about what the net zero goal really means, and deprive the media and opposition parties of the chance to speculate wildly about its costs.It would give investors much-needed certainty.France has already producedsuch a roadmap, and other countriesare also committedto doing so. Britain should join them.Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime ministerExplore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOpinionClimate crisisEnergyOil and gas companiesCarbon capture and storage (CCS)Energy industryGascommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: A music festival isn’t a music festival without children | Iman Amrani | The Guardian
description: Ignore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of events, says writer and producer Iman Amrani
Author: Iman Amrani
Headline: Ignore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of events, says writer and producer Iman Amrani
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onFestivalsThe hill I will die on: A music festival isn’t a music festival without childrenIman AmraniIgnore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of eventsMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTShareThe woman I used to be died the day I gave birth to twins. That life – full of spontaneous travel, impulsive decisions and a decorated social calendar – evaporated, giving way to a blank canvas of motherhood and two glorious little human beings. While I was inside that summer, many of my friends continued on their child-free paths. They posted pictures of themselves enjoying festivals, sleeping in tents with pop-up communities that I used to be a part of.So when the twins turned one last summer and we’d found our rhythm, I decided to take on the challenge ofsharing the magic of live music with them. It went better than I expected. Before their second birthday, we had danced at day festivals such as Situation Dance, put on by Femi Koleoso from Ezra Collective, camped out overnight in the Brecon Beacons for Green Man and been to the child-focused TOTFest.Some people think it’s wild, bordering on neglectful, to take children to festivals that also cater to adult punters. They tend to think that children and families need to be separated entirely from spaces where there is any drinking or adult fun happening. Mothers, especially, are used to being told that everything we could possibly enjoy ourselves is going to damage our children. Thankfully, wise women around me whose kids are now grown up have reminded me to ignore these pressures, and go with my maternal instincts.Taking young children to festivalsdoesrequire another level of research and responsibility. Ear defenders are packed; festivals more aligned with drugs and debauchery are avoided. But different worlds can coexist. Selecting the family camping area when you book is game-changing. The adult audiences get their late-night raving in, and the early risers include not just families, but the wellbeing crowd heading to yoga or for a swim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding | Amelia TaitRead moreHaving families around often has a positive effect on an event. People operate more within the realm of moderation when there are kids present, and you have to be a real Scrooge to get upset at barefoot children with glitter on their faces having fun alongside their parents.I, for one, don’t want to spend the rest of my life solely listening to the Wiggles, and made the tactical decision early on to expose my babies to a wide range of sounds. We’ve got instruments at home and they’re fascinated by how it all works. They’ve taken to live music so easily, it’s a joy to watch them engage with something so human and far away from any screens.People often say that other countries in Europe are ahead of us in terms of being inclusive of families and children, but I’d say the UK really shines duringits festival season. My favourite ones are a microcosm of what coexisting can look like in the real world. I’ve found my village in the fields and car parks that host these events. My motherhood canvas is filling up with music, and I’ve found festivals are places where we can all get a bit of something that we want.Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producerExplore more on these topicsFestivalsThe hill I will die onParents and parentingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Marine Le Pen’s career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than ever | Mujtaba Rahman | The Guardian
description: No longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan Bardella, says Mujtaba Rahman of Europe at Eurasia Group
Author: Mujtaba Rahman
Headline: No longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan Bardella, says Mujtaba Rahman of Europe at Eurasia Group
Content: ‘The other candidates were wary of Jordan Bardella [left], but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.’Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The other candidates were wary of Jordan Bardella [left], but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.’Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionMarine Le PenMarine Le Pen’s career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than everMujtaba RahmanNo longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan BardellaMon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTShareFrance loves a battle-scarred survivor. Charles de Gaulle, François Mitterrand and Jacques Chirac clawed their way back from political failure to become presidents of the republic. There is a significant chance thatMarine Le Penwill be next.Now that the Paris appeal courthas unshackled herfrom an electoral ban for fraud, the far-right veteran has double appeal in the race for the French presidency next year. She will run, as always, as an outsider and a scourge of the political elites – despite continuously holding electoral office since 1998. She can also now pose as a “miraculous survivor”, a “mother courage” and “a battling granny”, as senior French political figures, including former ministers, described her to me during recent conversations in Paris.Le Pen will be a much more formidable candidate than her young understudy Jordan Bardella might have been. The other candidates were wary of Bardella, but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.Her party, theNational Rally(RN), has a new campaign slogan: “Renaissance”. The rebirth of Le Pen’s political career, the party says, foretells the rebirth of France.One might almost think Le Pen had been acquitted of fraud on 7 July.She was not. The judges essentially ruled that voters, not the courts, should decide who is president. They reduced Le Pen’s five-year ban from electoral politics, imposed by the Paris criminal court last year, to time already served.She is now a twice-convicted embezzler of more than €4m in EU funds. If her final appeal to France’s highest court is heard rapidly and rejected, she might have to campaign next spring wearing an electronic tag on her ankle.And yet. Two opinion polls since her reprieve suggest that she coulddefeat all imaginable opponentsin the two-candidate second round next year.Previous polls were almost as good for Bardella, but there were reasons to believe that he would not stay the course. The two-week-long second-round campaign traditionally stress-tests the capacity of the candidates not just to govern France but to represent it. Voters will wonder: do they have astature présidentielle? Bardella will be 31 in September. He has been an RN party apparatchik since he dropped out of college at the age of 19. Would voters have been able to imagine this talented but glib young man toe-to-toe with a Vladimir Putin or a Donald Trump?That question – presidential weight – is especially important for older voters. Of the 50 million registered French voters, 28% are over 65. Unlike younger people, they turn out in huge numbers.A recent Ifop poll showed Le Pen beating the former prime minister Édouard Philippe, the strongest of the many candidates looking to carry Emmanuel Macron’s centrist torch, by 54% to 46% in the second round. She had almost exactly the same lead among the over-65s. It is the first time any poll in any national election put the RN ahead with the “grey vote”.Bardella was also popular with older voters but his appeal to young and old was starting to fade. He comes from a working-class, Italian migrant family but had begun to show a Nicolas Sarkozy-like attraction to the high life, including, reportedly, a romance with anheiress from Italy’s remnant nobility.Le Pen was born into a wealthy family and political business but cultivates an image as a gruff-voiced people’s champion, a single grandmother living with her best friend,a breeder of catsand, above all, a survivor.There is, however, another issue that is crucial for older voters: economic stability. Le Pen’s feeble TV debate performances on the economyin 2017and 2022 helped Macron to defeat her.The RN’s economic policies remain an incoherent jumble of high social spending and low taxes, free markets and state interference. Bardella tried to shift the party towards a more traditional rightwing, low-tax policy and a more reformist approach to the EU, taking inspiration from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Le Pen’s return means a return to “Marinomics” and a policy ofwrecking the EU from the inside. With France€3.5tn in debtand permanently teetering on the brink of fiscal crisis, the prospect of a far-right government may disturb older and better-off voters.Le Pen will have an obvious riposte. Macron bamboozled you all twice with his clever people’s talk, she will say. Look where that got you: another €1tn in debt. Time to give a down-to-earth woman a chance. I could hardly do worse.But she could. Much, much worse.A President Le Pen or a President Bardella would take France and the EU into dangerous new territory. Bardella, at least, appeared aware of the difficulty of being so outlandishly anti-EU, and of trying to govern with slogans. Le Pen does not.A Le Pen presidency from next May is not a certainty. But it is, for the first time in seven decades of the family’s involvement in politics, a strong possibility. The comfort blanket for mainstream parties of right, left and centre – the implausibility of a 31-year-old slightly more pragmatic President Bardella – has been snatched away.Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director forEuropeat Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firmExplore more on these topicsMarine Le PenOpinionNational RallyFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Tiananmen vigil convictions: Hong Kong too has been silenced. Others should speak out | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Two activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crime
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Two activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crime
Content: A candlelight vigil for victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre, at Victoria Park, Hong Kong, in 2019.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreenA candlelight vigil for victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre, at Victoria Park, Hong Kong, in 2019.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APOpinionHong KongThe Guardian view on the Tiananmen vigil convictions: Hong Kong too has been silenced. Others should speak outEditorialTwo activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crimeMon 24 Aug 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTShareFor decades,Hong Kongmourned when the mainland could not. Its huge annual Tiananmen vigil kept alive the memory of the 1989 pro-reform protests in Beijing, and of the massacre that suppressed them. Along with Macau, it was the only place in China where the anniversary could be publicly marked and the truth preserved.But the crackdown onthe 2019 uprising in Hong Konghas crushed the freedoms that the region once enjoyed. That year’s vigil was the last. On Friday, two leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which organised the commemoration,were convictedof incitement to subversion under the draconian national security law. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face up to 10 years in jail.A third defendant, the 74-year-old former legislator Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. All three have been imprisonedsince their arrestsin 2021. The court ruled that the alliance’s stated aim to “end one-party dictatorship” in itself constituted using unlawful means to overthrow the Chinese government – despite acknowledging that the group never used or advocated violence, or even set out a path to its goal.The convictions are shameful, but not surprising. They follow the jailing of the prominent pro-democracy activists known as the “Hong Kong 47” in late 2024 and the 20-year sentence handed to the media tycoon and activistJimmy Lai in February. Yet while this trial shows the authorities’ determination to eradicate Hong Kong’s previous freedoms, it also reflects the Communist party’s determination tocontrol and rewrite history across China.View image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesHundreds, perhaps thousands, of people were killed in the 1989 massacre. Xi Jinpingmade a rare referenceto the events last week, reaffirming the party’s “correct” response, in a speech paying tribute to the former leader Jiang Zemin. But the subject remains one of the most taboo in a country long adept at erasing uncomfortable truths – so sensitive that even words such as “remember” and “today” arecensored on social mediaon the anniversary. This June, the Tiananmen Mothers group of bereaved relatives, who have long mournedunder heavy police escort, were barred fromvisiting their loved ones’ graveson the date of the killings.Against such brutal edicts, memory appears fragile. Most younger people on the mainland have no idea of what happened. Yet late last year, previously unseen footagesuddenly emergedof the court martial of a general who defied the order to use force against demonstrators. The video was posted on YouTube – which is blocked in China – andsheds new lighton events. General Xu Qinxian, who was jailed and lived under heavy restrictions until his death in 2021, said that a commander imposing the order might become “a sinner in history”. Whoever leaked the footage, and whatever their reasons for doing so, it is clear that some still resist the national amnesia.Remembrance and mourning are not crimes. In a message to Andy Burnham, Ms Chow, a barrister who studied law in the UK, warned that Britain had a “non-delegable duty to adopt a more robust stance” to China. She was right. The UK was the other signatory of the treaty that supposedlypreservedHong Kong’s relative autonomy until 2047. For years in the annual vigils, Ms Chow, Mr Lee and other courageous Hong Kong people stood up for those on the mainland who had been silenced. Others should now stand up and speak for them as they pay the price for that solidarity.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsHong KongOpinionTiananmen Square protests 1989Asia PacificChinaProtestHuman rightsFreedom of speecheditorialsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Better than The Godfather’: how we made brutal Yorkshire crime classic Red Riding | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: ‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’
Content: ‘I had to eat a raw Findus Crispy Pancake’ … Mark Addy as lawyer John Piggott in Red Riding.Photograph: CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYView image in fullscreen‘I had to eat a raw Findus Crispy Pancake’ … Mark Addy as lawyer John Piggott in Red Riding.Photograph: CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYHow we madeCulture‘Better than The Godfather’: how we made brutal Yorkshire crime classic Red Riding‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’Interviews byMichael HoganMon 24 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Grisoni, screenwriterI’d been writing screenplays with Michael Winterbottom and in 2006, his producer Andrew Eaton said: “There’s this quartet of novels by David Peace. Are you interested in adapting them?” I read the first, 1974, and was drawn to it and repelled at the same time. It was strong meat, full of anger and injustice. It’s anchored in reality, especially thePeter SutcliffeandStefan Kiszkocases, but heightened and stylised. “Fiction torn from the facts,” David called it.I was scared stiff because the novels were so experimental but I desperately wanted to do it – even if adapting all four would mean waving goodbye to several years of my life. The books span a decade with a huge cast of characters, so I condensed a lot.Eaton was keen on a different director and format for each film. It meant each had its own reference points. I thought about Chinatown a lot with 1974. The design and costumes were all smoky and brown, like the 70s. The cast went for the material big time. David Morrissey really did his research and Sean Harris is nothing if not method. It’s a very masculine story but we wanted strong female characters too – we had Maxine Peake and Rebecca Hall. I kept the most horrendous violence off-screen. Violence you imagine is much worse than anything you’ll see. Your mind does the work.double quotation markI kept the most horrendous violence off-screen. Violence you imagine is much worseThe police interrogation scenes, where they torture suspects, are terrifying and deliberately so. Stefan Kiszko, on whom Daniel Mays’s character is based, was released in 1992 and died 18 months later, having been wrongly imprisoned for 16 years. A man with a mind of a 12-year-old who just wanted his mum. The corruption and brutality in Red Riding are bleak, but so is the real world. While I was writing, the headlines were full of cases like Stephen Lawrence, Madeleine McCann, Natascha Kampusch, Shannon Matthews, Josef Fritzl …I was warned that Sutcliffe was litigious, so I should use what he actually said in his police interview. That was fine. I couldn’t have made it up anyway. Red Riding was compared to James Ellroy and described as Yorkshire noir, which is spot-on, although David said it was a pity they used a French word. He preferred Yorkshire dark. I added some redemption at the end because I needed to save somebody and finish on a note of love.Allow dailymotion content?This article includes content provided bydailymotion. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWe made 1974, 1980 and 1983 but, for budgetary reasons, not 1977, which broke my heart. It was always intended as a quartet, so it felt like vandalism. I hold out hope that somehow we’ll get to do the missing fourth. The films got a theatrical release in the US, screened back-to-back, which is full-on, but a cult audience went for it. Critic David Thomson called it “better than The Godfather”. Nic Pizzolatto said it influenced True Detective. People are still discovering it. They tend to say: “But you seem like quite a nice guy!”Mark Addy, actorMy agent sent me the scripts but said: “Just to warn you, there’s no money in this.” I got halfway through the first episode, phoned her back and asked: “Who else is attached?” She said: “Sean Bean, David Morrissey, Paddy Considine, Peter Mullan and Maxine Peake.” I said: “Put my name on the list please.” The scripts were so well-written, it was a no-brainer.Everyone was on Equity minimum, there were no trailers, not even a green room area. It was a tremendous experience to have a cast of that calibre, throwing their all into something that wasn’t going to buy them more than a pair of shoes.David Peace’s books put you inside the mind of each character and are dense with detail. They were a major resource for building my character, washed-up solicitor John Piggott. In one scene, he flashes back to finding his father’s body. They literally strapped a camera rig on to me, so viewers see it through Piggott’s eyes. He becomes the unlikely hero, despite being a dope-smoking, heavy-drinking loser. He takes on the might of the crooked West Yorkshire police and partly succeeds. Amid the darkness, he’s a bit of light at the end of the tunnel.Piggott’s a shoddy, unkempt idiot – he sleeps in his suit and at one point, he eats a raw Findus Crispy Pancake – but he saves the girl at the end. He carries her out of a mineshaft in his arms, like a Bruce Willis action hero. Shooting scenes in the underground paedophile’s lair was grim. There was a room with the dentist’s chair in it, mattresses on the floor, a child’s shoe. It brought home the horrors of what these monsters were doing. You needed a shower at the end of the day.View image in fullscreen‘People are still discovering it’ … Sean Bean in Red Riding.Photograph: Contract Number (Programme)/CHANNEL 4 PICTURE PUBLICITYI grew up in York during the 1970s and vividly remember the Ripper era. I used to cycle back from my then-girlfriend’s house in the pitch black. Tension on the streets was palpable – you’d pedal home as quickly as you could. Everyone felt Sutcliffe’s elusiveness and how the police were overwhelmed. The show’s hardly a tourist advert for Yorkshire. On location, set dressing would be a burnt-out car on the grass verge, maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals were like: “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”Red Riding is an extraordinary achievement. Three different directors and formats. It’s hard for me to fault it. It had ripple effects on my career. Ridley Scott had just started work on Robin Hood with Russell Crowe. The casting director gave him a Red Riding DVD because it had so many British actors. He watched it one weekend and, on Monday morning, phoned up to acquire the US rights, then cast me as Friar Tuck. He must’ve seen me eat the frozen Crispy Pancake and thought: “That’s my man!”The Red Riding Trilogy is available to stream on Amazon’s Studiocanal Presents channelExplore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeTelevisionDavid PeacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A rock star on her own terms’: why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White | The White Stripes | The Guardian
description: Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer
Author: Annie Zaleski
Headline: Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer
Content: Meg White in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Rideaux/Rex FeaturesView image in fullscreenMeg White in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Rideaux/Rex FeaturesThe White Stripes‘A rock star on her own terms’: why we’re still so fascinated by Meg WhiteRecent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummerAnnie ZaleskiMon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 2011, theWhite Stripesannouncedthey were no longer going to tour or release new music. The decision wasn’t based on “artistic differences” or “health issues”; instead, the decision was “mostly to preserve what is beautiful and special about the band and have it stay that way”.In the ensuing years, vocalist-guitarist Jack White cultivated a wildly successful solo career and continued working sporadically with his other bands, the Raconteurs and the Dead Weather. Drummer Meg White, meanwhile, retreated from music, preferring instead to be a private citizen. In recent years, she politely declined to speak for a 2023 Elle story and didn’t attend the White Stripes’ 2025 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.Daily Mail accused of stalking woman mistaken as White Stripes drummer Meg WhiteRead moreAs a culture, we’re fascinated by musicians who stay out of the spotlight. Over the years, journalists have tried to track down elusive artists such as Cleveland singer-songwriter Bill Fox (who actually gave several interviews last year) or Suburban Lawns’Su Tissue. We’re not entitled to know details of their personal lives, of course, which is why this fascination occasionally slides into pernicious territory – like the now-deletedDaily Mail articlethat recently attempted to find Meg but instead stalked the wrong person.Meg had an uneasy relationship with being a public figure during the White Stripes’ active existence. She was notoriously shy, once tellingNPRabout the advice a teacher gave her: “She wrote in my yearbook to speak softly and carry a big stick, you know? And I took to that heart.” The White Stripes alsocanceledtour dates in 2007 due to Meg’s “acute anxiety”, something Jackspokeabout candidly and empathetically later. “To go full-speed from a dead-halt is overwhelming, and we had to take a break.”Such vulnerability made Meg enormously relatable, someone you wanted to root for to succeed. But people also feel protective of her because she was often treated so poorly when the White Stripes were an active band. Meg started playing drums in 1997 at Jack’s behest – the first song the duo played together was David Bowie’s Moonage Daydream – skipping formal music lessons in favor of more unvarnished creativity.View image in fullscreenMeg White in 2004.Photograph: Jean Baptiste Lacroix/WireImageThis irked people who expected virtuosity. A now-archived2016 article– Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her – outlined the sexism in exhaustive detail, from Pitchfork calling her drumming “pancake-handed” to a 2007 Pearl Jam message board thread titled “Official Meg White can’t play thread.” (Both jabs are still online.) Long after the White Stripes ceased recording, the negativity persisted. In 2023, a journalistapologizedafter intense outcry to his offhand comment that “the tragedy of the White Stripes is how great they would’ve been with a half-decent drummer.”The observation is especially absurd because the White Stripes were great precisely because of her approach to drumming. She and Jack complemented each other perfectly; her combination of steely focus and serene nonchalance balanced his more outgoing presence. “Meg is the best part of this band,” JacktoldRolling Stone in 2005, adding: “When she started to play drums with me, just on a lark, it felt liberating and refreshing.”Indeed, Meg was a powerful player who propelled the White Stripes’ blues/punk/garage rock hybrids with a steady hand. Her thumping kickdrum propels The Hardest Button to Button like a thundering metronome; the garage-rock classics Fell In Love With a Girl and Hotel Yorba lift off due to her buoyant, ramshackle playing. Later-era singles like Icky Thump and Blue Orchid boast a heavier edge thanks in no small part to Meg’s seething, sizzling grooves.And, unlike other duos, the White Stripes didn’t hire additional musicians to flesh out their live sound. It was always Meg and Jack against the world – her forceful rhythmic backbone anchoring his wild-hair extroversion, whether a grimy guitar line, a soulful organ, antique piano part or even a lively marimba.Criticized at the time, the White Stripes’ Glastonbury 2005 performance looks like a revelation through a modern lens; Meg looks unflappable, even ecstatic, as she mouths along with the words and steers the set. On the pair’sominous coverof Dolly Parton’s Jolene, her light-touch cymbal hits generate tension for much of the song – until it explodes as she ferociously attacks her entire drumkit, mirroring the moment when the narrator collapses in anguish.“It will always be us two,” JacktoldRolling Stone in 2005. “I will never do the White Stripes with another drummer. She’ll never do it with another guitarist.”He’s kept his word: when the duo was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Jack didn’t perform in Meg’s absence. Instead, Twenty One Pilots whacked through Seven Nation Army, while Olivia Rodrigo and Feist picked through a delicate We’re Going To Be Friends. However, Meg sent a note of gratitude that Jack read; he also noted she helped write and shape the speech he gave. “A lot of punctuation corrections too,” he quipped. “She’s pretty good at that.”With this honor, Meg became just the third female drummer inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, after Gina Schock of the Go-Go’s and Velvet Underground’s Moe Tucker. Like those two artists, Meg reinforced the idea that you could be in a band, create your own style and carve out your own destiny. She didn’t wait around for permission to be an artist.Meg’s iconoclastic music career and drumming skills are finally receiving their due, in no small part because younger fans and musicians aren’t saddled by the same sexist cultural baggage. Speaking to Elle in 2023, Rodrigo noted Meg’s playing and the White Stripes themselves taught her “the value of simplicity in music … that a truly great song doesn’t need to have crazy production or layers of sound. It just needs to move you. You can sense her passion in every song she plays.” But in the end, Meg proved you could be a rock star on your own terms – both duringandafter your music career.This article was amended on 24 August 2026. The article titled Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her was published in 2016, not 2006 as an earlier version stated.Explore more on these topicsThe White StripesPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Green Man review – Wolf Alice, Shame and secret sets keep the Welsh festival’s flame burning | Green Man | The Guardian
description: The traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Wolf Alice, Tamikrest and Westside Cowboy
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: The traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Wolf Alice, Tamikrest and Westside Cowboy
Content: Commanding … Wolf Alice.Photograph: Patrick GunningView image in fullscreenCommanding … Wolf Alice.Photograph: Patrick GunningGreen ManReviewGreen Man review – Wolf Alice, Shame and secret sets keep the Welsh festival’s flame burningBannau Brycheiniog, WalesThe traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Four Tet, Tamikrest and Westside CowboyOlive PometseyMon 24 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDriving towards the bucolic Welsh valley that’s home to theGreen Manfestival feels a little apocalyptic this year. Charred peat and grassland smoulder on the hillsides, the remnants of one of the 20 wildfires that blazed through south and west Wales the previous week. The dangerously dry conditions pose a problem for the festival organisers: the traditional closing ceremony, during which a towering effigy of the titular Green Man adorned with punters’ handwritten wishes is set alight, has been cancelled. A sensible decision, but one that left longtime festival-goers with a serious question: where would all those wishes go?Then, the heavens open. Manchester quartetWestside Cowboypack out the main stage arena on Friday afternoon, thousands of soggy cagoules bobbing along to the band’s charmingly ramshackle blend of British indie and amiable Americana. “We were over there last year,” grins vocalist and guitarist Jimmy Bradbury, gesturing towards the significantly smaller Rising stage. They’re clearly over the moon – and it’s infectious. To close the set, the band down instruments – save a guitar and a handheld drum – and gather round one mic for a rallying performance of In the Morning. The recorded version sounds like a lullaby, but here they transform it into a euphoric boot-stomping finale.That energy charges through the rest of the day, even as the rain clears up. With his exhilarating blend of highlife, funk and electro, Ghanaian singer Ata Kak bounds across the stage with enough zeal to fuel a small army. London post-punks Shame incite endless moshpits with their rowdy, self-deprecating swagger and calls to “free Palestine”. Dry Cleaning’s Florence Shaw delivers a typically off-kilter performance of her jaded, spoken-word indie, bringing out Jeff Tweedy – of headliners Wilco – for the first ever duo performance of My Soul/Half Pint. Over in the Far Out tent, Karla Chubb of Sprints plucks a teenager out of the crowd to take over her guitar during their final song, Little Fix, freeing her up to crowd surf on one condition: “You have to promise to not touch my bum,” she tells the audience.View image in fullscreenRowdy and self-deprecating … Shame.Photograph: Patrick GunningMalian rock band Tamikrest supply the psychedelic desert blues, and Gambian party-starter Suntou Susso orchestrates a giant conga line through the crowd. Cult producer Daniel Avery maintains the intensity, but in a surprising way:: all headbanging metal guitars and ferocious live drum’n’bass beats, only briefly punctuated by the pulsating techno he’s better known for. Anyone left slightly disappointed gets their fill at Four Tet’s headline slot, which crescendoes from ambient techno into body-rattling bass.Green Man’s lineup is hardly built around old-school star power. Still, both buzzy New York electro duo Fcukers andWolf Alicemake a convincing case for energetic performers, the latter in particular during the weekend’s final headline set. Clad head-to-toe in leather, Wolf Alice’s Ellie Rowsell commands the stage with powerhouse vocals that oscillate between indie crooning, near-operatic belting and snarling, punky screams, and leads the crowd in a collective howl at the moon. After a performance of that wattage, the replacement for the burning ceremony can’t help but feel a bit anticlimactic: Scotland’s Pictish Trail lead an acoustic performance of the Waterboys’ The Whole of the Moon, accompanied by aerial acrobats in glittering costumes, but the restless crowd never really get going.Thankfully, a secret closing set brings together Fcukers, Hot Chip’s Alexis Taylor, Way Dynamic, the Itch, Another Country $$$$ and SNL UK comedian Jack Shep for rounds of back-to-back DJ sets with crowd-pleasing Madonna remixes and a Don’t You Want Me singalong. It makes for a euphoric finale, and wish fulfilment of the highest order.Explore more on these topicsGreen ManFestivalsMusic festivalsWilcoDry CleaningWolf AlicePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Breakout indie band Westside Cowboy on rejecting tech and loving imperfection: ‘We’re not hermits!’ | Music | The Guardian
description: Despite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Despite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?
Content: ‘We’re not cool’ … Reuben Haycocks, Jimmy Bradbury, Aoife Anson O’Connell and Paddy Murphy, AKA Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannView image in fullscreen‘We’re not cool’ … Reuben Haycocks, Jimmy Bradbury, Aoife Anson O’Connell and Paddy Murphy, AKA Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannMusicInterviewBreakout indie band Westside Cowboy on rejecting tech and loving imperfection: ‘We’re not hermits!’Daniel Dylan WrayDespite their fast rise, the Manchester indie-pop band are happily going at their own pace. But what – if anything – did they learn from the advice of Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon?Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Westside Cowboy played Later … With Jools Holland earlier this year, fellow guests Duran Duran offered some advice. “Nerves are just your mind telling you that you’re about to do something extraordinary,” Simon Le Bon told the band, who were “cacking their pants”. Le Bon’s words didn’t really help. “I was hoping for some real advice,” says vocalist and guitarist Reuben Haycocks, laughing. “Like, where do I look?”The Manchester band have had to learn the ropes quickly. By 2025, only two years after forming, they had won Glastonbury’s emerging talent competition, supported Geese on the year’s buzziest indie tour and signed to a major label.“We’d be lying if we said there wasn’t a little bit of pressure,” says vocalist and guitarist Jimmy Bradbury.Not that you can hear it on their hotly anticipated debut album, It Goes On. Recalling the likes of the Feelies, Parquet Courts and Courtney Barnett, the album touches upon the muscular end of indie-pop, a little midwestern emo and has a chugging drive inspired by the Velvet Underground. “We weren’t trying to make some career-defining thing,” says drummer Paddy Murphy, as we cram into their tour van backstage at Tramlines festival in Sheffield. “We love the way debut albums sound when a band feels hungry but still not quite settled. There’s unnecessary pressure on new bands to bottle everything on the first attempt. It doesn’t have to be that way. Just do whatever feels right.”Westside Cowboy: Pin Up Boys – videoWestside Cowboy are all aged 23 to 26, but – as their taste in music and resistance to the grind may indicate – share an old-school mindset. Most of them have brick phones, use MP3 players and collections of analogue gear, from radios to CD players and cassette decks. They’re even considering setting up a PO box address for fans to send letters to. “We’re not hermits,” insists Bradbury. “We still have laptops and send emails, but taking away that single-use device, like a phone, really helps free up headspace. These things are designed to be addictive, and it’s trying to find a way to control it, because you don’t have to buy into that.”It’s the same with their music. Bassist and vocalist Aoife Anson-O’Connell finds it “really stifling creatively and personally isolating” being locked perpetually on screens, while Haycocks’ previous band, he says, became frozen by the “option paralysis” of overusing technology. “It feels like the only way for people of our age, but we reject that. Starting this band, we thought we’d go for the most simple thing possible and that’s also seeped into our daily lives.”View image in fullscreen‘Britanicana is as pointless as all other genres’ … Westside Cowboy.Photograph: Clementine SchneidermannOn stage later on, they play an explosive 4pm set to a rammed tent, contrasting sharp, noisy blasts of guitar with layered vocal harmonies. But back in the van, they are a modest and self-deprecating bunch. “We’re not doing anything revolutionary,” says Anson-O’Connell. Bradbury states: “We’re not cool.”All band members share songwriting duties; when Haycocks writes he tries to channel frontmen he feels possess more panache, such as Lou Reed or the Magnetic Fields’ Stephin Merritt (it might explain the American twang to his vocal delivery). “I’m not someone who feels at my coolest when I’m Reuben Haycocks,” he says. “There’s a certain level of bravado you need to try to write a song, so to get myself over the line, I’ll be X person for an hour – as I will never be able to reach that level of awesomeness.” This role play works for figuring out tone, too. One instruction Murphy gave to Bradbury when working out a guitar part was to imagine early rock’n’roller Link Wray “trying to scare kids”.Their love of folk, skiffle, Americana and early rock’n’roll led to them coining their own genre, Britanicana, to capture this hybrid. Now they call it a joke that got out of hand. “A very tongue-in-cheek thing,” says Murphy.“If people want to use Britanicana, be my guest,” Haycocks adds. “It’s as equally pointless as all other genres.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We’re really good. I don’t mean that arrogantly’: Yard Act on bullying, imposter syndrome and their heavy new albumRead moreAs much as Westside Cowboy feel like a band happily at home in the past, they’re just as invested in improving their own era. Alongside the indie bands Holly Head, Pushbike and Martial Arts, they run a night called No Band Is an Island, which programmes bands and leftwing political speakers to raise money for Medical Aid for Palestine. Although you won’t find explicitly political lyrics in their songs. “We are all political people,” offers Haycocks, who is wearing a T-shirt calling for animal liberation. “But we don’t think our music suits going on stage and shouting about politics because that’s not who we are, personally.”In hindsight, the fabulously slick Le Bon was probably never going to have much good advice for a band like this. Westside Cowboy’s own musical heroes are artists who have embraced imperfection. Haycocks scrolls through his MP3 player and finds Tom Waits’ Mule Variations. “It’s like, oh my God, how has he managed to write two of the most goofy songs in the world among five of the greatest?” he says, comparing the likes of Chocolate Jesus with Picture in a Frame.Bradbury jumps in: “You’ve got to have your duds!” Haycocks agrees, inadvertently summing up the band’s MO. “Duds are what make music human.”It Goes On is out now on IslandExplore more on these topicsMusicIndieinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffin | Photography | The Guardian
description: Bloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then men
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Bloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then men
Content: ‘It made me realise that life is very short’ … Lawrence, left, and Philipp, whose lives are recorded in Chronograph. All photographs: courtesy the artist and Mack.View image in fullscreen‘It made me realise that life is very short’ … Lawrence, left, and Philipp, whose lives are recorded in Chronograph. All photographs: courtesy the artist and Mack.Photography‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffinBloody noses, ear cleanings, the first sproutings of armpit hair … the photographer reveals how he captured his two babies growing into boys and then menTim JonzeMon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot many family photo albums open with images of the twin towers on fire. But for Nick Haymes, it made perfect sense. “When 9/11 happened,” he says, “I realised life was very short.” At the time, he was living in New York, trying to forge a career, while his friend, colleague and future wife Lina was dealing with the fallout of her previous marriage. “It made us realise we should probably get together and have a family. It was this huge historical event, but on a very micro level, it also shaped my relationship with my wife and children.”Chronograph is a photography book that runs from those terrorist attacks to the present day, tracing the journey of Haymes’s two sons, Philipp and Lawrence, as they grow from drooling babies into young men. We are given a ringside seat as arms get broken, beloved pets die and hairs start sprouting from armpits. The mundane side of life – verrucas, messy kitchens, Lina cleaning out an ear with a cotton bud – is captured in the same way as birthday parties and rites of passage.double quotation markLawrence would joke: ‘You photograph me when I’m crying rather than dealing with it’“Because we lived in this tiny, 800 sq ft apartment in Manhattan, you don’t miss a thing, all the ups and downs, all the mood swings,” says Haymes. “There was no door slamming, because there was nowhere to go!”View image in fullscreenIndeed, we are not spared from seeing the children at their least flattering: “We used to have a running joke where Lawrence would say: ‘You’re the only parent that would photograph me when I’m crying rather than deal with the issue straight away,’” admits Haymes, “but I like to think I was attentive. It was a funny balance because the camera was always around, but it seemed to work.”There are also multiple shots of the boys naked – not just running around the house as young children but as they transition into adulthood too. I suspect most teenagers would not be cool with this, but Haymes insists he had their approval. “They don’t have an issue,” he says. “I’ve been lucky enough to have some very nice photographers in my household at various times, so they’re aware of the creative process.” He shrugs: “There are bigger themes in the book than child nudity. That was just a part of our daily life.”Besides, when Philipp and Lawrence reach their teens – all bleached hair, tattoos and stubble – they work out an ingenious method of rebellion. Instead of sulking or turning away from the camera, Haymes says his kids smiled and put their thumbs up, knowing that the last thing their dad wanted was a posed family portrait. “That was basically their way of telling me to clear out of their lives,” he says.View image in fullscreenBorn in Stratford-upon-Avon, Haymes hoped to study art but ended up dropping out. “I took way too many drugs in my 20s and had a bit of a breakdown,” he says. After couch-surfing in London for a bit, he found work in a photo studio, eventually assisting Jürgen Teller. In 1999, he packed two cameras into a bag and decided to try his luck in New York. It was here he met Lina, a Jewish refugee who, as a teenager, had moved to the US with her parents from Ukraine – then part of the Soviet Union. She was working on a magazine and gave him a commission that allowed him to get a visa and stay.Haymes’s own difficult transition from youth to adulthood is perhaps what draws him to his subjects. Between Dog and Wolf captured his road trips across California and Oklahoma with a group of young skateboarders. Follow-up Gabe TM unfurled over many years hanging out with Gabe Nevins, the teenage star of Gus Van Sant’s Paranoid Park. Unexpectedly, Haymes found himself chronicling Nevins’s homelessness and addiction in the wake of making the movie. Dancing on the Fault Line, published in 2024, was another mammoth excursion, following teenager Love Bailey and her extended queer family right up to her decision to transition in her 30s.Haymes is still in touch with his previous subjects: he shot Bailey’s wedding; Gabe is living a “normal life” now in Oregon; the skaters have children of their own. Haymes doesn’t intend to foster such deep relationships with his subjects. “I always think, ‘Oh, I’ll just do a nice quick shoot.’ But then I get attached to everybody, they become part of my life. You can become a father figure to them, or a therapist maybe. That’s part of it, and that’s part of the educational process for me, just to be with people and understand them.”View image in fullscreenIt was during Covid that Haymes found the time to go through all his family negatives and work out what to do with them. “It moved me pretty heavily,” he says. “I also had to try to be as impartial as I could because I didn’t want it to be saccharine.”Did he know, as he took them, that the photos of his children would end up in a published book? “I suppose, as a photographer, yes. But I really did it for personal memory, and as a little self-analysis. To think about how I was as a parent. Also, I shoot on film and at the time, in the early 2000s, digital photography had kicked in so I was finding myself more and more unemployable. I thought, ‘OK, I am becoming a house husband.’ But I wanted to be a photographer still, so the family life around me is what I photographed.”Besides Lina and the boys, the other key figures in the book are Lina’s parents Nadia and Mikhail. “They werebigcharacters,” says Haymes. “I had to learn how to become a little more emotional and a little more warm and compassionate.”One striking image is of Mikhail sitting with wrapping paper on his head. He’s in a full tracksuit, giving off a slightly intimidatingPaulie Walnutsvibe. “He was a very loving person,” says Haymes, “but yeah, maybe a bit of a rogue. Whereas my mother-in-law had her issues and I think maybe undiagnosed bipolar disorder. She also became a victim of prescription medication in the US, and we had to deal with that. She was certainly a tough mother-in-law, but at some point you fall in love with her anyway.”There are some portentous images in the book. Scars on Mikhail’s stomach mirror Lina’s caesarean scars, although we can only guess why he’s been cut open. Then there is the pet hamster, who we see being held, adored and then grieved for as it rests in its cardboard coffin.View image in fullscreenThe book’s closing passages are extremely moving, as we see Nadia and Mikhail in hospital together, their conditions slowly deteriorating. “We were bringing two people to dialysis every day, which was two pretty gruelling years.” At some point, Haymes converted the home art gallery into a hospice.In the book, it appears as if the couple died at the same time. In reality it was a year apart and the couple had gone through a divorce by that point. “There are things that don’t need to be known,” says Haymes of the story his book tells. “Everybody has a family album, and through those you only remember certain parts.”Despite their divorce, Nadia and Mikhail were buried together in Los Angeles. “I’m not sure if Lina’s father is enjoying that right now, but that’s what happened,” says Haymes with a smile.He says he had been asked to make a photography book of his family for 15 years but it was only when the grandparents died that he realised the project was complete. “The book starts with death and ends with death,” he says. “It’s gone full circle.”Interspersed with beautiful, closeup images of flowers received at the funeral, we see Philipp and Lawrence standing by the graveside with the urn. “For them to be able to communicate those emotions and to speak at a service, for me that felt like, ‘OK, they’re on their own now. They’ve become men.’”He pauses, then laughs like only a father can. “Having said that,” he adds, “they’re still on my Uber account.”Chronograph(SPBH Editions, 2026) by Nick Haymes is published by Mack, £55Explore more on these topicsPhotographyFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Guardian-produced Gaza documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli directors of No Other Land to screen at Venice film festival | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the war
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Film directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the war
Content: NAZA, selected for the Venice film festival.Photograph: Venice Film Festival/APView image in fullscreenNAZA, selected for the Venice film festival.Photograph: Venice Film Festival/APMoviesGuardian-produced Gaza documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli directors of No Other Land to screen at Venice film festivalFilm directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, co-directors of No Other Land along with  Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal , investigates ‘Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians’ during the warAndrew PulverMon 24 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new documentary about Israel’s bombing campaign in Gaza, directed by Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, is to receive its world premiere at theVenice film festival.The film, called NAZA, has been produced with Jim Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind The Zone of Interest, and is the only documentary that will compete this year for Venice’s prestigious Golden Lion.Abraham and Szor are the two Israeli directors of the four behind No Other Land, whichwon the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.Announcing the news, the film-makers said: “Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.”The Guardian addedin a statementthat NAZA is an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.The documentary builds on original investigative reporting between 2023 and 2025 by Israeli-Palestinian publication+972, Hebrew-language outletLocal Calland the Guardian.No Other Land, which was directed by Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal alongside Abraham and Szor,was described as a “sombre, sobering work”by the Guardian’s chief film critic Peter Bradshaw.Shortly after No Other Land’s Oscar win,Ballal was attacked by Israeli settlers and briefly arrested, following whichthe Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciencesapologised after failing to name Ballal or the film in a statement of support.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsVenice film festivalFestivalsGazaPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: The comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?
Content: ‘I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy’…Russ Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy’…Russ Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe big interviewTV comedyInterview‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked awaySimon HattenstoneThe comedian dominated Saturday night TV in the 1980s, with his sketch shows attracting 18 million viewers. Next came the West End musicals and sitcoms. But in 2016 he quietly disappeared from the limelight. What happened?Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe electronic gates slide open to reveal a gorgeous Portuguese villa, a swimming pool and a beansprout of a man. “You’ve made me feel very important,” says Russ Abbot with a smile. “Come in!”It’s more than 30 years since Abbot, aged 78, dominated Saturday night TV with his sketches, songs and impersonations. He appealed to all sorts. Kids, parents and grandparents united around the TV – first for Russ Abbot’s Madhouse, which ran from 1980 to 1985, then The Russ Abbot Show, from 1986 to 1991. He was joined by the inimitable Bella Emberg and a cast of young comics, including Les Dennis, Dustin Gee and Michael Barrymore. But make no mistake, it was Abbot’s show and the 80s was his decade. At his peak, he attracted 18 million viewers an episode.When TV commissioners tired of his brand of sketch comedy, he did stints in the sitcoms Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine and played it straight in the moving TV drama September Song. There was a run of West End musical smashes – Fagin in Oliver!, Roger de Bris in The Producers, Alfred P Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Then, in 2016, he quietly retired.
