For the past seven years, he has split his time between Barbados and the Algarve, where I find him today.View image in fullscreenAbbot and Trish have been married for 60 years.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianAbbot introduces me to his wife, Trish, who has a smart silver bob and a northern accent. How long have you two been married, I ask her. “Sixty years,” she says quietly. “Not even the Train Robbers got that!” Trish, 80, giggles.We’re standing in a large, airy hall. On a table are figurines of Laurel and Hardy – Abbot’s heroes. Upstairs, I can make out lots of framed photos. He takes me on a tour. There are pics of him with the great entertainers of his era (Brucey, Elton, Tarby, Shaky) and the royals (Philip, Anne, Charles). We pass the silver discs from his brief period as Britain’s unlikeliest pop star (who can forget Atmosphere?). “That’s a certificate acknowledging the biggest box office in summer season history,” he says, like an accountant conducting an audit of his success. “And that’s whatshisname.” He squints at a picture. “Live Aid. Bob Geldof.”Pride of place is a photo of him dressed as Cooperman, with Tommy Cooper. Cooperman was one of Abbot’s more surreal mashup characters – Superman meets the brilliantly bumbling comic giant, who died on stage in 1984. He adored Cooper. “It was so funny at the funeral. All the faces were there. Max Bygraves, Eric Sykes, me. And when the cortege came in, we’d forgotten he’d got a younger brother who looked just like him. He walked in and we’re like: ‘Oh God! Another Tommy prank.’ When the curtain closed on the coffin, I thought: he’s going to come out in a minute because he was such a practical joker.”View image in fullscreenWith his band the Black Abbots, with whom he won Opportunity Knocks.Photograph: Anwar Hussein/AlamyHe pauses. Now he sounds emotional. “After the funeral, we were walking out paying our respects to his wife, Gwen, and she said to me: ‘He thought you were the cat’s whiskers!’ I filled up. Amazing.”More photos. Dennis and Gee, the double act who memorably impersonated Coronation Street’s Mavis Riley and Vera Duckworth on his show. Gee died in 1986, at 43. “So talented. Died too young.” We come to a picture of Abbot dressed as CU Jimmy, the incomprehensible, ranting Scottish stereotype that he’d struggle to get away with today. He says the character was based on his Scottish mother, whose accent got thicker the nearer the family got to Scotland for their holidays. He impersonates her – and she sounds as incoherent as Jimmy.Abbot’s mother, Elizabeth, was in domestic service to the Duke of Westminster at Eaton Hall in Cheshire when she met his father, Don Roberts, a tanker driver for Pratt’s Oil who went on to become an area manager. Young Russell Roberts was a bright lad who went to Chester Grammar. But he became obsessed with drumming, flunked his O-levels and left school at 16 to join a band called the Black Abbots. He supplemented his income with a job as a stagehand at the Royalty theatre in Chester, where the band had a residency.They soon became a comedy band, with Abbot dismounting the drums to tell daft jokes. The band won the talent show Opportunity Knocks six weeks in a row, became huge in the working men’s clubs, but never had a hit record. By 1973, Abbot was appearing on the TV standup comedy show The Comedians and his manager, Mike Hughes, didn’t think Russell Roberts had a ring to it. He suggested he become Russ Abbot. “He said: ‘Think about it, if your bill is in alphabetical order, you’ll always be top of the bill.’ He said: ‘Abba could top you, but that’s about it.’ That’s clever, isn’t it?”View image in fullscreenIn Russ Abbot’s Madhouse in the 1980s.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockBy the late 1970s, Abbot was well known as a comic and starred in the original Madhouse series with the more famous Freddie Starr. After 17 years as a Black Abbot, he left to go solo. Within months, Russ Abbot’s Madhouse started on ITV (The Russ Abbot Show would move during its run to the BBC) and he was a Saturday night fixture.We join Trish outside in the shade. She’s made us coffee and piled a plate with digestive biscuits. Did life change when he became a household name? “No.” He looks at her for confirmation. “Just in the sense we moved up the ladder homewise, didn’t we, Trish? So we started in the caravan. Trish’s dad had a win on the pools that paid for the caravan as a wedding present. Then my dad got us a place with £1-a-week rent. Two up, two down. Then we got a £10,000 bungalow and sold it for twice the price.”“Yep,” says Trish.‘Then we moved down south, we moved to Wentworth. We looked at this nice house …”“And that was it, yes,” says Trish.“We bought it, cash.”Were loads of women interested in you? “Not really, no,” he says. There’s a glint in his eye. “Oh, I suppose in my drumming days. Early.” The glint vanishes. “Actually, it was more the singers. Because I was just the drummer in the back.” He tells me how he met Trish. “She came to the stage door of the British Legion in Ellesmere Port as I was packing my drums up. We had a bass player in those days called Paul Dodd. He ended up a policeman. Trish says: ‘Is the bass player around?’ I said: ‘No, he’s gone, love.’ She said: ‘Oh, that’s a shame, I wanted to say hello to him.’”Did you fancy the bass player, I ask Trish.“Yeah.”So you got the wrong bloke?“Yeah, I got him instead.”“I said: come on, I’ll buy you a drink. Then I said: let me give you a lift home. She said: I only live across the road. I said: you can’t walk alone at this time of night. So I left with a kiss and a cuddle. And it all started from there, didn’t it, Trish?”Did she find him funny? “Oh no. Very normal. Lovely brothers, lovely mum and dad. Just normal, like the boy next door.” Did she like comedy? “Oh God, no!” Actually, she says, there was one occasion when he really made her laugh. “He opened the garden fete and chopped his nose off instead of cutting the ribbon.”Genuinely?“Yes, he was rushed to hospital. That’s what made me laugh.”“I had stitches all round my nose.”Trish is in stitches at the memory.“But that wasn’t intentionally funny,” Abbot protests.“No,” says Trish, still hooting. “But it was very funny, Russell. And we’ve laughed ever since.”He must have been stopped a lot over the years by fans. “No, not really,” he says. “It was always a nod and a wink and a smile. There’s one funny story. We went to the opening show of Miss Saigon.” Trish is already giggling. “We go into the VIP area. We sit there and Trish nudges me. All these heads are turning. And I say: ‘It’s all right! The lights will go down in a minute.’ I say: ‘Trish, it’s acompliment.’ And she nudges me again and says: ‘Look who’s sitting next to me!’ And it was Burt Lancaster. She fell about. Lovely story.”View image in fullscreenIn Cooperman getup, with his good friend Bella Emberg as Blunderwoman, in the late 1980s.Photograph: ITV/Rex/ShutterstockAbbot never considered himself a star. “I always think I’m playing that role of Russ Abbot. I go in the stage door as Russ Abbot and come out as Russell Roberts.” And he was too reserved to play the big I am. “I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy and I found them embarrassing. It’s like, now I’m retired, I’m not so shy and I can talk about it because it’s past.”Trish has always been his biggest fan, he says. Then he corrects himself. “Trish and my mum. She used to do handouts for the WI. I’d sign the autograph and she’d sign the back: ‘Russ’s mum!’ She loved it!” In her 70s, his mother got dementia. She went into a home, but Abbot didn’t realise how bad it had got until he arranged for her to come to a show. “Trish brought her up to the dressing room and Mum walked in and said: ‘What a pleasure to meet you. Thank you so much, I’ve been so entertained. It was absolutely marvellous, and now to meet you in person.’“I stood there and said: ‘Mum, it’s me,’ and she said: ‘I’ll have to go now, my family’s waiting for me.’ So Trish took her back. I slammed the dressing room door three times. It was terrible. It’s a terrible illness. She died about a year later. She was still a very elegant lady, very smartly dressed. She didn’t act like she had dementia. She just couldn’t remember who I was.”Abbot worked incredibly hard in his heyday. “In 1984, I worked 363 days.” Meanwhile, Trish was working incredibly hard, too, bringing up their four children. “Trish raised them all. I was always away, summer season tour or pantomime. Pantomimes, gosh! You’d get home Christmas Eve, put the presents under the tree, go to bed, have breakfast, watch the kids open the toys and then go back to do a matinee.”View image in fullscreenWith Les Dennis in The Russ Abbot Show, circa 1991.Photograph: TV Times/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesBut, he says, they were great times. He tells me of all the wonderful people he worked with. It sounds like an Oscar acceptance speech.Barry Cryerwrote much of his material, but there was a whole team involved and there is not an actor, producer, writer or manager he misses out.He was the ideas man, he says, rather than the wordsmith. “I loved it. All the nonsense.” He talks about the silly names they invented for characters. “My favourite was Miss Funnyfanny intead of Miss Moneypenny. I think that was my cousin Russell. I loved Basildon Bond because of the silliness of it.”Suddenly he’s quoting a 40-year-old monologue from a sketch featuring his James Bond parody. ‘My name’s Bond. Basildon Bond, licence to kill and drive a heavy-goods vehicle. I’d been away on holiday when I was summonsed back to headquarters to see my boss P … ‘Was it a good holiday Bond?’ I said: ‘Yes, thank you, sir, I went away for a bit of peace and quiet. I found a nice little piece. I just hope she keeps quiet.’ He said: ‘Don’t bother me with a silly little thing like that.’ I said: ‘It’s funny, that’s what she said.’”He quotes the monologue word-perfect, in all its anachronistic glory. For all the inappropriateness, there’s also an innocence to it, as there is to him. I notice he doesn’t swear and I ask if he’s religious. “Oh, I believe in God. I say my prayers every night.”Abbot fell out of fashion in the 1990s, as did virtually all the standup rooted in working men’s clubs and seaside summer seasons. Did he mind when his TV show got cancelled? “I wasn’t distressed or angry or anything. It came about when the head of entertainment gave an interview and said: ‘The BBC’s going to change. No more of this, no more of that,’ and somebody said: ‘Does that mean Russ Abbot?’ and he said yes, meaning the sketch shows. So then it became ‘BBC sacks Russ Abbot’, but that didn’t bother me. I thought: well, I’ve had a very good run. Also, I’d just cracked the West End, so I was doing everything I wanted to do without the stress of the TV shows.”Why did he fall out of fashion? “It was when the new wave came in. Alternative comedy. I thought, alternative comedy? What’s it alternative to? If the thing’s funny, it’s funny. Political correctness came in, and you can’t laugh at each other and you can’t laugh at yourself. At the same time, a lot of comedy started going blue and I thought: I’m not going down that road.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ve had a wonderful career,’ says Abbot.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSo much of his show’s humour was rooted in stereotyping and many of the jokes were at the expense of his great friend Emberg’s weight. Did he understand why that was no longer acceptable? “Yes. Some of the scripts I used to look at myself and wonder. I’d say: ‘Bella, have you read the script?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, I think it’s funny’. I’d say: ‘Are you sure?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, why?’ ‘I’m just asking your opinion,’ and she’d say: ‘I think it’s hilarious,’ and I’d say: ‘So do I!’” Did she ever get upset? “No, she never got upset once.” Emberg died in 2018 at 80. Of all the people he’s worked with, he says he misses her most.I loved it when Emberg as Blunderwoman lifted Abbot over her shoulders and carried him off. Even at his heaviest, he weighed only 12 and a half stone. Not much for a man over six foot tall. These days, Emberg would have had even less trouble. He’s lost two and a half stone. He knows Trish is worried, but he’s had every test going and nothing has been diagnosed. As for Trish, he says, she’s had two strokes in the past year, so they are taking it easy. Which doesn’t mean they’re not up to a round of golf. Abbot is a fine player and used to play off a handicap of 12, but he insists Trish is better than him. To be fair, so does she.Stories circulated that Abbot retired because he was embittered that comedy had changed and no straight roles were being offered to him. It’s true that he’s not a great fan of today’s comedy, he says, and he was disappointed when Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine were cancelled, but he insists the stories are nonsense. He actually retired because Hughes, his manager, was retiring and he thought it was a good time to call it quits and spend more time with Trish and have a social life.“I’ve seen something on YouTube saying ‘The tragedy of Russ Abbot’ and ‘He’s run away to Portugal’.” He smiles.“We just watched it once,” says Trish. “I said, don’t watch it, Russell.”It doesn’t look much of a tragedy to me, I say, glancing out at the cloudless sky, swimming pool and topiaried bushes.“Thank you,” Trish says.“I’ve had a wonderful career,” Abbot says.“Wonderful!”“He’s always said that,” Trish says.And now you’re enjoying a richly deserved retirement? “Absolutely,” he says.How would Trish feel if he decided to go back to work? Her eyes light up. “Happy,” she says. Why? “I’d like him to do something like Last of the Summer Wine. I think he does miss it, I’ve got to say.”Abbot gives her a look. “Yeah!” he says. “But not desperately, Trish.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Post your questions for Alex Winter | Movies | The Guardian
description: The 80s icon and star of The Lost Boys and Bill & Ted has also had a storied career behind the camera and on stage. Now, he’ll answer your (non-bogus) questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The 80s icon and star of The Lost Boys and Bill & Ted has also had a storied career behind the camera and on stage. Now, he’ll answer your (non-bogus) questions
Content: Winter is coming … to tend to your queries.Photograph: Jordan Strauss/Invision/APView image in fullscreenWinter is coming … to tend to your queries.Photograph: Jordan Strauss/Invision/APFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Alex WinterThe 80s icon and star of The Lost Boys and Bill & Ted has also had a storied career behind the camera and on stage. Now, he’ll answer your (non-bogus) questionsRich PelleyMon 24 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou probably still think of Alex Winter as Kiefer Sutherland’s bloodsucking, peroxide-haired vampire biker mate Marko in 1987’s The Lost Boys, or the air-guitaring slacker Bill S Preston Esq alongside Keanu Reeves’s Ted “Theodore” Logan in the Bill & Ted franchise.But Winter actually started out as a child actor on Broadway, appearing in The King and I with Yul Brynner before making his big-screen debut opposite Charles Bronson in 1985’s Death Wish 3. As well as the above, he played poet and physician John William Polidori in 1988’s Haunted Summer, and co-wrote, co-directed and starred in the 1993 cult comedy Freaked.Since then, Winter has mainly been behind the camera: he wrote and directed the well-received psychological thriller Fever, starring ET the Extra-Terrestrial’s Henry Thomas, in 1999, and has made documentaries on everything from the dark web to child stardom and Frank Zappa. In 2020, he reunited with his old buddy Reeves for a third Bill & Ted film; and then reunited with himagainin 2025, playing Vladimir opposite Reeves’s Estragon in Waiting for Godoton Broadway.So, what to ask him? Post your questions below by 12pm this Thursday 27 August and we’ll publish his most triumphant answers as part of our readers’ interview series. And in the meantime, be excellent to each other. title: Goodbye Dandelion review – ode to a fabulous friendship with a 50-year age gap | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Maddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger one
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Maddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger one
Content: Sunny … Maddie Rice in Goodbye Dandelion.Photograph: Harry ElletsonView image in fullscreenSunny … Maddie Rice in Goodbye Dandelion.Photograph: Harry ElletsonEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewGoodbye Dandelion review – ode to a fabulous friendship with a 50-year age gapUnderbelly, EdinburghMaddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger oneMark FisherMon 24 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn unexpected theme on this year’s Edinburgh fringe is assisted dying. It is central to Morna Young’sAfter Party, about a matriarch who chooses to die after her 80th birthday, and Ben Harrison’s adaptation of Andrew O’Hagan’sMayflies, in which a terminally ill man travels to Dignitas. It is hinted at in Eilidh Loan’sCathy, about a woman adjusting to bereavement. And it is here again in this breezy storytelling show by sibling duo Maddie and Marcus Rice.The semi-fictional tale is about Maddie’s befriending of the 87-year-old Darcy O’Shea, an artist and piano teacher 50 years her senior, who is full of zest and vigour. As Maddie puts it, she is “unapologetically herself”, a woman living a life of happy self-reliance with limited tolerance for anyone else. A long-gone partner nicknamed her Dandelion because of her sticky-up hair, and it suits her personality.View image in fullscreenMarcus Rice at the piano plays songs and background music.Photograph: Harry ElletsonDarcy tells it as she sees it and does not mind shaming the younger woman for failing to change the things that weigh her down: life is too short not to plunge in headfirst.As a narrator, Maddie has a sunny disposition and relates the story with some wit. Lest she get maudlin, she has Marcus on hand as a counterbalance. Playing pretty waltzes on the piano throughout, he launches into songs that draw on the language of officialdom to comic effect. There is even some heartening audience participation.Knowing that death is coming can make plays on this theme feel like one long delaying tactic, especially here where the story has so little friction. Directed by Katie Pesskin, it is best – if briefest – on the impact the encounter has on Maddie and the way it propels her to make changes in her own life.At Underbelly, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreSpoken wordAssisted dyingEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things review – a show to make you shudder with laughter | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance art
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: From Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance art
Content: Brooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreenBrooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress … Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFrankie Thompson: Horrible Things review – a show to make you shudder with laughterPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghFrom Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance artBrian LoganMon 24 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are plenty of works-in-progress on the fringe.Frankie Thompsoninsists (or has the voice of Peppa Pig do so) that her show is a work-in-regress, an expunging of Horrible Things from the deepest recesses of her, and our, recollection. Thompson, whose brand of clowning-meets-performance art more or less guarantees something interesting will happen on stage, parades these Things as lip-synced audio and audience-terrorising stunts, all marshalled by our brisk and wild-eyed host, brooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress.Women in the crowd can relax: Thompson’s Horrible Things are usually male, her victims in the crowd likewise. The first sketch sound clips an interview with 12-year-old Jacob Rees-Mogg, and if you ever doubted lip-sync as an art form, I offer you Thompson’s performance here as the very junior minister. As his every word damns the way this country’s ruling classes are raised, her hyper-expressive face and nanosecond-precise timing pass sharper commentary than a thousand satirical words ever could.There’s more where this came from: a collage of interviews laying bare the tawdry machismo of the whips’ office; a skit questioning the wholesomeness of Cliff Richard and his Summer Holiday. Occasionally, the theme is diluted, with a song about paint sample names, say. But there’s always another shudder of horrible around the corner, as when Thompson recruits a mime orchestra from the audience to accompany a recording of Frank Sinatra’s bizarre 1980 release Trilogy: Past Present Future, the final album of which is a sci-fi fantasia of the male ego unleashed, in which Ol’ Blue Eyes disappears entirely up his own Uranus.Those People review – a double act with raw passion and no filterRead moreRevenge is then wreaked on the men present in several interactive interludes, in which chaps are dragooned on stage to dance, be babies, be stabbed, be expelled from the room. I will never love members of the public looking ill-at-ease on stage, but if it must happen, let it happen in the hands of a comic as adroit as Thompson – who backs herself into uncomfortable corners too, now licking the floor, now lathering herself in shaving cream. By doing so, in this airing of some dank corners of our cultural memory, she posits laughter not as the best medicine, but the best exorcism.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 9-21 November.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)TheatreClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSSO/Canellakis review – electrifying trio of women unleash the horror in Strauss’s Elektra  | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Making the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realised
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Making the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realised
Content: Exceptional clarity … conductor Karina Canellakis and BBCSSO in Strauss’s Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalView image in fullscreenExceptional clarity … conductor Karina Canellakis and BBCSSO in Strauss’s Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBBCSSO/Canellakis review – electrifying trio of women unleash the horror in Strauss’s ElektraUsher Hall, EdinburghMaking the most of a huge orchestra, conductor Karina Canellakis treated the dissonant score with relish, but the evening belonged to the singers, with even the tiniest role superbly realisedMichael DownesMon 24 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristopher Nolan’s filmThe Odysseycarries a content warning for “strong violence and intense mythological horror”, but even its goriest scenesdo not matchthe mythological horror Richard Strauss produced nearly 120 years earlier inElektra, whose special effects are confined to the 111-piece orchestra. The heckelphones, basset horns and Wagner tubas Strauss adds to an already outsized band makes staging Elektra unfeasible for all but the best-resourced companies. But the extraordinary colours he draws from the orchestra and the storytelling he entrusts to it make concert performances particularly rewarding.View image in fullscreenOutstanding singing from Karen Cargill, Vida Miknevičiūtė and Ingela Brimberg … Elektra.Photograph: © Andrew Perry/Edinburgh International FestivalThe BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra played Strauss’s most dissonant score with relish, responsive toKarina Canellakis’s efficient, economical gestures. Brutal climaxes were suitably overwhelming, but equally striking was the refined string sound in occasional moments of repose. Clarity was exceptional, as whips crackled, flutes fluttered and trombones groaned; balance almost always excellent.All the roles were superbly sung, even the tiniest. Lea Shaw and Emma Morwood were outstanding among the maidservants who launch the action; Lee Bisset,a notable Brunnhilde, shone as their Overseer. Men often receive short shrift in Strauss: here it’s more than an hour before one is heard. But Günther Groissböck’s resonant bass made Oreste’s nobility obvious from the first bar, even if Elektra took longer to cotton on, and tenor John Daszak introduced a note of camp entirely in keeping with the text’s contemptuous depiction of Aegisthus.The evening was dominated, however, by outstanding performances in the three female roles at the heart of the psychodrama.Karen Cargillcompellingly charted Klytämnestra’s breakdown, snarling and sneering without ever compromising vocal beauty. Vida Miknevičiūtė produced the concert’s most radiant singing in her touching portrayal of Chrysothemis, a woman who longs only for the normality of family life. In the notoriously demanding title role, meanwhile, Ingela Brimberg combined seemingly tireless vocal powers with attentiveness to every textual nuance.Everything was as impressively acted as it was sung: devising mise-en-scene without directorial input, singers deployed the small playing space with imagination and eloquence, highlighting the story’s horrors with a focus that even the most elaborate staging – or Hollywood movie – would struggle to match.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsClassical musicBBC Scottish Symphony Orchestralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Guns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says Europol | Museums | The Guardian
description: EU police agency says shift could point to involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific artefacts
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: EU police agency says shift could point to involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific artefacts
Content: Armed police guarding the recovered helmet of Coțofenești in April after it was stolen from the Drents Museum in the Netherlands.Photograph: Sem van der Wal/EPAView image in fullscreenArmed police guarding the recovered helmet of Coțofenești in April after it was stolen from the Drents Museum in the Netherlands.Photograph: Sem van der Wal/EPAMuseumsGuns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says EuropolEU police agency says shift could point to involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific artefactsSam JonesMon 24 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way into buildings and display cases, according to a report by Europol.The EU police agency said that while museum thefts were generally seen as a non-violent form of organised property crime, member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts.The report says: “Unlike typical cultural goods traffickers, who usually avoid violence and specialise in organised property crime or the theft of cultural goods, these individuals often have histories of involvement in other types of crime.“Additionally, some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other. This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.”View image in fullscreenPolice outside the Louvre in Paris, where there was a heist last October.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersThe report, published on Monday, found that precious metals and jewellery were the preferred targets because of their increasing value and the ease with which gold and silver could be melted down and jewels removed from their settings.“Similarly, ancient Chinese porcelain artefacts are likely targeted by cultural goods traffickers for financial gain,” it says. “Driven by high demand, they are likely to be easily sold on the art market.”Europol said a number of recent heists showed some thieves had few qualms when it came to using explosives or employing violence. In January 2025, a gang blasted its way into the Drents Museum in the Netherlands andstole several Dacian artefacts, many of which were subsequently recovered.The report adds: “In some cases, offenders use firearms to intimidate security personnel and visitors. Some museum thefts have involved direct physical assaults on staff such as tying them up or using brute force against them. Across reported cases, the use of force is closely linked to targeted operations, suggesting prior identification of specific objects and preplanned execution.”It pointed out that four hooded suspects equipped with baseball bats and axes had stolen seven gold and diamond-adorned objects from the Cognacq-Jay art museum in Paris in 2024, while theheist at the Louvre in October 2025had involved similar violence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“To access the targeted artefacts, the [Louvre] thieves broke a window and threatened guards and visitors,” the report says. “Theysmashed the display casesin the Apollo Gallery, and stole jewellery worth an estimated €88m.”Europol said that while more evidence needed to be gathered, it was possible low-level museum thieves were being randomly recruited “on a crime-as-a-service basis”.It added: “Alternatively, some criminal actors and networks, typically active in other criminal markets, [have] realised the low-risk, high-profit potential of museum heists.”Explore more on these topicsMuseumsEuropePoliceOrganised crimeEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies a year after son | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Gardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Gardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020
Content: Jo Gardiner and her son Sam in Chapultepec, Mexico City, taking part in Race Across the World.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenJo Gardiner and her son Sam in Chapultepec, Mexico City, taking part in Race Across the World.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PATelevision & radioRace Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies a year after sonGardiner, who had cancer, is remembered as ‘one of a kind’ after competing in BBC show with son Sam in 2020Kevin Rawlinsonand agencyMon 24 Aug 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTributes have been paid to the Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner, who has died a year after her son and co-star Sam was killed in a car crash.The physiotherapist fromManchesterdied after “a long and courageous battle with cancer”, relatives said. She was 61 and is survived by her other son, Charlie.She and Sam competed in the second series of the BBC’s global travel competition, journeying across South America together in 2020.Relatives remembered her as “an intrepid adventurer” who was “brave, kind, witty and endlessly loving”.Her family said: “She had a rare gift for making everyone around her feel more alive. She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves. She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism. Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best.“To us, she was more than all of these things. She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure. We know how deeply Jo was loved, and we take comfort in knowing that her laughter, her courage, her kindness and her wonderfully outrageous spirit will live on in the many people whose lives she touched.”View image in fullscreen‘She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves,’ Gardiner’s family said.Photograph: Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe family asked that those who knew and loved her “do exactly what she would have wanted: tell the funny stories, raise a glass, have an adventure, laugh loudly and live life to the full.”They added: “She was one of a kind. There will never be another her.”Sam Gardiner died in June 2025 at the age of 24 after his car came off the road, rolled and landed on its side.The mother and son competed on Race Across the World because Jo wanted to have a travel adventure with Sam, who had ADHD. They competed against four other pairs of contestants racing from Mexico City down to Ushuaia in Argentina.A spokesperson for the programme said: “On behalf of the Studio Lambert production team, the BBC and the whole Race Across the World cast, we offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo’s son Charlie and her wider family and friends.“Millions of people remembered their transformative journey across Latin America in 2020 and we hold that memory in our hearts as we fondly recall Jo’s passion for life, her kindness, her strength and above all her utter devotion to Sam and her family.”Jo Gardiner had type 1 diabetes and was an ambassador for Diabetes UK. Her family has set up aJustGiving pagein her name and said all donations are to support the charity.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioReality TVManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount Skydance after it accuses him of using ‘antisemitic tropes’ | Mark Ruffalo | The Guardian
description: Actor says highlighting role of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in media company’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery has been ‘dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel’
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Actor says highlighting role of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in media company’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery has been ‘dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel’
Content: Actor Mark Ruffalo pictured at the Golden Globe Awards in January 2026. The actor has rejected criticism from media company Paramount Skydance that comments he made about its merger with Warner Bros Discovery were ‘antisemitic’.Photograph: Michael Tran/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenActor Mark Ruffalo pictured at the Golden Globe Awards in January 2026. The actor has rejected criticism from media company Paramount Skydance that comments he made about its merger with Warner Bros Discovery were ‘antisemitic’.Photograph: Michael Tran/AFP/Getty ImagesMark RuffaloMark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount Skydance after it accuses him of using ‘antisemitic tropes’Actor says highlighting role of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in media company’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery has been ‘dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel’Sian CainSun 23 Aug 2026 22.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Ruffalo has fired back at Paramount Skydance after the media company accused him of invoking “antisemitic tropes” in his criticism of its $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD).The actor, who has long been outspoken against Israel’s military conduct in Gaza and for the rights of Palestinians, shared a statement on social media on Friday in which he highlighted the links between Paramount Skydance, run by CEO David Ellison, and Oracle, the technology company run by Ellison’s father, Larry.Oracle has supplied software to the Israel Defense Forces, ministry of defense, air force, government and police for decades. Shmulik Hauser, head of Oracle’s sales division,told Ynet last year: “Supporting Israel is in our DNA – even if it costs us clients. That’s our agenda.”On Friday Ruffalo shared a video of Oracle executive vice-chair, Safra Catz, describing the “really profoundly scary technology”it provided toIsraelafter the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023. Above the video, Ruffalo took aim at Larry Ellison, who he accused of “using [Oracle] to fund his son David’s Warner Bros acquisition”.Larry Ellison, who is worthan estimated $189bn,agreed to personally backstop $40.4bnin equity financing to help Paramount Skydance acquire WBD in a $110.9bn deal.“These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you,” Ruffalo wrote. “Look how [Catz] revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered byOracle.”Ruffalo urged his followers to oppose the merger, which he argued would be “catastrophic” for the entertainment industry due to job losses and reduced competition.Paramount agrees to pause $110bn Warner Bros merger as case plays outRead moreThough the US department of justiceapproved the merger in June, it remains on hold while a federal judge considers a lawsuit from a coalition of 12 US states who have challenged the deal on antitrust grounds.In a rare statement on Saturday, Paramount responded to Ruffalo, saying it was “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute”.“Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong – they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe,” Paramount said. “This doesn’t deserve a response in kind – and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.”On Saturday, Ruffalo responded to Paramount with a written statement.“Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people,”Ruffalo wrote. “This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel.”The actor said his views “come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect. Everything I know about acting, activism, and humanism has been profoundly shaped by the Jewish friends, colleagues, and loved ones who have been integral and family throughout every point of my life.”“This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country,” he added. “Scrutinizing the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. The $111bn deal would hand one family control over CNN, HBO andWarner Bros., backed in part by foreign money whose influence on editorial decisions has never been fully explained to the public.”A Paramount spokesperson told NBC that it would make no further comment. The Guardian has contacted Oracle and Catz for comment.The Simon Wiesenthal Center, a Jewish human rights organisation, praised Paramount for “refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism”.Ruffalo was among thousands of actors and film industry workers who pledged last year not to work with Israeli film institutions “implicated in genocide and apartheid against the Palestinian people”.A Paramount-WBD merger would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood, as well as a host of TV networks, streaming libraries and news operations. That would include Warner’s HBO Max and CNN coming under the same roof of Paramount-owned CBS and the Paramount+ streaming service.If the merger does not close by 30 September, it could cost Paramount Skydance around $7m a ‌day in fees ‌it agreed to pay Warner Bros ‌shareholders in the event of a delay.Explore more on these topicsMark RuffaloParamount PicturesWarner BrosOracleIsrael-Gaza warIsraelAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Academy of St Martin in the Fields/Marquise Gilmore review – bassoon earns its spotlight in Thea Musgrave’s Out of the Darkness | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Amy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to Mozart
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Amy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to Mozart
Content: Lyrical … Amy Harman plays bassoon with the Academy of St Martin in the Fields at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenLyrical … Amy Harman plays bassoon with the Academy of St Martin in the Fields at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewAcademy of St Martin in the Fields/Marquise Gilmore review – bassoon earns its spotlight in Thea Musgrave’s Out of the DarknessRoyal Albert Hall, LondonAmy Harman brought a warm baritonal vocalise to premiere from nonagenarian Thea Musgrave, while Felix Klieser bent his unique horn technique to MozartFlora WillsonMon 24 Aug 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid this year’s crop of Proms premieres, one stood out a mile – long before any of us had heard a note of it. Out of the Darkness is a new bassoon concerto by the98-year-old Scottish composer Thea Musgrave, whose music was first heard at the Proms in 1960. Sixty-six years later, Musgrave is one of classical music’s most eminent elder stateswomen; hernext opera will make its debut next year. But bassoon concertos remain a rare breed.The first performance of Out of the Darkness emerged from a dark grumble of the Academy of St Martin in the Fields’ percussion and bass instruments, whichbassoonist Amy Harmananswered from the back of the stage, weaving a warm, baritonal vocalise through the orchestral duskiness. Only the solo violin line of ASMF’s director Benjamin Marquise Gilmore offered a lighter, brighter sound, until it was picked up by the rest of the violins. The musical material was all beguiling loops and phrases ending in question marks, Harman’s tone deliciously lyrical. Nothing was spelled out, except her journey around the orchestra, the bassoon gathering rhythmic vitality as she walked to join the trumpets, then double basses, finally arriving at the front – a soloist’s standard spot – in time for the disarmingly near-tonal final chord.View image in fullscreenSole music … Felix Klieser performs at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe remainder of the programme mixed Mozart and 20th-century British music. A fast, ultra-precise performance of Britten’s Simple Symphony was followed by a pleasant take on Mozart’s Horn Concerto No 3 in E flat major, K447 withFelix Klieserthe soloist. Klieser’s ability to play the instrument with his feet remains astonishing, but this surely should not be the most interesting feature of a performance. Harman returned to the stage post-premiere for Elgar’s charming Romance for bassoon and orchestra, allowing this period instrument ensemble a rare opportunity for voluptuous tone and a spot of Edwardian passion. In Mozart’s Symphony No 35 “Haffner”, K385, the ASMF were back on repertorial home turf, their playing neat, fleet-footed and tremendously classy. It was just a shame that the subtle drama of their approach could make only a limited impact in a space as cavernous as the Royal Albert Hall.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicAcademy of St Martin in the FieldsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: On Donetsk’s ‘life or death’ highway with the Khyzhak brigade – photo essay | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehicles
Author: Julia Kochetova
Headline: The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehicles
Content: The road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone nets.The road to Kostyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehiclesByJulia KochetovaMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Holy yeah! Yeaaaah! Done!”Booooooom.“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!” Dzhangofrom the Khyzhak brigade shouts in English. He has just shot down a Russian FPV drone.View image in fullscreenDzhango firing to shoot down a Russian FPV-drone.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenRussian waiting drone after being shot on the road by a mobile firing crewView image in fullscreenDzhango, a shooter, gets ready before the daily shiftView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenDzhango loads a magazine while brushing his teeth in the dugout before the daily shift. Inside the dugout of the mobile firing crew of Khyzhak brigadeView image in fullscreenYoung and Dzhango taking a break after the shift.A small moving target that wants to kill you is a challenge with an asterisk.I don’t manage to photograph the drone above us, but I’m glad that Dzhango shoots more accurately. The normal rule is for everyone else is to stay under cover and not stick your head out.View image in fullscreenThe remains of burned vehicles on the roadView image in fullscreenA ground robot returning from a logistic missionThe tasks of Dzhango’s mobile fire group are different – to stand watch and shoot down Russian drones.The H20 highway runs from the frontline city of Kramatorsk to the battlefield in Kostyantynivka in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The last road always becomes either the “road of life” or the “road of death”. Drone warfare is deadly simple – everything flies toward the road; any movement is a target. Us too.View image in fullscreenThe moon over the roadThe road is covered with scars: FPV drones, cluster munitions, artillery, glide bombs – a map of modern war. Pears on the ground are entangled with fibre-optic cable – this harvest will not be gathered. Anti-drone nets fall on to a highway strewn with burned-out ground robots, pickup trucks, and armoured vehicles. Donetsk is crumbling before my eyes.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenA Russian fibre optic drone flies above the mobile firing crew. Dzhango loads a magazine during the shiftThe fighters of the Khyzhak brigade are police patrol officers who joined up. The five of them share a dugout with Zhuzha, a dog that came to them in search of food and cuddles. A shower, a washbasin, a kitchen, even a plasma TV playing Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us – a parallel universe built underground. The peace sign on Jackson’s T-shirt contrasts with the sound of loading magazines.View image in fullscreenThe mobile firing unit of Khyzhak brigade on dutyView image in fullscreenSoldiers from Khyzhak brigade fire on a Russian drone during the rotation. Borya, a shooter on dutyView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSoldiers stop for a quick chat – they use scooters to drive between positionsAbove, the kill zone, which lives by its own rules: food and water are delivered by ground robots, via electric scooters, or through the sky while Ukrainian Vampire drones carry supply packages above.“We try as much as possible to shoot down whatever is flying toward us. We understand that it’s someone’s ground robot, or someone’s car, or even – someone’s life,”Dzhango tells me.He is 31, from Chernivtsi, which is more than 1,000km away.View image in fullscreenDzhango and Young during a shiftView image in fullscreenDzhango near the ruins of a homeIn the morning he talks to his family on a video call – on the screen there’s a beach, white sand, colourful umbrellas, his son – a parallel world. “What I miss most is my family, my child … living through the coolest moments of his childhood from a distance. His first baby teeth fell out! And I wanted to pull them out with a string, as my father did.”His son knows exactly what Dzhango’s job looks like and asks: “Bring me an FPV!”Dzhango does not bring FPVs home.His son’s birthday is tattooed on his right arm. On the left – a long scar and a tattoo: “Jump off the cliff and wings will grow.” It is a reminder of his father’s advice and of a police shift in Chernivtsi, when he was wounded – three bullets – and his 22-year-old colleague, Taisiia Tataryn, was killed. After a long rehabilitation, he joined the combat unit.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenYoung and Dzhango pass a burned-out scooter. A soldier was injured while driving on it and evacuated from the combat area. Fibre optic cable mixed with pears on the ground in Donetsk regionView image in fullscreenRemains of a shot-down Russian FPVEvery morning we walk the same streets and tree lines, but the landscape changes – fresh craters, fallen trees, smoke on the horizon. The remains of drones and munitions form a map of the area – here a Molniya, a Russian kamikaze drone, is stuck in a tree.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe body of a civilian covered with plastic sheeting near the road to Kostyantynivka. The body of a Ukrainian soldier – which was evacuated a few days laterHere – since the beginning of July – a dead civilian has been lying under a black plastic bag. A little further on – a soldier from a neighbouring unit, his body will be evacuated in a couple of days. In the tree line – a burned scooter, an FPV strike; a fighter from another unit was evacuated, but the soldiers will say that he died in hospital that night.View image in fullscreenSoldiers driving on a buggy at high speed, risking being spotted by a drone“Something’s flying!” – within seconds the guys start shooting.Dzhango’s comrade, 41-year-old Young, associates every successful shoot-down with adrenaline and a rush. He served almost eight years in the police and almost two years in the Khyzhak brigade.View image in fullscreenYoung, a shooter from Khyzhak brigade, on duty with the mobile firing crewView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenYoung collecting apricots next to the road. Young taking a breakOn his very first combat mission, two small fragments entered his body; he calls it luck. On the next one – an FPV drone hit the side window of his armoured vehicle – the shaped charge flew inside. “A flash behind me – out of the corner of my eye I see that something exploded inside. Sparks, smoke, you can’t see anything, it’s impossible to breathe,” he recalls.View image in fullscreenOne of his brothers-in-arms died instantly; a second was seriously wounded: “I guess the shaped charge passed through him, and then hit the floor where another fighter was sitting … And it exploded between his legs.”Now his task is to make sure another FPV does not reach his comrades’ vehicle.The only intact building among the erased skeletons of houses is the church.View image in fullscreenDzhango lighting a candle in a damaged churchView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHoly images inside the damaged church near the road to KostyantynivkaA blue eye looks out. Some of the saints are on the floor, others remain by the altar. Dzhango lights a candle – according to tradition, a candle is lit either for the health of the living or for the repose of those no longer here. Half an hour later, the artillery shelling will begin, and the church will come under fire. A week later I receive a short message: “The church burned down.”While waiting for the rotationout, we sit along the highway on scattered chairs and stools under the dense cover of the trees.View image in fullscreenTsygan from Khyzhak brigade is driving soldiers for rotation on the road towards Kostyantynivka, Donetsk regionView image in fullscreenSoldiers from Khyzhak brigade after the rotationDzhango plays Madonna’s Music from his phone, then Justin Timberlake’s Mirrors, and dances a little. From time to time he pauses – to stop and listen whether something is flying.Then he turns the music back on and sings along again.Even in abnormal circumstances, inside war – at least you can always choose the soundtrack.View image in fullscreenThe road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone netsView image in fullscreenA sunset over the road to KostyantynivkaThe next day Dzhango will write saying that they shot down another nine drones.And then – send a video of how another morning in the dugout began with “Good Morning, good morning to you” from the musical Singin’ in the Rain.“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!”, he said.Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayUkraineEuropeRussiaDrones (military)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Revival review – step up, Walking Dead fans! This is the most moving zombie show ever  | Television | The Guardian
description: The undead are climbing out of their graves all over town, so gore levels are high – but this noirish miniseries sets itself apart by being delightfully offbeat and genuinely poignant
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The undead are climbing out of their graves all over town, so gore levels are high – but this noirish miniseries sets itself apart by being delightfully offbeat and genuinely poignant
Content: What yikes and yuks will come next? … Revival on NetflixPhotograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenWhat yikes and yuks will come next? … Revival on NetflixPhotograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewRevival review – step up, Walking Dead fans! This is the most moving zombie show everThe undead are climbing out of their graves all over town, so gore levels are high – but this noirish miniseries sets itself apart by being delightfully offbeat and genuinely poignantLucy ManganMon 24 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAteenage girl is pale, withdrawn and seems not to be fully in or of this world. Could she be … a zombie? “She just likes the Cure,” weary police officer Dana Cypress (Wynonna Earp’s Melanie Scrofano) assures the anxious mother at the station.It’s good to get the mandatory goth joke out of the way early in an undead-centred show, and Revival – a 10-part adaptation of the comic books by Tim Seeley and Mike Norton – is briskly efficient. It begins with a man bashing his way out of a crematorium furnace while others in the corpse-queue start to stir and the recently buried start to climb out of their graves and wonder, frankly, WTF is going on.As, of course, do we, the delighted viewers, already aware that we are in confident, capable hands and eager to see what yikes and yuks come next.WTF is going on is that, in the pre-smartphone era in the small, nondescript town of Wausau, Wisconsin, on a random day, everyone who died in the previous fortnight is resurrected. After the event, it takes the town a while to work out the parameters – how far it went, who qualified and so on, hence the goth problem. And, although by the end of the subsequent month-long lockdown imposed on the town, the police chief (Dana’s father) has compiled a list of the Revivers, as they become known, Dana points out that it may not be complete. Anyone who died alone and in their sleep, for example, and woke up apparently normally would not necessarily know he or she was dead. Hmm, says the astute viewer. Noted, our Dana. Noted.View image in fullscreenSearching for the undead … Revival.Photograph: NetflixBut ordinary crime goes on, especially once the lockdown is lifted – although the town remains in quarantine, so is still cut off from the outside world. Dana begins investigating the case of a mutilated horse in the woods, only to find a handful of torn-out human teeth beside it and … well, uh-oh. It seems that, alongside the ability to self-heal, some of the undead have developed strengths and tastes that are unlikely to add to the general harmony of small-town life. They do, however, add to the gore level, which is good news for anyone who prefers their zombie tales more at the Walking Dead end of the spectrum and bad news for anyone who shrieks into the sofa whenever the top of someone’s head gets sliced off by a farm implement.There is also, for Dana, the matter of her troubled little sister, Em (Romy Weltman). Em has a difficult relationship with their loving but volatile father, but the sibling bond still holds fast. Drug addiction after a car accident that killed their mother and an entanglement with her college professor have brought chaos to Em’s life, but Dana isthere to help. They once dreamed of getting out of Wausau – Dana had just handed in her notice to her father and was leaving for a job in Chicago when Revival Day hit – and now they are trapped there by forces beyond their control. There have been worse and less tenderly drawn metaphors for the collapse of the American dream.That’s really what marks Revival out from the herd of noirish, murder-mystery miniseries (whether driven by superheroes, zombies or something in between) with which we are inundated. For all its lightness and speed, and its cleaving to well-tested tropes, it contains moments of real poignancy. The sisters’ love for each other feels lumpy and real. The woman whose husband died one day too soon to qualify for revival and is driven mad by her compounded grief is immediately comprehensible. And the Reviver mother who cannot die and climbs into her son’s coffin at his funeral reminds us that there are horrors far beyond what brain-eating monsters can offer. As the hostility towards Revivers grows in the town, it is the young Reviver girl asking her schoolfriend why, if people are always so sad when someone dies, they aren’t happy that she is alive that stops them from becoming too heavy-handed a representation of racism and contemporary anti-immigrant sentiment and keeps the story supple.Add to that Scrofano’s performance: she has an offbeat and idiosyncratic energy that makes her mesmerising but still so credible that she only adds to the show’s quality rather than throwing it off its stride – and you have a three-and-a-half-star show that I’m rounding up to four because she deserves it – and we deserve more of her.Revival is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Michael Sheen exposes a toxic scandal in north Wales | Television | The Guardian
description: The actor concludes his investigation into Monsanto by meeting people with cancer who blame the company for their illness. Plus: a devastating story of foundling sisters reunited. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The actor concludes his investigation into Monsanto by meeting people with cancer who blame the company for their illness. Plus: a devastating story of foundling sisters reunited. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Michael Sheen meets Katie Witherden.Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsView image in fullscreenMichael Sheen meets Katie Witherden.Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Michael Sheen exposes a toxic scandal in north WalesThe actor concludes his investigation into Monsanto by meeting people with cancer who blame the company for their illness. Plus: a devastating story of foundling sisters reunited. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellMon 24 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBuried With Michael Sheen9pm, BBC TwoThere’s a lagoon in Ruabon, north Wales, that is so toxic that the barrels containing the chemicals dumped in it have rotted away. Until about 20 years ago, children used to play around it. Michael Sheen’s compassionate and enraging exposé of the alleged poisoning of parts of his homeland decades ago by contractors working for the now defunct chemical company Monsanto concludes with the actor meeting people with cancer who are searching for accountability. Spoiler alert: it’s an uphill battle.Phil HarrisonMartin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip8pm, Channel 4The final leg of the father and son’s tour takes them to a snowy Northern Ireland. They spend a night in Ballygally Castle – said to be the most haunted hotel in the country – play a game of hurling, vampire-hunt, and swim in the freezing sea. You can’t accuse them of not getting stuck in.Hollie RichardsonMy Life Is Murder8pm, U&AlibiMore low-stakes antipodean crime-solving fun with Lucy Lawless as investigator Alexa Crowe. This time, she deals with the case of a wealthy woman who is killed amid a dog custody dispute. She finds herself in the bizarre world of millionaire dating, before racing to save another pet victim.HRLong Lost Family: Born Without Trace – What Happened Next9pm, ITV1The lovely but devastating show speaks to another pair of foundling siblings: Natasha and Lee-Ann want to know who left them as babies, two years apart, in the toilets of two different south London hospitals. And nurse Liz updates on what has happened since she shared her story of being found severely ill as a baby in a hedge.HRCelebrity Hunted9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenScarlette Douglas takes to the water in Scotland in Celebrity Hunted.Photograph: Shine TVCelebrity status adds a different dimension to this entertaining if always mildly sinister nationwide game of hide and seek. Is it really possible to blend in with the civilians? In this penultimate episode, one of our celebrities makes a basic error and seeks refuge with a known contact in Scotland. Oops.PHSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives10pm, Channel 4The buzzy reality show starring Gypsy influencer Trewley Precious ends its first season on a high with the social media star celebrating her 26th birthday in typically boisterous style. But there is also an emotive wedding dress fitting for her sister Pearly and a potentially problematic brand partnership to consider.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceView image in fullscreenA class apart … Helen Schlegel (Helena Bonham Carter) with Leonard Bast (Samuel West) in Howards End.Photograph: United Archives/AlamyHowards End (James Ivory, 1992), 1.15pm, Film4EM Forster’s 1910 novel about class, money, love and a house in the country was styled into a prestige period drama by Merchant Ivory, aided by Ruth Prawer Jhabvala’s Oscar-winning script. Three levels of society come into conflict in a story of chance encounters, misguided charity and patriarchal hypocrisy. Anthony Hopkins’s rigid, rich businessman, Henry Wilcox, is drawn to the bohemian, privileged Schlegel sisters, Margaret (Emma Thompson) and Helen (Helena Bonham Carter), while they get involved in the life of a poor clerk, Leonard Bast (Samuel West).Simon WardellNightcrawler (Dan Gilroy, 2014), 9pm, Sky AtlanticIt may have dated somewhat in this age of people filming everything on their phones, but Dan Gilroy’s dark 2014 drama is still wholly relevant in its clear-eyed critique of the public’s obsession with true crime. Jake Gyllenhaal – hollow of eye and creepy of smile – plays Louis, a sociopathic petty thief who finds a new job driving around LA shooting graphic footage of police incidents for the local TV news. If it bleeds it leads, with his ratings-chasing boss, Nina (Rene Russo), encouraging Louis’ worst tendencies.SWLive sportPremier League football: Fulham v Chelsea6.30pm, Sky Sports Main Event.Crystal Palace v Manchester City is on Friday at 7pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Disappearers by Marlon James review – a scorching exposé of homophobia in Jamaica | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queer
Author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
Headline: This Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queer
Content: Bleak and uncompromising … Marlon James.Photograph: Rahim Fortune/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBleak and uncompromising … Marlon James.Photograph: Rahim Fortune/The GuardianBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Disappearers by Marlon James review – a scorching exposé of homophobia in JamaicaThis Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queerYagnishsing DawoorMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Asense of sweep,” repliedMarlon James, when asked what moves him most in literature. “Sweep isn’t just about external journeys, but internal as well. It can be over years and decades, or across land and sea.” If that explanation is still hazy, pick up his mighty new novel, which is longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and is tirelessly – sometimes exhaustingly – grand and peripatetic. Mounting a grisly exposé of Jamaican homophobia, this polyphonic 640-page doorstopper is an emotionally bruising narrative that roves “uptown, downtown, ghetto and gully” through Aids-era Kingston with sidetrack excursions to 1950s England and a closing leap to 2000s United States.The novel’s defining event is a gruesome mob attack on eight queer men who have clandestinely come together to work on bringing John Herbert’s 1967 gay prison play, Fortune and Men’s Eyes, to the stage. The goal, in the words of director Havelock Titus, is to shatter “the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality”. “Because prison,” he explains, “is the ultimate male institution and yet masculine sexualities that could never happen outside in the normal world flourish in there all the time.”The spunk and sass of these men, their banter and squabbles as they feel each other out and ease into their roles, as well as their fears, insecurities and motivations for doing the play, are relayed by one of the actors: Eddy Porteous, a “white-ish” Belgian Jamaican college student from a well-heeled family. His diary entries over the course of the month preceding the assault make up the novel’s expositional first quarter, illuminating the interplay of class, race and colourism in the experience of Jamaican queerness.The narrative kicks into gear with the section on the attack. Now we are thrust, chillingly, into the minds of the perpetrators, among whom are a policeman, a self-loathing closet case, a deacon and a reggae singer named Streggeh Don whose hit, Batty Is Not Pussy, is the rallying-cry-cum-soundtrack for the splatterfest. Violence is James’s shtick and a hallmark of his fiction, from torture and sexual abjection in his subversive slavery epic, The Book of Night Women, and gang warfare in his Booker-winning novel,A Brief History of Seven Killings, to the near-ceaseless carnage in his ongoingDark Star fantasy trilogy. But here, far from the glib relish of which James has been accused throughout his writing career, one senses an unequivocal ethical purposefulness. “I think evil is a choice,” one survivor asserts, “and an ongoing one. Even in the midst of committing wickedness there are choices of how wicked one will be, which is made by the minute.” In order to grasp this statement in all its wounded, furious profundity – to see the outsize hate unleashed on these men as deeply volitional – the reader must bear witness not only from within the action, but also from within the consciousness of the perpetrators.One man has a branch shoved into his anus and dies. Another has both his eyes gouged out. All but Eddy, who had skipped rehearsal on that fateful night, are battered, gashed and maimed. Two of them will later vanish without a trace. Wrestling with survivor’s guilt, Eddy teams up with fellow actor Jordan to try to find them. More so than Eddy, it is Jordan who is the novel’s beating heart. A gleeful, foul-mouthed “sometime prostitute”, animated by the dangerous, liberatory ethos of American author John Rechy’s 1977 book The Sexual Outlaw, which he obsessively reads for affirmation, he is the Jamaican homophobe’s “battymonster” come to life.double quotation markFizzing with filth, snark and venom, the novel hawks and spits at conventionJordan and Eddy’s journeys into the promiscuous gay underground and the dark heart of heterosexual Jamaica are recounted in a series of interview transcripts, as the pair take turns speaking to a journalist from an American media outlet. Their frustrations gather further poignancy within the broader tragedy of the Aids epidemic engulfing Jamaica’s gay community: “This is what Aids is after all, isn’t it? One long set of disappearing acts. First is watching the friends and family disappear. Second act is when people try to disappear you. Third act is watching your body vanish from itself and wondering where the fuck you going, piece by piece, until all of you gone … If there is a fourth act it’s when everybody erase your name as if you were never born in the first place. Certainly no Christian church ever christened you.”The Disappearers is a bleak and uncompromising exploration of rage and survival; of trauma and its afterlife; of the terrible intimacy that binds victims to their perpetrators, and survivors to the dead, as well as revenge’s lure for those who are not given their due. Throughout, the narrative obsesses over the questions of whether meaning can emerge from the devastation of atrocity, and whether the void left by the missing is a mystery to be solved, or a limbo to be helplessly inhabited. What if the disappeared, done with being part of a world bent on eliminating them, didn’t want to be found? Fizzing with filth, snark and venom, the novel hawks and spits at convention, especially the politics of respectability that insists on restraint; it strafes down on homophobia with ruthless abandon. Few books have mapped the beleaguered realities of queer existence with such psychological depth, harrowing realism and searing condemnation.The formal design, however, is not without flaws. The overlong narrative sags in places, tarrying where it should speed along, and the intertextuality – most obviously the revenge plot’s debt to Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon – can veer into self-conscious pastiche. While the book’s conversation with the queer canon is richly rewarding (besides Herbert and Rechy, Gide, Genet, Vidal, Wilde, Baldwin and Holleran are some of the visiting spectres), I struggled with the fact that a significant chunk of the action is reported rather than dramatised. As well as the interview transcripts, we have letters from Havelock to a friend; some pivotal moments are thus experienced either at a temporal and affective remove, or inevitably somewhat summarised.Ultimately, these are redeemable shortcomings in an otherwise remarkable novel. James makes room for the contradictions of queer life, its intimacies, estrangements and hungers, in utterly indelible ways. His prose is a consistent triumph: bitter and hilarious, lyrical, bawdy, pugnacious and scorchingly, ravishingly queer. The Booker judges have described this novel as a “reckoning”; it is incontestably also a haunting.The Disappearers by Marlon James is published by Hamish Hamilton (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionBook of the dayLGBTQ+ rightsMarlon JamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Betrayal by Luke Harding review – could Donald Trump be a Russian asset? | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind it
Author: Lawrence Freedman
Headline: A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind it
Content: Putin and Trump at an Anchorage airbase ahead of their Alaska summit in August 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPutin and Trump at an Anchorage airbase ahead of their Alaska summit in August 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewBetrayal by Luke Harding review – could Donald Trump be a Russian asset?A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind itLawrence FreedmanMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican presidents have struggled to get the measure ofVladimir Putin. When George W Bush met him in 2001, he reported that he had “looked the man in the eye”, got a “sense of his soul” and found him “trustworthy”. Barack Obama thought Putin was making a mistake with his interventions in Ukraine and Syria, but didn’t do much about it. Joe Biden backed Ukraine’s resistance to the Russian invasion, yet his fear that Putin would reach for the nuclear button if backed into a corner made him risk averse. He worried about the impact of the sort of long-range strikes against Russian territory that Kyiv is now launching on a daily basis.This caution frustrated Ukrainians to the point that they looked forward toDonald Trumpshaking things up after he won re-election. Be careful what you wish for: the returning president thought his rapport with Putin would be enough to get Russia to sign up to an immediate ceasefire. In Trump’s head it was President Zelenskyy, fighting a war he was bound to lose, who was the problem.This led to the betrayal that gives Guardian correspondent Luke Harding’s book its title. Instead of increasing the pressure on Moscow, the new administration set about abandoningUkraine. In the UN General Assembly, the US voted with the dregs of Russia’s supporters against a resolution condemning its aggression (even China abstained). Trump denounced his predecessor, Biden, for the support given to Ukraine, exaggerated its value (claiming it was $350bn when it was close to $70bn) and demanded privileged access to Ukraine’s mineral wealth as a form of repayment. Then came the greatest indignity of all as Zelenskyy was baited in the Oval Office, with JD Vance accusing him of disrespecting the president, after he had merely tried to correct falsehoods about how his country was coping with the war. He was ushered out of the White House and subjected to further denunciations. Intelligence was even cut off to Ukraine’s frontline forces for a short but critical period.double quotation markAs Zelenskyy was being ambushed in front of the world’s press, Harding was in Odessa, visiting a clinic that had been hit by a Russian droneTrump’s delusions about Putin persisted. Later that year he invited him to Alaska for a summit, where he was treated with extraordinary deference, in the mistaken belief that he was prepared to compromise. The only compromise Putin had in mind involved Ukraine handing over its territory without a fight. (Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, is still denying Russian claims that this was agreed in principle at the summit.) In any case, the meeting was a failure, with Trump left irritated by one of Putin’s long disquisitions on the history of Russian-Ukrainian relations. It ended before lunch.Harding demonstrates Trump’s betrayal less through accounts of negotiations and summits than in his reporting from Ukrainian cities under constant attack from the air. As Zelenskyy was being ambushed in front of the world’s press, Harding was in Odessa, visiting a clinic that had been hit by an Iranian-designed Russian Shahed drone. As she viewed the wreckage of the gutted children’s clinic in which she worked, Olena Palsh lamented: “We fashioned it with love. The work of five years was destroyed in an instant.” Harding tells many such stories of the suffering and devastation inflicted by Putin on a country he considers to be a natural part of Russia.In this way, he creates a sobering chronicle of a long and vicious conflict. He is skilled at describing the individuals caught up in events, including Ri Chol-nam, a North Korean soldier who was surprised to find himself fighting for Russia, and for whom the shame of being captured by the Ukrainians led to a suicide attempt. The wider context is also deftly conveyed, with chapters on how China is trying to make the most of the situation and how Putin seeks to intimidate Europeans, sabotaging internet cables on the seabed or flying drones into their airspace.The villains at the core of the book are undoubtedly Trump and Putin. Harding discusses the question of whether Trump might himself be a Russian asset. Is it just that he enjoys the company of tyrants and envies their supreme power, or do they have embarrassingkompromatthat he wants to ensure doesn’t see the light of day (though admittedly this is a man who seems to know no shame)? Harding concludes with a question in the subjunctive: “If Trumpwerea Russian agent, what exactly would he do differently?”Yet now Putin seems disappointed by Trump, for he has not delivered the Ukrainian surrender he sought. Which leads to a different question: given Trump’s readiness to accommodate Putin, how come the Russian leader has been unable to make the compromises that would have allowed him to close the deal? It’s a shame that Harding is no longer allowed into his old stomping ground of Moscow, where his contacts might have helped him to explore the biggest puzzle: why Putin persists with a futile and costly war he can’t win.Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest by Luke Harding is published by Guardian Faber (£20).
