title: ‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movie | Horror films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise
Content: Cary Elwes in Saw.Photograph: Cinetext/Lions Gate/AllstarView image in fullscreenCary Elwes in Saw.Photograph: Cinetext/Lions Gate/AllstarMy feelgood movieHorror films‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchiseEmma MaddenMon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas petsitting recently for a white suburban family, with the typical streaming habits therein. They had two kids; their most-watched shows, according to the history that showed up on the screen, were Bluey for the kids and The Office for the adults. When they came home from their weeklong trip, they would’ve found their watch history upheaved. The Bingos and Michael Scotts all erased by Saw I, Saw II, Saw III, Saw IV, Saw V, Saw VI, Saw 3D, Saw Spiral, Saw Jigsaw and, finally, my new favourite, Saw X.‘Fated to become a cult classic’: why Barcelona is my feelgood movieRead moreI was obsessed with the Saw franchise well before I ever saw it. At 11, as Jigsaw puppets became Halloween costumes, I went to bed each night convinced Jigsaw was going to scoop me up in a van because the word “hell”a popped into my head. By 13, I looked up every film on Wikipedia and read through each trap with terrified excitement. By 14, I drank my first can of Stella and typed Saw II into YouTube, watching it in 12 installments. It was utterly horrifying. And so, so, so much fun.I am now 31 and have seen every film so many times I could count on both hands – which Jigsaw would sever finger by finger – how many times I’ve seen them. Somewhere along the way, Saw became my feel-good film.The reasons why are mostly shallow and unsophisticated. It’s not like I care for the nonsensical storyline, or the dubstep editing, or the ham acting. No one’s exactly raving about Saw’s mise-en-scene. Its morality – the murderer keeps insisting he’s not actually murdering anyone – is deeply specious, and it’s never fully clear whether the film-makers are aware of this or not. But I obviously do not care. Just as I don’t care if a rollercoaster has any “worldbuilding”. I just want it to go whoosh and loop the loop.The one thing about Saw – other than its asinine-cop B-storylines – is that I’m guaranteed not to be bored. I just cannot tap out while watching a man in a revolving crucifix, his bones crushed one by one, or a woman cutting off her leg and extracting her bone marrow. Even typing that is making me squirm.When I first started watching these films, I looked away; now I stare them down blankly. I think watching horror is a bit like meditation, or doing planks. You go through waves of discomfort and the feeling that you can’t go on, but then you do. You subject yourself to something counterintuitive and unpleasant, and then you discover that you are still there at the end of it.It feels sort of embarrassing to dignify Saw with any kind of seriousness – and to say this in light of the films – but I’ve struggled with suicidal ideation my entire life. I think I am so benumbed that I am utterly beyond pain, but then I watch Saw and find myself wincing. As a suicidal person, I would undoubtedly qualify as one of Jigsaw’s “victims”. He would say that I don’t appreciate life.But when I watch Saw, I think:Thank God I’m not stuck at the bottom of a vat, with liquefied pig carcasses drowning me.Annoyingly, life is all about learning to let go: of others, of ego, of the flesh. Martyrs, a much better film in every way, takes those ideas seriously, treating suffering and transcendence as something profound and spiritual. But it’s no fun. Saw takes the sacrifice of life at its absolute stupidest and turns it into a game. No matter how much you think you want to die, you probably do have a bit of survival instinct left. “Live or die” is the Jigsaw villain’s catchphrase, and of course, living is much harder. It requires constant attention and struggle. But that’s the choice almost everyone makes.As I watch Saw, I put myself in the victims’ positions every single time: whatwouldI do if I had 60 seconds to cut into my eye or die? I’d rather not answer, but if I had to,hadto, I think I might choose to dig right in.If on another day I’d feel like throwing the scalpel down and just giving up, I’ll put on Saw once again, and remember what it costs to choose otherwise.Saw is available to rent digitally in the US and UK and on Stan and Binge in AustraliaIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsMy feelgood movieThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limbo | Movies | The Guardian
description: This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting
Content: Intriguing notes of absurdity … The Visitor.View image in fullscreenIntriguing notes of absurdity … The Visitor.MoviesReviewThe Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limboThis portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up driftingPhil HoadMon 24 Aug 2026 06.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt one point in this Nordic-Baltic homecoming film, Danielius (Darius Šilėnas) refuses an invite for beachfront karaoke, preferring to watch from behind a polythene partition. At another, a neighbour glimpses him exercising across the courtyard, through the window of the flat in an end-of-summer Lithuanian resort that Danielius is trying to sell. Having returned from Norway to settle up accounts, this prodigal son is often holding the world at arm’s length – and director Vytautas Katkus does his best to help him with this distanced technique in this quizzical and faintly existential drama.Little tangible is disclosed. Danielius is a thirtysomething father who skipped the funeral of his own dad the year before. Preparing the flat to go on the market, he walks the dog of his neighbour, Vismante (Vismantė Ruzgaitė), hangs speculatively at beach gatherings and falls asleep in pine forests. Ice-cream is eaten at every available opportunity. He’s not alienated exactly, but somewhat out of step. As he looks for new anchorage, even the film seems to question whether Danielius has sufficient main character energy: it periodically drifts to follow another resident, Tomas (Rokas Siaurusaitis), who is caring for his grandmother over the way.Given Katkus’s cinematography background, it’s not surprising that this smalltown ennui comes gracefully shot, with stray snippets of quirk, like the fairground diplodocus poking its head over the treetops as Danielius arrives. But with much of The Visitor’s long runtime devoted to simply surveilling this entropic purgatory and little else, it leaves it until late before openly broaching the matter of its protagonist’s diffidence. Is it because of guilt for returning too late? Or tied up with feelings about his own recent fatherhood? Or just common nostalgia about his old family life? All of the above, possibly.With the paternal issue apparently settled by a strange request over breakfast to Vismante’s father, Katkus – steadfast in his love of the mid-shot thus far – abandons his previous reserve. Where a character being gifted a red lifeguard beach inflatable prompted a diegetic burst of the Baywatch theme tune in the first half, the second half sees the film break with realism almost entirely for another seafront musical number. If not as stridently deadpan and stylised as the likes of Aki Kaurismäki, it brings gentler, intriguing notes of absurdism and human warmth to this seaside haven.The Visitor is at the ICA, London, from 21 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsLithuaniaNorwayEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Marching in the Dark review – rural Indian widows show stunning resilience as they battle poverty and taboos | Movies | The Guardian
description: Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront together
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront together
Content: Invisible suffering … Marching in the Dark.Photograph: SNG Film (Studio Nieuwe Gronden)View image in fullscreenInvisible suffering … Marching in the Dark.Photograph: SNG Film (Studio Nieuwe Gronden)MoviesReviewMarching in the Dark review – rural Indian widows show stunning resilience as they battle poverty and taboosKinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront togetherPhuong LeMon 24 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOut in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms.Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.Marching in the Dark is on True Story from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsIndiaFarmingSouth and central AsiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Disciples review – fresh-faced boys are sucked into a nightmare of extremism in India | Movies | The Guardian
description: A prestigious school in the holy city of Varanasi and its controversial, dogmatic teachings are the subject of this shocking documentary
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: A prestigious school in the holy city of Varanasi and its controversial, dogmatic teachings are the subject of this shocking documentary
Content: Dubious honour … DisciplesView image in fullscreenDubious honour … DisciplesMoviesReviewDisciples review – fresh-faced boys are sucked into a nightmare of extremism in IndiaA prestigious school in the holy city of Varanasi and its controversial, dogmatic teachings are the subject of this shocking documentaryPhuong LeMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi,India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert toHinduismor leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.Disciples is atBertha DocHouse, London, from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsIndiaHinduismReligionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ab-sol-utely incredible!’ The blockbuster ballet that says Pandora’s box unleashed AI | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: She was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her tale
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: She was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her tale
Content: ‘Dancers are heroes’ ... Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Chris HardyView image in fullscreen‘Dancers are heroes’ ... Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Chris HardyEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Ab-sol-utely incredible!’ The blockbuster ballet that says Pandora’s box unleashed AILyndsey WinshipShe was the first woman, according to myth, and she let loose all the evils and sorrows of humanity. But Aszure Barton thinks Pandora’s had a bad rap – and she’s using dance to reimagine her taleMon 24 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAszure Barton is taking herself back to the creation of Mere Mortals, remembering the creative buzz of the studio at San Francisco Ballet. “Sam was fiddling around making magic in one corner,” she says – that’s Sam Shepherd, AKA electronic musician Floating Points, who plays live in the show. Digital art duo Hamill Industries were there too, designing visuals for giant LED screens. “I was in a corner with the dancers,” says Barton. “Principals and apprentices, everyone working together. It was a really shared experience, which I loved.” In fact, it’s a “curiosity for real collaboration” that drives the Canadian-American choreographer. “If it was just about me,” she says, “the work wouldn’t be as powerful.”Mere Mortals, which opened in San Francisco in 2024, is finally getting a European premiere, at this year’s Edinburgh international festival. While Barton’s memories of making the show are all about human connection, the subject matter is quite the opposite: artificial intelligence. It’s inspired by the myth of Pandora’s box, but instead of a box unleashing the evils and sorrows of humanity, it is reimagined as a cautionary tale about AI.double quotation markI have to be in the back, bouncing up and down like I’m at a raveThe idea came from SF Ballet’s artistic director Tamara Rojo, who took over the company in 2022 after 26 years in the UK, notably as a principal dancer at the Royal Ballet and artistic director of English National Ballet. “She was very hands-off in terms of the work itself,” says Barton, but Rojo assembled a crack international team for her ambitious commission which garnered some rave reviews for the intensity of its scale, score and visual impact.View image in fullscreenDazzling … Wei Wang and San Francisco Ballet in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Alexander Reneff-OlsonBarton had worked with Rojo before, when she choreographed Fantastic Beings for English National Ballet in 2016, a dance full of endlessly inventive, quirky movement. Beyond that, the 50-year-old isn’t well known on this side of the Atlantic (Rojo has called her “completely underrated”), although she’s been choreographing for more than two decades with major companies all over the world, as well as for her own, Aszure Barton & Artists. She was mentored by the great Mikhail Baryshnikov at his Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York. What did she learn from him? “On day one, he said, ‘Never ask me for money’ and ‘I like your willingness to work your ass off.’”In the making of Mere Mortals, it turns out the richest conversations were not about the perils of AI, but the myth of Pandora, or “a myth that had been misconstrued”, says Barton. “A false story spread throughout history of this powerful being who didn’t have any agency and was toxic.”There’ll always be different tellings of Greek myths, but Pandora does seem to have had a bad rap. She was the first woman, an Eve-like figure, created from clay and given by Zeus to Epimetheus, unbeknownst to him, as a punishment for his brother Prometheus giving humans fire. “One of the things I was really driven by was the fact that she was an agent of change,” says Barton.As well as looking to a fictional figure from the past, however, Barton also used what was right in front of her in the present: the dancer in the lead role, Jennifer Stahl. “Ab-sol-utely incredible!” she says of Stahl, wide-eyed. “This stunning, powerful, amazing woman that I was getting to create with made my job very sweet.” Stahl, who has danced with SF Ballet for 20 years, will be returning to the Pandora role, having had a baby in between premieres.View image in fullscreenNot anti-AI … Aszure Barton.Photograph: Lindsey RalloIn the same way the inspiration for Pandora was right there in the studio, the show’s theme was all around her in San Francisco, the AI centre of the world. “You’re living the reality,” says Barton, “the systems and the chaos and the beauty, and I was really intuitively responding to that moment.” Barton uses lots of tech in her working life, not so much AI, more video, to endlessly document, analyse and deconstruct her way through the creative process. She calls choreography “the most magical Legoland for me”, but it always comes back to bodies. “I love dance because it’s so human and so beautiful. You can do some cool stuff with technology, but there’s nothing like sharing a space with a dancer.”She’s not anti-AI. Some choreographers use AI as a tool to interrupt their creative habits and find new ideas. “That’s cool,” says Barton, although her own creativity is sparked by interacting with dancers. “You never have choreographer’s block if you’re open to what’s right there in front of you,” she says. “Dancers are heroes. They don’t get credited enough for their input.”Barton hopes that all the fizzing creativity that went into making Mere Mortals is tangible to the audience. She wants them to be “showered with energy”. She can’t sit in her chair and watch it, she says. “I have to be in the back, bouncing up and down like I’m at a rave.” Between the dancers and the musicians (from the Royal Scottish National Orchestra) there are 87 performers in the show. “Masses of people sharing themselves, sharing this raw beauty,” says Barton. “It’s delicious.”Mere Mortals is atEdinburgh Playhouse, 28-30 August andSadler’s Wells, London, 9-12 September.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceEdinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Slayyyter live review – raucous show announces a new princess of sleaze-pop | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesse
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: The cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesse
Content: Slayyyter performing at Coachella on 10 April 2026.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty Images for CoachellaView image in fullscreenSlayyyter performing at Coachella on 10 April 2026.Photograph: Amy Sussman/Getty Images for CoachellaPop and rockReviewSlayyyter live review – raucous show announces a new princess of sleaze-popShrine Auditorium, Los AngelesThe cult star proves she is ready for pop’s big leagues in a show that blends chaotic punk energy with technical finesseEmma MaddenMon 24 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last timeSlayyytertoured, in 2023, she struggled to break even and had to fly home boxes of unsold merch. Back then, she was still largely the domain of Twitter gays: a subcultural figure to those who assessed music in terms of “flops” and “bops”.Then, midway through 2025, she released the electro-trashy Beat Up Chanel$, and suddenly caught everyone’s attention. With a career-defining Coachella set earlier this year, she had broken through into the mainstream alongside a class of flop-no-more artists –Zara Larsson,RayeandTinashe– who had spent years seeming cruelly shut out of its central sphere, only to break through with a surprise big hit. For these artists, and Slayyyter in particular, the urgency of a last chance had become as galvanizing as the urgency of a first.‘I didn’t think anyone would be into it’: Slayyyter turns midwest trash into pop goldRead moreFollowing what she described to the Switched on Pop podcast as the “financial failure” of her previous tour, Slayyyter’s fourth studio album, Wor$t Girl in America, became that final chance. She intended it to be the last album she’d ever record, trading the pinkish, delusional chic of her earlier work for Middle American sleaze. CloserBrittany Murphy, a song about depression and suicidal ideation, doubled as a meta-farewell to the chase for musical relevancy: “Do you notice all I’ve done? Do you know it’s all I want?”When she announced the accompanying North American leg of herWorst Girl in the World tour in March this year, it sold out in minutes. Her team immediately set to work on venue upgrades and added extra dates; tonight and tomorrow night at the Shrine inLos Angelessold out almost instantaneously, a venue that Slayyyter said midway through the set was a place she “always dreamed of playing”.At her first of these two packed Los Angeles shows, she finally got the answer she wanted to the question she posed on her album’s closer: a crowd screaming those lyrics back at her. Three songs into the set, she told them, seemingly unaware of the connection to Brittany Murphy, “This is all I’ve ever wanted.”She came out to devilish howls from the crowd, which almost drowned out her version of St Francis’s prayer. She walked, at first somberly, across the stage, which consisted of a tiny Missouri home, likely similar to the one she grew up in in St Louis; a lone carousel horse, a washing line full of Slayyyter-branded white tees, a crucifix poking out of the ground, and a high-exposure timelapse of a blue Missouri sky over a wheat field. As the sky turned from blue to gray and then lightning, Slayyyter detonated, bringing the energy of a hardcore show to a pop performance.Slayyyter’s production was distinct, self-contained and grand without losing its sense of scum. It was aHarmony Korine-like meeting of the baroque and Americana, finding beauty in a pack of Marlboro Reds and a gas-station T-shirt with a ganja leaf on it.Like the album, the set married pop and hard techno with Americana scuzz. While Slayyyter sang and screamed on the record through punkish distortion, with most of the music happening in the low end, live, you heard the clarity of her voice and just how incredible it was. When she sang, she belted in a single note with the heft of Dua Lipa, the hiccups of Chappell Roan, the girlish trails of Ariana Grande and the inferno of Courtney Love.She performed mostly with a rock band set-up: drummer, guitarist, bass; aproperlive show. Early in her career, when she came up among the first wave of hyperpop artists, she proved she could do it alone and make low budget look cool. Now, more impressively, she can make a much larger budget look cool, too.Trash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreEverything else was equally precise: the crowd work, the stage blocking, the hairography (and what hair!) were all on point. There was something deeply gratifying about hearing Slayyyter and seeing her vision so clearly, welcomed with such enthusiasm. It was particularly satisfying if you had followed her long enough to remember when the idea of this many people standing in a room to hear her sing would have seemed slightly delusional.The crowd had changed, too. Slayyyter had built a visual brand strong enough that the audience could wear it back to her. A great majority of the 5,000 in attendance came dressed in gas-station trucker caps, boxy thrifted tees, and oversized camo khakis. Everyone was mercifully at her feet while she fed the 5,000. When she sang bloghouse banger Old Technology, repeating the lyrics, “I’m doing drugs tonight,” a woman in the crowd with a bleach-blond skullet vomited into a bin.Rounding off the night with Beat Up Chanel$, Slayyyter stood beneath the blue Missouri sky as thousands screamed for her not to go. The prayer that opened the show had asked for grace in a world of suffering. Finally, she received a room full of people who knew exactly what she was trying to say. Her prayers had been answered.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockLos AngelesElectronic musiclive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: My Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territory | Games | The Guardian
description: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Author: Bex April May
Headline: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb
Content: What if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesView image in fullscreenWhat if your own arm turned to crime? … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesSummer games previewsGamesMy Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territoryDevelopers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limbBex April MayMon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost stealth games cast you as a spy, an assassin or a master thief. My Arms Are Longer Now dispenses with most of the criminal person, to send in just one spectacularly badly behaved limb. It slithers across floors, winds around furniture, steals things and slaps anyone within reach – finally answering the question nobody asked: what if your own arm turned to crime?As TootGamesco-founder Matthew Jackson puts it: “You are the bad thing that happens to the people.”The idea began as a much simpler prototype made during a weekend game jam themed around the idea of lost and found. Jackson and fellow Toot co-founderMillie Holten, who met through Melbourne’s improv and sketch comedy community, wanted an idea that could be understood – and raise a laugh – in a single still image. A grotesquely extended arm proved to be just that.Since then, the game has been all about comedy. It has more than 40 speaking characters, voiced by Australian comedians who perform the written dialogue before improvising alternative takes. “It’s a vessel for jokes,” Jackson says. For almost a year, development largely involved trying to “cram jokes into the game”; only later did the team realise the physics of the increasingly sophisticated arm had become fun in their own right. Players can personalise its skin tone, hair and accessories, making it less somebody else’s disembodied crime spree than a freaky extension of their own body.The stealth here owes something toUntitled Goose Game: characters react to your crimes, but, Jackson says, “There are no fail states in the game.” A museum guard might smack the arm, or beg it to stop before they are fired. Anyone can be slapped, including an infant. While searching for a publisher, Jackson repeatedly asked: “Is someone going to come and tell us you can’t slap the baby?”Jackbox Games, thankfully, did not.View image in fullscreen‘A vessel for jokes’ … My Arms Are Longer Now.Photograph: Toot GamesMaking that slap possible required rather more sophistication than the joke might suggest. The original game was flat and 2D, but Holten’s concept art showed the arm looping over tables, under chairs and around objects. Six months into development, the studio took the risky decision to rebuild in 3D. Working with developer Cherie Davidson, Jackson created a procedural, tube-like limb and a system that uses forced perspective to preserve the illustrated style while allowing the physical collisions the game needs.The work never quite ends. The team calls another session tinkering with the troublesome appendage “going into the armpit”.That labour is particularly demanding because comedy is finite. “You can hit a joke, and that joke’s done. You’ve burnt that,” Jackson says. Some publishers suggested adding more puzzles, but Toot feared they would obstruct the punchlines. Jackbox understood that it was meant to be “a good time, not a long time”, with players who do poke into every corner rewarded with optional interactions and voice lines.Jackson’s ultimate ambition for the game is appropriately simple: “I hope players say it was funny. That’s truly it.” And after three years in the armpit, 48 speaking characters, and one non-negotiable baby slap, Toot Games has gone to extraordinary lengths to reach gaming’s funny bone.My Arms Are Longer Now is in development forPC, with release planned for 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: David Olusoga’s extraordinary new show: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’
Author: Nell Frizzell
Headline: The historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’
Content: David Olusoga presents A Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten Massacre.Photograph: Jon Parker Lee/Findmypast/PAView image in fullscreenDavid Olusoga presents A Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten Massacre.Photograph: Jon Parker Lee/Findmypast/PABest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioDavid Olusoga’s extraordinary new show: best podcasts of the weekThe historian shares the astonishing story of a Peterloo massacre survivor. Plus, a delightfully wholesome new pod that is ‘Desert Island Discs … for words’Nell FrizzellandHollie RichardsonMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 03.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekA Family History of … Peterloo: Britain’s Forgotten MassacreFrom the People’s History Museum, thisseriesis about the Peterloo massacre in Manchester, 1819, which the host David Olusoga calls the “ground zero of industrial capitalism”. Touching on systematic disenfranchisement (Manchester didn’t have a single MP) and state-sanctioned violence through the extraordinary story of survivor William Cheatham, it’s an invigorating if sobering listen.Nell FrizzellWidely available, episodes weeklyWriting FunnyAnalysing what makes something funny is the artistic equivalent of trying to peel a raw egg. And yet, funny people are fun to have in your ears. The Comedy Women in Print prize has anew podcast, presented by the award’s founder, Helen Lederer, and the author Chrissie Manby, in which they will tackle everything from a writer’s journey to writing comedy in dark times.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyWodcastView image in fullscreenElif Shafak, a guest on Wodcast.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesMabel Evans and Benjamin Aston turn their Word of the Day project into a very wholesomeseriesdescribed as “Desert Island Discs for words”. They ask guests to expand on the words that shape their lives, starting with Elif Shafak. Future guests include Stephen Fry and Tim Rice.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weeklyBig Little InterestsWhen I last worked in an office I watched videos of large boats misjudging their stopping distances and crashing into walls. Which is probably why I like the premise ofBig Little Interests: a podcast dedicated to the strange, funny hyper-fixations that make different comedians’ brains feel smooth and shiny. Episode one, with Steve Bugeja, features bull semen.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyCivilian Or SpyAs told by CNN’s Isabelle Chapman, this is the compellingstoryof how Russian-born American citizen Ilya Beloozerov was shot by the FBI outside a Super 8 hotel in 2024. With the relationship between the US and Russia as compelling today as during any cold war escapade of the 1970s, this investigation definitely has wider implications. Just don’t call it the new Serial.NFWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat are you listening to at the moment? title: ‘Everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place’: Brescia, Lombardy’s hidden gem | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: The city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change that
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: The city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change that
Content: The winding alleys of the Carmine district in Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardainView image in fullscreenThe winding alleys of the Carmine district in Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardainItaly holidays‘Everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place’: Brescia, Lombardy’s hidden gemThe city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change thatKevin RushbyMon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe have hardly begun walking before I spot the side alley, curving away from the main road in a patchwork of sunlit yellow walls, shuttered windows and shadowy archways. “What’s up there?” Elena, my guide to the city, pulls a wry smile. “That is Carmine. As a kid, I was warned not to go there.”I turn up the alley. There’s a lot of graffiti. Next to an anarchy symbol, someone has sprayed “morte al decoro” – death to decorum. I’m intrigued. We go further, finding a labyrinth of colourful streets filled with bars and restaurants, a few just opening up for the day.Like the bohemian quarter at its heart, Brescia is an Italian city that is easily missed: it’s near the Dolomites and Lake Garda, but not close enough to be a base for them. Tourists tend to speed past on their way to Milan or Verona. Fiercely proud of her city, Elena is on a mission to convince me it is worth a stop. “You’ll see. We’ve got everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place.”View image in fullscreenAndrea, manager of I Dù dela Contrada bar in Carmine, Brescia.Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianHer confidence is matched by Andrea, the manager ofi Dù dela Contrada, a Carmine bar that we step into for a coffee. Quirky bric-a-brac is dotted around, the bar itself plastered with passport photos, donated by its many fans. “Twenty years ago, this was an area for prostitutes and thieves,” Andrea tells me. “Now it’s safer but still vibrant, and growing.”I tell him Elena’s mission and he nods. “She’s right, ask anyone.”“OK. Who shall I ask next?”“Piera at Ostería dei Mercanti. She’s a real character.”And so begins a magical day in the city where we wander, one person leading to the next, each encounter enriched by Elena’s deep knowledge of her home town.We find Piera sitting among a gaggle of friends, the table covered in coffee cups and one or two glasses of Brescia’s favourite aperitivo,pirlo. “The drinks here are special,” she tells me. “We’ve got the Franciacorta wine region on our doorstep. I came 17 years ago and knew instantly I would stay.”double quotation markWithin 20 minutes, I’m sitting outside eating the best pizza of my life – for breakfastShe sends us to meet her friend Maria. That means passing through the medieval square of the city, Piazza della Loggia, which is dominated by theTorre dell’Orologio, a magnificent clock that features two lifesize automatons, “the lunatics of time”, who have been bashing out the hours on a large bell since 1581. We can’t find Maria, but bump into her amiable friend Antimio, whoseLestro restaurantis both a homage to the 1970s and a laboratory where he experiments tirelessly, perfecting the pizza.Next thing, I’m in his kitchen getting a swift lesson in the mix of special flours, the best kneading methods, how to prep the cheeses … “I like to mix smoked scamorza and mozzarella, but my favourite isbagòss, a local speciality.” Within 20 minutes, I’m sitting outside, listening to the lunatics hammer out the hour and eating the best pizza of my life – for breakfast.View image in fullscreenPiazza della Loggia.Photograph: Bogdan Lazar/Getty Images/iStockphotoThus fortified, Antimio sends us around the corner to visit Roberto atBrescia’s sumptuous Teatro Grande. The theatre was founded in the 1660s and is considered one of Italy’s finest. The palatial cafe with its murals is a popular spot formerenda, the traditional afternoon cake stop, but the tour adds wonderful details, such as the way horses were steered on stage and how Puccini, chastened by the rejection of his new opera, Madama Butterfly, at Milan’s La Scala, brought it here in 1904 and won acclaim.Roberto’s tip is the church of San Cristo, but first we divert through Piazza Vittoria which Mussolini, at the peak of his power in 1932, had remodelled on fascist principles, kicking out residents to erect monuments to youth, energy and strength; in other words thuggish neo-classical blocks round a massive male nude statue. A decade later, Mussolini was back, this time as a German puppet, governing the republic of Salò, a rump state that included Brescia. In recent years, the piazza has been renovated, but the male nude remains warehoused, and the large capital letter “M” on one building does not refer to the fallen dictator.I’m beginning to understand why Elena believes Brescia is a microcosm of Italian history and culture. She now takes me back to the medieval Piazza della Loggia to point out something I had missed, a small pillar marking the spot where a bomb exploded in 1974, killing eight people. The political forces of the Mussolini era reached a terrible climax in the 1970s and 80s, theanni di piombi, “years of lead”, when fascist groups and the leftwing Red Brigades traded lethal bombings, kidnappings and assassinations. The extent of the carnage is revealed in hundreds of pavement plaques that lead up to Brescia’s medieval castle above the city, each plaque representing a victim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPiera at Osteria dei Mercanti: ‘I came 17 years ago and knew instantly I would stay.’Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianAfter this sombre digression, we cool off inChiesa di San Cristo, a 16th-century church known as “the Sistine Chapel of Brescia” for the luminous murals that cover every available space. A few doors down the lane isOsteria del Savio, a famous spot for local cuisine where we tuck intocasoncelli, a ravioli made with sage and butter, thenmalfatti, a local mountain gnocchi, while owner Michaela explains why there is a Roman column in the middle of her restaurant. “It actually goes down another 5 metres and my neighbours have the capital off it – they use it as a coffee table.”double quotation markChiesa di San Cristo is known as the Sistine Chapel of Brescia for the luminous murals that cover every available spaceFinding history hidden under columns is a Bresciano tradition. Back in the 1820s, archaeologists decided to dig under the top of a Roman column in a city garden that was being used as a picnic table. What they discovered was a vast temple complex and a bronze statue, the Winged Victory, that has been dated back to the first century BC.A short walk down the lane brings us to that spot, now a partly subterraneanarchaeological site. Other Roman artefacts are in the nearbySanta Giulia Museum, a warren of ancient buildings that could easily occupy a day, but we whip through because it is time to go and taste some wine.If Brescia keeps below the mass tourism radar, its wine district, the Franciacorta, is also a well-kept secret. Planted on volcanic soils south of Lake Iseo, these vineyards produce sparkling wine so good that the locals drink most of it.View image in fullscreenMonte Isola, an island on Lake Iseo.Photograph: Faber 1893/Getty ImagesI stay by the lake shore in Sulzano, a 30-minute drive from Brescia, then next day catch the ferry across to Monte Isola, an island in the lake. Ringed by mountains and a popular day trip for the Bresciani, the island still keeps its home-spun friendliness. At the fishing net shop, Paolo demonstrates the knots to make a net using a double-ended needle that “is the same tool they found in Pompeii”. Further on, in the small net factory, owner Daniela points to a photo of her grandmother mending nets, then tells me that most Serie A football nets are now made here. In the shop round the corner, they give me a taste of their local salami – they are very proud of that. But the climax, for me, is when I wander, unannounced, into the Archetti boatyard.This is the kind of place where royalty and billionaires buy handmade wooden boats, but Andrea and his dad have no time for airs and graces. They are craftsmen, proudly showing me works in progress. “Our ancestors were gondola-makers in Venice,” says Andrea. “In 1640, they came here and liked Brescia and its surrounding area so much, they stayed.” It was a decision, I admit to Elena, that I can heartily endorse.The trip was provided byVisit Brescia. Doubles atHotel Lenelin Bresciafrom€183, and atHotel Rivalagoin Sulzanofrom€209.Kevin Rushby travelled to Brescia by train, via Milan. title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos | Snacks | The Guardian
description: A fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alike
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alike
Content: Georgina Hayden’s charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Louie Waller. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.Quick and easySnacksGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachosA fun and easily customisable snack, to be enjoyed by kids and adults alikeGeorgina HaydenMon 24 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCorn is a late-summer staple in our house, but its arrival often leaves me feeling a little blue (end of summer and all that). So, instead, I like to entertain more and make the most of the warm, light evenings. These nachos are a great snack for adults and kids alike (just adjust the chilli for younger palates), and a solid base that can be tweaked any which way. Have some lovely ripe tomatoes to hand? Chop them up and throw them in, too. Avocados at their peak? A side of guacamole would be a dream. Got a well-stocked spice cupboard? Add a little sweet smoked paprika and even some crushed coriander seeds to the fried beans. Make it to your liking and pantry, and enjoy with friends, ideally in the evening sun.Charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachosWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook20 minServes4-62 ears of corn, kernels cut off the core2 tbsp vegetable oil200g tinnedblack beans, drained and rinsed (net weight)½ tsp cumin seeds, lightly groundSea salt andblack pepper2 limes½ bunch coriander, finely chopped2jalapeños, or green chillies, stalks, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped200g tortilla chips75g grated mozzarella100g mature cheddar, gratedSouredcream, to servePut a large frying pan on a high heat, add the corn and fry for five to 10 minutes, until the kernels start to char. Transfer to a large bowl.Pour the vegetable oil into the pan, then add the black beans and ground cumin, and season well. Fry on a high heat for about five minutes, until the beans start to crisp up and pop a little, then tip into the bowl of charred corn.Finely grate in the zest of one of the limes, and squeeze in the juice of one and a half limes. Add most of the chopped coriander and chilli, then toss well. Tweak and adjust the seasoning to taste, adding more lime juice or salt as required.Meanwhile, heat the grill to high. Spread out the tortilla chips on a baking sheet or tray, and cover with both grated cheeses. Pop under the grill for a couple of minutes, until the cheese turns oozy – if if starts to catch, turn off the heat and leave it to finish melting in the residual heat.Transfer the cheesy nachos to a platter and dot with the corn salsa. Dot with the soured cream and finish with the remaining coriander and chillies scattered over the top.Explore more on these topicsSnacksQuick and easyFoodVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkSide dishesMexican food and drinkSummer food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Courgette kraut and fermented pepper sauce: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s Czech pickle recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: In an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-round
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-round
Content: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s courgette kraut.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenŠárka Otevřel Camrdová’s courgette kraut.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodCourgette kraut and fermented pepper sauce: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s Czech pickle recipesIn an extract from her new book, the Prague-born food writer shares two ways to preserve summer vegetables so they can be savoured year-roundŠárka Otevřel CamrdováMon 24 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePreserving the abundance of summer produce is a wonderful way to extend the season long after the gardens have faded. Opening a jar in the colder months offers more than just something good to eat; it also holds joy, patience and memories. When winter comes knocking, we are ready with something sweet, sour or salty waiting on the shelf, reminding us that summer will return and the sun will shine again.Courgette krautWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThis kraut can be used much like traditional sauerkraut, though its flavour is milder and its texture more delicate. Sauteed with onions in a little butter or lard, it makes an excellent accompaniment to roast meats and sausages; it can also be added to potato pancakes or used as a filling for savoury pies and pastries.Prep5 minCook40 minFerment2 weeksMakes3-4x 650ml jars2kgcourgettes2tbsp (25g) granulated sugar1½tbsp (25g) salt65mldistilled white vinegar(8% acidity)1½tsp caraway seeds, crushedWash the unpeeled courgettes and pat them dry. Cut the courgettes in half lengthways, scrape out the seeds and shred or coarsely grate the flesh into a bowl.Mix the sugar, salt and vinegar, then pour this over the courgettes. Sprinkle in the caraway seeds, mix well and set aside for 15-30 minutes. Adjust the seasoning to taste, adding sugar or vinegar as required.Transfer the courgettes to sterilised jars, leaving a space of about 2cm between the veg and the rim of the jar, and making sure everything is completely covered in the liquid. Cover the jars tightly, place them on a rack or folded tea towel in a large pot, add warm water until it comes about three-quarters of the way up the sides of the jars, and keep at a steady at 85-90C (185-195F) for 15 minutes. Carefully lift out the jars, leave to cool completely, then store in a cool, dark place for about two weeks before use.Fermented bell pepper sauceWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenŠárka Otevřel Camrdová’s fermented bell pepper sauce.You can modify this recipe to suit your taste, by using different types of bell peppers, for example, or replacing some of the peppers with tomatoes, or adding other herbs and spices. You can also use this recipe to make your own hot sauce – just replace the bell peppers with chilli peppers. Fermented bell pepper sauce has a flavour that is reminiscent of the Balkan red pepper condimentajvar, which means you can use it in a similar way: as a sauce for grilled meat and kebabs, burgers or sandwiches; as a dip for different vegetable side dishes; as an accompaniment for bulgur and couscous; or spread it on toast.Prep15 minCook30 minFerment5 days+Makes3 x750ml bottles1lwater1tbsp (20g) salt6 red or orange bell peppers,halved lengthways, stalks, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh washed and cut into chunks3 sprigsflat-leaf parsley, or lovage1 onion,peeled and cut into wedges3-5garlic cloves,peeled and halved3-6 bay leaves(optional)To make the brine, put the water in a saucepan, bring to a boil, then leave to cool completely. Add the salt and stir until it’s all dissolved.Divide the pepper pieces between three sterilised jars, then add a parsley sprig, a few pieces of onion and garlic, and a bay leaf or two, if using, to each one. Leave at least a 3cm gap between the contents of the jar and the rim. Pour the brine over the vegetables – the pepper pieces should be completely covered to prevent contact with the air, so, if need be, use a sterilised fermentation weight to keep them in place. Leave some space between the salt solution and the rim of the jar to allow room for the formation of foam on the surface of the liquid.Close the jars with their lids, but do not tighten them. Put the jars on a tray or baking sheet and leave in a dark place at room temperature (preferably at 18-21C/65-70F) to ferment for five to seven days: the exact time will depend on the temperature of the room (a warmer temperature speeds up the fermentation process). Check and taste the contents of the jars regularly (always use an impeccably clean fork) – the peppers are ready when no more bubbles form or the foam dissipates, and they should now have a pleasantly sour and mildly spicy taste.Fine-strain the contents of the jars and collect the liquid. Discard the bay leaves. Puree the vegetables and herbs until thick and creamy, diluting the sauce, if need be, with some of the reserved liquid. Fill sterilised bottles with the sweet pepper sauce and use immediately or store in the fridge.These recipes are edited extracts from God is a Pickle: Recipes and Stories for Preserving the Seasons – A Culinary Journey Through the Czech Republic, byŠárka Otevřel Camrdová, published by Gestalten at £35.
